questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a cellulose molecule. (2)
hints: Which isomer of glucose is it made from?
Think about how neighbouring chains are held together.
questions.solution:
Made of β-glucose (monomers) [B1]
Joined by 1-4 glycosidic bonds (alternate monomers inverted) [B1]
Straight / unbranched chains [B1]
Chains linked by hydrogen bonds to form microfibrils. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Cellulose is a polymer of β-glucose joined by 1-4 glycosidic bonds, with alternate monomers inverted, giving long straight unbranched chains held together by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils. (Any 2 points.)

questions.prompt: Starch is made of two polysaccharides, amylose and amylopectin. Describe the structure of starch. (2)
hints: Both are made from the same monomer.
questions.solution:
Polymer of α-glucose [B1]
Amylose: 1-4 glycosidic bonds, unbranched (helical) [B1]
Amylopectin: 1-4 and 1-6 glycosidic bonds, so branched. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Starch is a polymer of α-glucose. Amylose has only 1-4 glycosidic bonds and coils into an unbranched helix; amylopectin has 1-4 and 1-6 bonds, so it is branched. (Any 2 points.)

questions.prompt: Explain two ways in which the structure of glycogen makes it suitable as an energy store in animal cells. (2)
hints: Think about how quickly glucose needs to be released.
Think about its effect on water potential.
questions.solution:
Highly branched, so many ends for (rapid) hydrolysis / enzyme action [B1]
Insoluble, so does not affect water potential / osmosis [B1]
Compact, so a lot stored in a small space [B1]
Large molecule, so cannot leave the cell. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any two explained features, e.g. it is highly branched so there are many ends for enzymes to hydrolyse quickly; it is insoluble so it doesn't change the cell's water potential.

questions.prompt: Describe how sucrose is formed, and how you would test a solution to show it contains sucrose. (4)
questions.solution:
Glucose and fructose joined by a condensation reaction [B1]
Forming a glycosidic bond (water released) [B1]
Benedict's test negative first (no reducing sugar) [B1]
Boil with acid, neutralise, then heat with Benedict's: brick-red precipitate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how maltose is formed from glucose and how it is broken down in the human digestive system. (4)
hints: Which isomer of glucose and which bond?
questions.solution:
Two α-glucose molecules join by condensation [B1]
Forming a 1-4 glycosidic bond [B1]
Maltase hydrolyses the glycosidic bond, producing glucose [B1]
Maltase is bound to the cell-surface membranes of ileum epithelial cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe tests to show that a food sample contains starch, protein and a reducing sugar. (5)
hints: Each test has a reagent and a colour change.
One of the tests needs heating.
questions.solution:
Starch: add iodine solution [B1]
Blue-black colour [B1]
Protein: add biuret reagent — purple / lilac [B1]
Reducing sugar: heat with Benedict's reagent [B1]
Green / yellow / orange / brick-red precipitate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you could use Benedict's reagent and a colorimeter to find the concentration of reducing sugar in an unknown solution. (5)
hints: You need a set of known concentrations.
questions.solution:
Make a range of known glucose concentrations [B1]
Add the same volume of Benedict's to each and heat for the same time and temperature [B1]
Remove precipitate / filter, then measure absorbance (or transmission) with a colorimeter [B1]
Plot a calibration curve of absorbance against concentration [B1]
Test the unknown the same way and read its concentration from the curve. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to test for a non-reducing sugar, and explain the reason for each step. (5)
hints: Why do the Benedict's test first?
Why is acid used, and why must it be neutralised?
questions.solution:
Heat with Benedict's first — no colour change shows no reducing sugar [B1]
Heat a new sample with dilute hydrochloric acid [B1]
Acid hydrolyses glycosidic bonds, producing monosaccharides (reducing sugars) [B1]
Neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate because Benedict's works in alkaline conditions [B1]
Heat with Benedict's — red precipitate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare and contrast the structures of starch, glycogen and cellulose. (5)
hints: Which isomer of glucose does each use?
questions.solution:
All are polysaccharides made of glucose joined by glycosidic bonds [B1]
Starch and glycogen are made of α-glucose; cellulose of β-glucose [B1]
Glycogen is more highly branched than amylopectin (1-4 and 1-6 bonds) [B1]
Amylose is unbranched and helical [B1]
Cellulose forms straight chains linked by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how glycogen is made from glucose and how glucose is released from glycogen. (5)
questions.solution:
α-glucose molecules joined by condensation reactions (water released) [B1]
Forming 1-4 glycosidic bonds [B1]
and 1-6 glycosidic bonds at branch points [B1]
Glycogen hydrolysed (using water) to release glucose [B1]
Many branch ends allow rapid hydrolysis when glucose is needed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Glucose has the formula C₆H₁₂O₆. Give the formula of maltose and explain how it is formed. (2)
questions.solution:
C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ [B1]
Two glucose molecules joined by a condensation reaction, removing water and forming a glycosidic bond. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the molecular formula of a trisaccharide made from three glucose molecules (C₆H₁₂O₆), and explain how you worked it out. (2)
hints: How many water molecules are removed?
questions.solution:
Two water molecules removed in two condensation reactions [B1]
C₁₈H₃₂O₁₆. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the two monosaccharides that make up lactose and the bond that joins them. (2)
hints: The other is found in milk sugar.
questions.solution:
Glucose and galactose [B1]
Glycosidic bond (formed by condensation). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the main polymer in bacterial cell walls and the main storage polysaccharide in plants. (1)
hints: The bacterial one is also called peptidoglycan.
questions.solution: Murein (peptidoglycan) and starch (both needed). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the main storage polysaccharide in animals and in fungi. (1)
hints: It is the same in both.
questions.solution: Glycogen (both). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the monomer of cellulose and the monomer of glycogen. (1)
hints: They differ in the position of one OH group.
questions.solution: β-glucose (cellulose) and α-glucose (glycogen). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the disaccharide formed from glucose and fructose. (1)
questions.solution: Sucrose. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the disaccharide formed from glucose and galactose. (1)
questions.solution: Lactose. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the bond that joins two monosaccharides in a disaccharide. (1)
questions.solution: Glycosidic bond. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare and contrast the structures of glycogen and starch. (6)
hints: What do they have in common?
How do they differ in branching?
questions.solution:
Both are polysaccharides of α-glucose [B1]
Both have 1-4 glycosidic bonds [B1]
Both are insoluble storage molecules / compact [B1]
Starch is found in plants; glycogen in animals (and fungi) [B1]
Starch contains amylose, which is unbranched and helical [B1]
Glycogen is more highly branched than amylopectin (more 1-6 bonds). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of cellulose is related to its function in plant cell walls. (6)
hints: Which glucose isomer, and how are monomers arranged?
questions.solution:
Made of β-glucose [B1]
Alternate monomers inverted, giving long straight unbranched chains [B1]
Hydrogen bonds form between parallel chains [B1]
Chains form microfibrils and fibres [B1]
Giving strength [B1]
Cell wall resists turgor pressure / stops cells bursting. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of starch makes it suitable as an energy store in plants. (6)
hints: Think about shape, solubility and size.
How quickly can glucose be released?
questions.solution:
Polymer of α-glucose — releases glucose for respiration when hydrolysed [B1]
Amylose is helical, so compact [B1]
Amylopectin is branched, with many ends for rapid hydrolysis [B1]
Insoluble, so does not affect water potential [B1]
Large, so cannot leave the cell [B1]
Stored in starch grains / amyloplasts. [B1]

questions.prompt: Chitin is a polymer of a modified form of β-glucose. Suggest why chitin, like cellulose, is strong. (3)
questions.solution:
Monomers alternate / every other one inverted, giving straight unbranched chains [B1]
Hydrogen bonds form between parallel chains [B1]
Chains group into fibres / microfibrils, giving strength. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three differences between cellulose and glycogen. (3)
hints: Which glucose isomer is in each?
questions.solution:
Cellulose made of β-glucose; glycogen α-glucose [B1]
Cellulose unbranched; glycogen highly branched [B1]
Cellulose has only 1-4 bonds; glycogen 1-4 and 1-6 [B1]
Cellulose forms microfibrils with hydrogen bonds between chains; glycogen is compact / coiled [B1]
Cellulose structural (plants); glycogen storage (animals). [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Two α-glucose molecules join to form maltose. Describe which atoms are lost and name the bond formed and the reaction. (3)
questions.solution:
H from the OH on carbon 4 of one glucose and OH from carbon 1 of the other are removed (as water) [B1]
1-4 glycosidic bond formed [B1]
Condensation reaction. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mixture of lactose, maltose and glucose is completely hydrolysed. How many different types of monosaccharide are produced? (1)
questions.solution: Two (glucose and galactose). [B1]

questions.prompt: A mixture of starch and sucrose is completely hydrolysed. How many different types of monosaccharide are produced? (1)
questions.solution: Two (glucose and fructose). [B1]

questions.prompt: A mixture of maltose, lactose and sucrose is completely hydrolysed. How many different types of monosaccharide are produced? (1)
hints: List the monosaccharides from each disaccharide.
questions.solution: Three (glucose, galactose and fructose). [B1]

questions.prompt: Honey contains glucose and fructose. Describe how to test honey for reducing sugar and give the expected result. (3)
hints: Are glucose and fructose reducing sugars?
questions.solution:
Add Benedict's reagent to a solution of honey [B1]
Heat in a water bath (boiling) [B1]
Orange / brick-red precipitate, because glucose and fructose are reducing sugars. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student heated a solution of pure sucrose with Benedict's reagent. Describe and explain the result. (3)
questions.solution:
Solution stays blue / no precipitate [B1]
Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar [B1]
Because the reducing groups of glucose and fructose are used in the glycosidic bond. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the Benedict's test can be used to compare the reducing sugar concentration of different solutions. (3)
hints: What must be kept the same?
questions.solution:
Colour / amount of precipitate depends on reducing sugar concentration (blue → green → yellow → orange → red) [B1]
Use the same volume of sample and Benedict's, and heat for the same time [B1]
Compare with colour standards of known concentration (or use a colorimeter). [B1]

questions.prompt: For each of starch, lactose and RNA, state which of these apply: contains glucose; contains galactose; contains phosphate; is a polymer. (3)
questions.solution:
Starch: contains glucose; is a polymer [B1]
Lactose: contains glucose and galactose (not a polymer) [B1]
RNA: contains phosphate; is a polymer. [B1]

questions.prompt: For each of cellulose, maltose and ATP, state which of these apply: contains glucose; contains phosphate; is a polymer; formed by condensation. (3)
hints: Which one is a nucleotide derivative?
All three are formed by condensation reactions.
questions.solution:
Cellulose: contains glucose; polymer; formed by condensation [B1]
Maltose: contains glucose; formed by condensation (not a polymer) [B1]
ATP: contains phosphate; formed by condensation (not a polymer). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between α-glucose and β-glucose and how it affects the polymers they form. (2)
hints: Where is the OH group on carbon 1?
What must happen for β-glucose to join?
questions.solution:
OH on carbon 1 is below the ring in α-glucose and above it in β-glucose [B1]
So β-glucose monomers must be inverted to bond, forming straight chains, while α-glucose forms coiled / branched chains. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cellulose forms straight chains but amylose forms a helix. (2)
questions.solution:
Cellulose: β-glucose with alternate monomers inverted, giving straight chains [B1]
Amylose: α-glucose with 1-4 bonds all in the same orientation, so the chain coils. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why plants store carbohydrate as starch rather than glucose. (2)
hints: What would lots of glucose do to water potential?
questions.solution:
Glucose is soluble and would lower water potential, causing water to enter by osmosis [B1]
Starch is insoluble (no osmotic effect) and too large to leave the cell. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the branching of amylopectin is an advantage for an energy store. (2)
hints: How quickly can glucose be released?
questions.solution:
Many branch ends [B1]
Enzymes can hydrolyse many ends at once, releasing glucose rapidly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the helical shape of amylose makes it good for storage. (2)
hints: Does a helix take up much space?
questions.solution:
Helix is compact [B1]
So a lot of glucose can be stored in a small space. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how cellulose microfibrils make plant cell walls strong. (3)
hints: How are cellulose chains held together?
questions.solution:
Long straight cellulose chains lie parallel [B1]
Hydrogen bonds form between chains [B1]
Forming microfibrils / fibres with high tensile strength. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the cell wall prevents a plant cell from bursting when it is placed in water. (3)
questions.solution:
Water enters the cell by osmosis and the cell swells [B1]
Cellulose cell wall is strong / inelastic [B1]
So it resists the pressure — the cell becomes turgid rather than bursting. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of cellulose helps support a non-woody plant. (3)
hints: What does the wall do when cells are turgid?
Where does the strength come from?
questions.solution:
Cellulose microfibrils give the wall strength [B1]
Turgid cells press against the strong walls [B1]
Turgor pressure keeps the plant upright / provides support. [B1]

questions.prompt: For each of starch, triglyceride and DNA, state the monomer (if any), the type of bond joining the units, and whether it's a polymer. (3)
questions.solution:
Starch: α-glucose, glycosidic bonds, polymer [B1]
Triglyceride: glycerol + 3 fatty acids, ester bonds, not a polymer [B1]
DNA: nucleotides, phosphodiester bonds, polymer. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a phospholipid and explain how phospholipids form a bilayer in water. (5)
hints: Compare with a triglyceride — what replaces one fatty acid?
Which parts are attracted to water?
questions.solution:
Glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group [B1]
Joined by ester bonds [B1]
Phosphate head is hydrophilic / polar [B1]
Fatty acid tails are hydrophobic / non-polar [B1]
Heads face the water on both sides, tails face inwards, away from water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the structure of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids, and explain how this affects the properties of triglycerides. (5)
hints: What is the difference in the hydrocarbon chain?
How does a kink affect packing?
questions.solution:
Both have a hydrocarbon chain and a carboxyl group [B1]
Saturated: no C=C double bonds [B1]
Unsaturated: one or more C=C double bonds [B1]
Double bonds cause kinks, so molecules cannot pack closely [B1]
So triglycerides with unsaturated fatty acids are liquid (oils) at room temperature; saturated are solid (fats). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a triglyceride is formed and explain why triglycerides are good energy stores. (5)
hints: How many fatty acids join to glycerol, and by what reaction?
Think about C–H bonds and solubility.
questions.solution:
Glycerol + three fatty acids [B1]
Condensation reactions forming ester bonds (releasing 3 water) [B1]
Many C–H bonds, so lots of energy released when oxidised / high energy per gram [B1]
Insoluble, so no effect on water potential [B1]
Release water when oxidised (metabolic water). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a phospholipid is formed. (3)
questions.solution:
Glycerol joined to two fatty acids and a phosphate group [B1]
By condensation reactions [B1]
Forming ester bonds (water released). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the hydrolysis of a triglyceride. (3)
questions.solution:
Ester bonds are broken [B1]
Using three molecules of water [B1]
Producing glycerol and three fatty acids (catalysed by lipase). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the emulsion test for lipids. (3)
hints: What is the sample mixed with first?
What is it then added to?
questions.solution:
Mix / shake the sample with ethanol [B1]
Pour into (or add) water [B1]
A white / milky emulsion shows lipid is present. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Use the table. Which fatty acid is polyunsaturated?

Choose one answer.

A  Lauric
B  Palmitic
C  Oleic
D  Linolenic (1)
hints: Polyunsaturated = more than one double bond.
questions.solution: D [B1]
questions.table:
Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds
Lauric | 12 | 0
Palmitic | 16 | 0
Oleic | 18 | 1
Linolenic | 18 | 3

questions.prompt:
Use the table. Which two fatty acids are saturated?

Choose one answer.

A  Lauric and palmitic
B  Lauric and oleic
C  Oleic and linolenic
D  Palmitic and linolenic (1)
hints: Which have 0 in the last column?
questions.solution: A [B1]
questions.table:
Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds
Lauric | 12 | 0
Palmitic | 16 | 0
Oleic | 18 | 1
Linolenic | 18 | 3

questions.prompt:
Use the table. Which fatty acid would be most likely to make a triglyceride that is liquid at room temperature?

Choose one answer.

A  Lauric
B  Palmitic
C  Oleic
D  Linolenic (1)
questions.solution: D [B1]
questions.table:
Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds
Lauric | 12 | 0
Palmitic | 16 | 0
Oleic | 18 | 1
Linolenic | 18 | 3

questions.prompt: Two populations of a fish species live in warm and cold water. The table shows the percentage of saturated fatty acids in their membranes and their swimming speeds at two temperatures. Use the data to show how each population is better adapted to its own environment. (4)
hints: Compare swimming speeds at each temperature.
How does saturation affect membrane fluidity in the cold?
questions.solution:
Warm-water fish swim faster at 25 °C; cold-water fish swim faster at 10 °C [B1]
Cold-water fish have more unsaturated fatty acids, which keep membranes fluid at low temperature [B1]
Warm-water fish have more saturated fatty acids, so membranes do not become too fluid / leaky at high temperature [B1]
Enzymes may also have different optimum temperatures in each population. [B1]
questions.table:
Population | % saturated | Speed at 25 °C / cm s⁻¹ | Speed at 10 °C / cm s⁻¹
Warm water | 45 | 50 | 20
Cold water | 30 | 35 | 32

questions.prompt: Use the table. Name the fatty acid with 18 carbon atoms that is saturated. (1)
hints: Look for 18 carbons and 0 double bonds.
questions.solution: Stearic. [B1]
questions.table:
Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds | Melting point / °C
Lauric | 12 | 0 | 44
Palmitic | 16 | 0 | 63
Stearic | 18 | 0 | 70
Oleic | 18 | 1 | 13
Linoleic | 18 | 2 | −5

questions.prompt: Use the table. Name the fatty acid that is monounsaturated. (1)
hints: Which has exactly one double bond?
questions.solution: Oleic. [B1]
questions.table:
Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds | Melting point / °C
Lauric | 12 | 0 | 44
Palmitic | 16 | 0 | 63
Stearic | 18 | 0 | 70
Oleic | 18 | 1 | 13
Linoleic | 18 | 2 | −5

questions.prompt: Use the table. Name the fatty acid that would be liquid at the lowest temperature. (1)
questions.solution: Linoleic. [B1]
questions.table:
Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds | Melting point / °C
Lauric | 12 | 0 | 44
Palmitic | 16 | 0 | 63
Stearic | 18 | 0 | 70
Oleic | 18 | 1 | 13
Linoleic | 18 | 2 | −5

questions.prompt: Use the table. Describe how the number of C=C double bonds affects the melting point of fatty acids with 18 carbon atoms. (1)
questions.solution: More double bonds, lower melting point. [B1]
questions.table:
Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds | Melting point / °C
Lauric | 12 | 0 | 44
Palmitic | 16 | 0 | 63
Stearic | 18 | 0 | 70
Oleic | 18 | 1 | 13
Linoleic | 18 | 2 | −5

questions.prompt: Use the table. Describe how chain length affects the melting point of saturated fatty acids. (1)
questions.solution: Longer chain (more carbon atoms), higher melting point. [B1]
questions.table:
Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds | Melting point / °C
Lauric | 12 | 0 | 44

questions.prompt: Explain why fatty acids with more C=C double bonds have lower melting points. (1)
hints: What shape do double bonds cause?
questions.solution: Double bonds cause kinks, so molecules cannot pack closely together (weaker attractions). [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which equation represents the formation of a dipeptide?

Choose one answer.

A  dipeptide + water → amino acid + amino acid
B  amino acid + amino acid + water → dipeptide
C  amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water
D  amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + ATP (1)
hints: Is a dipeptide formed by condensation or hydrolysis?
Which side of the equation is water on?
questions.solution:
C [B1]

Model answer:
C: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water (a condensation reaction).

questions.prompt: Name the four groups attached to the central carbon atom of an amino acid. (1)
hints: One group is basic and one is acidic.
One group varies between amino acids.
questions.solution: Amine group (NH₂), carboxyl group (COOH), R group and hydrogen atom (all four). [B1]

questions.prompt: There are 20 different amino acids found in proteins. How do they differ from each other? (1)
hints: Which part of the structure varies?
The other groups are the same in all of them.
questions.solution: They have different R groups (side chains). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the bond that joins two amino acids and the molecule released when it forms. (1)
hints: The bond is named after the molecules it makes.
questions.solution: Peptide bond; water (both needed). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how polypeptides and DNA are formed from their monomers and how they are broken down. (5)
hints: Name the monomer and bond for each.
questions.solution:
Amino acids joined by condensation reactions, forming peptide bonds [B1]
Polypeptide hydrolysed by proteases / peptidases (using water) [B1]
Nucleotides joined by condensation, forming phosphodiester bonds [B1]
DNA polymerase catalyses this [B1]
DNA hydrolysed by nucleases (breaking phosphodiester bonds). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a dipeptide is formed from two amino acids. (2)
questions.solution:
Condensation reaction between the amine group of one and the carboxyl group of the other [B1]
Forms a peptide bond and releases water. [B1]

questions.prompt: A tripeptide is completely hydrolysed. Name the products and state how many water molecules are used. (2)
hints: How many peptide bonds are in a tripeptide?
questions.solution:
Three amino acids [B1]
Two water molecules (one per peptide bond). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a polypeptide always has a free amine group at one end and a free carboxyl group at the other. (2)
hints: Which groups are used in each peptide bond?
What about the first and last amino acids?
questions.solution:
Each peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of the next [B1]
So the amine of the first amino acid and the carboxyl of the last are left unbonded. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two elements found in proteins but not in carbohydrates. (2)
hints: What is in an amine group?
Which element is in some R groups?
questions.solution:
Nitrogen [B1]
Sulfur. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which bond holds together the primary structure of a polypeptide?

Choose one answer.

A  Disulfide
B  Hydrogen
C  Ionic
D  Peptide (1)
hints: Primary structure is the chain of amino acids.
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which bond forms between the R groups of two cysteine molecules?

Choose one answer.

A  Disulfide
B  Hydrogen
C  Ionic
D  Peptide (1)
hints: This is a strong covalent bond.
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which bond forms between R groups with opposite charges?

Choose one answer.

A  Disulfide
B  Hydrogen
C  Ionic
D  Peptide (1)
hints: It's easily broken by pH changes.
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the primary structure of a protein. (1)
questions.solution: The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the tertiary structure of a protein. (1)
hints: It is the overall 3D shape of one polypeptide.
questions.solution: Further folding of the polypeptide into a specific 3D shape, held by hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one example of a protein with a quaternary structure and explain why it has one. (1)
hints: Quaternary structure needs more than one polypeptide.
Think of the oxygen carrier in red blood cells.
questions.solution: Haemoglobin (or antibody / collagen) because it is made of more than one polypeptide chain. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a polypeptide folds into its tertiary structure. (5)
hints: Which bonds hold the final shape?
questions.solution:
Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids [B1]
Secondary structure: α-helix / β-pleated sheet held by hydrogen bonds [B1]
Further folding into a specific 3D shape [B1]
Held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and disulfide bridges between R groups [B1]
Hydrophobic R groups tend to cluster inside, hydrophilic outside. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the four levels of protein structure. (5)
hints: Which level is just the sequence?
Which level needs more than one chain?
questions.solution:
Primary: sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds [B1]
Secondary: α-helix or β-pleated sheet held by hydrogen bonds [B1]
Tertiary: further folding into a specific 3D shape [B1]
Held by hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds [B1]
Quaternary: more than one polypeptide chain joined together (e.g. haemoglobin). [B1]

questions.prompt: When a peptide bond forms between two amino acids, which atoms are removed from each amino acid? Name the reaction. (3)
hints: Which group of the first amino acid reacts?
questions.solution:
OH removed from the carboxyl group of one amino acid [B1]
H removed from the amine group of the other [B1]
Condensation reaction (water released). [B1]

questions.prompt: For each of a triglyceride, a protein and glycogen, state which of these apply: contains nitrogen; is a polymer; formed by condensation. (3)
questions.solution:
Protein: contains nitrogen; polymer; condensation [B1]
Glycogen: polymer; condensation (no nitrogen) [B1]
Triglyceride: formed by condensation only (not a polymer, no nitrogen). [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the structures and properties of globular and fibrous proteins. (5)
questions.solution:
Globular: compact, spherical tertiary structure [B1]
Globular: soluble — hydrophilic R groups on the outside; e.g. enzymes, haemoglobin [B1]
Fibrous: long parallel chains / little folding [B1]
Fibrous: insoluble and strong, with cross-links between chains [B1]
Fibrous: structural roles, e.g. collagen, keratin. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the biuret test for proteins and explain why proteins with different structures all give a positive result. (5)
hints: Which bond do all proteins have?
questions.solution:
Add biuret reagent (sodium hydroxide and copper sulfate) to the sample [B1]
Purple / lilac colour shows protein [B1]
Blue colour stays if no protein [B1]
Biuret reacts with peptide bonds [B1]
All proteins contain peptide bonds, whatever their sequence or shape. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how changes in pH can affect the structure and function of a protein. (5)
hints: What do H⁺ ions interact with?
questions.solution:
Change in H⁺ concentration alters the charges on R groups [B1]
Ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds are broken [B1]
Tertiary structure changes / protein denatures [B1]
Active site or binding site changes shape [B1]
So it can no longer bind its substrate / function. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two features of proteins that allow them to be separated by gel electrophoresis. (2)
questions.solution:
Size / mass (number of amino acids) [B1]
Overall charge (due to R groups). [B1]

questions.prompt: Insulin is a protein. Explain why people with type I diabetes inject insulin rather than taking it by mouth. (2)
hints: What enzymes act on proteins in the stomach and intestine?
Could the whole molecule be absorbed?
questions.solution:
Insulin would be hydrolysed by proteases / endopeptidases and exopeptidases in the gut [B1]
Too large to be absorbed intact / would no longer have its tertiary structure, so wouldn't bind to receptors. [B1]

questions.prompt: An inactive protein hormone is converted to its active form when bone cells produce an acidic environment. Suggest how low pH makes the hormone active. (2)
hints: What do H⁺ ions do to ionic / hydrogen bonds?
questions.solution:
H⁺ ions affect ionic / hydrogen bonds in the protein [B1]
Changes its tertiary structure, so it becomes complementary to its receptor / can bind. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the bonds that maintain the tertiary structure of a protein. (2)
questions.solution:
Hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds between R groups [B1]
Disulfide bridges between cysteines (and hydrophobic interactions). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name one body protein whose loss would reduce muscle power, and one whose loss would reduce immunity. (2)
questions.solution:
Muscle: actin / myosin [B1]
Immunity: antibodies / receptors on lymphocytes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two proteins involved in transport in the body and what they transport. (2)
questions.solution:
Haemoglobin — oxygen [B1]
Carrier / channel proteins — ions / glucose (or albumin etc.). [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two structural proteins and where they are found. (2)
questions.solution:
Collagen — tendons / bones / skin / artery walls [B1]
Keratin — hair / nails. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why protein from food can't be built directly into body proteins. (3)
questions.solution:
Proteins are hydrolysed into amino acids during digestion [B1]
Amino acids absorbed and used to make new proteins [B1]
By translation, in the sequence coded by the person's own genes. [B1]

questions.prompt: A tripeptide has R groups (from left to right) CH₃, CH₂OH and H. Using the table, name the three amino acids. (2)
hints: Glycine has the simplest R group.
questions.solution:
Alanine, serine, glycine. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.
questions.table:
Amino acid | R group
Alanine | CH₃
Asparagine | CH₂CONH₂
Aspartic acid | CH₂COOH
Glycine | H
Serine | CH₂OH

questions.prompt: A tripeptide has R groups (left to right) CH₂COOH, H and CH₂CONH₂. Using the table, name the amino acids. (2)
hints: COOH in the R group = acid.
questions.solution:
Aspartic acid, glycine, asparagine. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.
questions.table:
Amino acid | R group
Alanine | CH₃
Asparagine | CH₂CONH₂
Aspartic acid | CH₂COOH
Glycine | H
Serine | CH₂OH

questions.prompt: Draw (or describe) the general structure of an amino acid and name the bond that forms between two amino acids. (2)
questions.solution:
Central carbon bonded to H, an amine group (NH₂), a carboxyl group (COOH) and an R group [B1]
Peptide bond, formed by condensation (water released). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the general structure of an amino acid. (1)
questions.solution: Central carbon with an amine group (NH₂), carboxyl group (COOH), hydrogen and a variable R group. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the reaction that joins two amino acids and the molecule released. (1)
questions.solution: Condensation, releasing water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe a chemical test for proteins and the positive result. (1)
questions.solution: Add biuret reagent — turns from blue to purple / lilac. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which statement about protein structure is correct?

Choose one answer.

A  Primary structure is held by hydrogen bonds
B  Secondary structure includes α-helices held by hydrogen bonds
C  All proteins have quaternary structure
D  Tertiary structure is the sequence of amino acids (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which level of structure is the sequence of amino acids?

Choose one answer.

A  Primary
B  Secondary
C  Tertiary
D  Quaternary (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which bond is broken when a protein is heated but NOT when it is denatured by mild pH change?

Choose one answer.

A  Hydrogen bonds
B  Ionic bonds
C  Peptide bonds
D  Disulfide bridges (1)
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt:
An enzyme was incubated with excess substrate at 30 °C and at 60 °C. The graph shows the mass of product formed over time.

Explain the shapes of both curves. (4)
hints: Compare the initial rates first — what does temperature do to kinetic energy?
Why does the 60 °C curve level off at a lower mass of product?
questions.solution:
At 60 °C, faster initial rate because more kinetic energy, so more enzyme–substrate complexes formed [B1]
At 60 °C, enzyme denatured (over time) — hydrogen / ionic bonds broken, changing the tertiary structure [B1]
Active site changes shape so substrate no longer fits / is not complementary, so no more product formed (curve levels off) [B1]
At 30 °C, slower rate but enzyme not denatured, so product keeps increasing (reaches a higher total). [B1]

questions.prompt:
The graph shows the effect of pH on the rate of reaction of an enzyme.

Explain why the rate of reaction is low at pH 2 and at pH 12. (4)
hints: What do H⁺ and OH⁻ ions affect in a protein?
Link the change in structure to enzyme–substrate complexes.
questions.solution:
Concentration of H⁺ / OH⁻ ions changes [B1]
Breaks ionic / hydrogen bonds (in the tertiary structure) [B1]
Active site changes shape / substrate no longer complementary [B1]
Fewer enzyme–substrate complexes formed. [B1]

questions.prompt:
The graph shows the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction at different substrate concentrations, with and without an inhibitor.

Explain the results shown in the graph. (4)
hints: At high substrate concentration the two curves almost meet — what type of inhibitor does that suggest?
Why does the curve without inhibitor level off?
questions.solution:
Inhibitor is competitive / similar shape to substrate, so binds to the active site [B1]
At low substrate concentration, inhibitor occupies active sites, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes / lower rate [B1]
At high substrate concentration, substrate outcompetes inhibitor, so rate approaches the same maximum [B1]
Without inhibitor, rate levels off because all active sites are occupied / enzyme concentration is limiting. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug inhibits an enzyme in a malaria parasite but does not inhibit the human enzyme that catalyses the same reaction. Suggest why. (1)
hints: Same reaction does not mean same protein.
questions.solution: Different amino acid sequence / primary structure, so different tertiary structure / shape of binding site, so drug not complementary. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the induced-fit model of enzyme action. (2)
hints: Is the active site exactly complementary before the substrate binds?
What happens to bonds in the substrate?
questions.solution:
Active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, becoming complementary [B1]
This puts strain on bonds in the substrate / lowers activation energy. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an enzyme only catalyses one type of reaction. (2)
hints: What determines the shape of the active site?
questions.solution:
Active site has a specific shape (determined by tertiary structure) [B1]
Only a substrate with a complementary shape can bind / form an enzyme–substrate complex. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some enzymes join two substrate molecules together. Suggest how forming an enzyme–substrate complex speeds up this reaction. (2)
hints: How likely is it that two molecules meet in the right position by chance?
questions.solution:
Holds the substrates close together / in the correct orientation [B1]
Reduces repulsion / lowers activation energy. [B1]

questions.prompt: A non-competitive inhibitor lowers the maximum rate of an enzyme reaction, even at high substrate concentrations. Explain why. (3)
hints: Where does a non-competitive inhibitor bind?
Why can't more substrate overcome it?
questions.solution:
Binds to a site other than the active site (allosteric site) [B1]
Changes the tertiary structure / shape of the active site, so substrate no longer complementary [B1]
Fewer enzyme–substrate complexes; adding more substrate does not compete with / displace the inhibitor. [B1]

questions.prompt: An activator molecule binds to an enzyme at a site away from the active site. The enzyme then catalyses its reaction faster at low substrate concentrations. Suggest how the activator does this. (3)
hints: Think of the opposite of a non-competitive inhibitor.
What happens to the shape of the active site?
questions.solution:
Binds to an allosteric site / site other than the active site [B1]
Changes the tertiary structure / shape of the active site [B1]
Active site becomes more complementary to the substrate, so more enzyme–substrate complexes form. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a metabolic pathway, the final product inhibits the first enzyme of the pathway. Explain how this controls the amount of product made. (3)
hints: When there is a lot of product, what happens to the first enzyme?
What happens when product levels fall?
questions.solution:
Product binds to the first enzyme (non-competitively / at an allosteric site), reducing its activity [B1]
So less product is made when there is plenty [B1]
Binding is reversible: when product levels fall it detaches and the enzyme becomes active again. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a competitive inhibitor slows down an enzyme-controlled reaction. (3)
hints: Where does a competitive inhibitor bind?
What happens if you add more substrate?
questions.solution:
Inhibitor has a similar shape to the substrate [B1]
Binds to / blocks the active site [B1]
So fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form [B1]
Effect reduced by increasing substrate concentration. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why increasing the substrate concentration can overcome competitive inhibition but not non-competitive inhibition. (3)
hints: Do the two inhibitors bind at the same site?
Can substrate displace an inhibitor at a different site?
questions.solution:
Competitive inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site; more substrate means substrate more likely to bind [B1]
Non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere (allosteric site) and changes the shape of the active site [B1]
Substrate cannot displace it / active site stays non-complementary however much substrate is added. [B1]

questions.prompt: Mercury ions bind to sulfur atoms in the R groups of cysteine. Suggest how mercury ions inhibit enzymes. (3)
hints: Link the bond change to the active site.
questions.solution:
Break / prevent disulfide bridges [B1]
Changes the tertiary structure [B1]
Active site changes shape, so substrate no longer complementary / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes. [B1]

questions.prompt: With inhibitor Y, the rate of an enzyme reaction is lower at low substrate concentrations, but at high substrate concentrations it reaches the same maximum rate as without the inhibitor. What type of inhibitor is Y? Explain your answer. (1)
hints: Which type can be outcompeted by substrate?
Look at what happens at high substrate concentration.
questions.solution: Competitive, because at high substrate concentration the substrate outcompetes the inhibitor and the same maximum rate is reached. [B1]

questions.prompt: With inhibitor Z, the maximum rate of an enzyme reaction is lower than without it, even at very high substrate concentrations. What type of inhibitor is Z? Explain your answer. (1)
hints: Can more substrate cancel the effect?
questions.solution: Non-competitive, because the maximum rate is not reached even when substrate concentration is high. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why adding more substrate does not reduce the effect of a non-competitive inhibitor. (1)
hints: Is it competing for the active site?
questions.solution: It binds at a site other than the active site, so substrate is not competing with it / cannot displace it. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an enzyme experiment, each sample was placed in ice as soon as it was collected. Explain why. (2)
hints: What does cold do to enzyme activity?
Why does this matter for the measurement?
questions.solution:
Low temperature means low kinetic energy / few enzyme–substrate complexes, so the reaction almost stops [B1]
So the concentration measured is what it was when the sample was taken. [B1]

questions.prompt: Samples from a protease reaction were added to acid as soon as they were collected. Explain why. (2)
hints: What does a large pH change do to an enzyme?
questions.solution:
Change in pH denatures the enzyme [B1]
Stops the reaction, so the sample shows the amount of product at that time. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an enzyme experiment, a control tube contained boiled enzyme. Explain the purpose of this control. (2)
hints: What does boiling do to an enzyme?
What does the control rule out?
questions.solution:
Boiled enzyme is denatured [B1]
Shows that any change in the test tubes is due to (active) enzyme, not other factors. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the lock-and-key model of enzyme action and explain why the induced-fit model is now preferred. (3)
hints: In lock-and-key, is the active site's shape fixed?
What does induced fit explain about activation energy?
questions.solution:
Lock and key: active site has a fixed shape exactly complementary to the substrate [B1]
Induced fit: active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, becoming complementary [B1]
Induced fit explains how bonds in the substrate are strained, lowering activation energy. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction. (3)
hints: What happens to bonds or to substrate positions?
questions.solution:
Enzyme–substrate complex forms [B1]
Active site changes shape (induced fit), putting strain on / distorting bonds in the substrate, or holds substrates close together [B1]
So less energy is needed for the reaction / more reactions occur at body temperature. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the primary structure of an enzyme determines the shape of its active site and its specificity. (3)
hints: How does amino acid sequence affect folding?
Which bonds hold the tertiary structure?
questions.solution:
Sequence of amino acids determines where bonds form [B1]
Hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds hold the specific tertiary structure [B1]
Gives the active site a specific shape complementary to only one substrate. [B1]

questions.prompt: An enzyme was immobilised on beads. Suggest how a reaction using these beads could be stopped after exactly 2 minutes, and explain why your method works. (2)
hints: Could you take the enzyme out?
What happens with no enzyme present?
questions.solution:
Remove the beads (e.g. sieve / filter / lift out the bead bag) [B1]
No enzyme present, so no enzyme–substrate complexes form. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why heating a reaction mixture to 95 °C stops an enzyme-controlled reaction. (2)
hints: Which bonds break at high temperature?
What happens to the active site?
questions.solution:
Hydrogen / ionic bonds in the tertiary structure break — the enzyme is denatured [B1]
Active site changes shape, so no enzyme–substrate complexes can form. [B1]

questions.prompt: The rate of an enzyme reaction increases as substrate concentration increases, then levels off. Explain this. (2)
hints: What limits the rate at low substrate concentration?
What limits it at high concentration?
questions.solution:
At low concentrations, substrate is limiting — more substrate means more enzyme–substrate complexes [B1]
At high concentrations all active sites are occupied, so enzyme concentration is limiting. [B1]

questions.prompt: With a fixed, small amount of substrate, the initial rate rises as enzyme concentration increases, then levels off. Explain this. (2)
hints: What becomes limiting at high enzyme concentration?
questions.solution:
At first more enzyme means more active sites and more enzyme–substrate complexes [B1]
Then substrate becomes limiting — there are more active sites than substrate molecules. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an enzyme reaction, the mass of product rises quickly at first, then levels off. Explain why. (2)
hints: What happens to the substrate over time?
questions.solution:
As substrate is used up, fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form, so the rate falls [B1]
Product levels off when all substrate has been converted. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the activity of the same enzyme from bacteria living in a hot spring and in soil. Use the data to explain how each is adapted to its environment. (4)
hints: Which enzyme works better at each temperature?
What would make an enzyme resistant to heat?
questions.solution:
Hot-spring enzyme has high activity at 70 °C; soil enzyme has high activity at 30 °C [B1]
Hot-spring enzyme has more bonds (e.g. disulfide / hydrogen) holding its tertiary structure, so it does not denature at 70 °C [B1]
Soil enzyme denatures at 70 °C — its active site changes shape [B1]
Hot-spring enzyme has low activity at 30 °C as molecules have less kinetic energy / fewer collisions. [B1]
questions.table:
Source | Activity at 70 °C | Activity at 30 °C
Hot spring | 90 | 20
Soil | 5 | 60

questions.prompt: The same enzyme from two species differs in 40% of its amino acid sequence but catalyses the same reaction. Explain how. (2)
hints: What needs to be the same?
questions.solution:
The active sites have the same / very similar shape, complementary to the same substrate [B1]
The differences are in other parts of the molecule. [B1]

questions.prompt: An enzyme from a bacterium living in hot springs catalyses the same reaction as a human enzyme but has a different amino acid sequence. Suggest why. (2)
hints: What would happen to the human enzyme at 80 °C?
What extra bonds could prevent this?
questions.solution:
The hot-spring enzyme has more bonds (e.g. disulfide / ionic / hydrogen) to stop it denaturing at high temperature [B1]
Its active site is still complementary to the same substrate. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the activity of enzymes P and Q at three pH values. Give three conclusions from the data. (3)
hints: Find each enzyme's best pH in this range.
questions.solution:
P has highest activity at pH 7 (optimum near 7) [B1]
Q has highest activity at pH 8 (optimum 8 or higher) [B1]
P more active than Q at pH 6 and 7; Q more active at pH 8 [B1]
Q is more affected by low pH. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.
questions.table:
pH | Activity of P | Activity of Q
6 | 20 | 5
7 | 45 | 25
8 | 30 | 50

questions.prompt: The table shows the activity of two protein-digesting enzymes at three pH values. Give three conclusions and suggest where each enzyme works in the body. (3)
hints: Which enzyme works best in acid?
Which part of the gut is acidic?
questions.solution:
Enzyme A works best at pH 2 / in acid; enzyme B works best at pH 8 [B1]
Neither works well at the other's optimum pH [B1]
A probably works in the stomach; B in the small intestine. [B1]
questions.table:
pH | Enzyme A | Enzyme B
2 | 60 | 2
5 | 15 | 20
8 | 1 | 55

questions.prompt: The table shows the activity of two enzymes at three temperatures. Give three conclusions. (3)
hints: Find each enzyme's best temperature in this range.
Which loses activity at high temperature?
questions.solution:
X has highest activity at 40 °C; Y at 50 °C (or higher) [B1]
X loses most activity at 50 °C — likely denatured [B1]
Y is more heat-stable / X more active at lower temperatures. [B1]
questions.table:
Temperature / °C | Enzyme X | Enzyme Y
30 | 30 | 10
40 | 50 | 25
50 | 8 | 45

questions.prompt: Explain how a non-competitive inhibitor differs from a competitive inhibitor in where it binds and in its effect. (3)
hints: How does substrate concentration affect each?
questions.solution:
Competitive binds to the active site; non-competitive to another (allosteric) site [B1]
Non-competitive changes the shape of the active site [B1]
Competitive inhibition can be overcome by more substrate; non-competitive cannot. [B1]

questions.prompt: A non-competitive inhibitor binds permanently. Explain why adding more enzyme can restore the reaction rate but adding more substrate cannot. (3)
hints: What happens to inhibitor molecules once all are bound?
questions.solution:
Each inhibitor molecule permanently inactivates one enzyme molecule [B1]
Extra enzyme provides new, unaffected active sites, so more enzyme–substrate complexes form [B1]
More substrate cannot displace the inhibitor, which is not in the active site. [B1]

questions.prompt: Apple variety X turns brown more slowly than variety Y when cut. Suggest two explanations. (2)
hints: Browning is caused by an enzyme acting on a substrate.
What could be present in smaller amounts?
questions.solution:
Variety X has less enzyme (polyphenol oxidase) [B1]
Or less substrate (phenols) / more inhibitor (e.g. vitamin C) / a less active form of the enzyme. [B1]

questions.prompt: Liver from two different animals released oxygen from hydrogen peroxide at different rates. Suggest an explanation. (2)
hints: Which enzyme breaks down hydrogen peroxide?
questions.solution:
Different concentration / amount of catalase per gram of liver [B1]
So more enzyme–substrate complexes form per second in one liver. [B1]

questions.prompt: Tissue from potatoes stored for six months produced less product than tissue from fresh potatoes. Suggest why. (2)
hints: What could happen to enzymes over time?
questions.solution:
Less enzyme present — some broken down / denatured during storage [B1]
Less enzyme synthesised in stored tissue. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how apple tissue could be prepared so that browning happens faster, without changing its mass, and explain why. (3)
hints: How could you release more enzyme and substrate?
questions.solution:
Grind / blend the tissue (or cut into smaller pieces) [B1]
Breaks open more cells / larger surface area [B1]
More enzyme and substrate released and mixed, so more enzyme–substrate complexes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why liver that has been blended releases oxygen from hydrogen peroxide faster than a single cube of the same mass. (3)
hints: Where is catalase in the cube?
questions.solution:
Larger surface area [B1]
More cells broken open, so more catalase exposed / released [B1]
More enzyme–substrate complexes per second. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one change to the temperature of an enzyme investigation that would shorten the time for a colour change, and explain why. (3)
hints: What does heat do to molecules?
What would happen if it got too hot?
questions.solution:
Increase temperature towards the optimum (e.g. 35 °C) [B1]
Molecules have more kinetic energy, so more collisions [B1]
More enzyme–substrate complexes per second (but not so hot it denatures). [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which method measures catalase activity by measuring the product formed?

Choose one answer.

A  Volume of oxygen collected in a gas syringe
B  Biuret test on the mixture
C  Iodine test on the mixture
D  Mass of the liver (1)
hints: What does catalase produce from hydrogen peroxide?
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which method measures amylase activity by measuring the disappearance of substrate?

Choose one answer.

A  Benedict's test at the start
B  Biuret test at the end
C  Time until iodine no longer turns blue-black
D  Measuring oxygen released (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which method measures lipase activity by measuring a product formed?

Choose one answer.

A  Emulsion test
B  Fall in pH measured with a pH probe
C  Iodine test
D  Volume of oxygen collected (1)
hints: What do fatty acids do to pH?
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
In an energy diagram, the substrate has 40 kJ of energy. The highest energy point is 120 kJ without an enzyme and 80 kJ with an enzyme. The products have 10 kJ. What is the activation energy with the enzyme?

Choose one answer.

A  40 kJ
B  80 kJ
C  70 kJ
D  30 kJ (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
Using the same values (substrate 40 kJ; peak 120 kJ without enzyme, 80 kJ with; products 10 kJ), by how much does the enzyme lower the activation energy?

Choose one answer.

A  30 kJ
B  40 kJ
C  70 kJ
D  80 kJ (1)
hints: Find the activation energy with and without.
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Using the same values (substrate 40 kJ; products 10 kJ), how much energy is released by the reaction?

Choose one answer.

A  10 kJ
B  20 kJ
C  30 kJ
D  40 kJ (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt: An early idea was that enzymes speed up reactions just by being present, without binding to the substrate. Explain how evidence from enzyme experiments shows that enzymes do bind their substrates. (4)
hints: Why does rate level off at high substrate concentration?
What does competitive inhibition tell you?
questions.solution:
Rate levels off at high substrate concentration — active sites become saturated, so a limited number of binding sites [B1]
Competitive inhibitors with a similar shape to the substrate reduce the rate, so substrate must bind a specific site [B1]
Enzymes are specific to substrates of one shape [B1]
Enzyme–substrate complexes have been detected / imaged. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by enzymes being 'unchanged at the end of a reaction', and why this means only small amounts are needed. (4)
hints: What happens to the enzyme after products form?
How many times can it act?
questions.solution:
Products are released from the active site [B1]
Enzyme has the same shape as before / is not used up [B1]
So it can bind another substrate molecule and be reused [B1]
Each enzyme molecule catalyses many reactions per second, so small amounts are enough. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the induced-fit model accounts for both the flexibility and the specificity of enzymes. (4)
hints: What must the substrate still be?
questions.solution:
Active site is flexible and changes shape slightly when substrate binds [B1]
So it moulds around the substrate, straining bonds and lowering activation energy [B1]
Substrate must still be close to complementary in shape / charge to start binding [B1]
So only one or a few similar substrates can bind — specificity. [B1]

questions.prompt: An enzyme converts substrate S into product P. Molecule I has a similar shape to S. The table shows the amount of P after 10 minutes. Explain the result in each tube. (4)
hints: Can I be converted into P?
questions.solution:
Tube Q: no inhibitor, so many enzyme–substrate complexes form — most product [B1]
Tube P: I has a similar shape to S and binds to the active site (competitive inhibition) [B1]
So fewer enzyme–substrate complexes / less product [B1]
Tube R: no substrate, so no product (I is not converted into P). [B1]
questions.table:
Tube | Contents | Product / mg dm⁻³
P | S + I + enzyme | 60
Q | S + water + enzyme | 150
R | I + water + enzyme | 0

questions.prompt: Lactase hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose. As galactose builds up, the rate of the reaction slows. Explain why, using your knowledge of competitive inhibition. (4)
questions.solution:
Galactose has a similar shape to part of lactose [B1]
So it can bind to the active site of lactase [B1]
It competes with lactose, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form [B1]
As more galactose is produced, inhibition increases and the rate slows. [B1]

questions.prompt: Malonate is a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase, which uses succinate as its substrate. Explain the effect of increasing succinate concentration on the inhibition. (4)
hints: Malonate and succinate compete for what?
Which wins at high succinate concentration?
questions.solution:
Malonate has a similar shape to succinate and binds to the active site [B1]
Malonate and succinate compete for active sites [B1]
More succinate means succinate is more likely to bind than malonate [B1]
So inhibition decreases and the rate approaches the uninhibited maximum. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you could confirm that an inhibitor is competitive, and give the expected result. (2)
hints: What can overcome a competitive inhibitor?
What would happen to the rate?
questions.solution:
Increase the substrate concentration in the tube with inhibitor [B1]
Rate / product increases towards the value without inhibitor. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you could show that an inhibitor is non-competitive, and give the expected result. (2)
hints: What would happen if you add lots of substrate?
Does it reach the uninhibited maximum?
questions.solution:
Increase the substrate concentration in the tube with inhibitor [B1]
Rate does not return to the uninhibited maximum. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you could show that an inhibitor binds reversibly, and give the expected result. (2)
questions.solution:
Remove the inhibitor (e.g. by dilution / dialysis / washing the enzyme) [B1]
Enzyme activity is restored. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the initial rate of an enzyme reaction is higher at 45 °C than at 25 °C. (2)
hints: What does temperature do to molecules?
questions.solution:
Molecules have more kinetic energy [B1]
More collisions / more enzyme–substrate complexes formed per unit time. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an enzyme reaction is very slow at 5 °C, and why the rate increases again when the mixture is warmed. (2)
questions.solution:
Low kinetic energy, so few collisions / enzyme–substrate complexes [B1]
Enzyme is not denatured, so activity increases when warmed. [B1]

questions.prompt: A reaction is faster at 37 °C than at 20 °C, but the final amount of product is the same. Explain why. (2)
hints: What decides how much product in total?
questions.solution:
Higher kinetic energy at 37 °C, so more enzyme–substrate complexes per second [B1]
Same amount of substrate, so the same total amount of product eventually forms. [B1]

questions.prompt: Between 10 and 30 minutes, the amount of product at 50 °C stopped increasing, while at 30 °C it continued to increase slowly. Explain these results. (4)
hints: What has happened to the enzyme at 50 °C?
questions.solution:
At 50 °C the enzyme has denatured — hydrogen / ionic bonds broken [B1]
Active site changes shape, so no more enzyme–substrate complexes / product stops increasing (even though substrate remains) [B1]
At 30 °C the enzyme is still active, so product continues to form [B1]
But rate slows as substrate is used up. [B1]

questions.prompt: At two temperatures, the product curves level off at the same final amount but at different times. Explain why. (4)
questions.solution:
Same amount of substrate in both, so the same final amount of product [B1]
Curves level off when all the substrate has been used [B1]
At the higher temperature, more kinetic energy / more enzyme–substrate complexes, so it levels off sooner [B1]
Neither enzyme is denatured. [B1]

questions.prompt: An enzyme from a bacterium that lives in hot springs shows no fall in rate after 30 minutes at 60 °C, whereas the same enzyme from a soil bacterium stops working. Explain. (4)
hints: What holds an enzyme's tertiary structure together?
Why might the hot-spring enzyme not denature?
questions.solution:
Hot-spring enzyme has more bonds (e.g. disulfide / ionic / hydrogen) stabilising its tertiary structure [B1]
So it is not denatured at 60 °C — the active site keeps its shape [B1]
Soil enzyme denatures — active site changes shape, so no enzyme–substrate complexes [B1]
Hot-spring enzyme also benefits from higher kinetic energy at 60 °C. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a metabolic pathway, enzyme activity was 100% with no end product present, 60% with a low concentration of end product and 10% with a high concentration. Evaluate the conclusion that the end product inhibits the enzyme. (3)
hints: Is that proof of direct inhibition?
questions.solution:
Activity decreases as end-product concentration increases, supporting the conclusion [B1]
Consistent with end-product (negative feedback) inhibition [B1]
But only three concentrations / no repeats or SD; inhibition could be indirect — need to test the purified enzyme. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the advantage to a cell of end-product inhibition. (2)
hints: What happens when there's plenty of product?
questions.solution:
Production stops / slows when enough product is present [B1]
So energy (ATP) and substrates are not wasted. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some enzymes only bind to their substrate after a phosphate group is added to them. Explain why. (2)
hints: What does phosphorylation do to shape?
questions.solution:
Phosphorylation changes the tertiary structure / shape of the enzyme [B1]
Active site becomes complementary to the substrate, so enzyme–substrate complexes can form. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a non-competitive inhibitor reduces the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction. (2)
hints: What happens to the active site?
questions.solution:
Binds to a site other than the active site (allosteric site) [B1]
Changes the shape of the active site, so substrate can't bind / fewer E–S complexes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an enzyme only catalyses one type of reaction. (2)
questions.solution:
Active site has a specific shape due to its tertiary structure [B1]
Only complementary to one substrate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an enzyme from the stomach works best at pH 2 but is inactive at pH 8. (2)
hints: What holds the active site in shape?
questions.solution:
pH changes the charges on R groups, breaking ionic / hydrogen bonds [B1]
Active site changes shape at pH 8, so substrate can't bind / no E–S complexes. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug has a similar shape to the substrate of an enzyme that is needed to make nucleotides. Explain how the drug slows cell division. (3)
questions.solution:
Drug is a competitive inhibitor — similar shape so binds to the active site [B1]
Fewer enzyme–substrate complexes, so fewer nucleotides made [B1]
Less DNA replication, so cells can't complete the cell cycle / mitosis slowed. [B1]

questions.prompt: An RNA nucleotide contains a phosphate group. Name the other two components of an RNA nucleotide. (1)
hints: Compare with a DNA nucleotide: one component is different.
One component is a pentose sugar.
questions.solution: Ribose and a (nitrogenous / organic) base (both needed); accept a named base A, U, C or G. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three differences between the structure of DNA and the structure of RNA. (3)
questions.solution:
DNA contains deoxyribose; RNA contains ribose [B1]
DNA contains thymine; RNA contains uracil [B1]
DNA is double-stranded; RNA is single-stranded [B1]
DNA molecules are longer. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Which of the following contain phosphorus: glucose, DNA, triglyceride, phospholipid, ATP, amino acid? (2)
questions.solution:
DNA, phospholipid and ATP (and no others). [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of an RNA nucleotide and how RNA nucleotides join to form a polynucleotide. (5)
questions.solution:
Ribose (pentose sugar) [B1]
Phosphate group [B1]
Nitrogenous base: adenine, uracil, cytosine or guanine [B1]
Joined by condensation reactions [B1]
Phosphodiester bonds between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of DNA is related to its functions. (5)
hints: How does it help store information?
questions.solution:
Two strands held by hydrogen bonds, which are easily broken for replication / transcription [B1]
Complementary base pairing allows accurate copying [B1]
Sugar–phosphate backbone / phosphodiester bonds give stability [B1]
Very long molecule stores lots of information [B1]
Double helix protects the bases / base sequence codes for amino acids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three differences between DNA and mRNA. (3)
questions.solution:
DNA double-stranded; mRNA single-stranded [B1]
DNA has deoxyribose; mRNA ribose [B1]
DNA has thymine; mRNA uracil [B1]
DNA much longer / mRNA has no hydrogen bonds between bases. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Give three differences between a DNA molecule in a eukaryotic nucleus and a tRNA molecule. (3)
questions.solution:
DNA is a double helix; tRNA a single folded strand (clover-leaf) [B1]
DNA contains thymine and deoxyribose; tRNA uracil and ribose [B1]
DNA is much longer [B1]
tRNA has an anticodon and amino acid binding site. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Give three similarities between DNA and RNA. (3)
questions.solution:
Both made of nucleotides containing a phosphate, a pentose sugar and a base [B1]
Both have phosphodiester bonds / sugar–phosphate backbone [B1]
Both contain adenine, cytosine and guanine [B1]
Both can form hydrogen bonds between complementary bases. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a DNA nucleotide and how nucleotides form a DNA double helix. (6)
hints: How are the two strands held together?
questions.solution:
Deoxyribose, phosphate group and a nitrogenous base [B1]
Bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine, guanine [B1]
Nucleotides joined by phosphodiester bonds forming a sugar–phosphate backbone [B1]
Two antiparallel strands [B1]
Held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (A–T, C–G) [B1]
Twisted into a double helix. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a phosphodiester bond forms between two nucleotides. (3)
hints: Which part of one nucleotide joins to which part of the next?
questions.solution:
Phosphate group of one nucleotide reacts with the pentose sugar (OH on carbon 3) of the next [B1]
Water is released — condensation reaction [B1]
Forms the sugar–phosphate backbone (catalysed by DNA polymerase). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the three components of a DNA nucleotide. (1)
questions.solution: Deoxyribose, phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. [B1]

questions.prompt: Which part of a nucleotide, together with phosphate, forms the backbone of a DNA strand? (1)
questions.solution: Deoxyribose (sugar). [B1]

questions.prompt: Which part of the nucleotides forms the hydrogen bonds that hold the two DNA strands together? (1)
questions.solution: The bases. [B1]

questions.prompt: In one strand of DNA, 22% of bases are A, 30% C and 18% G. Give the percentage of each base in that strand that is T, and the percentages of A, T, C and G in the complementary strand. (2)
hints: The four percentages in a strand add up to 100.
A in one strand = T in the other.

questions.prompt: In a double-stranded DNA molecule, 28% of the bases are adenine. Give the percentages of thymine, guanine and cytosine. (2)
hints: C = G, and all four add up to 100.
questions.solution:
Thymine 28% [B1]
Guanine 22% and cytosine 22%. [B1]

questions.prompt: One DNA strand contains A 18%, T 26%, C 30% and G 26%. Give the percentages of each base in the complementary strand. (2)
hints: Swap A with T and C with G.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the two strands of DNA being antiparallel, and why this is important. (4)
hints: What is at each end of a strand?
How do the strands line up?
questions.solution:
Each strand has a 5′ end (phosphate) and a 3′ end (sugar OH) [B1]
The strands run in opposite directions — the 5′ end of one is opposite the 3′ end of the other [B1]
This allows complementary bases to align and hydrogen bond [B1]
And determines the direction in which DNA polymerase can copy each strand. [B1]

questions.prompt: For each molecule — DNA, ATP, an enzyme, a phospholipid — state whether it (i) contains peptide bonds, (ii) is formed by condensation and (iii) is a polymer. (3)
questions.solution:
Peptide bonds: enzyme only [B1]
Formed by condensation: all four [B1]
Polymer: DNA and enzyme only. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three differences between the structure of DNA and ATP. (3)
questions.solution:
DNA has deoxyribose; ATP has ribose [B1]
DNA is a polymer of many nucleotides; ATP is a single (modified) nucleotide [B1]
ATP has three phosphate groups; DNA nucleotides have one / DNA has four bases, ATP only adenine. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which equation represents the hydrolysis of ATP?

Choose one answer.

A  ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ
B  ADP + Pᵢ → ATP + H₂O
C  ATP → ADP + Pᵢ + H₂O
D  ATP + H₂O → AMP + Pᵢ (1)
hints: Hydrolysis uses water as a reactant.
questions.solution:
A [B1]

Model answer:
A: ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ (hydrolysis uses water and removes one phosphate).

questions.prompt:
Which statement about ATP is correct?

Choose one answer.

A  ATP contains deoxyribose
B  ATP synthase catalyses condensation of ADP and Pᵢ
C  ATP hydrolase joins ADP and Pᵢ
D  ATP is a long-term energy store (1)
hints: Think about how ATP is made in the light-dependent reaction and respiration.
questions.solution:
B [B1]

Model answer:
B: ATP synthase catalyses a condensation reaction between ADP and Pᵢ.

questions.prompt: Describe how a protein can be phosphorylated and suggest how this can activate it. (2)
hints: Where does the phosphate come from?
What happens to the protein's shape?
questions.solution:
ATP is hydrolysed and the phosphate group is attached to the protein (by a kinase enzyme) [B1]
This changes the protein's tertiary structure / shape, e.g. making an active site complementary. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which enzyme catalyses the synthesis of ATP?

Choose one answer.

A  ATP hydrolase
B  DNA polymerase
C  ATP synthase
D  RNA polymerase (1)
hints: It is named after its product.
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which molecule is produced, along with inorganic phosphate, when ATP is hydrolysed?

Choose one answer.

A  AMP
B  ADP
C  Adenine
D  Ribose (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which sugar is found in a molecule of ATP?

Choose one answer.

A  Deoxyribose
B  Glucose
C  Fructose
D  Ribose (1)
hints: It is the same sugar as in RNA.
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt: Name all of the elements found in a molecule of ATP. (2)
hints: It contains a base, a sugar and phosphates.
questions.solution:
Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus. [B2]
5 correct = 2 marks; 4 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of ATP and explain why it is suited to its role as the immediate energy source in cells. (5)
hints: How is energy released, and how much?
questions.solution:
Adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups [B1]
Hydrolysis of the bond to the last phosphate releases energy [B1]
Releases a small, manageable amount of energy in one step [B1]
Rapidly resynthesised from ADP and Pi [B1]
Phosphate can be transferred to other molecules, making them more reactive. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how ATP is resynthesised in cells. (4)
hints: Which reaction joins ADP and Pi?
questions.solution:
ADP + Pi joined by a condensation reaction [B1]
Catalysed by ATP synthase [B1]
During respiration (glycolysis / oxidative phosphorylation) [B1]
During photosynthesis (light-dependent reaction). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why ATP is a good immediate source of energy but not a good long-term energy store. (4)
hints: How much energy is released, and how fast?
questions.solution:
Hydrolysis releases a small, manageable amount of energy [B1]
In a single step, so energy is available quickly [B1]
ATP is quickly resynthesised from ADP and Pi [B1]
But ATP is unstable / not stored in large amounts — glycogen and lipids are long-term stores. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe four uses of ATP in cells. (4)
hints: Think about transport, movement and synthesis.
questions.solution:
Active transport [B1]
Muscle contraction [B1]
Protein synthesis / DNA replication (anabolic reactions) [B1]
Phosphorylating molecules to make them more reactive (e.g. glucose in glycolysis) [B1]
Secretion (vesicle movement / exocytosis). [B1]
Any 4 of these points — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Give two ways in which ATP is suitable as the immediate energy source for cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Releases a small, manageable amount of energy / little lost as heat [B1]
Rapidly hydrolysed in one step / easily resynthesised / can phosphorylate other molecules. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how ATP is resynthesised from ADP. (2)
hints: Where does the energy come from?
questions.solution:
ADP + Pi joined by ATP synthase (condensation reaction) [B1]
Energy from respiration / photosynthesis (light energy). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why ATP cannot be stored in large amounts and how cells overcome this. (2)
questions.solution:
ATP is unstable / readily hydrolysed [B1]
Cells continuously make ATP by respiration / store energy as glucose, fat or phosphocreatine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain, in terms of energy, why some enzyme-catalysed reactions use phosphorylated substrates. (1)
hints: What does phosphorylation do to a molecule's reactivity?
questions.solution: Phosphorylated substrate is more reactive / lowers activation energy needed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why glucose is phosphorylated at the start of glycolysis. (1)
questions.solution: Makes glucose more reactive / lowers activation energy for the next reactions (and traps it in the cell). [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one way in which ATP hydrolysis is coupled to an energy-requiring reaction. (1)
questions.solution: Released phosphate phosphorylates another molecule, making it more reactive (or energy released is used directly). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the properties of water make it important for organisms living in ponds and lakes. (5)
hints: What happens when a pond freezes?
Think about temperature, dissolving and light.
questions.solution:
Ice is less dense than water, so it floats and insulates the water beneath [B1]
High specific heat capacity, so water temperature is stable [B1]
Good solvent, so oxygen / ions / nutrients dissolve [B1]
Transparent, so light reaches plants for photosynthesis [B1]
Cohesion / surface tension, so some insects can walk on the surface. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how hydrogen bonding between water molecules gives water properties that are important in plants. (5)
hints: Link hydrogen bonds to cohesion, heat and solvent properties.
questions.solution:
Water is polar, so hydrogen bonds form between molecules [B1]
Cohesion — water is pulled up the xylem as a continuous column [B1]
Adhesion to xylem walls helps water rise [B1]
High latent heat of vaporisation — evaporation (transpiration) cools leaves [B1]
Good solvent — minerals dissolve and are transported [B1]
Water is a reactant in photosynthesis / hydrolysis. [B1]
Any 5 of these points — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of iron ions, hydrogen ions, sodium ions and phosphate ions in organisms. (5)
hints: One is in haemoglobin, one affects pH.
One is used in co-transport, one in ATP and DNA.
questions.solution:
Iron ions (Fe²⁺) are part of haem in haemoglobin, binding oxygen [B1]
Hydrogen ions determine pH (affecting enzymes) / used in chemiosmosis [B1]
Sodium ions are needed for co-transport of glucose / amino acids [B1]
Phosphate ions are part of ATP / nucleotides (DNA, RNA) [B1]
Phosphate is part of phospholipids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Other than the nucleus, name the two organelles in a plant cell that contain their own DNA. (1)
hints: Think about which organelles are thought to have evolved from free-living prokaryotes.
One of them is the site of aerobic respiration.
questions.solution: Mitochondria and chloroplasts (both needed). [B1]

questions.prompt: Penicillin prevents bacteria forming cell walls. Suggest why penicillin does not harm human cells. (1)
hints: What structure does a human cell lack?
What are bacterial cell walls made of?
questions.solution: Human cells do not have a cell wall / murein (peptidoglycan). [B1]

questions.prompt: An antibiotic binds to bacterial 70S ribosomes and stops translation. Suggest why it does not stop translation in the cytoplasm of human cells. (1)
hints: Are human cytoplasmic ribosomes the same size as bacterial ones?
questions.solution: Human (cytoplasmic) ribosomes are 80S / larger / a different shape, so the antibiotic does not bind. [B1]

questions.prompt: Contrast the structure of prokaryotic cells with the structure of eukaryotic cells. (6)
hints: Give paired differences: prokaryotes have … whereas eukaryotes have …
Think about DNA, organelles, ribosomes and the cell wall.
questions.solution:
Prokaryotes have no nucleus — DNA free in cytoplasm; eukaryotes have a nucleus [B1]
Prokaryotic DNA circular; eukaryotic DNA linear [B1]
Prokaryotic DNA not associated with histones; eukaryotic DNA is [B1]
Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles (e.g. mitochondria); eukaryotes do [B1]
Prokaryotes have smaller (70S) ribosomes; eukaryotes have larger (80S) ribosomes [B1]
Prokaryotic cell wall made of murein / peptidoglycan; plant / fungal walls made of cellulose / chitin [B1]
Prokaryotes may have plasmids / capsule / flagella of different structure [B1]
Prokaryotic cells are smaller. [B1]
Any 6 of these points — max 6 marks.

Model answer:
Any 6 contrasting points (each must state both sides).

questions.prompt: Describe how a protein made in a cell is modified to form a glycoprotein and transported to the cell-surface membrane. (4)
hints: Where are proteins for export made?
questions.solution:
Polypeptide made on ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum [B1]
Transported in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus [B1]
Carbohydrate added in the Golgi (glycoprotein formed) [B1]
Vesicles carry it to the cell-surface membrane and fuse with it. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the main structural polysaccharide in the cell walls of (i) plants, (ii) fungi and (iii) bacteria. (3)
hints: Each group uses a different polysaccharide.
The bacterial one is also called peptidoglycan.
questions.solution:
(i) Cellulose [B1]
(ii) Chitin [B1]
(iii) Murein / peptidoglycan. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name one structure that is found in: (i) both prokaryotic cells and plant cells but not animal cells; (ii) plant cells but not prokaryotic or animal cells; (iii) all three types of cell. (3)
hints: Think about the outside of the cell first.
Which organelle is only in photosynthetic eukaryotes?
questions.solution:
(i) Cell wall [B1]
(ii) Chloroplast / large permanent vacuole [B1]
(iii) Ribosomes / cell-surface membrane / cytoplasm. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three structural differences between a plant cell and an animal cell. (3)
hints: Think about what surrounds the cell.
Think about organelles for photosynthesis and storage.
questions.solution:
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall [B1]
Plant cells have chloroplasts [B1]
