Plant cells have a large permanent vacuole [B1]
Plant cells store starch, animal cells glycogen. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Give four differences between the structure of a virus and the structure of a bacterium. (4)
hints: Compare the outer layers and the genetic material.
questions.solution:
Virus has no cell-surface membrane / cytoplasm [B1]
Virus has no ribosomes [B1]
Virus has a protein capsid, bacterium a murein cell wall [B1]
Virus genetic material may be RNA; bacterium always DNA (circular, plasmids) [B1]
Virus is much smaller. [B1]
Any 4 of these points — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain two features of a red blood cell that make it efficient at carrying oxygen. (2)
questions.solution:
Biconcave shape, so large surface area for diffusion / short diffusion distance [B1]
No nucleus (or few organelles), so more room for haemoglobin [B1]
Small and flexible, so fits through capillaries. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain two features of a palisade mesophyll cell that make it efficient at photosynthesis. (2)
questions.solution:
Many chloroplasts, to absorb lots of light [B1]
Tall / column shape near the upper surface, so lots of light reaches it [B1]
Large vacuole pushes chloroplasts to the edge of the cell, near the light / CO₂. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain two features of a sperm cell that help it fertilise an egg. (2)
hints: How does it move, and what powers this?
How does it get through the outer layer of the egg?
questions.solution:
Flagellum / tail, so it can swim [B1]
Many mitochondria, to provide ATP for movement [B1]
Acrosome contains enzymes to digest the egg's outer layer [B1]
Haploid nucleus. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Give two features of mitochondria that suggest they evolved from bacteria. (2)
questions.solution:
Contain circular DNA [B1]
Contain 70S ribosomes [B1]
Divide by binary fission [B1]
Double membrane. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Give one feature of chloroplasts that allows them to make some of their own proteins, and one way this feature differs from the equivalent in the cytoplasm. (2)
hints: What is needed to make proteins?
questions.solution:
Contain ribosomes (and DNA) [B1]
Chloroplast ribosomes are smaller (70S) than cytoplasmic ribosomes (80S). [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two features of a chloroplast and explain how each helps photosynthesis. (2)
questions.solution:
Thylakoid membranes / grana with chlorophyll — large surface area for light absorption [B1]
Stroma contains enzymes for the light-independent reaction [B1]
Contains starch grains to store products. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: A drug is attached to an antibody that binds to a receptor on cancer cells. The complex is taken into the cell. Describe how the drug could be released inside the cell. (3)
hints: How is the complex taken in?
questions.solution:
Antibody binds to the complementary receptor / antigen on the cell surface [B1]
Cell membrane engulfs it, forming a vesicle (endocytosis) [B1]
Lysosome fuses with the vesicle; hydrolytic enzymes break down the antibody / linker, releasing the drug. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how lysosomes are involved in breaking down worn-out organelles. (3)
questions.solution:
Organelle enclosed in a vesicle / membrane [B1]
Lysosome fuses with it [B1]
Hydrolytic enzymes (lysozymes) digest the organelle; products reused by the cell. [B1]

questions.prompt: Contrast the structure of a plant cell with the structure of an animal cell. (5)
hints: Think about walls, plastids, vacuoles and storage.
questions.solution:
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall; animal cells do not [B1]
Plant cells have chloroplasts; animal cells do not [B1]
Plant cells have a large permanent vacuole; animal vacuoles small / temporary [B1]
Plant cells store starch; animal cells glycogen [B1]
Animal cells have centrioles (most plant cells do not). [B1]

questions.prompt: Contrast the structure of a fungal cell with the structure of a bacterial cell. (5)
questions.solution:
Fungal cell has a nucleus; bacterium has DNA free in the cytoplasm [B1]
Fungal wall made of chitin; bacterial wall of murein [B1]
Fungal cell has 80S ribosomes; bacterium 70S [B1]
Fungal cell has membrane-bound organelles (e.g. mitochondria); bacterium does not [B1]
Fungal DNA linear with histones; bacterial DNA circular / plasmids [B1]
Fungal cell is larger. [B1]
Any 5 of these points — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a bacterial cell. (5)
hints: Which structures are only in some bacteria?
questions.solution:
Cell wall made of murein [B1]
Cell-surface membrane [B1]
Cytoplasm with 70S ribosomes [B1]
Circular DNA (not in a nucleus, no histones) [B1]
Plasmids [B1]
May have a capsule and / or flagellum. [B1]
Any 5 of these points — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure and function of a mitochondrion. (4)
hints: How many membranes, and is the inner one folded?
questions.solution:
Double membrane [B1]
Inner membrane folded into cristae (large surface area) [B1]
Matrix contains enzymes, 70S ribosomes and circular DNA [B1]
Site of aerobic respiration / produces ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure and functions of the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus. (4)
hints: What is on the surface of the rough ER?
What does the Golgi do to proteins?
questions.solution:
RER: system of membranes / cisternae with ribosomes on the surface [B1]
RER: synthesises and transports proteins [B1]
Golgi: stack of flattened membrane sacs (cisternae) with vesicles [B1]
Golgi: modifies proteins (e.g. adds carbohydrate), packages them into vesicles / forms lysosomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure and functions of a chloroplast. (4)
hints: Where do the two stages of photosynthesis happen?
questions.solution:
Double membrane (envelope) [B1]
Thylakoids stacked into grana, containing chlorophyll — site of the light-dependent reaction [B1]
Stroma contains enzymes — site of the light-independent reaction [B1]
Contains its own DNA / 70S ribosomes / starch grains. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two features found in all eukaryotic cells but not in prokaryotic cells. (1)
hints: Where is the DNA kept in a eukaryote?
questions.solution: Two from: nucleus / membrane-bound organelles / 80S ribosomes / linear DNA with histones. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two structures found in some, but not all, prokaryotic cells. (1)
hints: Think of small extra loops of DNA.
Think of structures outside the cell wall.
questions.solution: Two from: plasmids / capsule / flagellum. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two structures found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: ribosomes / cell-surface membrane / cytoplasm / DNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: The antibiotic polymyxin binds to a molecule found only in the outer membrane of some bacteria. Suggest why polymyxin does not damage human cells. (2)
hints: Do human membranes contain that molecule?
Can the drug bind without it?
questions.solution:
Human cell membranes do not contain the molecule [B1]
So polymyxin cannot bind to / damage them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Lysozyme in tears kills some bacteria but does not harm human cells. Suggest why. (2)
hints: Do human cells have this structure?
questions.solution:
Lysozyme hydrolyses murein / peptidoglycan in bacterial cell walls [B1]
Human cells have no cell wall / murein. [B1]

questions.prompt: After centrifugation, the fraction containing chloroplasts also contained ribosomes and DNA. Explain why. (3)
hints: Do chloroplasts contain their own DNA and ribosomes?
questions.solution:
Chloroplasts contain their own (circular) DNA [B1]
And their own (70S) ribosomes [B1]
So these are isolated together with the chloroplasts. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the functions of the capsid and the attachment proteins of a virus. (2)
hints: What do attachment proteins bind to?
questions.solution:
Capsid: protein coat that protects the nucleic acid [B1]
Attachment proteins: bind to complementary receptors on host cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name three structural features found in all viruses. (2)
hints: What is the genetic material inside?
What surrounds it and helps it attach?
questions.solution:
Nucleic acid (DNA or RNA); capsid; attachment proteins. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Explain why viruses are described as acellular. (2)
hints: What structures does every cell have?
questions.solution:
Not made of cells [B1]
No cell-surface membrane / cytoplasm / organelles such as ribosomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why viruses are not considered to be living organisms. (2)
hints: Can they reproduce on their own?
questions.solution:
Cannot reproduce outside a host cell [B1]
No metabolism / do not respire / do not grow. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why viruses can only replicate inside host cells. (2)
hints: What do they lack for making proteins?
questions.solution:
Have no ribosomes / enzymes to make their own proteins or nucleic acids [B1]
Use the host cell's ribosomes, enzymes and ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why antibiotics are not prescribed to treat influenza. (1)
questions.solution: Influenza is caused by a virus; antibiotics target bacterial structures (e.g. murein walls, 70S ribosomes) that viruses lack. [B1]

questions.prompt: Murein is made of polysaccharide chains cross-linked by short peptide chains. Suggest how this structure makes bacterial cell walls strong. (3)
hints: What must a bacterial wall resist?
questions.solution:
Long polysaccharide chains [B1]
Cross-linked by peptide chains (covalent bonds), forming a net / mesh [B1]
Resists osmotic pressure, so the cell does not burst. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name one structure visible in an electron micrograph that would show a cell is eukaryotic. (1)
questions.solution: Nucleus / mitochondria / endoplasmic reticulum / Golgi apparatus (any membrane-bound organelle). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name one structure that would show that a eukaryotic cell is a plant cell. (1)
questions.solution: Chloroplast / cellulose cell wall / large permanent vacuole. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name one feature visible in an electron micrograph that would show that a cell is prokaryotic. (1)
questions.solution: DNA free in the cytoplasm / no nucleus / no membrane-bound organelles / plasmids / murein wall. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two functions of lysosomes. (2)
hints: Think about pathogens and old organelles.
questions.solution:
Digest pathogens engulfed by phagocytes [B1]
Break down worn-out organelles [B1]
Release enzymes out of the cell by exocytosis / cause cell death (autolysis). [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe two functions of the rough endoplasmic reticulum. (2)
hints: What happens to proteins after they are made?
questions.solution:
Protein synthesis (on its ribosomes) [B1]
Folds and transports proteins / packages them in vesicles to the Golgi. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two functions of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum. (2)
hints: Which type of molecule does it deal with?
questions.solution:
Synthesises and processes lipids [B1]
Stores / transports lipids (or carbohydrates). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why phagocytosis requires a fluid cell-surface membrane. (3)
hints: What must the membrane do to engulf a pathogen?
What happens after the vesicle forms?
questions.solution:
Membrane must change shape / flow around the pathogen [B1]
Membrane fuses to form a vesicle (phagosome) [B1]
Vesicle membrane must fuse with lysosomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of organelles in producing and secreting a protein hormone such as insulin. (5)
hints: Where are mRNA, ribosomes and the Golgi involved?
How does it leave the cell?
questions.solution:
Nucleus: gene transcribed to mRNA, which leaves through nuclear pores [B1]
Ribosomes on RER translate mRNA into a polypeptide [B1]
RER folds / transports the protein in vesicles to the Golgi [B1]
Golgi modifies and packages it into secretory vesicles [B1]
Vesicles fuse with the cell-surface membrane (exocytosis); mitochondria supply ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how lysosomes are formed and how they help destroy an engulfed pathogen. (5)
questions.solution:
Hydrolytic enzymes made on ribosomes of the RER [B1]
Transported to the Golgi apparatus [B1]
Golgi packages them into vesicles — lysosomes [B1]
Lysosome fuses with the phagosome containing the pathogen [B1]
Lysozymes hydrolyse the pathogen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of organelles in producing a protein that becomes part of the cell-surface membrane. (5)
hints: How does the protein end up in the membrane?
questions.solution:
Nucleus: transcription produces mRNA [B1]
Ribosomes on RER translate it [B1]
Protein enters the RER and is folded [B1]
Transported in vesicles to the Golgi, where it may be modified (e.g. glycoprotein) [B1]
Vesicle fuses with the cell-surface membrane, inserting the protein. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the function of each of these structures found in some prokaryotic cells: plasmid, capsule, flagellum. (2)
hints: What extra genes do plasmids carry?
What does a capsule protect against?
questions.solution:
Plasmid: carries extra genes, e.g. antibiotic resistance; capsule: protection (from drying out / phagocytosis); flagellum: movement. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Name three structures found in all prokaryotic cells. (2)
hints: What do all cells use to make proteins?
questions.solution:
Three from: cell-surface membrane; cytoplasm; ribosomes (70S); circular DNA; cell wall. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Name three structures found in eukaryotic cells but not in prokaryotic cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Three from: nucleus; mitochondria; endoplasmic reticulum; Golgi apparatus; lysosomes; chloroplasts. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: What name is given to a group of similar cells working together to carry out a particular function? (1)
hints: It is a level of organisation.
questions.solution: A tissue. [B1]

questions.prompt: What name is given to a group of tissues working together to perform a function? (1)
hints: The heart and the leaf are examples.
questions.solution: An organ. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name a plant organ and two tissues found in it. (1)
hints: Which tissues does a leaf contain?
questions.solution: e.g. leaf: palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, xylem, phloem, epidermis (any two). [B1]

questions.prompt: Vesicles are moved from the Golgi apparatus to the cell-surface membrane along protein filaments. Explain how this movement requires energy and where the energy comes from. (2)
questions.solution:
Motor proteins move along the cytoskeleton (microtubules / actin) — needs ATP hydrolysis [B1]
ATP is produced by mitochondria (aerobic respiration). [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which statement is true of both a virus and a bacterium?

Choose one answer.

A  Both have ribosomes
B  Both have a cell wall
C  Both contain nucleic acid
D  Both have a cell-surface membrane (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which structure is found in a bacterium but NOT in a virus?

Choose one answer.

A  Capsid
B  Ribosomes
C  Attachment proteins
D  Nucleic acid (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which is found in a virus but not in a bacterium?

Choose one answer.

A  Capsid
B  Plasmid
C  Murein cell wall
D  70S ribosomes (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two features of mitochondrial DNA that differ from nuclear DNA in eukaryotes. (2)
questions.solution:
Circular (not linear) [B1]
Not associated with histones / shorter / no introns. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe what stem cells are and explain why bone marrow stem cells can be used to replace a patient's immune cells. (5)
hints: Which cells come from bone marrow?
questions.solution:
Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and differentiate [B1]
Bone marrow stem cells are multipotent [B1]
They differentiate into blood cells including lymphocytes [B1]
Transplanted cells divide to repopulate the immune system [B1]
Must be tissue-matched to reduce rejection. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which is true of all prokaryotic cells?

Choose one answer.

A  They contain mitochondria
B  Their DNA is circular and not associated with histones
C  They all have a capsule
D  They have 80S ribosomes (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which structure is found in prokaryotic cells but not in animal cells?

Choose one answer.

A  Ribosomes
B  Cell-surface membrane
C  Murein cell wall
D  Cytoplasm (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
How do prokaryotic cells divide?

Choose one answer.

A  Binary fission
B  Mitosis
C  Meiosis
D  Budding with spindle fibres (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt: A receptor protein in a cell-surface membrane is taken into the cell and destroyed by a lysosome. Explain how. (2)
questions.solution:
Receptor taken in by endocytosis in a vesicle, which fuses with a lysosome [B1]
Lysosome releases hydrolytic enzymes (proteases) that hydrolyse the receptor. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium. (2)
questions.solution:
Engulfs the bacterium by phagocytosis into a phagosome [B1]
Lysosome fuses and releases lysozymes that hydrolyse the bacterium. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of the rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus in producing a membrane receptor. (2)
questions.solution:
RER: ribosomes synthesise the protein, which is folded / transported in the RER [B1]
Golgi modifies (e.g. adds carbohydrate) and packages it into vesicles that fuse with the membrane. [B1]

questions.prompt: After a heart attack, rats were given stem cells with a functioning receptor (c-KIT⁺), stem cells without it (c-KIT⁻), or no stem cells (control). The receptor activates an enzyme that triggers differentiation into heart muscle cells. Mean ventricular blood pressure was highest in c-KIT⁺, lower in c-KIT⁻ and lowest in the control. Explain the results. (4)
questions.solution:
Control: no stem cells, so damaged tissue not replaced — low pressure [B1]
c-KIT⁺: receptor activated, triggers differentiation into new cardiomyocytes [B1]
More muscle cells to contract, so higher ventricular pressure [B1]
c-KIT⁻: some differentiation by other pathways / fewer new cells, so intermediate pressure. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the differences between totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent and unipotent stem cells. (4)
questions.solution:
Totipotent: can become any cell type, including placenta (early embryo) [B1]
Pluripotent: any body cell type, not placenta (embryonic stem cells) [B1]
Multipotent: a limited range of cell types (e.g. bone marrow) [B1]
Unipotent: only one cell type (e.g. cardiomyocytes from some heart stem cells). [B1]

questions.prompt: An electron micrograph of a plant cell shows an organelle with stacks of flattened membranes (W) and a large membrane-bound sac filled with cell sap (Z). Name W and Z and give a function of each. (2)
questions.solution:
W: chloroplast — photosynthesis [B1]
Z: vacuole — keeps the cell turgid / stores substances. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the organelle with a double membrane whose inner membrane is folded into cristae, and give its function. (2)
questions.solution:
Mitochondrion [B1]
Site of aerobic respiration — produces ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the structure made of cellulose around a plant cell and give its function. (2)
questions.solution:
Cell wall [B1]
Provides strength / prevents the cell bursting when turgid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare and contrast the scanning electron microscope (SEM) and the transmission electron microscope (TEM). (6)
hints: Where does the electron beam go in each one?
questions.solution:
Similarity: both use a beam of electrons (focused by electromagnets) [B1]
Similarity: both need a vacuum, so specimens must be dead [B1]
Similarity: both have higher resolution than optical microscopes / produce black-and-white images [B1]
TEM: electrons pass through the specimen; SEM: electrons are scattered / bounce off the surface [B1]
TEM gives 2D images of internal structure; SEM gives 3D images of surfaces [B1]
TEM has higher resolution (about 0.1 nm) than SEM [B1]
TEM specimens must be extremely thin; SEM specimens need not be [B1]
Both may show artefacts from preparation. [B1]
Any 6 of these points — max 6 marks.

Model answer:
Any 6 points; at least one similarity and one difference.

questions.prompt: Describe how cell fractionation and ultracentrifugation can be used to obtain a sample of mitochondria from liver tissue. Explain the conditions used. (6)
hints: Explain why the solution is cold, isotonic and buffered.
Which organelle forms the first pellet?
questions.solution:
Cold — reduces enzyme activity / stops organelles being digested [B1]
Isotonic — prevents osmosis, so organelles do not burst or shrink [B1]
Buffered — keeps pH constant so proteins / enzymes are not denatured [B1]
Homogenise (blend) tissue, then filter to remove debris / whole cells [B1]
Centrifuge at low speed; nuclei form the first pellet [B1]
Spin supernatant at a higher speed; mitochondria form the next pellet. [B1]

Model answer:
6 points.

questions.prompt: Lipid was shaken with bile salts. When viewed with an optical microscope, no large lipid droplets could be seen. Explain why. (2)
hints: What do bile salts do to lipids?
What is the smallest thing an optical microscope can resolve?
questions.solution:
Bile salts emulsify the lipid into very small droplets / micelles [B1]
Droplets are smaller than the resolution of an optical microscope (about 0.2 µm). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why ribosomes cannot be seen with an optical microscope. (2)
hints: What limits the resolution of an optical microscope?
questions.solution:
Ribosomes are very small (about 20–30 nm) [B1]
Smaller than the resolution of an optical microscope, which is limited by the wavelength of light. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why increasing the magnification of an optical microscope beyond about × 1500 does not reveal more detail. (2)
hints: What is the difference between magnification and resolution?
questions.solution:
Resolution is limited by the wavelength of light / points closer than about 0.2 µm cannot be distinguished [B1]
So the image gets bigger but more blurred / no extra detail. [B1]

questions.prompt: In cell fractionation, explain why (i) the homogenate is filtered, and why the solution is (ii) ice-cold, (iii) isotonic and (iv) buffered. (4)
hints: What would whole cells and debris do?
Think about enzymes, osmosis and pH.
questions.solution:
(i) Removes whole cells / large debris [B1]
(ii) Reduces enzyme activity, so organelles are not broken down [B1]
(iii) Prevents osmosis, so organelles don't burst or shrink [B1]
(iv) Keeps pH constant, so proteins / enzymes are not denatured. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how nuclei can be isolated from plant tissue by cell fractionation and ultracentrifugation. (4)
hints: What do you do to the tissue first?
Which fraction comes out first in the centrifuge?
questions.solution:
Cut tissue and homogenise in a cold, isotonic, buffered solution [B1]
Filter to remove debris [B1]
Centrifuge at low speed [B1]
Nuclei (largest / densest) form the first pellet. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the order in which organelles form pellets during differential centrifugation. (4)
hints: What decides which organelles sink first?
questions.solution:
Densest / largest organelles sediment first [B1]
Nuclei first, then chloroplasts / mitochondria [B1]
Then lysosomes / endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes last [B1]
Supernatant is spun at increasing speeds each time. [B1]

questions.prompt: Gold particles attached to antibodies are used to show the location of proteins in transmission electron micrographs. Explain why gold is used. (3)
hints: How does gold interact with electrons?
questions.solution:
Gold is dense / does not let electrons through, so appears as a dark spot [B1]
Particles are very small, so position can be pinpointed [B1]
Antibody binds specifically to the protein, so the gold marks where the protein is. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a transmission electron microscope, rather than an optical microscope, is needed to see individual protein molecules in membranes. (3)
questions.solution:
Proteins are a few nanometres across, smaller than the resolution of an optical microscope (about 200 nm) [B1]
Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light [B1]
So TEM has much higher resolution (about 0.1 nm). [B1]

questions.prompt: After nuclei have been removed from a liver homogenate, describe how a sample of mitochondria could be obtained. (2)
hints: What do you do with the supernatant?
questions.solution:
Centrifuge the supernatant at a higher speed [B1]
Mitochondria form the pellet. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how whole cells and large debris are removed from a homogenate before ultracentrifugation. (2)
hints: What can let organelles through but not whole cells?
questions.solution:
Filter (e.g. through gauze / muslin) [B1]
or centrifuge at a low speed and discard the pellet. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the supernatant is centrifuged at increasing speeds during differential centrifugation. (2)
hints: Do all organelles sink at the same speed?
questions.solution:
Each speed makes organelles of a particular size / density form a pellet [B1]
Smaller / less dense organelles need greater force to sediment. [B1]

questions.prompt: Detergent was added to a liver homogenate before centrifugation. Ribosomes that normally pellet with the endoplasmic reticulum were then found in the supernatant. Explain why. (3)
hints: What does detergent do to membranes?
questions.solution:
Detergent dissolves lipids / membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum [B1]
Ribosomes are released from the RER [B1]
Free ribosomes are small, so are not pelleted at that speed. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mixture of 80S and 70S ribosomes was centrifuged through a density gradient. Explain where each type would be found. (3)
questions.solution:
80S ribosomes are larger / denser [B1]
So they move further down the tube [B1]
70S ribosomes form a band higher up. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why stains are used when viewing cells with an optical microscope. (2)
hints: What does a stain bind to?
questions.solution:
Most cell structures are transparent / colourless [B1]
Stains bind to particular structures, giving contrast so they can be seen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Methylene blue stains the nucleus of a cheek cell dark blue. Suggest why the nucleus takes up more stain than the cytoplasm. (2)
hints: What molecule is concentrated in the nucleus?
questions.solution:
Nucleus contains DNA [B1]
Stain binds to DNA (e.g. to its negatively charged phosphate groups). [B1]

questions.prompt: When leaf cells are stained with iodine, parts of the chloroplasts turn blue-black. Explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Iodine stains starch blue-black [B1]
Chloroplasts contain starch grains (product of photosynthesis). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why specimens for a transmission electron microscope must be cut extremely thin. (2)
hints: The image is formed by electrons passing through the specimen.
What happens to electrons in a thick specimen?
questions.solution:
Electrons must pass through the specimen [B1]
Thick specimens absorb / scatter electrons, so the image would be dark / unclear. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a coverslip is placed on a wet-mount specimen before viewing it with an optical microscope. (2)
hints: What would the specimen do without one?
questions.solution:
Flattens the specimen to an even thickness / single layer [B1]
Prevents the specimen drying out / protects the objective lens. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why thin sections of tissue are needed to see individual cells clearly with an optical microscope. (2)
hints: Light must pass through the specimen.
questions.solution:
Light must be able to pass through the specimen [B1]
Thick sections have overlapping layers of cells, so structures can't be distinguished. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain how to obtain a sample of chloroplasts from leaf tissue. (6)
hints: Explain each condition of the solution.
questions.solution:
Cut up leaves and homogenise / blend in a solution [B1]
Solution is cold — reduces enzyme activity that could damage organelles [B1]
Isotonic — prevents osmosis so chloroplasts don't burst / shrink [B1]
Buffered — keeps pH constant so proteins aren't denatured [B1]
Filter to remove debris / whole cells [B1]
Centrifuge at low speed to remove nuclei; spin supernatant faster — chloroplasts form the next pellet. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain how to obtain a sample of ribosomes from animal tissue by differential centrifugation. (6)
questions.solution:
Homogenise tissue in cold, isotonic, buffered solution (with reasons) [B1]
Filter to remove debris [B1]
Centrifuge at low speed — nuclei form the pellet; supernatant kept [B1]
Centrifuge supernatant at higher speeds — mitochondria, then ER / lysosomes pellet [B1]
Highest speed — ribosomes form the final pellet [B1]
Smallest / least dense organelles need the greatest force. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how cell fractionation could be used to find out which organelle contains a particular enzyme. (6)
hints: How do you test each fraction?
questions.solution:
Homogenise tissue in cold, isotonic, buffered solution [B1]
Filter, then centrifuge at increasing speeds [B1]
Collect each pellet (fraction) separately [B1]
Add the same volume of substrate to each fraction [B1]
Measure product formed / rate of reaction in each [B1]
The fraction with the highest activity contains the enzyme (identify organelle by microscopy). [B1]

questions.prompt: Use the table. Choose the best microscope (1) to watch living Paramecium cells (about 100 µm long) swimming, and (2) to see the internal thylakoid membranes of a chloroplast. Give two reasons for each choice. (4)
hints: Can electron microscopes view living specimens?
questions.solution:
(1) Optical: specimens can be alive (no vacuum) [B1]
(1) Paramecium is much larger than the resolution limit of 0.25 µm [B1]
(2) TEM: highest resolution, needed for structures only nanometres thick [B1]
(2) Shows internal structure (thin sections). [B1]
questions.table:
Microscope | Resolution / µm
Optical | 0.25
SEM | 0.02
TEM | 0.0002

questions.prompt: Use the table. Choose the best microscope (1) to count red blood cells (8 µm diameter) in a blood smear, and (2) to see the 3D surface of a pollen grain. Give two reasons for each. (4)
hints: Is 8 µm above the optical microscope's resolution?
questions.solution:
(1) Optical: 8 µm is well above the 0.25 µm resolution [B1]
(1) Quick / cheap / simple preparation, colour stains [B1]
(2) SEM: produces 3D images of surfaces [B1]
(2) Higher resolution than optical, to see fine surface detail. [B1]
questions.table:
Microscope | Resolution / µm
Optical | 0.25
SEM | 0.02
TEM | 0.0002

questions.prompt: Use the table. Choose the best microscope (1) to see individual ribosomes (0.025 µm) and (2) to see the shape of living bacteria (2 µm). Give two reasons for each. (4)
hints: Is 0.025 µm smaller than the optical and SEM resolutions?
questions.solution:
(1) TEM: resolution 0.0002 µm is fine enough; optical (0.25) and SEM (0.02) are too close / too coarse [B1]
(1) Ribosomes are inside cells, so need thin sections / TEM [B1]
(2) Optical: specimens can be living (no vacuum) [B1]
(2) 2 µm is larger than its resolution of 0.25 µm. [B1]
questions.table:
Microscope | Resolution / µm
Optical | 0.25
SEM | 0.02
TEM | 0.0002

questions.prompt: Explain why chloroplasts are isolated in an ice-cold solution. (2)
hints: What does low temperature do to enzymes?
questions.solution:
Low temperature reduces enzyme activity [B1]
So enzymes (e.g. from lysosomes) do not damage / digest the chloroplasts. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the solution used to isolate chloroplasts is buffered. (2)
hints: What does a buffer keep constant?
What would a pH change do to proteins?
questions.solution:
Keeps pH constant [B1]
So enzymes / proteins in the chloroplasts are not denatured. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the homogenate is filtered before chloroplasts are separated by centrifugation. (2)
hints: What is still in the homogenate?
What do you want to remove?
questions.solution:
Removes unbroken cells / large debris [B1]
So they don't contaminate the chloroplast pellet. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an electron micrograph a bacterium is 45 mm long at a magnification of ×15 000. A bacteriophage is 30 mm long at ×150 000. Calculate how many times longer the bacterium is than the phage. (2)
A bacterium is 36 mm long in an image at ×12 000. A virus is 25 mm long at ×250 000. Calculate how many times longer the bacterium is than the virus. (2)
A bacterium is 20 mm long in an image at ×10 000. A virus is 40 mm long at ×200 000. Calculate how many times longer the bacterium is than the virus. (2)
A stain made cell nuclei appear dark blue. Explain how this allowed white cells to be counted among red cells. (1)
hints: Do red blood cells have nuclei?
questions.solution: Mature red cells have no nucleus, so only white cells (with nuclei) are stained dark blue. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why specimens are stained before viewing with a light microscope. (1)
questions.solution: To increase contrast / make transparent structures visible. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a light microscope can't be used to see ribosomes. (1)
questions.solution: Ribosomes are smaller than the resolution limit of light (about 0.2 µm). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a detergent that dissolves lipids could release a protein from inside cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Detergent dissolves the phospholipids of the cell-surface membrane (and nuclear envelope) [B1]
So the cell breaks open and its contents, including the protein, are released. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why tissue is placed in a cold, isotonic buffer before cell fractionation. (2)
questions.solution:
Cold reduces enzyme activity that could break down organelles; isotonic prevents osmosis bursting / shrinking organelles [B1]
Buffer keeps pH constant so proteins don't denature. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how cells are broken open and large debris removed in cell fractionation. (2)
questions.solution:
Homogenise / blend the tissue [B1]
Filter to remove large debris / whole cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how ultracentrifugation separates a protein from heavier cell components. (2)
questions.solution:
Spin at increasing speeds; heaviest / densest components form a pellet first [B1]
Remove supernatant and spin faster — protein remains in the supernatant until high speed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the order in which nuclei, mitochondria and ribosomes are separated by differential centrifugation, and explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Nuclei, then mitochondria, then ribosomes [B1]
Heaviest / largest organelles sediment at the lowest speeds. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how you could confirm that a pellet from ultracentrifugation contains mainly mitochondria. (2)
questions.solution:
View under an electron microscope for cristae / double membrane [B1]
Or test for an enzyme found only in mitochondria (e.g. Krebs cycle enzyme). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to make a temporary mount of a piece of plant tissue to observe starch grains with a light microscope. (4)
questions.solution:
Cut a thin section / single layer of tissue with a scalpel [B1]
Place on a slide in a drop of water [B1]
Add iodine in potassium iodide solution to stain starch blue-black [B1]
Lower coverslip at an angle with a mounted needle to avoid air bubbles. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to use a light microscope to view a prepared slide at high power. (4)
questions.solution:
Clip the slide onto the stage and start with the lowest-power objective [B1]
Use the coarse focus to bring the specimen into focus [B1]
Switch to a higher-power objective [B1]
Use only the fine focus at high power, adjusting light / diaphragm. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to use an eyepiece graticule and stage micrometer to measure a cell. (4)
questions.solution:
Line up the eyepiece graticule with the stage micrometer [B1]
Find how many micrometers one graticule division equals for that objective [B1]
Measure the cell in graticule divisions [B1]
Multiply by the calibration value. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an image showing internal membranes of a chloroplast must have been produced by a transmission electron microscope. (2)
questions.solution:
Thylakoid membranes are too small to resolve with a light microscope — TEM has higher resolution [B1]
TEM shows internal structures (thin section), SEM only surfaces. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two differences between transmission and scanning electron microscopes. (2)
questions.solution:
TEM passes electrons through a thin specimen; SEM scans the surface [B1]
TEM gives 2D images with higher resolution; SEM gives 3D images. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two limitations of electron microscopes compared with light microscopes. (2)
questions.solution:
Specimens must be in a vacuum, so must be dead [B1]
Black and white only / complex preparation causing artefacts / expensive. [B1]

questions.prompt: A scale bar representing 1 µm measures 25 mm on an image. Calculate the magnification. (1)
A scale bar representing 2 µm measures 40 mm on an image. Calculate the magnification. (1)
A scale bar representing 0.5 µm measures 15 mm on an image. Calculate the magnification. (1)
Viruses are not cells and cannot divide. Describe how a virus is replicated. (2)
hints: What does the virus put into the host cell?
questions.solution:
Attachment proteins bind to (complementary) receptors on the host cell [B1]
Viral nucleic acid (DNA / RNA) enters the host cell [B1]
Host cell (ribosomes / enzymes) makes viral nucleic acid and proteins, which are assembled into new viruses. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any 2 points.

questions.prompt: Give two ways in which binary fission in bacteria differs from mitosis in eukaryotic cells. (2)
hints: Think about the form of the DNA in a bacterium.
Does a bacterium have a nucleus or spindle?
questions.solution:
Binary fission involves circular DNA / no chromosomes or histones [B1]
No spindle (fibres) formed [B1]
No nucleus / nuclear envelope to break down [B1]
Plasmids are also replicated. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any 2 differences.

questions.prompt: Describe what happens to a bacterium's DNA and cytoplasm during binary fission. (2)
hints: There are two types of DNA in many bacteria.
How does the cell finally split?
questions.solution:
Circular DNA replicates (and plasmids replicate) [B1]
DNA loops move to opposite poles of the cell [B1]
Cytoplasm divides, producing two daughter cells (each with one copy of circular DNA and a variable number of plasmids). [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any 2 points.

questions.prompt:
A photograph of a root-tip cell shows chromosomes lined up across the middle of the cell. Each chromosome is made of two chromatids, and homologous chromosomes are not paired with each other.

Give two pieces of evidence that this cell is in metaphase of mitosis, and explain each. (2)
hints: How would meiosis I look different?
questions.solution:
Chromosomes on the equator / middle of the cell, which happens in metaphase [B1]
Chromosomes made of two chromatids, so chromatids have not yet separated (not anaphase) [B1]
Homologous chromosomes not in pairs, so not meiosis I. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt:
An animal has a diploid number of 24. A dividing cell from this animal contains 24 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids, and has no nuclear envelope.

Explain two pieces of evidence that this cell is dividing by mitosis rather than by meiosis II. (2)
hints: How many chromosomes would a cell in meiosis II contain?
questions.solution:
24 chromosomes = diploid number, whereas a cell in meiosis II would be haploid / have 12 [B1]
Homologous chromosomes are not paired (no bivalents), so not meiosis I. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why chromosomes can only be seen with an optical microscope while a cell is dividing. (2)
hints: What happens to the DNA at the start of division?
questions.solution:
During division the chromosomes condense / coil tightly (supercoil) [B1]
So they are thick enough to see / take up stain; in interphase DNA is uncoiled (chromatin). [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a dividing cell, sister chromatids are being pulled towards opposite poles of the cell. Which stage of mitosis is this?

Choose one answer.

A  Anaphase
B  Metaphase
C  Prophase
D  Telophase (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a dividing cell, nuclear envelopes are forming around two separate groups of chromosomes at opposite ends of the cell. Which stage is this?

Choose one answer.

A  Anaphase
B  Interphase
C  Prophase
D  Telophase (1)
hints: This is the last stage of mitosis.
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt:
In which stage of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?

Choose one answer.

A  Anaphase
B  Interphase
C  Metaphase
D  Prophase (1)
hints: It is not a stage of mitosis itself.
It is the longest part of the cell cycle.
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt: When preparing a root-tip squash, a student first put the root tips in warm hydrochloric acid. Suggest two reasons why this makes it easier to see chromosomes. (2)
hints: Why does a single layer of cells help?
questions.solution:
Acid hydrolyses / breaks down the middle lamella / bonds between cell walls, so cells separate [B1]
Cells can be spread into a single layer, so light passes through / chromosomes are not hidden by overlapping cells [B1]
Stops cell division / kills cells so cells are fixed at their stage; lets stain enter. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Drug X inhibits DNA polymerase. The table shows the percentage of cells replicating their DNA. Suggest explanations for these results. (3)
hints: What does the third result show about the inhibitor?
questions.solution:
DNA polymerase needed to join nucleotides, so drug X prevents replication [B1]
Inhibition is reversible / drug X is removed from the enzyme when washed out [B1]
So replication returns to near normal (or new enzyme made). [B1]
questions.table:
Treatment | % cells replicating DNA
Control | 45
Drug X | 3
Drug X, then washed out | 41

questions.prompt: Part of a rat's liver was removed. The table shows the percentage of liver cells in mitosis afterwards. Describe and explain the results. (2)
questions.solution:
Mitosis increases sharply after the operation (peak at day 1) to replace lost tissue / regenerate the liver [B1]
Then falls back to normal once the liver has regrown. [B1]
questions.table:
Day after operation | % cells in mitosis
0 | 0.5
1 | 6.2
3 | 3.0
7 | 0.4

questions.prompt: The table shows the percentage of cells in mitosis at different distances from the tip of a growing root. Describe and explain the results. (2)
hints: What do cells do further from the tip?
questions.solution:
Mitosis is highest near the tip and decreases with distance [B1]
Cells near the tip (meristem) divide; further away cells elongate / differentiate and no longer divide. [B1]
questions.table:
Distance from tip / mm | % cells in mitosis
0.5 | 18
2 | 6
5 | 0

questions.prompt: Describe what happens to the chromosomes and spindle fibres during prophase, metaphase and anaphase of mitosis. (5)
hints: Prophase: what happens to chromosomes and the nuclear envelope?
questions.solution:
Prophase: chromosomes condense / become visible [B1]
Prophase: spindle fibres form and nuclear envelope breaks down [B1]
Metaphase: chromosomes line up on the equator [B1]
Metaphase: spindle fibres attach to centromeres [B1]
Anaphase: centromeres divide; spindle fibres shorten, pulling sister chromatids to opposite poles. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why mitosis produces two genetically identical cells. (5)
hints: What happens to DNA before mitosis?
Where does each sister chromatid go?
questions.solution:
DNA is replicated (semi-conservatively) in interphase [B1]
So each chromosome has two identical sister chromatids [B1]
In metaphase each chromosome lines up individually on the equator [B1]
In anaphase sister chromatids separate, one going to each pole [B1]
So each new nucleus gets an identical set of chromosomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the stages of the cell cycle and what happens in each. (5)
questions.solution:
G1: cell grows, organelles replicated / proteins made [B1]
S phase: DNA replicates [B1]
G2: further growth / checks before division [B1]
Mitosis: nucleus divides (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) [B1]
Cytokinesis: cytoplasm divides into two cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) replicates. (3)
hints: How does the phage attach and what does it inject?
How are the new phages released?
questions.solution:
Attachment proteins bind to receptors on the bacterium [B1]
Phage injects its DNA into the bacterium [B1]
Bacterium's enzymes / ribosomes replicate the viral DNA and make viral proteins [B1]
New phages are assembled and released when the bacterium bursts (lysis). [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why it is difficult to develop drugs to treat viral infections. (3)
questions.solution:
Viruses replicate inside host cells using the host's enzymes / ribosomes [B1]
So drugs that stop replication may also harm host cells [B1]
Viruses have no metabolism / cell wall for antibiotics to target, and mutate rapidly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a virus particle. (3)
questions.solution:
Genetic material: DNA or RNA [B1]
Surrounded by a protein coat (capsid) [B1]
Attachment proteins on the surface [B1]
Some have a lipid envelope / enzymes such as reverse transcriptase. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: State whether each of the following happens in binary fission, mitosis or both: (i) replication of circular DNA, (ii) formation of a spindle, (iii) replication of plasmids, (iv) production of two daughter cells. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) binary fission; (ii) mitosis; (iii) binary fission; (iv) both. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2–3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: State the stage of the cell cycle in which each happens: (i) chromosomes condense, (ii) DNA replicates, (iii) chromatids are pulled to opposite poles, (iv) nuclear envelopes reform. (2)
hints: One is not a stage of mitosis.
questions.solution:
(i) prophase; (ii) interphase / S phase; (iii) anaphase; (iv) telophase. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2–3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: A drug stops cytokinesis but not mitosis. Describe how treated cells would look under a microscope and explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Cells would contain two (or more) nuclei / be larger [B1]
Nucleus divides but the cytoplasm does not. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug prevents spindle fibres forming. Describe what would be seen in root-tip cells treated with the drug. (2)
questions.solution:
Chromosomes condensed but not separated / many cells stuck at the start of mitosis [B1]
No cells in anaphase / telophase, because chromatids cannot be pulled to the poles. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug prevents DNA replication. Predict and explain its effect on the mitotic index of a tissue. (2)
hints: Can cells divide without replicating DNA?
questions.solution:
Mitotic index falls [B1]
Cells cannot complete interphase / enter mitosis without replicating DNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the appearance and behaviour of chromosomes during metaphase and telophase of mitosis. (4)
hints: Where are they in metaphase, and what holds them?
What happens at the poles in telophase?
questions.solution:
Metaphase: chromosomes (each two chromatids) line up on the equator [B1]
Attached to spindle fibres by their centromeres [B1]
Telophase: chromatids (now chromosomes) have reached the poles [B1]
They uncoil / become less visible and nuclear envelopes reform. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the percentage of onion root cells at each stage of the cell cycle at different distances from the root tip. Give three conclusions. (3)
hints: How does interphase change with distance?
Which stage of mitosis has most cells?
questions.solution:
Proportion in interphase increases further from the tip [B1]
Proportion in each stage of mitosis decreases further from the tip — dividing cells concentrated near the tip [B1]
Prophase has the most cells of any mitotic stage, so it is the longest stage of mitosis. [B1]
questions.table:
Distance / mm | Interphase % | Prophase % | Metaphase % | Anaphase % | Telophase %
1 | 70 | 15 | 6 | 4 | 5
3 | 85 | 8 | 3 | 2 | 2
5 | 98 | 1 | 0.5 | 0.3 | 0.2

questions.prompt: The mitotic index of three tissues was: root tip 0.12, leaf 0.01, root 5 mm from tip 0.02. Give three conclusions. (3)
questions.solution:
Root tip has the highest mitotic index — most cell division / growth [B1]
Leaf has the lowest — few cells dividing / mostly differentiated [B1]
Cell division falls with distance from the root tip. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the number of bacteria and the mean number of copies of a plasmid per cell during the growth of a culture. Give conclusions about binary fission and plasmid replication in each phase. (3)
hints: When does cell number rise fastest?
When does plasmid copy number change?
questions.solution:
Little binary fission in the lag phase, but plasmid copy number rises — plasmids replicate before cells start dividing [B1]
Log phase: rapid binary fission; copy number stays constant, so plasmid replication keeps pace with division [B1]
Stationary phase: no increase in cells and copy number falls — plasmids no longer replicated / lost or broken down. [B1]
questions.table:

Lag (0 h) | 1.0 × 10³ | 5
Lag (4 h) | 1.2 × 10³ | 12
Log (10 h) | 6.0 × 10⁵ | 12
Stationary (16 h) | 6.0 × 10⁵ | 4

questions.prompt: Bacteria growing rapidly may contain more copies of a plasmid than slowly growing bacteria. Suggest why, and explain why it matters that plasmids are replicated before binary fission. (3)
hints: How are plasmids passed to daughter cells?
What if there were too few copies?
questions.solution:
Plasmids are replicated independently of the chromosome [B1]
Rapidly dividing cells may replicate plasmids more often [B1]
Replication before division means each daughter cell is likely to receive copies (e.g. keeping antibiotic resistance genes). [B1]

questions.prompt: Put these stages of mitosis in order: anaphase, prophase, telophase, metaphase. (1)
hints: Then line up, separate, and reach the poles.
questions.solution: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. [B1]

questions.prompt: Put these descriptions of mitosis in order: W chromatids at the poles; X chromosomes condense; Y chromosomes on the equator; Z chromatids separating. (1)
questions.solution: X, Y, Z, W. [B1]

questions.prompt: What happens to the DNA content per cell when a cell divides by mitosis? (1)
hints: What does each daughter cell get?
questions.solution: It halves (back to the amount before replication). [B1]

questions.prompt: Some cancer drugs prevent spindle fibres forming. Explain how this slows the growth of a tumour. (3)
questions.solution:
Spindle fibres attach to centromeres and separate chromatids [B1]
Without them, chromatids can't separate at anaphase [B1]
Mitosis stops, so tumour cells can't divide. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why drugs that slow DNA replication also cause side-effects such as hair loss. (3)
questions.solution:
Drug affects all rapidly dividing cells, not just cancer cells [B1]
Hair follicle cells divide quickly [B1]
Their division is slowed, so hair falls out. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a root tip squash, root tips were soaked in hydrochloric acid for 12 minutes. Suggest why. (2)
questions.solution:
Breaks down the middle lamella / bonds between cells [B1]
So cells can be separated / spread into a single layer (and stops division). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a stain such as toluidine blue is used in a root tip squash. (2)
questions.solution:
Stains DNA / chromosomes [B1]
So chromosomes are visible and stages can be identified. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why root tips are used to observe mitosis. (2)
questions.solution:
Root tips contain meristem tissue [B1]
Where cells divide rapidly, so many cells are in mitosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why pressing down firmly on the coverslip helps to show the stages of mitosis. (2)
questions.solution:
Spreads cells into a single layer [B1]
So light passes through and individual cells / chromosomes can be seen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two safety precautions when preparing a root tip squash. (2)
questions.solution:
Wear goggles / gloves with hydrochloric acid [B1]
Cut away from fingers with a scalpel / care with glass slides. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why you should not twist or slide the coverslip when pressing down. (2)
questions.solution:
Twisting could break / smear cells [B1]
Chromosomes may be moved, making stages hard to identify. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a cell, chromosomes are lined up across the middle of the cell. Name the stage and explain its appearance. (2)
questions.solution:
Metaphase [B1]
Chromosomes attached by centromeres to spindle fibres at the equator. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a cell, two groups of chromatids are moving to opposite poles. Name the stage and explain its appearance. (2)
questions.solution:
Anaphase [B1]
Centromeres divide and spindle fibres shorten, pulling sister chromatids to opposite poles. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a cell, chromosomes are visible as condensed threads and the nuclear envelope is breaking down. Name the stage and explain. (2)
questions.solution:
Prophase [B1]
Chromosomes condense / supercoil and become visible; nuclear envelope disappears. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a field of view, 8 of 40 cells were in mitosis. Calculate the mitotic index. (1)
In a field of view, 15 of 50 cells were in mitosis. Calculate the mitotic index. (1)
In a field of view, 6 of 48 cells were in mitosis. Calculate the mitotic index. (1)
Other students using the same method got different mitotic indices. Suggest two explanations other than student error. (2)
questions.solution:
Different regions of root tip used (further from tip, fewer dividing cells) [B1]
Roots of different ages / plants / different times of day / only one field of view counted. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why counting several fields of view gives a more reliable mitotic index. (2)
questions.solution:
Cells dividing aren't evenly spread [B1]
Larger sample is more representative / reduces effect of anomalous fields. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a tumour tissue would have a higher mitotic index than normal tissue. (2)
questions.solution:
Cell division in tumours is uncontrolled [B1]
More cells are dividing at any one time. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe binary fission in bacteria. (3)
questions.solution:
Circular DNA replicates (and plasmids replicate) [B1]
DNA copies move to opposite poles of the cell [B1]
Cytoplasm divides (cell membrane / wall pinches in), giving two daughter cells, each with one copy of circular DNA and variable numbers of plasmids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how viruses replicate. (3)
questions.solution:
Attachment proteins bind to complementary receptors on host cell [B1]
Nucleic acid is injected / enters the cell [B1]
Host cell enzymes and ribosomes make new viral nucleic acid and proteins, which are assembled and released. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three differences between binary fission and mitosis. (3)
questions.solution:
Binary fission in prokaryotes; mitosis in eukaryotes [B1]
No spindle fibres in binary fission [B1]
Circular DNA and plasmids copied in binary fission; linear chromosomes in mitosis / no nuclear envelope breakdown. [B1]

questions.prompt: Root hair cells absorb water and mineral ions from the soil. Suggest two features of root hair cells that increase the rate of uptake, and explain how each feature does so. (2)
hints: Mineral ions are often taken up against a concentration gradient.
questions.solution:
Long thin extension, so large surface area [B1]
Many carrier proteins (in membrane), so more active transport of ions [B1]
Many mitochondria, so more ATP for active transport [B1]
Many aquaporins / channel proteins, so faster osmosis. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any two features, each with a linked explanation (1 mark each).

questions.prompt: Cells lining kidney tubules reabsorb large volumes of water. Suggest two features of the cell-surface membranes of these cells that would increase the rate of water reabsorption, and explain each. (2)
hints: Water crosses membranes through special proteins.
questions.solution:
Many aquaporins / water channel proteins, so more water moves by osmosis [B1]
Folded membrane / microvilli, so large surface area [B1]
Thin / short diffusion distance (phospholipid bilayer). [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any two features, each with a linked explanation (1 mark each).

questions.prompt: Describe how sodium ions are involved in the absorption of glucose by epithelial cells of the ileum. (3)
hints: Start with what happens on the blood side of the cell.
Sodium ions are pumped out of the cell into the blood…
questions.solution:
Na⁺ actively transported out of the epithelial cell into the blood (by Na⁺/K⁺ pump, using ATP) [B1]
This keeps a low Na⁺ concentration inside the cell / maintains a Na⁺ gradient [B1]
Na⁺ diffuses into the cell from the lumen through a co-transporter protein [B1]
Carrying glucose with it, against the glucose concentration gradient [B1]
Glucose then moves into the blood by facilitated diffusion. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Na⁺ is actively pumped out of the cell into the blood, keeping the Na⁺ concentration in the cell low. Na⁺ then diffuses in from the lumen down its gradient through a co-transporter, carrying glucose with it against glucose's gradient. Glucose leaves into the blood by facilitated diffusion. (Any 3 points.)

questions.prompt: A carrier protein in the cell-surface membrane of stomach lining cells moves hydrogen ions out of the cell in exchange for potassium ions moving in. It uses ATP. Use your knowledge of active transport to suggest how this carrier protein moves the ions. (3)
hints: What happens to ATP, and what effect does that have on the protein?
Ions bind on one side and are released on the other.
questions.solution:
ATP is hydrolysed (to ADP + Pi), releasing energy / phosphorylating the carrier [B1]
This changes the shape (tertiary structure) of the carrier protein [B1]
H⁺ binds inside and is released outside; K⁺ binds outside and is released inside [B1]
Ions move against their concentration gradients. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: A respiratory inhibitor is added to cells lining the ileum. The rate of amino acid absorption decreases. Explain why. (3)
hints: What does a respiratory inhibitor reduce?
Amino acids are absorbed by co-transport with sodium ions.
questions.solution:
Less ATP produced [B1]
Less active transport of Na⁺ out of the cell (Na⁺/K⁺ pump) [B1]
So the Na⁺ concentration gradient (lumen → cell) is not maintained [B1]
So less co-transport of amino acids with Na⁺. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt:
A drug blocks the glucose co-transporter in the ileum. Scientists gave the drug to one group of mice and a placebo to a control group. The table shows their results. The difference between the groups is significant (P < 0.05).

The scientists concluded that the drug reduces glucose absorption. Use the data and your knowledge of water potential to explain why the results support this conclusion. (4)
hints: If glucose stays in the gut, what happens to the water potential of the gut contents?
questions.solution:
More glucose remains in the lumen (of the gut) [B1]
Lowers the water potential of the gut contents [B1]
So less water leaves the gut by osmosis / water moves into the gut by osmosis [B1]
Faeces water content higher in drug group and the difference is significant (P < 0.05) / unlikely to be due to chance. [B1]
questions.table:
Group | Water in faeces / %
Control (placebo) | 58
Drug | 72

questions.prompt: People who are lactose intolerant produce very little lactase. Explain why drinking milk can cause them to have diarrhoea (watery faeces). (4)
hints: Lactose is a disaccharide — can it be absorbed?
Think about the water potential of the gut contents.
questions.solution:
Lactose is not hydrolysed (to glucose and galactose) [B1]
Lactose cannot be absorbed (only monosaccharides are absorbed) [B1]
Lactose lowers the water potential of the gut contents / lumen [B1]
Water moves into the lumen by osmosis, so faeces contain more water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Cholera toxin causes chloride ion channels in ileum epithelial cells to stay open, so chloride ions move out of the cells into the lumen. Explain how this leads to severe, watery diarrhoea. (4)
hints: What happens to the water potential of the lumen?
Where does the water come from?
questions.solution:
Chloride ions move into the lumen [B1]
Water potential of the lumen decreases / becomes lower than in the cells [B1]
Water moves out of the epithelial cells into the lumen by osmosis [B1]
Water then moves from blood / tissue fluid into the cells, so large volumes are lost in faeces. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why red blood cells burst when placed in pure water, but plant cells do not. (2)
hints: Which way does water move by osmosis?
Which cell has a structure that resists expansion?
questions.solution:
Water enters both cells by osmosis (from higher to lower water potential) [B1]
Red blood cells have no cell wall, so they swell and burst; plant cell wall resists expansion / cell becomes turgid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Animal cells were placed in a solution with a water potential slightly higher than that of their cytoplasm. Explain why the cells swelled. (2)
hints: Compare water potentials inside and outside.
questions.solution:
Water moves into the cells by osmosis [B1]
From higher water potential (solution) to lower water potential (cytoplasm) across the partially permeable membrane. [B1]

questions.prompt: The sodium–potassium pump in cell-surface membranes uses ATP. Explain the role of ATP hydrolysis in the pump's function. (2)
hints: What is released when ATP is hydrolysed?
What happens to the carrier protein's shape?
questions.solution:
Hydrolysis releases energy / a phosphate group that attaches to the carrier [B1]
Changes the shape of the carrier protein, moving Na⁺ out and K⁺ in against their concentration gradients. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why active transport stops when cells are treated with cyanide, which inhibits respiration. (2)
hints: What does a carrier need to change shape?
questions.solution:
No / less ATP produced [B1]
So no energy for carrier proteins to change shape / move substances against a gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cells that carry out a lot of active transport contain many mitochondria. (2)
questions.solution:
Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration [B1]
Produce (lots of) ATP needed for active transport. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the sodium–potassium pump on the blood side of ileum epithelial cells is essential for the absorption of glucose. (2)
hints: What does the pump do to the Na⁺ concentration inside the cell?
How does glucose enter from the lumen?
questions.solution:
Keeps the Na⁺ concentration in the cell low / maintains a Na⁺ gradient from lumen to cell [B1]
Na⁺ diffuses in through the co-transporter, carrying glucose with it. [B1]

questions.prompt: Ouabain inhibits the sodium–potassium pump. Predict and explain the effect of ouabain on amino acid absorption by the ileum. (2)
hints: Which ion gradient drives amino acid co-transport?
What happens to that gradient if the pump stops?
questions.solution:
Amino acid absorption decreases [B1]
Na⁺ gradient not maintained, so less co-transport of amino acids with Na⁺. [B1]

questions.prompt: The co-transporter protein that moves glucose into ileum cells does not hydrolyse ATP. Explain how glucose can still be moved against its concentration gradient. (2)
hints: Where does the energy come from?
What sets up the sodium gradient?
questions.solution:
Energy comes from Na⁺ moving down its concentration gradient (indirect active transport) [B1]
The Na⁺ gradient is maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, which uses ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the fluid mosaic model of membrane structure. (2)
questions.solution:
Phospholipid bilayer in which molecules can move (fluid) [B1]
Proteins scattered through it (mosaic), with cholesterol / glycoproteins / glycolipids. [B1]

questions.prompt: The part of a channel protein that sits within the membrane has many amino acids with hydrophobic R groups on its outer surface. Explain why. (2)
hints: What is the middle of the bilayer made of?
questions.solution:
Hydrophobic R groups interact with the hydrophobic fatty acid tails, holding the protein in the bilayer [B1]
Hydrophilic R groups line the channel / face the water, letting ions pass. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of cholesterol in cell-surface membranes. (2)
hints: How does that affect movement of phospholipids?
questions.solution:
Binds to fatty acid tails, restricting their movement [B1]
Makes the membrane less fluid / more stable / less permeable to water and ions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Beetroot pieces were placed in different concentrations of ethanol. The absorbance of the surrounding liquid increased with ethanol concentration. The red pigment cannot cross an undamaged membrane. Explain these results. (4)
hints: What does ethanol do to lipids?
Which membranes must the pigment cross to get out?
questions.solution:
Ethanol dissolves / disrupts phospholipids in membranes [B1]
Membranes (tonoplast and cell-surface membrane) become more permeable [B1]
Pigment leaks out of the vacuole / cell into the liquid [B1]
Higher concentration causes more damage, so more pigment and higher absorbance. [B1]

questions.prompt: Beetroot pieces were placed in water at different temperatures. Absorbance of the water rose slowly between 20 °C and 45 °C, then sharply above 50 °C. Explain these results. (4)
hints: What does heat do to phospholipids?
What happens to membrane proteins at high temperature?
questions.solution:
Higher temperature gives phospholipids more kinetic energy, so they move more / membrane more permeable [B1]
So a little more pigment leaks out as temperature rises [B1]
Above 50 °C membrane proteins denature [B1]
Leaving gaps in the membrane, so much more pigment leaks out. [B1]

questions.prompt: Beetroot pieces were placed in increasing concentrations of detergent. More pigment leaked out at higher detergent concentrations. Explain this using your knowledge of membrane structure. (4)
questions.solution:
Detergent dissolves / emulsifies the phospholipids [B1]
Disrupts the bilayer / membranes become more permeable [B1]
Pigment escapes from the vacuole and cell [B1]
More detergent disrupts more membrane, so more pigment. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how phosphorylation of a carrier protein can move a substance across a membrane. (2)
hints: Where does the phosphate come from?
What does it do to the protein?
questions.solution:
ATP hydrolysed, phosphate attached to the carrier [B1]
Carrier changes shape, moving the substance to the other side of the membrane (against its gradient). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how cells secrete large molecules such as proteins, and how phagocytes take in bacteria. (5)
hints: Taking in: what does the membrane do?
questions.solution:
Proteins packaged into vesicles by the Golgi apparatus [B1]
Vesicles move to and fuse with the cell-surface membrane, releasing contents (exocytosis) [B1]
Phagocytosis: membrane surrounds / engulfs the bacterium [B1]
Forming a vesicle / phagosome [B1]
Both processes need ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare and contrast facilitated diffusion and active transport. (5)
hints: Similarities: which proteins can both use?
questions.solution:
Both use carrier proteins (facilitated diffusion can also use channel proteins) [B1]
Both are specific to particular molecules / ions [B1]
Facilitated diffusion moves substances down a concentration gradient; active transport against it [B1]
Active transport uses ATP; facilitated diffusion is passive [B1]
Active transport can be stopped by respiratory inhibitors. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how surface area, concentration gradient, diffusion distance, temperature and membrane proteins affect the rate of movement of substances across membranes. (5)
hints: For proteins, think about channels and carriers.
questions.solution:
Larger surface area increases rate (more membrane / more proteins) [B1]
Steeper concentration gradient increases rate [B1]
Shorter diffusion distance (thinner) increases rate [B1]
Higher temperature increases kinetic energy / rate (until proteins denature) [B1]
More channel / carrier proteins increase the rate of facilitated diffusion / active transport. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why ions cannot diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer. (2)
hints: What is the middle of the bilayer like?
questions.solution:
Ions are charged / water-soluble [B1]
So cannot pass through the hydrophobic fatty acid tails / need channel proteins. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why glucose needs carrier or channel proteins to cross a cell-surface membrane. (2)
questions.solution:
Glucose is polar / water-soluble and relatively large [B1]
So cannot pass through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why oxygen and carbon dioxide can diffuse quickly through cell-surface membranes. (2)
questions.solution:
Small molecules [B1]
Non-polar / lipid-soluble, so pass through the phospholipid bilayer. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some antifungal drugs bind to ergosterol, a molecule found in fungal membranes. Human membranes contain cholesterol instead. Suggest why these drugs are less harmful to human cells. (2)
hints: Which sterol does the drug bind to?
Which sterol do human cells have?
questions.solution:
Drug binds to ergosterol, which human membranes lack [B1]
Binds less / not at all to cholesterol, so human membranes are not disrupted. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe an experiment to find out whether the cells of a seaweed have a lower water potential than sea water. (4)
hints: What would happen to the mass of seaweed pieces if their water potential were lower?
What must be kept the same?
questions.solution:
Cut pieces of the same size; blot and weigh [B1]
Place in sea water for a set time at constant temperature [B1]
Blot and reweigh; calculate percentage change in mass (repeat) [B1]
Increase in mass shows water entered by osmosis, so cells have a lower water potential than sea water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how onion epidermis and a range of salt solutions can be used to estimate the water potential of onion cells, using a microscope. (4)
hints: What happens to cells in a strong salt solution?
What proportion of cells is used as the end point?
questions.solution:
Place strips of epidermis in a range of salt concentrations for the same time [B1]
View each under a microscope [B1]
Count the percentage of cells that are plasmolysed [B1]
The concentration giving 50% plasmolysis has about the same water potential as the cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how Visking tubing can be used to find out which of two sugar solutions has the lower water potential. (4)
hints: How can you detect water movement?
questions.solution:
Fill tubing with solution A, tie it, and place it in solution B [B1]
Measure the change in mass of the tubing (or level in a capillary tube) after a set time [B1]
Water moves by osmosis towards the lower water potential [B1]
If the tubing gains mass, A has the lower water potential (repeat with solutions swapped). [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug binds to a carrier protein at a site away from where the transported molecule binds, and stops transport. Suggest how. (3)
hints: What happens to the protein's shape?
Can it still bind or change shape?
questions.solution:
Drug binds at a different site (like a non-competitive inhibitor) [B1]
Changes the tertiary structure of the carrier [B1]
Binding site no longer complementary / carrier cannot change shape to move the molecule. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some organisms living in cold conditions increase the proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in their membrane phospholipids. Explain the advantage of this. (3)
hints: What happens to membranes at low temperature?
questions.solution:
Unsaturated fatty acids have kinks, so phospholipids cannot pack tightly [B1]
Keeps the membrane fluid at low temperature [B1]
So membrane proteins / transport / endocytosis can still work. [B1]

questions.prompt: Removing cholesterol from cell membranes makes them more fluid. Suggest and explain the effect on the permeability of the membrane. (3)
hints: What gets through a more fluid membrane?
questions.solution:
Cholesterol normally restricts movement of phospholipids [B1]
Without it the membrane is more fluid / less stable [B1]
So more permeable to water and ions / small polar molecules. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe simple diffusion and osmosis across cell-surface membranes. (3)
hints: Osmosis is a special case for which molecule?
questions.solution:
Diffusion: net movement of molecules from high to low concentration [B1]
Passive — no ATP needed; small / non-polar molecules pass through the bilayer [B1]
Osmosis: net movement of water from higher to lower water potential across a partially permeable membrane (through aquaporins / bilayer). [B1]

questions.prompt: The rate of facilitated diffusion increases with concentration gradient, then levels off. Explain why. (3)
hints: What do molecules need to cross by facilitated diffusion?
questions.solution:
At first, a steeper gradient means more molecules reach carrier / channel proteins [B1]
Number of carrier / channel proteins is limited [B1]
When all are in use (saturated), rate cannot increase further. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the differences between channel proteins and carrier proteins. (3)
questions.solution:
Channel proteins form water-filled pores that ions / polar molecules pass through [B1]
Carrier proteins bind the molecule and change shape to move it across [B1]
Only carrier proteins are used in active transport. [B1]

questions.prompt: Vitamin C is water-soluble and vitamin E is lipid-soluble. Suggest how each crosses the membrane of an ileum epithelial cell. (3)
hints: Can a polar molecule cross the bilayer?
How does a lipid-soluble molecule reach the membrane?
questions.solution:
Vitamin C is polar, so it needs carrier proteins (facilitated diffusion / co-transport) [B1]
Vitamin E is delivered by micelles [B1]
And diffuses through the phospholipid bilayer. [B1]

questions.prompt: A Visking tubing bag containing concentrated sucrose solution was attached to a capillary tube and placed in water. The liquid rose up the capillary tube. Explain why. (3)
hints: Compare water potentials inside and outside.
questions.solution:
Sucrose solution has a lower water potential than the water outside [B1]
Water moves into the bag by osmosis across the partially permeable membrane [B1]
Volume inside increases, so liquid is pushed up the tube. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a plant cell becomes turgid when placed in water. (3)
hints: Where does water go in the cell?
questions.solution:
Water enters by osmosis (cell has lower water potential) [B1]
Vacuole swells and the protoplast pushes against the cell wall [B1]
Cell wall resists expansion, creating pressure — the cell is turgid. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an osmometer, liquid rises up a capillary tube for some hours, then stops. Explain why it stops. (3)
hints: What builds up as the column rises?
What happens to the water potentials?
questions.solution:
Hydrostatic pressure of the column increases [B1]
It balances the water potential difference / water potentials become equal [B1]
So there is no net movement of water. [B1]

questions.prompt: A 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution in an osmometer produced a pressure of 600 kPa. A modified solution produced 150 kPa. Suggest what was changed, using a calculation. (2)
hints: How many times smaller is the pressure?
What does that suggest about concentration?
questions.solution:
600 ÷ 150 = 4, so solution was diluted 4 times (≈ 0.25 mol dm⁻³) [B1]
Higher water potential, so less water entered by osmosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: A solution produced a pressure of 500 kPa in an osmometer. After changing the solution the pressure was 200 kPa. Suggest the change, using a calculation. (2)
hints: Pressure is proportional to solute concentration.
questions.solution:
Concentration reduced to 0.4 times / diluted 2.5 times [B1]
Higher water potential, so less osmosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Pressure in an osmometer doubled from 300 kPa to 600 kPa when the solution was changed. Suggest the change and explain. (2)
hints: What would double the osmotic effect?
questions.solution:
Solute concentration was doubled [B1]
Lower water potential, so more water moved in by osmosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why phospholipids form a bilayer, rather than a single layer, in the cell-surface membrane. (2)
hints: Is there water on one side of the membrane or both?
questions.solution:
There is water on both sides (cytoplasm and tissue fluid), so hydrophilic heads face outwards on both sides [B1]
Hydrophobic tails point inwards, away from water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the phospholipid bilayer is a barrier to water-soluble substances. (2)
hints: What is in the centre of the bilayer?
questions.solution:
Centre of the bilayer is made of hydrophobic fatty acid tails [B1]
Polar / charged substances cannot pass through it (need channel or carrier proteins). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why phospholipids can move within the membrane. (2)
hints: Are phospholipids covalently bonded to each other?
questions.solution:
Phospholipids are not covalently bonded — held by weak hydrophobic interactions [B1]
So they can move sideways, making the membrane fluid. [B1]

questions.prompt: In some plant cells, an ATP-driven pump moves H⁺ ions into the vacuole. A second carrier lets H⁺ ions flow back out while moving sucrose into the vacuole. Explain why the vacuole swells. (4)
hints: What does the pump set up?
What happens to the water potential when sucrose accumulates?
questions.solution:
H⁺ actively pumped into the vacuole using ATP, creating an H⁺ gradient [B1]
H⁺ diffuses out through the carrier, moving sucrose in (co-transport / antiport) [B1]
Sucrose accumulates, lowering the water potential of the vacuole [B1]
Water enters by osmosis, so the vacuole volume increases. [B1]

questions.prompt: Root hair cells take up nitrate ions from soil where nitrate concentration is lower than inside the cells. Explain how this happens, and the effect on water uptake. (4)
