hints: Can diffusion move ions against a gradient?
What do extra ions do to water potential?
questions.solution:
Active transport (or co-transport with H⁺) through carrier proteins [B1]
Uses ATP from respiration [B1]
Nitrate ions lower the water potential of the root hair cells [B1]
So more water enters by osmosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: A respiratory inhibitor was added to plant cells that pump H⁺ ions out of the cytoplasm. Explain why the pH of the cytoplasm decreased. (3)
hints: What does the inhibitor stop being made?
What happens to H⁺ ions that are no longer pumped out?
questions.solution:
Less / no ATP produced [B1]
H⁺ ions no longer actively pumped out of the cytoplasm [B1]
H⁺ concentration in the cytoplasm increases, so pH falls. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a plant cell, H⁺ is pumped into the vacuole using ATP and leaves through a co-transporter. Explain why the pH inside the vacuole rises when ATP production stops. (3)
questions.solution:
No ATP, so H⁺ is no longer pumped into the vacuole [B1]
H⁺ continues to leave through the co-transporter / by diffusion [B1]
H⁺ concentration in the vacuole falls, so pH rises. [B1]

questions.prompt: Cyanide stops the uptake of nitrate ions by root cells. Explain why. (3)
questions.solution:
Cyanide inhibits respiration [B1]
So no ATP is produced [B1]
Active transport of nitrate (or the proton pumps that drive co-transport) stops. [B1]

questions.prompt: Contrast simple diffusion with facilitated diffusion. (3)
questions.solution:
Simple diffusion through the phospholipid bilayer; facilitated diffusion through channel / carrier proteins [B1]
Simple diffusion for small / non-polar molecules; facilitated for polar molecules / ions [B1]
Facilitated diffusion is specific and has a maximum rate (limited by number of proteins). [B1]

questions.prompt: Contrast osmosis with active transport. (3)
questions.solution:
Osmosis moves water; active transport moves ions / molecules [B1]
Osmosis is down a water potential gradient; active transport against a concentration gradient [B1]
Osmosis is passive; active transport uses ATP and carrier proteins. [B1]

questions.prompt: Contrast direct active transport (e.g. a sodium–potassium pump) with co-transport. (3)
hints: What provides the energy in co-transport?
questions.solution:
Direct active transport uses ATP directly to change the carrier's shape [B1]
Co-transport uses the energy of one substance moving down its gradient (e.g. Na⁺) [B1]
Co-transport moves two substances together; the gradient is set up by a pump that uses ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Carrot discs were kept in a potassium solution bubbled with either oxygen or nitrogen. After 2 hours, uptake was 40 units with oxygen and 8 units with nitrogen. Explain these results. (4)
hints: How is K⁺ taken up against a gradient?
What does oxygen allow cells to produce?
questions.solution:
K⁺ is taken up by active transport, which needs ATP [B1]
With oxygen, aerobic respiration produces lots of ATP [B1]
With nitrogen, no aerobic respiration, so little ATP and little active uptake [B1]
Small uptake without oxygen due to diffusion / ATP from anaerobic respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Root tissue was placed in a solution of ions, with or without a respiratory inhibitor. In both, uptake rose rapidly for the first 15 minutes. After that, uptake continued only in the tissue without inhibitor. Explain. (4)
hints: What could happen in the first 15 minutes without ATP?
questions.solution:
Initial rapid uptake in both is by diffusion (into cell walls / down a gradient), which does not need ATP [B1]
Later uptake is by active transport, needing ATP from respiration [B1]
Inhibitor stops respiration, so no ATP and active uptake stops [B1]
Without inhibitor, active transport continues against the concentration gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Ion uptake by roots was low at 5 °C, high at 25 °C and fell again at 45 °C. Explain these results. (4)
questions.solution:
At 5 °C, low kinetic energy — slow respiration (enzymes), so little ATP and slow active transport [B1]
At 25 °C, faster respiration produces more ATP; carrier proteins move faster [B1]
At 45 °C, enzymes for respiration / carrier proteins begin to denature [B1]
So less ATP / fewer working carriers and uptake falls. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons why a large, polar drug given into the blood might not reach brain cells. (2)
hints: Can large polar molecules cross membranes easily?
questions.solution:
Large / polar molecules cannot easily cross phospholipid bilayers [B1]
Brain capillaries form a barrier (blood–brain barrier) that restricts what enters. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why small, non-polar molecules can cross cell-surface membranes quickly. (2)
hints: What is the core of the membrane made of?
questions.solution:
They dissolve in / pass between the hydrophobic phospholipid tails [B1]
No carrier or channel protein is needed — simple diffusion. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why siRNA molecules on their own are poorly taken up by cells. (1)
questions.solution: They are large and charged / polar, so cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why lipid vesicles (liposomes) can deliver molecules into cells. (1)
hints: What is a liposome's outer layer made of?
What can it do with a membrane?
questions.solution: Liposome lipid bilayer can fuse with the cell-surface membrane, releasing its contents inside. [B1]

questions.prompt: During exercise, calcium ions activate two transport proteins in muscle cell membranes: one that transports glucose and one that transports fatty acids. Suggest and explain how this is an advantage during exercise. (3)
hints: What are glucose and fatty acids used for?
questions.solution:
More glucose and fatty acids taken into muscle cells (facilitated diffusion) [B1]
More respiratory substrate for (aerobic) respiration [B1]
More ATP for muscle contraction. [B1]

questions.prompt: Insulin causes more glucose transport proteins to be added to the membranes of muscle cells. Explain how this lowers blood glucose concentration. (3)
hints: Where are the extra proteins stored?
What happens to glucose inside the cell?
questions.solution:
Vesicles containing channel / carrier proteins fuse with the cell-surface membrane [B1]
More glucose enters cells by facilitated diffusion [B1]
Glucose converted to glycogen / respired, maintaining the gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why red blood cells burst when placed in distilled water but plant cells don't. (2)
hints: What resists expansion in plant cells?
questions.solution:
Water enters both by osmosis because the cells have a lower water potential [B1]
Plant cell wall resists expansion / cell becomes turgid; red blood cells have no cell wall so they burst. [B1]

questions.prompt: A channel protein (aquaporin) allows both water and carbon dioxide to pass through it. Suggest two reasons why both molecules can use the same channel. (2)
questions.solution:
Both are small molecules (similar size) [B1]
Both have no overall charge / can fit and pass through the same pore. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why water can pass through membranes even though they contain a hydrophobic layer. (2)
questions.solution:
Water molecules are small, so some can pass between phospholipids [B1]
Aquaporins (channel proteins) allow rapid movement. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why sodium ions cannot diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer. (2)
questions.solution:
Ions are charged / water-soluble [B1]
Repelled by the hydrophobic fatty acid tails, so need channel / carrier proteins. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium. (3)
hints: How does the phagocyte recognise the bacterium?
questions.solution:
Phagocyte recognises foreign antigens / is attracted by chemicals [B1]
Engulfs the bacterium, forming a phagosome / vacuole [B1]
Lysosomes fuse with the phagosome [B1]
Lysozymes / hydrolytic enzymes digest / hydrolyse the bacterium. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Describe how a body cell infected with a virus is destroyed by the immune system. (3)
hints: How does the immune system know the cell is infected?
Which type of T cell kills infected cells?
questions.solution:
Infected cell presents viral antigens on its cell-surface membrane [B1]
Cytotoxic T cell with a complementary receptor binds to the antigen [B1]
T cell releases perforin, which makes holes in the cell membrane [B1]
Cell becomes freely permeable / dies. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Explain how vaccination leads to long-term immunity against a disease. (3)
hints: Which cells provide the long-term protection?
questions.solution:
Vaccine contains antigen (dead / weakened pathogen) [B1]
Triggers a primary immune response / B cells with complementary receptors activated and undergo clonal selection [B1]
Memory cells are produced [B1]
On reinfection, memory cells cause a faster, larger secondary response / more antibody before symptoms develop. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Describe the role of helper T cells in the immune response. (3)
hints: What does a helper T cell bind to?
What chemical messengers do they release, and what do these stimulate?
questions.solution:
Receptor on helper T cell binds to complementary antigen on an antigen-presenting cell [B1]
Helper T cell is activated and divides by mitosis (clones) [B1]
Releases cytokines [B1]
Which stimulate B cells to divide / phagocytes / cytotoxic T cells. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Describe the secondary immune response and explain why it is faster than the primary response. (3)
hints: Which cells remain after the first infection?
questions.solution:
Memory B cells (remain in the blood from the primary response) [B1]
Recognise / bind the complementary antigen quickly [B1]
Divide rapidly by mitosis and differentiate into plasma cells [B1]
Produce large amounts of antibody quickly, so pathogen destroyed before symptoms. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of an antibody and explain how antibodies lead to the destruction of bacteria. (3)
hints: How many polypeptide chains does an antibody have?
questions.solution:
Four polypeptide chains (two heavy, two light) held by disulfide bridges [B1]
Variable region forms an antigen-binding site complementary to a specific antigen [B1]
Forms antigen–antibody complexes / causes agglutination (clumping) of bacteria [B1]
Clumped bacteria are engulfed by phagocytes. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: A virus has a surface protein with a similar shape to a protein on insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. Suggest how infection with this virus could lead to type 1 diabetes. (2)
hints: What happens to the pancreatic cells?
questions.solution:
Antibodies / T cells made against the viral protein are also complementary to / bind the pancreatic cell protein [B1]
So the immune system destroys insulin-producing cells (so little insulin made). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a vaccine against one strain of influenza may not protect a person against a different strain. (2)
hints: What can change on the virus surface?
Will the memory cells still recognise it?
questions.solution:
Different strains have different (shaped) antigens / antigenic variability [B1]
Memory cells / antibodies from the vaccine are not complementary to the new antigen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Rheumatic fever can develop after a throat infection by streptococcal bacteria. Antibodies produced during the infection damage heart muscle. Suggest an explanation. (2)
hints: Compare the shapes of the bacterial antigen and a heart protein.
What do antibodies do when they bind?
questions.solution:
Bacterial antigen has a similar shape to a protein on heart cells [B1]
Antibodies are complementary to / bind heart cells, causing damage. [B1]

questions.prompt: A person bitten by a venomous snake is given antibodies against the venom rather than a vaccine. Explain why. (2)
hints: How long does a primary immune response take?
questions.solution:
Injected antibodies act immediately (passive immunity) [B1]
A vaccine would need time (days–weeks) for a primary response / antibody production, but venom acts quickly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two differences between active immunity and passive immunity. (2)
questions.solution:
Active involves memory cells; passive does not [B1]
Active is long-term; passive is short-term [B1]
Passive is immediate; active takes time to develop [B1]
Active: own antibodies made; passive: antibodies from outside. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how a newborn baby gains passive immunity, and why this immunity does not last. (2)
hints: Where do the baby's first antibodies come from?
What isn't produced in passive immunity?
questions.solution:
Antibodies pass across the placenta / in breast milk [B1]
No memory cells are made and the antibodies are broken down. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a vaccine against a bacterium contains several different strains of the bacterium. (2)
hints: Do different strains have identical antigens?
What must the memory cells recognise?
questions.solution:
Different strains have different antigens [B1]
So memory cells / antibodies are produced against all of them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Antivenom made using the venom of one snake species often does not work against bites from a different species. Explain why. (2)
hints: Venom contains proteins that act as antigens.
questions.solution:
Venom of a different species has different proteins / antigens with a different shape [B1]
Antibodies are not complementary to them, so cannot bind. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why antivenom is made using venom collected from snakes of the same species from many different regions. (2)
hints: Is venom identical in every snake of a species?
What do the antibodies need to bind to?
questions.solution:
Venom composition / antigens vary between populations [B1]
So antibodies are produced that are complementary to all the forms. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one reason why only a limited volume of blood is taken from an animal used to make antibodies. (1)
hints: What does the body need time to do?
questions.solution: So the animal does not become ill / anaemic / blood volume can recover. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one ethical issue with using animals to produce antibodies. (1)
hints: Injections and blood collection are involved.
questions.solution: Animals may suffer pain / stress / harm from injections of antigen or repeated bleeding. [B1]

questions.prompt: Antibodies made in mice are often modified to be more like human antibodies before being used as medicines. Suggest why. (1)
hints: How would a human immune system see a mouse protein?
What might it make against it?
questions.solution: Mouse antibodies are foreign / act as antigens, so the patient's immune system would attack / destroy them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a second (booster) dose of a vaccine is given some weeks after the first. (3)
hints: What cells remain after the first dose?
Compare the second response with the first.
questions.solution:
Second exposure triggers a secondary response [B1]
Memory B cells divide rapidly / differentiate into plasma cells [B1]
More antibody produced faster / more memory cells made, so longer-lasting immunity. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why antibody concentration rises more slowly after the first exposure to an antigen than after a second exposure. (3)
hints: How many B cells with the right receptor are there at first?
What must happen before they can divide?
questions.solution:
First exposure: few B cells with complementary receptors [B1]
They must be selected / activated by helper T cells before clonal expansion [B1]
Second exposure: many memory cells, which rapidly divide into plasma cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of plasma cells and memory cells in the humoral response. (3)
hints: Where do both cell types come from?
questions.solution:
B cell with complementary antibody binds antigen and is activated (by helper T cell cytokines) [B1]
Divides by mitosis (clonal expansion) into plasma cells and memory cells [B1]
Plasma cells secrete antibodies [B1]
Memory cells remain in the blood for a faster secondary response. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe how HIV replicates inside a helper T cell. (4)
hints: Which receptor does HIV bind to?
HIV's genetic material is RNA — what enzyme does it carry?
questions.solution:
Attachment protein binds to CD4 receptor on helper T cell [B1]
Viral RNA (and reverse transcriptase) enter the cell [B1]
Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from the viral RNA [B1]
Viral DNA inserted into host DNA [B1]
Host cell makes viral proteins and RNA, which assemble into new viruses that bud out. [B1]
Any 4 of these points — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how HIV infection leads to the symptoms of AIDS. (4)
hints: What do those cells normally activate?
questions.solution:
HIV infects and destroys helper T cells [B1]
Fewer helper T cells, so B cells not stimulated / fewer antibodies [B1]
Cytotoxic T cells / phagocytes not activated [B1]
So the person cannot fight infections and suffers opportunistic infections. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows data for two groups of people with HIV. Use the data to explain why people in group B are more likely to suffer from opportunistic infections. (3)
hints: What does a high viral load mean is happening?
What does a low CD4 count mean?
questions.solution:
Group B has a high viral load, so HIV is replicating / infecting many cells [B1]
Group B has fewer CD4 (helper T) cells, as they have been destroyed [B1]
So fewer B cells / cytotoxic T cells activated, less effective immune response. [B1]
questions.table:
Group | CD4 cells per mm³ | Viral load per cm³
A | 900 | 50
B | 200 | 80 000

questions.prompt: A person tests positive for antibodies to HIV but has no symptoms. Explain why the antibodies show the person is infected, and suggest why there are no symptoms yet. (3)
hints: Why would anti-HIV antibodies only be present after infection?
How long does it take for helper T cell numbers to fall?
questions.solution:
HIV antigens triggered a humoral response [B1]
Plasma cells made antibodies complementary to HIV antigens [B1]
Helper T cell numbers have not yet fallen enough / virus may be latent, so the immune system still works. [B1]

questions.prompt: Drugs that inhibit reverse transcriptase reduce viral load and delay the onset of AIDS. Explain how. (3)
hints: What happens if that step is blocked?
questions.solution:
Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from viral RNA [B1]
If inhibited, viral DNA is not made / inserted, so no new viruses [B1]
Fewer helper T cells destroyed, so the immune system keeps working. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how an ELISA test can detect a particular antigen in a sample. (3)
hints: What is fixed to the well first?
Where does the colour come from?
questions.solution:
Antibody complementary to the antigen is bound to the well; sample added and antigen binds [B1]
Well washed; second antibody with an enzyme attached added and binds to the antigen [B1]
Well washed; substrate added — colour change shows the antigen is present. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the well is washed between each stage of an ELISA test. (3)
hints: What could be left behind unattached?
What would happen if unbound enzyme-linked antibody remained?
questions.solution:
Removes unbound antigen / antibodies [B1]
So any colour is due only to enzyme-linked antibodies that are bound [B1]
Prevents a false positive result. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how an ELISA test can show that a person has antibodies to HIV in their blood. (3)
hints: This time the antigen is fixed to the well.
The second antibody binds to human antibodies.
questions.solution:
HIV antigen bound to the well; patient's plasma added — HIV antibodies bind if present [B1]
Wash; add second antibody (with enzyme attached) that binds to human antibodies [B1]
Wash; add substrate — colour change shows HIV antibodies are present. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of an antibody. (3)
questions.solution:
Four polypeptide chains: two heavy and two light [B1]
Held together by disulfide bridges [B1]
Variable regions form two antigen-binding sites [B1]
Constant region is the same in all antibodies of that class. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why an antibody can bind to two antigens, and why it is specific to one antigen. (3)
hints: What gives the binding site its shape?
questions.solution:
Has two antigen-binding sites (one on each arm) [B1]
Variable region has a specific amino acid sequence / tertiary structure [B1]
So the binding site is complementary to only one antigen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how antibodies cause bacteria to clump together (agglutination) and how this helps destroy them. (3)
hints: How many binding sites does each antibody have?
What do phagocytes do with clumps?
questions.solution:
Each antibody has two binding sites [B1]
Can bind antigens on two different bacteria, linking them into clumps [B1]
Phagocytes engulf the clumps more easily. [B1]

questions.prompt: Infection with cowpox virus gave people protection against smallpox. Suggest an explanation. (2)
hints: Compare the antigens on the two viruses.
What remains after the cowpox infection?
questions.solution:
Cowpox antigens have a similar shape to smallpox antigens [B1]
So memory cells / antibodies are also complementary to smallpox antigens. [B1]

questions.prompt: An antibody test for one virus sometimes gives a positive result for people infected with a closely related virus. Suggest why. (2)
hints: Do related viruses have similar antigens?
What does the antibody bind to?
questions.solution:
The related virus has antigens with a similar shape [B1]
So the antibody in the test can also bind to them (false positive). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an antibody normally binds to only one antigen. (2)
hints: What determines the shape of the binding site?
questions.solution:
Binding site has a specific shape due to the amino acid sequence / tertiary structure of the variable region [B1]
Only an antigen with a complementary shape can bind. [B1]

questions.prompt: Scientists measured a person's antibodies against a tick-saliva protein. The person was bitten by a tick in week 1 and again in week 8, and had an allergic reaction to red meat in week 11. Evaluate the hypothesis that an earlier immune response to the tick bite caused the allergy. (3)
hints: Compare the response after each bite.
questions.solution:
Antibody rose after the first bite (primary response) and rose much more after the second bite (secondary response, memory cells), supporting the idea of an immune response to the tick [B1]
Allergic reaction happened after the large secondary response, which supports the hypothesis [B1]
But only one person / correlation does not prove cause / the antibodies measured may not be the ones causing the allergy. [B1]
questions.table:
Week | Antibody / arbitrary units
0 | 1
3 | 20
6 | 18
10 | 95

questions.prompt: A child had no reaction the first time she ate peanuts, but had a severe reaction the second time, a month later. Antibodies against a peanut protein were found in her blood after the first exposure. Evaluate the idea that the first exposure caused the later reaction. (3)
hints: What do antibodies after the first exposure show?
What would the second exposure trigger?
questions.solution:
Antibodies after the first exposure show a primary immune response / memory cells were made [B1]
Second exposure triggered a faster, larger secondary response, consistent with the reaction [B1]
But one child only / other foods or factors could be involved / timing alone doesn't prove cause. [B1]

questions.prompt: A study found that hay fever symptoms in a group of people were worst on days with the highest pollen counts. Evaluate the claim that pollen causes hay fever symptoms. (3)
hints: What else changes on high-pollen days?
questions.solution:
Positive correlation between pollen count and symptoms supports the claim [B1]
Correlation does not prove causation — other factors (e.g. temperature, air pollution) also change with season [B1]
No information on significance / sample size; need evidence of an immune response to pollen antigens. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how monoclonal antibodies can be used to deliver a drug specifically to cancer cells. (3)
hints: What is special about the antibody's binding site?
Which cells have the matching antigen?
questions.solution:
Antibodies have a binding site complementary to an antigen found on cancer cells [B1]
Drug is attached to the antibody [B1]
So the drug binds only to / is taken into cancer cells, harming fewer healthy cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a monoclonal antibody that targets an antigen found only on cancer cells causes fewer side effects than chemotherapy. (2)
hints: Which cells will the antibody bind to?
questions.solution:
Antibody binds only to cancer cells with the complementary antigen [B1]
Healthy cells don't have that antigen, so are not affected. [B1]

questions.prompt: An antibody–drug treatment targets a protein found on cancer cells and also on heart muscle cells. Suggest why the treatment may damage the heart. (2)
questions.solution:
Antibody is also complementary to the protein on heart cells, so binds to them [B1]
Drug is delivered to / kills heart cells too. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how an antibody labelled with a fluorescent dye could be used to show where a particular protein is located in cells viewed with a light microscope. (3)
hints: What makes the antibody bind to one protein only?
questions.solution:
Antibody is complementary to / specific to the protein [B1]
Binds only where the protein is [B1]
Fluorescent label shows up (glows) at those locations under the microscope. [B1]

questions.prompt: HIV has a lipid envelope and contains the enzyme reverse transcriptase. Give the function of each. (2)
hints: Where does the envelope come from?
questions.solution:
Envelope (from host membrane) helps the virus fuse with / enter host cells [B1]
Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from viral RNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why antiviral drugs often target viral enzymes such as reverse transcriptase. (1)
hints: Do human cells use reverse transcriptase?
Would the drug harm host cells?
questions.solution: Human cells do not have / need these enzymes, so the drug harms the virus with few side effects. [B1]

questions.prompt: Patients with a bacterial gut infection were tested for antibodies against the bacterial toxin. Suggest how injecting anti-toxin antibodies would help, and which group of patients should receive them. (3)
hints: What do injected antibodies do immediately?
Which group is making few antibodies of their own?
questions.solution:
Injected antibodies bind to / neutralise the toxin straight away (passive immunity) [B1]
Patients who relapse make few antibodies of their own [B1]
So the relapse group should receive them; the quick-recovery group already produces plenty. [B1]
questions.table:
Day | Quick recovery | Relapse
0 | 5 | 4
3 | 40 | 6
6 | 80 | 10

questions.prompt: An unvaccinated person with a deep, dirty wound is given anti-tetanus antibodies. Explain why. (3)
hints: How long does a primary immune response take?
questions.solution:
Gives immediate protection (passive immunity) [B1]
Antibodies bind to and neutralise the toxin [B1]
No time for the person's own primary response before the toxin acts. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why passive immunity only lasts a short time, and why repeated injections of antibodies from horses might stop working. (3)
hints: How does the body see horse proteins?
questions.solution:
No memory cells are produced [B1]
Injected antibodies are broken down [B1]
Horse antibodies are foreign / act as antigens, so the patient makes antibodies against them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a lateral flow pregnancy test detects the hormone hCG in urine. (2)
hints: Which molecules move with the urine?
What is fixed at the test line?
questions.solution:
Mobile antibodies with a coloured label bind to hCG [B1]
The hCG–antibody complex is caught by fixed antibodies at the test line, which then shows a coloured line. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the test line of a lateral flow test only becomes coloured when the antigen is present. (2)
hints: What are the fixed antibodies at the test line complementary to?
How does the label get there?
questions.solution:
Fixed antibodies at the test line are complementary to the antigen [B1]
Labelled antibodies are held there only if they have bound antigen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a lateral flow test has a control line, and what the antibodies at the control line bind to. (2)
hints: What should happen whether or not the antigen is present?
questions.solution:
Control-line antibodies bind the labelled (mobile) antibody itself [B1]
So a line appears whenever the liquid has flowed and reagents work, showing the test is valid. [B1]

questions.prompt: What does it mean if no line appears at the control line of a lateral flow test? (1)
hints: What does the control line check?
questions.solution: The test has not worked / result is invalid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the antibodies at the control line bind to the labelled antibody rather than to the antigen. (1)
hints: Should the control line depend on the antigen?
questions.solution: So the line appears whether or not antigen is present, showing the liquid has flowed. [B1]

questions.prompt: A line appears at the test line but not the control line. Explain why the result should not be trusted. (1)
hints: What does a missing control line mean?
Could the test have run incorrectly?
questions.solution: Test did not work properly (e.g. reagents faulty / liquid didn't flow fully), so result is invalid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why B cells are fused with tumour cells to produce monoclonal antibodies. (2)
hints: What does each cell type contribute?
Do B cells divide in culture?
questions.solution:
B cells make the specific antibody but do not divide in culture [B1]
Tumour cells divide indefinitely, so the hybridoma divides and produces antibody continuously. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why all the antibodies produced by one hybridoma clone are identical. (2)
hints: Where does a clone come from?
questions.solution:
All cells come from one B cell (clone), so have the same antibody gene [B1]
So they make identical antibodies complementary to one antigen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a mouse is used to obtain B cells that make a specific antibody. (2)
hints: Where are B cells collected from?
questions.solution:
Mouse is injected with the antigen, triggering an immune response [B1]
B cells producing the antibody are removed (e.g. from the spleen). [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one ethical issue with using mice to produce monoclonal antibodies. (1)
questions.solution: Mice are injected / may suffer / are killed to obtain B cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one ethical argument in favour of using animals in medical research. (1)
hints: What might the research lead to?
questions.solution: It can lead to treatments that save / improve many human (or animal) lives. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an HIV antibody test may give a negative result in the first few weeks after infection. (2)
hints: How long does a primary immune response take?
questions.solution:
Primary immune response takes time — plasma cells have not yet produced many antibodies [B1]
So antibody levels are too low to detect. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a positive antibody test shows that a person has been exposed to a virus, but not whether they are still infected. (2)
hints: What happens to antibodies / memory cells after infection clears?
Do antibodies prove the virus is present?
questions.solution:
Antibodies / memory cells remain after the infection has cleared [B1]
So the test detects past exposure, not necessarily the virus itself. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how doctors decide that a person with HIV has developed AIDS. (2)
hints: What happens to helper T cells?
questions.solution:
Very low helper T (CD4) cell count [B1]
Presence of opportunistic infections. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an ELISA test for antibodies, explain why no colour change occurs if the patient has no antibodies to the antigen. (2)
hints: What would the second antibody bind to?
questions.solution:
No antibody binds to the antigen in the well, so the enzyme-linked second antibody has nothing to bind to [B1]
It is washed away, so no enzyme is present to convert the substrate to a coloured product. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a colour change only occurs in wells that test positive in an ELISA. (2)
hints: When is it kept in the well?
questions.solution:
The enzyme is attached to the second antibody, which only stays if the first antibody / antigen is bound [B1]
The enzyme converts the colourless substrate into a coloured product. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the intensity of colour in an ELISA well is related to the amount of antigen in the sample. (2)
hints: More antigen means more of what binding?
questions.solution:
More antigen means more antibody–enzyme complexes bound [B1]
More enzyme, so more coloured product formed in the same time. [B1]

questions.prompt: A baby tests positive for measles antibodies but has never had measles or the vaccine. Suggest why. (2)
hints: Where could the antibodies come from?
What type of immunity is this?
questions.solution:
Antibodies passed from the mother across the placenta / in breast milk [B1]
Passive immunity — the baby didn't make them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why antibodies passed from mother to baby disappear after a few months. (2)
hints: Does the baby make memory cells?
What happens to antibodies over time?
questions.solution:
Antibodies are broken down [B1]
No plasma cells / memory cells to replace them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why some vaccines are not given to babies until maternal antibodies have declined. (2)
hints: What would maternal antibodies do to vaccine antigen?
Would the baby make memory cells?
questions.solution:
Maternal antibodies would bind to / destroy the vaccine antigen [B1]
So the baby's own immune response (and memory cells) would not develop. [B1]

questions.prompt: An ELISA plate includes a control well with no antigen attached. Suggest two purposes of this control. (2)
hints: Could antibodies stick to the plastic?
What would colour in this well mean?
questions.solution:
Shows the antibodies / enzyme do not bind to the well itself [B1]
So any colour in test wells is due to specific binding to the antigen (shows washing was effective). [B1]

questions.prompt: An ELISA plate includes a well with a sample known to be positive. Suggest two purposes of this control. (2)
hints: What can you compare test wells with?
questions.solution:
Shows the test / reagents are working [B1]
Gives a colour to compare the test samples with. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons why each patient's sample is tested in more than one well. (2)
hints: Could one well give an odd result?
questions.solution:
Identifies anomalous results / errors [B1]
Increases reliability / allows a mean to be calculated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why antibodies can be used to purify one specific protein from a mixture of proteins. (2)
hints: What is special about the binding site?
How could the bound protein be separated?
questions.solution:
Antibody binding site is complementary to only that protein [B1]
So only that protein binds, and the antibody–protein complex can be separated (e.g. on beads). [B1]

questions.prompt: A pregnancy test antibody binds to the hormone hCG but not to LH, which is a similar hormone. Explain why. (2)
hints: Are hCG and LH identical in shape?
questions.solution:
Antibody binding site is complementary only to the shape of hCG (its specific epitope) [B1]
LH has a different tertiary structure / amino acid sequence at that site. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how changing one amino acid in an antigen could stop an antibody binding to it. (2)
hints: What determines the shape of the antigen?
questions.solution:
Changes the tertiary structure / shape of the antigen at the binding region [B1]
No longer complementary to the antibody's binding site. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why iPS cells made from a patient's own cells are not rejected when transplanted. (2)
hints: Which antigens are on their surface?
Does the immune system see them as foreign?
questions.solution:
They have the patient's own (self) antigens [B1]
So the immune system does not recognise them as foreign. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a bone marrow donor needs to be tissue-matched to the patient. (3)
hints: What could the donor's immune cells do?
questions.solution:
Matched donors have similar cell-surface antigens [B1]
Reduces rejection of donor cells by the patient's immune system [B1]
Also reduces donor immune cells attacking the patient's tissues (graft-versus-host). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why changing the amino acid sequence of an antibody's variable region changes which antigen it binds to. (2)
questions.solution:
Changes the tertiary structure / shape of the antigen-binding site [B1]
So it becomes complementary to a different antigen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why myasthenia gravis is described as an autoimmune disease. (2)
questions.solution:
The immune system makes antibodies against the body's own proteins (ACh receptors) [B1]
It fails to recognise them as self. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why vaccines against a virus with a rapidly mutating surface protein must be updated frequently. (2)
questions.solution:
Mutations change the shape of the antigen (antigenic variability) [B1]
Memory cells / antibodies are no longer complementary, so new vaccine needed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a monoclonal antibody can be used to target a drug to cancer cells. (3)
hints: What do cancer cells have that normal cells don't?
How does the drug get there?
questions.solution:
Cancer cells have specific antigens / receptors on their surface [B1]
Monoclonal antibody is complementary to that antigen and binds to it [B1]
Drug attached to the antibody is delivered only to cancer cells, so fewer side-effects. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced. (3)
questions.solution:
Inject a mouse with the antigen and extract the activated B cells / plasma cells [B1]
Fuse with tumour cells to form hybridoma cells that divide rapidly [B1]
Select the hybridoma producing the required antibody and clone it. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a vaccine provides protection against a disease. (2)
questions.solution:
Vaccine contains antigens that stimulate a primary immune response [B1]
Memory cells produced, giving a faster, larger secondary response on infection. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between active and passive immunity, with one example of each. (2)
questions.solution:
Active: own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells (e.g. vaccination / infection) [B1]
Passive: antibodies given from outside (e.g. via placenta / breast milk / injection), no memory cells, short-lived. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the response of B lymphocytes when an animal is vaccinated. You don't need to describe the cellular detail. (3)
questions.solution:
B cell with complementary receptor binds to the antigen (and stimulated by T helper cells) [B1]
Divides by mitosis (clonal selection / expansion) [B1]
Forms plasma cells that secrete antibodies and memory cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of T helper cells in the immune response. (3)
questions.solution:
T helper cell receptor binds to antigen presented on an antigen-presenting cell [B1]
Releases chemicals (cytokines) that stimulate B cells to divide / phagocytes [B1]
And activate cytotoxic T cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the secondary immune response is faster and larger than the primary response. (3)
questions.solution:
Memory cells already present that recognise the antigen [B1]
They divide rapidly into plasma cells [B1]
So more antibodies produced quickly, before symptoms appear. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how HIV replicates inside helper T cells. (4)
questions.solution:
Attachment proteins bind to receptors (CD4) on the helper T cell [B1]
HIV RNA enters the cell [B1]
Reverse transcriptase converts RNA to DNA [B1]
Viral DNA inserted into the host DNA, transcribed and translated; viral proteins and RNA assembled into new viruses which bud out. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how HIV infection leads to the symptoms of AIDS. (4)
questions.solution:
HIV destroys helper T cells [B1]
Fewer helper T cells to stimulate B cells / cytotoxic T cells / phagocytes [B1]
Immune system can't respond effectively to pathogens [B1]
Opportunistic infections / cancers cause illness and death. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why antibiotics are not effective against HIV, and how antiretroviral drugs work. (4)
questions.solution:
Antibiotics target bacterial structures / enzymes (e.g. cell walls, 70S ribosomes) [B1]
Viruses have none of these — they use host cells [B1]
Antiretrovirals inhibit viral enzymes like reverse transcriptase [B1]
So viral replication is slowed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two types of cell that can stimulate an immune response by presenting antigens. (2)
questions.solution: Two from: phagocytes / macrophages; cancer cells; virus-infected cells; transplanted cells; B cells. [B2]

questions.prompt: Describe what is meant by an antigen and give two examples of where antigens are found. (2)
questions.solution:
A molecule (usually protein) that triggers an immune response [B1]
On pathogens, cancer cells, transplanted cells or toxins. [B1]

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the cellular and humoral immune responses. (2)
questions.solution:
Cellular: involves T cells responding to antigens presented on cells [B1]
Humoral: involves B cells and antibodies in body fluids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Ear swelling measures the cellular (T-cell) response; antibody concentration measures the humoral response. Use the table to conclude how autoimmune disease affects these responses in male and female mice. (3)
hints: Compare autoimmune with healthy for each sex.
questions.solution:
Autoimmune males: larger cellular response (swelling 25.9 vs 17.9), humoral similar (14 vs 16) [B1]
Autoimmune females: larger humoral response (antibody 26 vs 14), cellular similar (16.7 vs 18.5) [B1]
So autoimmunity increases the cellular response in males and the humoral response in females. [B1]
questions.table:
Mice | Swelling / cm × 10⁻³ | Antibody / arbitrary units
Healthy male | 17.9 ± 4.1 | 16 ± 3
Healthy female | 18.5 ± 2.9 | 14 ± 4
Autoimmune male | 25.9 ± 4.5 | 14 ± 2
Autoimmune female | 16.7 ± 3.0 | 26 ± 7

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by an autoimmune disease. (3)
questions.solution:
Immune system fails to recognise self antigens [B1]
Lymphocytes / antibodies attack the body's own cells [B1]
Causing tissue damage / inflammation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of cytotoxic T cells. (3)
questions.solution:
Recognise antigens on infected / abnormal body cells [B1]
Release perforin, which makes holes in the cell membrane [B1]
So the cell is killed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how antibodies lead to the destruction of pathogens. (4)
questions.solution:
Antibody variable region is complementary to a specific antigen [B1]
Forms antigen–antibody complexes [B1]
Agglutination — clumps pathogens together [B1]
Makes it easier for phagocytes to engulf them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Complete the passage. 'Molecules on cell surfaces that trigger an immune response are called __1__. Antibodies made from a single clone of plasma cells are __2__ antibodies. Each antibody has two antigen-binding __3__. Antibodies are secreted by __4__ cells. A vaccine stimulates the production of __5__ cells. When enough of a population is vaccinated, the unvaccinated are protected by __6__ immunity.' (3)
questions.solution:
1 antigens; 2 monoclonal; 3 sites; 4 plasma; 5 memory; 6 herd. [B3]
6 correct = 3 marks; 4 or 5 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Complete the passage. 'Phagocytes engulf pathogens and display their antigens, acting as __1__ cells. T __2__ cells bind to these antigens and release __3__ that stimulate B cells. B cells divide by __4__ to form clones. This is called clonal __5__. Antibodies cause pathogens to clump together, called __6__.' (3)
questions.solution:
1 antigen-presenting; 2 helper; 3 cytokines; 4 mitosis; 5 selection / expansion; 6 agglutination. [B3]
6 correct = 3 marks; 4 or 5 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Complete the passage. 'Immunity gained by making your own antibodies is __1__ immunity. Antibodies received from the mother in breast milk give __2__ immunity, which is __3__-lived because no __4__ cells are made. The first response to an antigen is the __5__ response; a later, faster response is the __6__ response.' (3)
questions.solution:
1 active; 2 passive; 3 short; 4 memory; 5 primary; 6 secondary. [B3]
6 correct = 3 marks; 4 or 5 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Suggest one reason why there is no effective vaccine against HIV. (1)
questions.solution: HIV mutates rapidly, changing its antigens (antigenic variability) / hides inside helper T cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a new flu vaccine is needed every year. (1)
questions.solution: Flu virus antigens change (antigenic variability), so memory cells no longer recognise them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the ELISA test for HIV detects antibodies rather than the virus itself. (1)
questions.solution: Antibodies are present in large amounts and are specific to HIV antigens, so easier to detect. [B1]

questions.prompt: Antibiotic 1 breaks apart double-stranded DNA in bacteria; antibiotic 2 prevents cross-links between murein chains. Explain why neither works against HIV. (2)
questions.solution:
Antibiotic 1: HIV has RNA, not double-stranded DNA (and its DNA is inside host cells) [B1]
Antibiotic 2: HIV has no murein cell wall. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an antibiotic that inhibits bacterial 70S ribosomes doesn't harm human cells or viruses. (2)
questions.solution:
Human cells have 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm, which aren't affected [B1]
Viruses have no ribosomes — they use host ribosomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why antibiotics that stop cell wall synthesis cause bacteria to burst. (2)
questions.solution:
Water enters by osmosis [B1]
Without a strong murein wall, the cell can't resist expansion and bursts (osmotic lysis). [B1]

questions.prompt: One B cell gives rise to 3000 plasma cells, each making 2000 antibody molecules per second. Blood volume is 5.0 dm³. Calculate the number of antibody molecules per cm³ of blood after 12 hours. (2)
5000 plasma cells each make 1500 antibody molecules per second. Blood volume is 6.0 dm³. Calculate the number of antibody molecules per cm³ of blood after 24 hours. (2)
2000 plasma cells each make 2500 antibody molecules per second. Blood volume is 4.5 dm³. Calculate the number of antibody molecules per cm³ of blood after 6 hours. (2)

Young and old female mice were infected with the same flu virus and the number of B cells per gram of lung tissue measured over 8 days. Old mice had fewer B cells. Without referring to statistics, repeats or sample size, suggest three reasons why further investigation is needed before concluding that ageing reduces the immune response in humans. (3)
questions.solution:
Only female mice — males may differ [B1]
Mice not humans [B1]
Only B cells in lungs measured — not antibodies / T cells / other tissues / one virus strain only. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest three reasons why older people may have a weaker immune response. (3)
questions.solution:
Fewer new lymphocytes produced / thymus shrinks [B1]
Fewer naive B and T cells that can respond to new antigens [B1]
Slower clonal expansion / fewer plasma cells and antibodies. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the number of B cells in infected tissue rises over several days after infection. (3)
questions.solution:
B cells with complementary receptors are selected [B1]
Stimulated by T helper cells / cytokines [B1]
Divide by mitosis to form clones of plasma and memory cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some skin cancer cells have a faulty cell-surface receptor protein. Suggest why these tumour cells can be destroyed by the immune system. (3)
questions.solution:
Faulty protein has a different shape — recognised as a non-self antigen [B1]
Cytotoxic T cells with complementary receptors bind [B1]
And kill the tumour cell (perforin). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a drug that blocks a 'brake' receptor on T cells could help treat cancer. (3)
questions.solution:
Tumour cells can switch off T cells via the brake receptor [B1]
Blocking it keeps T cells active [B1]
So T cells continue to recognise and kill tumour cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why tumours often escape destruction by the immune system. (3)
questions.solution:
Tumour cells are the body's own cells, so many antigens are self [B1]
May reduce display of abnormal antigens [B1]
May release chemicals that suppress T cells. [B1]

category: Organisms exchange substances with their environment

questions.prompt:
Two agar cubes containing pink indicator have sides of 1 cm and 2 cm. They are placed in acid, which turns the indicator colourless.

Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each cube and explain which becomes colourless first. (3)
hints: Think about the distance from the surface to the centre.
questions.solution:
1 cm cube: 6 : 1 [M1]
2 cm cube: 3 : 1 [M1]
1 cm cube turns colourless first: larger SA:V ratio / shorter diffusion distance to the centre. [A1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a flatworm does not need a circulatory system. (1)
hints: How far are cells from the surface?
questions.solution: Flat / thin body, so large SA:V ratio / short diffusion distance to all cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a single-celled organism does not need a specialised gas exchange system. (1)
hints: Compare its SA:V ratio with a large organism.
questions.solution: Large SA:V ratio, so diffusion across the cell-surface membrane is enough. [B1]

questions.prompt: Mosses have no xylem. Suggest why mosses are always small. (1)
hints: How must water move without xylem?
Is that fast over long distances?
questions.solution: Water moves cell to cell by osmosis / diffusion, which is only fast enough over short distances. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why small mammals lose heat faster than large mammals, and how they make up for this. (3)
hints: How is heat produced in the body?
questions.solution:
Small mammals have a larger SA:V ratio [B1]
So more heat lost per unit volume / mass [B1]
They have a higher rate of respiration / metabolic rate (and eat more per gram) to generate heat. [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of cubes with sides of 2 cm and 6 cm. Use your answers to explain why large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces. (3)
hints: What happens to the ratio as size increases?
questions.solution:
2 cm cube: 24 ÷ 8 = 3 : 1 [B1]
6 cm cube: 216 ÷ 216 = 1 : 1 [B1]
Larger organisms have a smaller SA:V ratio / longer diffusion distances, so diffusion across the body surface is not enough. [B1]

questions.prompt: Hummingbirds are very small and need to feed almost continuously. Explain why. (3)
hints: Think about SA:V ratio and heat.
What do they need lots of for respiration?
questions.solution:
Very large SA:V ratio, so lose heat rapidly [B1]
High metabolic / respiration rate to keep warm (and fly) [B1]
Need a constant supply of respiratory substrate (sugar). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why insects are never very large. (2)
hints: How does oxygen reach insect cells?
questions.solution:
Oxygen reaches cells by diffusion through the tracheal system [B1]
Diffusion is too slow over long distances, so a large insect could not supply all its cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why multicellular animals need a mass transport system. (2)
hints: How far are many cells from the exchange surface?
Can diffusion alone supply them quickly enough?
questions.solution:
Small SA:V ratio / long distance between exchange surface and most cells [B1]
Diffusion too slow to supply cells with enough oxygen / nutrients for their metabolism. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a large tree needs xylem to supply water to its leaves. (2)
hints: How far is it from root to leaf?
Could water move fast enough by osmosis cell to cell?
questions.solution:
Long distance from roots to leaves / small SA:V [B1]
Osmosis / diffusion cell to cell would be too slow, so mass flow in xylem is needed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the relationship between surface area to volume ratio and metabolic rate in mammals. (3)
questions.solution:
Smaller animals have a larger SA : V ratio [B1]
Lose heat faster relative to their volume [B1]
So need a higher metabolic rate (more respiration) to keep body temperature constant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why large organisms need specialised gas exchange surfaces and transport systems. (3)
questions.solution:
Large organisms have a small SA : V ratio [B1]
Body surface too small to supply all cells by diffusion [B1]
Diffusion distances to inner cells too long, so a transport system is needed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why animals living in cold climates tend to be larger and have smaller ears than related species in warm climates. (3)
questions.solution:
Larger size gives a smaller SA : V ratio [B1]
Smaller ears reduce surface area [B1]
So less heat is lost to the surroundings. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which is NOT a possible explanation for two people having different SA : V ratios?

Choose one answer.

A  They have different body shapes
B  One has a higher mass
C  One is taller
D  They have the same height and mass (1)
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt:
A cube of side 2 cm has an SA : V ratio of:

Choose one answer.

A  1 : 1
B  2 : 1
C  3 : 1
D  6 : 1 (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
As a cube doubles in side length, its SA : V ratio:

Choose one answer.

A  doubles
B  halves
C  stays the same
D  quadruples (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

category: Organisms exchange substances with their environment

questions.prompt: Explain three features of the alveoli that make gas exchange efficient. (3)
hints: Fick's law: surface area, distance, gradient.
Give a feature and link it to one of those.
questions.solution:
Thin walls / one cell thick (squamous epithelium), so short diffusion distance [B1]
Many alveoli, so large surface area [B1]
Surrounded by a capillary network / ventilation, so a steep concentration gradient is maintained. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain three features of a leaf that make gas exchange efficient. (3)
hints: How do gases get into the leaf?
What is in the spongy mesophyll?
questions.solution:
Many stomata, so gases can enter / leave [B1]
Air spaces in spongy mesophyll, so gases diffuse quickly to cells [B1]
Thin leaf, so short diffusion distance [B1]
Large surface area of mesophyll cells for diffusion. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 features with explanation.

questions.prompt: Explain how an insect limits water loss while still exchanging gases. (3)
hints: How can the openings to the tracheal system be controlled?
questions.solution:
Spiracles can close (when less oxygen needed), reducing evaporation [B1]
Waxy cuticle, reducing evaporation from body surface [B1]
Hairs around spiracles trap moist air, reducing the water potential gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the counter-current mechanism makes gas exchange in fish gills efficient. (2)
hints: Which directions do blood and water flow?
What happens to the oxygen concentration gradient along the lamella?
questions.solution:
Blood and water flow in opposite directions [B1]
So a concentration gradient (of oxygen) is maintained along the whole length of the lamella / gill filament. [B1]

questions.prompt: Tuna are fast-swimming fish. They have a larger gill surface area per gram of body mass than slow-moving fish. Suggest why. (2)
hints: What is different about the metabolism of an active fish?
What does a larger surface area do?
questions.solution:
More active / higher (metabolic or respiratory) rate, so more oxygen needed [B1]
Larger surface area allows faster / more diffusion of oxygen. [B1]

questions.prompt: During flight, fluid at the ends of an insect's tracheoles is drawn into the muscle cells. Explain how this increases the rate of gas exchange. (2)
hints: Do gases diffuse faster in air or in water?
What is now in contact with more of the tracheole wall?
questions.solution:
Gases diffuse faster through air than through liquid [B1]
Larger surface area of tracheole wall exposed to air / more oxygen reaches muscle cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how oxygen moves from the air in an alveolus to haemoglobin in a red blood cell, and explain the features that make this process efficient. (6)
hints: Then link features to Fick's law.
questions.solution:
Oxygen diffuses down a concentration gradient [B1]
Across the alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium [B1]
Into the plasma and into the red blood cell [B1]
Walls are thin (squamous) / one cell thick, so short diffusion distance [B1]
Many alveoli, so large surface area [B1]
Ventilation and blood flow maintain a steep concentration gradient [B1]
Narrow capillaries slow red cells / press them against the wall. [B1]
Any 6 of these points — max 6 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the mechanism of breathing out (expiration) at rest and during exercise. (6)
hints: At rest, is expiration active or passive?
Which muscles help during forced expiration?
questions.solution:
At rest: external intercostal muscles relax [B1]
Ribcage moves down and in [B1]
Diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards [B1]
Volume of thorax decreases, so pressure increases above atmospheric [B1]
Air moves out down the pressure gradient [B1]
During exercise: internal intercostals contract, pulling ribs down further [B1]
Abdominal muscles contract, pushing the diaphragm up. [B1]
Any 6 of these points — max 6 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the gross structure of the human gas exchange system and how air is drawn in during inspiration. (6)
hints: Start at the trachea and work down.
Then describe the muscles and pressure changes.
questions.solution:
Trachea divides into two bronchi [B1]
Bronchi branch into bronchioles [B1]
Bronchioles end in alveoli [B1]
External intercostal muscles contract, ribcage moves up and out [B1]
Diaphragm contracts and flattens [B1]
Thoracic volume increases, pressure decreases below atmospheric [B1]
Air moves in down the pressure gradient. [B1]
Any 6 of these points — max 6 marks.

questions.prompt: Emphysema destroys the walls between alveoli and reduces their elasticity. Explain why this reduces gas exchange. (3)
questions.solution:
Fewer, larger air spaces, so smaller surface area [B1]
Less elastic recoil, so less air breathed out / poorer ventilation [B1]
Smaller concentration gradient, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: In pulmonary fibrosis, the walls of the alveoli become thickened with scar tissue. Explain why people with this disease are often breathless. (3)
hints: What does a thicker wall do to diffusion?
How does the body respond to low oxygen?
questions.solution:
Longer diffusion distance [B1]
So slower / less diffusion of oxygen into the blood [B1]
Less oxygen for aerobic respiration, so they breathe faster to compensate. [B1]

questions.prompt: During an asthma attack, the bronchioles narrow. Explain why this reduces gas exchange. (3)
hints: How much air reaches the alveoli?
What happens to the concentration gradient?
questions.solution:
Less air reaches the alveoli / reduced ventilation [B1]
Oxygen concentration in alveoli falls, so smaller concentration gradient [B1]
So less oxygen diffuses into the blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why fish use gills but land mammals use lungs. (2)
hints: What supports gill filaments in water?
What would happen to gills in air?
questions.solution:
Water supports gill filaments; in air they collapse / stick together, reducing surface area [B1]
Lungs are internal, so less water is lost by evaporation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the spiracles of land insects can open and close. (2)
hints: What is lost through open spiracles?
When do they need to be open?
questions.solution:
Closing reduces water loss (evaporation) [B1]
Opening lets gases in / out when oxygen demand is high. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the gas exchange surfaces of land animals are inside the body. (2)
hints: What would happen if they were exposed?
questions.solution:
Reduces water loss by evaporation [B1]
Protects the thin, delicate surface from damage. [B1]

questions.prompt: In fish gills, blood leaving the lamellae is about 80% saturated with oxygen. If blood and water flowed in the same direction, it could reach only about 50%. Explain which system is more efficient and why. (2)
hints: Which system keeps a concentration gradient along the whole lamella?
What happens in parallel flow halfway along?
questions.solution:
Counter-current system is more efficient — blood leaves more saturated (80% vs 50%) [B1]
Concentration gradient maintained along the whole lamella; in parallel flow it reaches equilibrium. [B1]

questions.prompt: Fish extract about 80% of the oxygen from water passing over their gills. Humans extract about 25% of the oxygen from air they breathe in. Does this mean fish have a more efficient gas exchange system? Explain. (2)
hints: Compare the oxygen content of air and water.
Is a higher percentage always more oxygen?
questions.solution:
Yes in terms of the proportion extracted — counter-current flow [B1]
But air contains much more oxygen per volume than water, so humans still get plenty / tidal breathing leaves residual air. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the one-way flow of water over fish gills makes gas exchange efficient. (2)
hints: Does water mix with water that has already been used?
What happens to the concentration gradient?
questions.solution:
Water enters the mouth and leaves through the gills — continuous flow in one direction [B1]
No mixing with deoxygenated water, so a steep concentration gradient is maintained. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a parallel-flow gas exchange system would be less efficient than the counter-current system in fish gills. (2)
hints: In parallel flow, what happens to the concentrations of blood and water?
Is there a gradient after that?
questions.solution:
In parallel flow, oxygen concentrations in blood and water reach equilibrium (about 50%) [B1]
After that there is no concentration gradient, so no more diffusion. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of gill filaments and lamellae increases the efficiency of gas exchange in fish. (2)
questions.solution:
Many filaments with many lamellae, giving a large surface area [B1]
Lamellae are thin with capillaries close to the surface, giving a short diffusion distance. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why blood leaving a fish's gills can contain a higher concentration of oxygen than the water leaving the gills. (2)
hints: Where does blood leaving the lamella meet water?
Which water has the most oxygen?
questions.solution:
Counter-current flow: blood about to leave meets water that has just entered (highest oxygen concentration) [B1]
So a concentration gradient is maintained all along the lamella. [B1]

questions.prompt: A disease makes the lamellae on a fish's gill filaments fuse together. Explain how this affects gas exchange. (3)
hints: Can water flow between the lamellae?
questions.solution:
Reduces surface area for diffusion [B1]
Water cannot flow between the lamellae / reduced ventilation [B1]
So less oxygen diffuses into the blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Uncontrolled cell division makes the epithelium of a fish's gill lamellae thicker. Explain how this affects the fish. (3)
hints: What does the fish need oxygen for?
questions.solution:
Longer diffusion distance [B1]
So slower / less diffusion of oxygen into the blood [B1]
Less aerobic respiration / less ATP, so the fish is less active. [B1]

questions.prompt: Pollution causes a thick layer of mucus to cover the gills of fish. Explain how this reduces gas exchange. (3)
questions.solution:
Increases diffusion distance [B1]
Reduces water flow over lamellae / lamellae stick together, reducing surface area [B1]
So less oxygen diffuses into the blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of rings of cartilage in the trachea. (2)
hints: What happens to pressure in the airways when breathing in?
questions.solution:
Keep the trachea open / stop it collapsing when pressure falls during inspiration [B1]
So air can flow freely to the lungs. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why insect tracheoles are thin-walled and highly branched. (2)
hints: How close do they get to cells?
questions.solution:
Thin walls give a short diffusion distance [B1]
Highly branched, giving a large surface area / reaching every cell. [B1]

questions.prompt: Insects can pump air through their tracheae by contracting abdominal muscles. Explain why it is important that the tracheae do not collapse. (2)
hints: What would a collapsed tube do to airflow?
questions.solution:
Collapse would block air flow [B1]
So less oxygen would reach respiring tissues. [B1]

questions.prompt: What are alveoli? (1)
questions.solution: Tiny air sacs at the ends of bronchioles where gas exchange occurs. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why air moves into the lungs when the volume of the thorax increases. (3)
hints: What happens to pressure when volume increases?
questions.solution:
Increasing volume decreases the pressure in the lungs [B1]
Pressure falls below atmospheric pressure [B1]
Air moves in down the pressure gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how elastic tissue in the walls of the alveoli helps expiration. (3)
hints: What happens to the elastic tissue when you breathe in?
questions.solution:
Elastic tissue stretches during inspiration [B1]
Recoils during expiration [B1]
Helping to push air out without muscle contraction (passive at rest). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by pulmonary ventilation rate and how it is calculated. (3)
questions.solution:
Volume of air breathed in (or out) per minute [B1]
Pulmonary ventilation rate = tidal volume × breathing rate [B1]
Units: dm³ min⁻¹. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the airway that has C-shaped rings of cartilage and divides into two bronchi. (1)
questions.solution: Trachea. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the smallest airways, which lead into the alveoli. (1)
questions.solution: Bronchioles. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the adaptations of the insect tracheal system for gas exchange. (4)
hints: How close do the tubes get to cells?
questions.solution:
Spiracles allow air in; tracheae branch into tracheoles [B1]
Tracheoles have thin walls — short diffusion distance [B1]
Highly branched — large surface area / reach every respiring cell [B1]
Abdominal pumping ventilates the system / fluid in tracheole ends withdrawn during activity. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the adaptations of the human lungs for gas exchange. (4)
hints: Think of surface area, distance and gradient.
How is the gradient kept steep?
questions.solution:
Millions of alveoli give a large surface area [B1]
Alveolar and capillary walls are one cell thick — short diffusion distance [B1]
Ventilation brings fresh air [B1]
Blood flow in capillaries maintains a steep concentration gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the adaptations of fish gills for gas exchange. (4)
hints: How do blood and water flow?
questions.solution:
Many filaments covered in lamellae — large surface area [B1]
Thin lamellae with capillaries close to the surface — short diffusion distance [B1]
Counter-current flow maintains a concentration gradient along the whole lamella [B1]
One-way ventilation of water over the gills. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the pathway taken by oxygen from the air outside an insect to a muscle cell. (4)
questions.solution:
Air enters through spiracles [B1]
Into the tracheae [B1]
Then into the tracheoles [B1]
Oxygen diffuses from the tracheoles into the muscle cells down a concentration gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the pathway taken by oxygen from the water around a fish into its blood. (4)
hints: How does water get to the gills?
questions.solution:
Water enters through the mouth and passes over the gills [B1]
Over the gill filaments and lamellae [B1]
Oxygen diffuses across the thin lamella epithelium into the blood [B1]
Counter-current flow maintains the concentration gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: At night, carbon dioxide produced by a mesophyll cell leaves the leaf. Describe its pathway. (4)
questions.solution:
CO₂ diffuses out of the cell (through the membrane and wall) [B1]
Into the air spaces in the spongy mesophyll [B1]
Diffuses through the air spaces to the stomata [B1]
Out through the stomata down a concentration gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: In asthma, FEV is reduced much more than FVC. In fibrosis, FEV and FVC are reduced by similar proportions. Use the table to decide which group has fibrosis. Explain your answer with calculations. (3)
hints: Calculate the percentage fall in FEV and FVC for each group.
Which group has similar falls in both?
questions.solution:
Group X: FEV falls 50% but FVC only 8% — pattern of asthma [B1]
Group Y: FEV falls 35% and FVC 36% — similar, so fibrosis [B1]
So group Y has fibrosis. [B1]
questions.table:
Group | FEV / dm³ | FVC / dm³
Healthy | 4.0 | 5.0
X | 2.0 | 4.6
Y | 2.6 | 3.2

questions.prompt: Explain why FEV is reduced in people with asthma, but FVC is affected much less. (3)
hints: Can the lungs still hold the same volume?
questions.solution:
Bronchioles are narrowed (muscle contraction / inflammation / mucus) [B1]
So air cannot be breathed out quickly — FEV falls [B1]
Alveoli are not damaged, so the total volume (FVC) is similar. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why FVC is reduced in people with pulmonary fibrosis. (3)
hints: What does scar tissue do to the alveoli?
questions.solution:
Scar tissue makes alveolar walls thicker / stiffer and less elastic [B1]
So the lungs cannot expand fully [B1]
Smaller volume of air can be breathed in and out. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why breathing rate stays high for a few minutes after vigorous exercise stops. (2)
questions.solution:
Lactate built up from anaerobic respiration [B1]
Extra oxygen needed to oxidise lactate / repay oxygen debt and remove CO₂. [B1]

questions.prompt: During exercise, CO₂ production rises, yet breathed-out pCO₂ rises only slightly. Suggest one physiological change that explains this and how it removes extra CO₂. (2)
questions.solution:
Increased breathing rate / depth (ventilation) [B1]
Removes CO₂ from the alveoli faster, maintaining the diffusion gradient — CO₂ diluted in more air. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how ventilation maintains a steep concentration gradient for oxygen in the alveoli. (2)
questions.solution:
Brings fresh air with high oxygen into the alveoli [B1]
Removes air with low oxygen / high CO₂, while blood flow carries oxygen away. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how inspiration happens. (2)
questions.solution:
External intercostal muscles and diaphragm contract — ribs move up and out, diaphragm flattens [B1]
Volume of thorax increases, pressure falls below atmospheric, air moves in. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two structural features of fish gills that increase the surface area for gas exchange. (1)
questions.solution: Many gill filaments; many lamellae on each filament. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the mechanism in fish gills that keeps a diffusion gradient along the whole lamella. (1)
questions.solution: Counter-current flow / exchange. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two features of the insect tracheal system that make gas exchange efficient. (1)
questions.solution: Many tracheoles reaching cells (short diffusion distance); thin walls / fluid at tracheole ends / spiracles. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles in increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity. (2)
questions.solution:
Diaphragm contracts and flattens (moves down) [B1]
External intercostals contract, moving ribcage up and out. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe forced expiration. (2)
questions.solution:
Internal intercostal muscles contract, pulling ribs down and in (abdominal muscles push diaphragm up) [B1]
Volume decreases, pressure rises above atmospheric, air forced out. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the pathway taken by air from the nose to the alveoli. (2)
questions.solution:
Trachea, bronchi, bronchioles [B1]
To alveoli. [B1]

questions.prompt: Asbestosis can be diagnosed without a biopsy if five conditions are met. Three are scar tissue on a lung scan, reduced gas exchange and shortness of breath. Asbestosis appears 15–40 years after exposure. Suggest the other two conditions. (2)
questions.solution:
A history of exposure to asbestos [B1]
At least 15 years since first exposure / other causes ruled out. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why fibrosis reduces the efficiency of gas exchange. (2)
questions.solution:
Scar tissue thickens the alveolar walls, increasing diffusion distance [B1]
Lungs less elastic, so less air ventilated / smaller surface area. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why people with emphysema are often short of breath. (2)
questions.solution:
Alveolar walls broken down, so smaller surface area [B1]
Less oxygen diffuses into the blood / less elastic so less air exhaled. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two advantages of diagnosing a lung disease without a biopsy. (2)
questions.solution:
Avoids an invasive procedure — less pain / risk of infection / damage [B1]
Faster / cheaper diagnosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two ways lung function can be measured without surgery. (2)
questions.solution:
Spirometer — measure tidal volume / vital capacity / FEV₁ [B1]
Peak flow meter / blood oxygen saturation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how FEV₁ (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) indicates lung disease. (2)
questions.solution:
Narrowed airways / less elastic lungs reduce how fast air can be breathed out [B1]
So FEV₁ is lower than normal. [B1]

category: Organisms exchange substances with their environment

questions.prompt: Epithelial cells lining the ileum absorb glucose rapidly. Suggest two features of these cells that increase the rate of absorption, and explain how each feature does so. (2)
hints: Glucose absorption uses co-transport, which depends on ATP.
questions.solution:
Microvilli, so a large surface area (for carrier proteins / diffusion) [B1]
Many carrier / co-transporter proteins, so more glucose transported at once [B1]
Many mitochondria, so more ATP for active transport (of Na⁺ out of the cell). [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any two features, each with a linked explanation (1 mark each).

questions.prompt: Amylase is secreted into the lumen of the gut, but maltase is attached to the cell-surface membranes of epithelial cells in the ileum. Suggest an advantage of maltase being membrane-bound. (2)
hints: Where is glucose produced if the enzyme is on the membrane?
Think about what glucose has to reach to be absorbed.
questions.solution:
Glucose is produced close to the co-transporter / carrier proteins [B1]
So it is absorbed quickly / maintains a concentration gradient / is not lost or used by gut bacteria. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of membrane-bound disaccharidases in the ileum. (2)
hints: Name a disaccharide and its products.
Why does it matter that the products are small?
questions.solution:
Hydrolyse disaccharides (e.g. maltose / sucrose / lactose) into monosaccharides [B1]
Monosaccharides can then be absorbed (by co-transport / facilitated diffusion). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how endopeptidases and exopeptidases work together to digest proteins. (2)
hints: The prefixes endo- and exo- tell you where on the chain they act.
How does one enzyme help the other?
questions.solution:
Endopeptidases hydrolyse peptide bonds within the polypeptide / between amino acids in the middle [B1]
Exopeptidases hydrolyse peptide bonds at the ends, removing single amino acids / dipeptides [B1]
Endopeptidases create more ends for exopeptidases to act on. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any 2 points.

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of bile salts and lipase in the digestion of lipids. (2)
hints: Bile salts don't digest anything — what do they do to fat droplets?
questions.solution:
Bile salts emulsify lipids into small droplets, increasing surface area (for lipase) [B1]
Lipase hydrolyses (ester bonds in) triglycerides into monoglycerides / glycerol and fatty acids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Amylase was mixed with starch solution at 37 °C. The table shows the composition of samples taken at 10 and 30 minutes. Explain the differences between the two samples. (3)
hints: Why is there no starch left at 30 minutes?
questions.solution:
Amylase hydrolyses glycosidic bonds in starch, producing maltose [B1]
More time, so more starch hydrolysed / more maltose [B1]
By 30 minutes all the starch has been hydrolysed (substrate used up). [B1]
questions.table:
Sample | Starch / mg cm⁻³ | Maltose / mg cm⁻³
10 min | 4.0 | 1.2
30 min | 0.0 | 3.5

questions.prompt: A protease was mixed with a protein solution. The table shows samples taken at 20 and 60 minutes. Explain the differences. (3)
questions.solution:
Protease hydrolyses peptide bonds [B1]
Protein broken down into peptides / amino acids, so protein falls and amino acids rise [B1]
More hydrolysis over the longer time. [B1]
questions.table:
Sample | Protein / mg cm⁻³ | Amino acids / mg cm⁻³
20 min | 5.0 | 0.8
60 min | 1.0 | 3.6

questions.prompt: Lipase was added to a milk and sodium carbonate mixture. The pH fell from 8.0 to 6.5 over 20 minutes, falling quickly at first, then slowly. Explain these results. (3)
hints: What are the products of lipid hydrolysis?
Why does the rate slow down?
questions.solution:
Lipase hydrolyses triglycerides (ester bonds) [B1]
Producing fatty acids, which lower the pH [B1]
Rate slows as the substrate is used up / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how monoglycerides and fatty acids are absorbed by ileum epithelial cells and leave them as chylomicrons. (3)
hints: How do the products reach the cell?
questions.solution:
Micelles carry monoglycerides and fatty acids to the cell surface [B1]
They diffuse across the membrane (lipid-soluble) [B1]
Recombined into triglycerides in the endoplasmic reticulum [B1]
Packaged with proteins into chylomicrons (Golgi), which leave by exocytosis into lacteals / lymph. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.
