questions.prompt: Explain why fatty acids can cross the cell-surface membrane by simple diffusion but glucose cannot. (3)
hints: Which part of the membrane must the molecule cross?
Is each molecule polar or non-polar?
questions.solution:
Fatty acids are non-polar / lipid-soluble [B1]
So they pass through the phospholipid bilayer [B1]
Glucose is polar / water-soluble, so needs carrier or channel proteins. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the roles of bile salts in the digestion and absorption of lipids. (3)
hints: What do bile salts do to large fat droplets?
What structures do they form with the products?
questions.solution:
Emulsify lipids into small droplets, increasing surface area for lipase [B1]
Form micelles with monoglycerides and fatty acids [B1]
Micelles carry these to the epithelial cells / maintain a concentration gradient for diffusion. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the complete digestion of protein in a mammal. (4)
questions.solution:
Endopeptidases hydrolyse peptide bonds within the chain [B1]
Exopeptidases hydrolyse bonds at the ends, removing amino acids [B1]
Membrane-bound dipeptidases hydrolyse dipeptides into amino acids [B1]
Final stage at the epithelium of the ileum. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the complete digestion of lipids in a mammal. (4)
hints: Which enzyme, and what are the products?
questions.solution:
Bile salts emulsify lipids into small droplets, increasing surface area [B1]
Lipase hydrolyses ester bonds [B1]
Producing monoglycerides and fatty acids [B1]
These form micelles with bile salts. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the complete digestion of sucrose and lactose in a mammal. (4)
questions.solution:
Sucrase and lactase are membrane-bound on ileum epithelial cells [B1]
They hydrolyse glycosidic bonds [B1]
Sucrose → glucose + fructose [B1]
Lactose → glucose + galactose. [B1]

questions.prompt: Untreated coeliac disease damages the villi of the small intestine. Explain why people with this disease may lose weight. (3)
hints: What do villi do to surface area?
What happens to absorption of products of digestion?
questions.solution:
Damaged villi give a smaller surface area [B1]
So less absorption of glucose / amino acids / fatty acids [B1]
So less energy / materials available, leading to weight loss. [B1]

questions.prompt: Damage to the microvilli removes membrane-bound disaccharidases from the ileum. Explain why this causes diarrhoea. (3)
hints: What do they do to water potential?
questions.solution:
Disaccharides are not hydrolysed, so not absorbed [B1]
They lower the water potential of the gut contents [B1]
Water moves into the lumen by osmosis, giving watery faeces. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how villi increase the rate of absorption in the small intestine. (3)
hints: Think about distance and blood supply.
questions.solution:
Large surface area (and microvilli increase it further) [B1]
Thin epithelium gives a short diffusion distance [B1]
Good blood supply maintains a steep concentration gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why insulin cannot be taken as a tablet. (3)
hints: What type of molecule is insulin?
What happens to proteins in the gut?
questions.solution:
Insulin is a protein [B1]
Hydrolysed by endopeptidases / exopeptidases in the gut [B1]
Broken into amino acids / loses its shape, so it no longer works. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a protein drug taken by mouth would be digested. (3)
hints: What happens at the ileum epithelium?
questions.solution:
Endopeptidases hydrolyse peptide bonds within the polypeptide [B1]
Exopeptidases remove amino acids from the ends [B1]
Dipeptidases on the ileum epithelium hydrolyse dipeptides into amino acids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why protein digestion is faster when endopeptidases and exopeptidases work together. (3)
questions.solution:
Endopeptidases break the polypeptide into many shorter chains [B1]
Creating more ends [B1]
So more sites for exopeptidases to act on, speeding up hydrolysis. [B1]

questions.prompt: What are villi? (1)
hints: What do they do to surface area?
questions.solution: Finger-like projections of the small intestine wall that increase surface area. [B1]

questions.prompt: Vitamin D is lipid-soluble. Suggest why people who produce very little bile may become deficient in vitamin D. (3)
hints: What do bile salts form with lipids?
How does vitamin D reach the epithelium?
questions.solution:
Bile salts needed to emulsify lipids / form micelles [B1]
Vitamin D is carried to epithelial cells in micelles [B1]
Fewer micelles, so less vitamin D absorbed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how micelles increase the rate of absorption of fatty acids. (3)
hints: Are fatty acids soluble in the watery gut contents?
What do micelles carry and where?
questions.solution:
Micelles carry insoluble fatty acids / monoglycerides through the watery lumen to the epithelium [B1]
Release them close to the cell-surface membrane [B1]
Maintaining a high concentration there / steep gradient, so faster diffusion. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the rate of lipid digestion increases when bile salts are present. (4)
hints: What do bile salts do to large fat droplets?
questions.solution:
Bile salts emulsify lipids into many small droplets [B1]
Larger surface area of lipid exposed [B1]
More lipase can bind / more enzyme–substrate complexes form [B1]
So triglycerides are hydrolysed faster. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of lipase and micelles in the digestion and absorption of lipids. (4)
hints: What do micelles carry, and where?
questions.solution:
Lipase hydrolyses ester bonds in triglycerides [B1]
Producing monoglycerides and fatty acids [B1]
These combine with bile salts to form micelles [B1]
Micelles carry them to the epithelium, where they are released and diffuse into the cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: A gallstone blocks the bile duct, so no bile reaches the small intestine. Explain why the person's faeces contain a lot of fat. (4)
hints: What do bile salts normally do?
Without them, what happens to digestion and absorption?
questions.solution:
No emulsification, so smaller surface area for lipase [B1]
Less lipid hydrolysed [B1]
No micelles formed, so less absorption of fatty acids / monoglycerides [B1]
Undigested / unabsorbed lipid passes out in the faeces. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why humans can digest starch but not cellulose. (2)
hints: Do humans make an enzyme for β-glycosidic bonds?
questions.solution:
Amylase's active site is complementary to starch / α-glycosidic bonds [B1]
Humans have no enzyme (cellulase) complementary to the β-glycosidic bonds in cellulose. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how amino acids are absorbed into the blood from the ileum. (4)
hints: Amino acids are absorbed like glucose.
questions.solution:
Na⁺ actively pumped out of epithelial cells into the blood (Na⁺/K⁺ pump) [B1]
Keeps a low Na⁺ concentration in the cell [B1]
Na⁺ diffuses in from the lumen through a co-transporter, carrying amino acids [B1]
Amino acids move into the blood by facilitated diffusion. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why proteins must be digested into amino acids before they can be absorbed. (4)
hints: What carriers are in the membranes?
questions.solution:
Proteins are too large to cross cell membranes [B1]
Hydrolysis produces small, soluble amino acids [B1]
Amino acids can be absorbed by co-transport / carrier proteins [B1]
Amino acids are used to build the body's own proteins. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how dipeptides are hydrolysed and the products absorbed in the ileum. (4)
questions.solution:
Membrane-bound dipeptidases on the epithelial cells [B1]
Hydrolyse the peptide bond, producing two amino acids [B1]
Amino acids absorbed by co-transport with Na⁺ [B1]
Then pass into the blood by facilitated diffusion. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons why insulin is injected rather than taken as a tablet. (2)
hints: What type of molecule is insulin?
questions.solution:
Insulin is a protein, so it would be hydrolysed by proteases in the gut [B1]
Too large to be absorbed intact across the gut wall. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons why a drug made of a short DNA molecule cannot be taken by mouth. (2)
hints: What would digest nucleic acids in the gut?
questions.solution:
It would be hydrolysed by nucleases in the gut [B1]
It is too large / charged to be absorbed intact into the blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how endopeptidases and exopeptidases together increase the rate of protein digestion. (2)
questions.solution:
Endopeptidases hydrolyse peptide bonds within the polypeptide, producing shorter chains [B1]
This creates more ends for exopeptidases, which remove amino acids from the ends. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how amino acids are absorbed in the ileum. (2)
questions.solution:
Sodium ions actively transported out of epithelial cells into the blood, lowering their concentration in the cell [B1]
Amino acids enter by co-transport with sodium ions, then diffuse into the blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the enzyme and the bond broken in the final stage of protein digestion at the epithelial membrane. (2)
questions.solution:
Dipeptidase [B1]
Peptide bond (by hydrolysis). [B1]

questions.prompt: During chewing, salivary amylase acts on starch in cooked wheat. State which reducing sugar is produced and give a reason. (2)
questions.solution:
Maltose [B1]
Amylase hydrolyses glycosidic bonds in starch to give maltose. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the test for reducing sugars and the positive result. (2)
questions.solution:
Add Benedict's reagent and heat in a water bath [B1]
Colour changes from blue to green / yellow / orange / brick red. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to test for a non-reducing sugar. (2)
questions.solution:
Negative Benedict's test, then boil with dilute hydrochloric acid and neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate [B1]
Repeat Benedict's test — positive result shows a non-reducing sugar. [B1]

questions.prompt: A gut model uses pancreatic amylase. Name the other enzyme needed to digest starch completely to glucose. (1)
questions.solution: Maltase. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the enzyme that hydrolyses sucrose. (1)
questions.solution: Sucrase. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the enzyme that hydrolyses lactose and its products. (1)
questions.solution: Lactase — glucose and galactose. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a gut model, food was mixed with water, hydrochloric acid and pepsin at 37 °C for 30 minutes. State the purpose of this step. (1)
questions.solution: To model digestion in the stomach (protein digestion by pepsin in acid). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why amylase stops working in the stomach. (1)
questions.solution: Low (acidic) pH changes / denatures the active site of amylase. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why gut models are kept at 37 °C. (1)
questions.solution: To match body temperature so enzymes work as they would in the body. [B1]

questions.prompt: Chewed wheat released reducing sugar faster than blended wheat in a gut model. Explain what this suggests about chewing and starch digestion. (3)
questions.solution:
Chewing mixes food with salivary amylase, starting starch digestion [B1]
Breaks food into smaller pieces — larger surface area for enzymes [B1]
So starch hydrolysed to maltose faster. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how bile helps digest lipids. (3)
questions.solution:
Bile salts emulsify lipids into small droplets [B1]
Larger surface area for lipase [B1]
Bile salts form micelles that carry fatty acids / monoglycerides to the epithelium. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cooked starch is digested faster than raw starch. (3)
questions.solution:
Cooking breaks down starch granules / swells them (gelatinisation) [B1]
More glycosidic bonds exposed to amylase [B1]
So faster hydrolysis. [B1]

category: Organisms exchange substances with their environment

questions.prompt: A person with a protein-deficient diet has a low concentration of protein in their blood plasma. Explain why tissue fluid accumulates in their body. (2)
hints: How does plasma protein affect water potential?
At which end of the capillary does water usually return?
questions.solution:
Water potential of plasma is higher / less negative [B1]
So less water returns to the capillary by osmosis (at the venule end). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a person with high blood pressure may produce more tissue fluid than normal. (2)
hints: What forces fluid out at the arteriole end of a capillary?
What happens if that force increases?
questions.solution:
Higher hydrostatic pressure (at the arteriole end of capillaries) [B1]
So more fluid / water and small molecules forced out of the capillaries. [B1]

questions.prompt: A parasite blocks the lymph vessels in a person's leg. Explain why the leg swells. (2)
hints: Not all tissue fluid returns to the capillaries.
Where does the excess normally go?
questions.solution:
Excess tissue fluid normally drains into the lymph vessels (and back to the blood) [B1]
If blocked, tissue fluid accumulates (in the tissues). [B1]

questions.prompt: Haemoglobin from species A is 50% saturated at 2.5 kPa of oxygen; haemoglobin from species B is 50% saturated at 5.0 kPa. One species lives at high altitude. Explain which species has the higher affinity for oxygen, and which is likely to live at high altitude. (3)
hints: Which one needs less oxygen to be half-saturated?
What is the partial pressure of oxygen like at altitude?
questions.solution:
Species A has the higher affinity (50% saturated at a lower partial pressure / curve further left) [B1]
Species A likely lives at high altitude [B1]
Because the partial pressure of oxygen is low there, so its haemoglobin can still load oxygen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the Bohr effect and how it helps respiring tissues. (3)
questions.solution:
High CO₂ concentration lowers the pH of the blood [B1]
Changes the shape of haemoglobin, lowering its affinity for oxygen (curve shifts right) [B1]
So more oxygen is unloaded in respiring tissues. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve is S-shaped. (3)
hints: Is the first oxygen easy to load?
What happens to the protein's shape after it binds?
questions.solution:
The first oxygen binds with difficulty (shape of haemoglobin) [B1]
Binding changes the quaternary structure, making it easier for further oxygens to bind (cooperative binding) [B1]
Last oxygen binds less easily as there are few free sites. [B1]

questions.prompt: Small mammals have oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curves further to the right than large mammals. Explain the advantage of this. (2)
hints: Right-shifted curve = lower or higher affinity?
Small mammals have high metabolic rates.
questions.solution:
Lower affinity, so oxygen unloads more readily to respiring tissues [B1]
Supports a high rate of (aerobic) respiration / metabolic rate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Fetal haemoglobin has a dissociation curve to the left of adult haemoglobin. Explain the advantage of this. (2)
hints: Where does the fetus get its oxygen?
questions.solution:
Higher affinity for oxygen [B1]
So fetal haemoglobin can load oxygen from the mother's haemoglobin at the placenta (low partial pressure). [B1]

questions.prompt: Lugworms live in burrows where oxygen levels are low. Their haemoglobin curve is far to the left. Explain how this helps them survive. (2)
hints: What does a left-shifted curve mean for loading?
What is the partial pressure of O₂ in the burrow?
questions.solution:
High affinity, so haemoglobin can load oxygen at low partial pressures [B1]
Enough oxygen is obtained for respiration (lugworms are inactive / have low oxygen needs). [B1]

questions.prompt: At the start of ventricular systole, pressure in the left ventricle rises but no blood leaves the ventricle. Explain why. (2)
hints: Compare the ventricle pressure with the aortic pressure.
questions.solution:
Atrioventricular valve is closed and the semilunar valve is still closed [B1]
Because ventricular pressure is still lower than pressure in the aorta. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the atrioventricular valve closes at the start of ventricular systole. (2)
hints: Compare pressures in the atrium and ventricle.
What would happen if it stayed open?
questions.solution:
Pressure in the ventricle becomes higher than in the atrium [B1]
Valve is pushed shut, preventing backflow into the atrium. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain when and why the semilunar valve in the aorta opens. (2)
hints: It is a pressure difference again.
questions.solution:
When pressure in the ventricle rises above pressure in the aorta [B1]
Blood pushes the valve open and is forced into the aorta. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how pressure in the aorta is kept high when the ventricle relaxes. (2)
hints: Which valve stops blood flowing back?
What does the aortic wall do?
questions.solution:
Semilunar valve closes, preventing backflow into the ventricle [B1]
Elastic tissue in the aorta wall recoils, maintaining pressure. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of elastic tissue in the walls of arteries. (2)
questions.solution:
Stretches when blood is pumped in (systole) [B1]
Recoils during diastole, maintaining pressure / smoothing blood flow. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the semilunar valve closes at the start of ventricular diastole, and why this is important. (2)
hints: Compare pressures as the ventricle relaxes.
Where would blood go if it stayed open?
questions.solution:
Ventricle pressure falls below aortic pressure, so blood pushes the valve shut [B1]
Prevents backflow of blood into the ventricle. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the right ventricle. (2)
hints: Where does each ventricle pump blood?
questions.solution:
Left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body; right ventricle only to the lungs [B1]
So left needs to generate higher pressure — more muscle. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one similarity and one difference between pressure changes in the pulmonary artery and in the aorta during a cardiac cycle. (2)
hints: Do the ventricles contract at the same time?
Which has the higher peak pressure?
questions.solution:
Similarity: both rise and fall at the same time / same shape / same volume pumped [B1]
Difference: pressure in the pulmonary artery is much lower. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one similarity and one difference between pressure changes in the left atrium and the left ventricle during a cardiac cycle. (2)
questions.solution:
Similarity: pressure rises when each contracts / both fall when relaxed [B1]
Difference: ventricle reaches a much higher pressure / contracts after the atrium. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two structural differences between an artery and a vein. (2)
hints: Compare wall thickness and lumen size.
questions.solution:
Artery has a thicker wall with more muscle and elastic tissue [B1]
Artery has a smaller lumen (relative to wall) [B1]
Veins have valves. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of a capillary suits it to its function. (2)
questions.solution:
Wall one cell thick (endothelium), so short diffusion distance for exchange with tissues [B1]
Narrow lumen slows red blood cells / presses them against the wall; many capillaries give large surface area. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why veins have valves but arteries (other than at the heart) do not. (2)
hints: What could happen to blood in veins?
questions.solution:
Blood pressure in veins is low [B1]
Valves prevent backflow; in arteries high pressure keeps blood moving forwards. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two differences between the circulatory system of a fish and that of a mammal. (2)
hints: How many times does blood pass through the heart in one circuit?
questions.solution:
Fish: single circulation (blood passes through the heart once per circuit); mammal: double [B1]
Fish heart has two chambers; mammal heart has four [B1]
Fish blood reaches the body at low pressure after the gills. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain the advantage to mammals of having a double circulation. (2)
hints: What happens to blood pressure in the lung capillaries?
questions.solution:
Blood returns to the heart after the lungs to be pumped again at high pressure, so oxygen reaches body tissues quickly [B1]
Lower pressure can be used in the lungs, avoiding damage to delicate capillaries. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the blood vessel that: (i) carries blood from the heart to the lungs, (ii) carries blood away from the kidneys, (iii) supplies the heart muscle with blood. (2)
hints: (i) It's an artery that carries deoxygenated blood.
questions.solution:
(i) pulmonary artery; (ii) renal vein; (iii) coronary arteries. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen. Explain why carbon monoxide poisoning reduces oxygen delivery to tissues. (3)
hints: What happens to the binding sites?
Is less oxygen loaded or unloaded?
questions.solution:
CO binds to the haem groups (irreversibly / very strongly) [B1]
Fewer binding sites available for oxygen, so less oxygen loaded in the lungs [B1]
So less oxygen is carried to / unloaded at the tissues. [B1]

questions.prompt: Smokers can have 5–10% of their haemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide. Explain why they tire more quickly during exercise. (3)
hints: How much oxygen can their blood carry?
What happens if muscles lack oxygen?
questions.solution:
Less haemoglobin available to carry oxygen [B1]
Less aerobic respiration in muscles [B1]
More anaerobic respiration, producing lactate, causing fatigue. [B1]

questions.prompt: People who move to high altitude make more red blood cells over several weeks. Explain the advantage. (3)
hints: What is the partial pressure of oxygen at altitude?
questions.solution:
Lower partial pressure of oxygen, so haemoglobin is less saturated in the lungs [B1]
More red blood cells / haemoglobin increase oxygen-carrying capacity [B1]
So enough oxygen reaches the tissues for respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Damaged capillaries let plasma proteins leak into the tissue fluid. Explain how this affects the return of tissue fluid to the capillaries. (2)
hints: What do proteins in tissue fluid do to its water potential?
questions.solution:
Water potential of tissue fluid is lowered / gradient between capillary and tissue fluid is reduced [B1]
So less water returns to the capillaries by osmosis, and tissue fluid builds up. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how tissue fluid is formed at the arteriole end of a capillary. (2)
hints: What is pushed out, and what stays behind?
questions.solution:
High hydrostatic pressure forces fluid out of the capillary [B1]
Water and small molecules leave; cells and large proteins stay in the blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why plasma proteins normally remain in the blood, and why this matters. (2)
hints: How big are proteins compared with gaps in capillary walls?
What do they do to water potential?
questions.solution:
Proteins are too large to pass through the capillary wall [B1]
They keep the water potential of the plasma low, so water returns by osmosis at the venule end. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of haemoglobin and explain how it is related to its function. (5)
hints: How many polypeptides and haem groups?
How does binding of one oxygen affect the others?
questions.solution:
Quaternary structure: four polypeptide chains (two α, two β) [B1]
Each has a haem group containing Fe²⁺, which binds one O₂ — four O₂ in total [B1]
Binding of the first O₂ changes the shape, making it easier for others to bind (cooperative binding) [B1]
Soluble / globular, so carried in red blood cells [B1]
Affinity falls in high CO₂ (Bohr effect), so oxygen is unloaded in respiring tissues. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the blood vessel that carries deoxygenated blood from the heart towards the alveoli. (1)
questions.solution: Pulmonary artery. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two structural features of the wall of a vein and link each to its function. (2)
hints: How much muscle does a vein wall have?
questions.solution:
Thin muscle / elastic layer — blood is at low pressure [B1]
Valves — prevent backflow [B1]
Wide lumen — less resistance to flow. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Give two structural features of the wall of an arteriole and link each to its function. (2)
hints: What can arterioles do to their diameter?
questions.solution:
Thick muscle layer — contracts to narrow the lumen / relaxes to widen it, controlling blood flow to tissues [B1]
Less elastic tissue than arteries — pressure surges are lower here. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two features of the wall of the aorta, other than elastic tissue, and link each to its function. (2)
questions.solution:
Collagen / thick wall — strength to withstand high pressure [B1]
Smooth endothelium — reduces friction; muscle layer — maintains pressure. [B1]

questions.prompt: Raising body temperature shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the right. Explain the effect on oxygen loading in the lungs and unloading in active muscles. (2)
hints: At high pO₂, is saturation much changed?
At low pO₂, does more or less oxygen unload?
questions.solution:
In the lungs (high pO₂), haemoglobin still becomes almost fully saturated — little effect on loading [B1]
In muscles (low pO₂), affinity is lower so more oxygen is unloaded. [B1]

questions.prompt: A lower blood pH shifts the dissociation curve to the right. Explain the effect on loading and unloading of oxygen. (2)
hints: Where is pH lowest in the body?
questions.solution:
Loading in the lungs is barely affected (high pO₂ still saturates haemoglobin) [B1]
More oxygen unloads in respiring tissues where CO₂ / acid lowers pH. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a cold-blooded animal, low temperature shifts the dissociation curve to the left. Explain the effect on loading and unloading of oxygen. (2)
hints: Where does higher affinity matter most?
questions.solution:
Loading at the gas exchange surface is similar (or slightly easier) [B1]
Less oxygen is unloaded in tissues — but the animal's cold tissues need less oxygen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the pathway taken by blood from the lungs to the liver. Name the blood vessels, heart chambers and valves involved. (5)
hints: Which vessel brings blood back from the lungs?
questions.solution:
Pulmonary vein to the left atrium [B1]
Through the left atrioventricular (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle [B1]
Through the semilunar valve into the aorta [B1]
Aorta to the hepatic artery [B1]
Hepatic artery to the liver. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the pathway taken by blood from the legs to the lungs. Name the blood vessels, heart chambers and valves involved. (5)
hints: Which large vein enters the heart?
Which side of the heart pumps to the lungs?
questions.solution:
Veins of the legs to the (inferior) vena cava [B1]
Vena cava to the right atrium [B1]
Through the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) valve into the right ventricle [B1]
Through the semilunar valve into the pulmonary artery [B1]
Pulmonary artery to the lungs. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the pathway taken by absorbed glucose from the ileum to the heart muscle. Name the main blood vessels and heart chambers. (5)
hints: Blood from the gut goes to the liver first.
Which arteries supply the heart muscle?
questions.solution:
Hepatic portal vein to the liver, then hepatic vein to the vena cava [B1]
Right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs [B1]
Pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle [B1]
Left ventricle → aorta [B1]
Coronary arteries (branching from the aorta) supply the heart muscle. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the pressure and volume changes and valve movements in the left side of the heart during one cardiac cycle. (5)
questions.solution:
Atrial systole: atrium contracts, pressure rises, blood pushed into ventricle through open AV valve [B1]
Ventricular systole: ventricle contracts, pressure exceeds atrium so AV valve closes [B1]
When ventricle pressure exceeds aorta, semilunar valve opens and blood leaves [B1]
Diastole: ventricle relaxes, pressure falls below aorta so semilunar valve closes [B1]
Pressure falls below atrium, AV valve opens and ventricle fills. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of the heart and its vessels ensures blood flows in one direction only. (5)
hints: What makes them open and close?
questions.solution:
Atrioventricular valves between atria and ventricles [B1]
Semilunar valves in the aorta and pulmonary artery [B1]
Valves open when pressure is higher behind them and close when pressure is higher in front [B1]
Prevents backflow into atria / ventricles [B1]
Tendons (chordae tendineae) stop AV valves turning inside out. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why binding of one oxygen molecule to haemoglobin makes it easier for a second oxygen molecule to bind. (2)
questions.solution:
Binding of the first oxygen changes the tertiary / quaternary structure of haemoglobin [B1]
Uncovering another haem group binding site. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin is S-shaped. (2)
hints: Is the first oxygen easy to load?
questions.solution:
First oxygen binds with difficulty, then changes shape making it easier for more to bind (steep part) [B1]
Final oxygen harder to bind as most sites are full (curve levels off). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the Bohr effect and its advantage during exercise. (2)
hints: What does CO₂ do to affinity?
questions.solution:
Higher CO₂ lowers blood pH, reducing haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen (curve shifts right) [B1]
So more oxygen unloads to respiring muscles. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the valve between the left atrium and left ventricle, and the chamber that pumps blood into the aorta. (1)
questions.solution: Bicuspid / mitral (atrioventricular) valve; left ventricle. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the blood vessel that carries blood from the right ventricle and the valve at its base. (1)
questions.solution: Pulmonary artery; semilunar valve. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the blood vessel that brings oxygenated blood to the heart, and the chamber it enters. (1)
questions.solution: Pulmonary vein; left atrium. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how an atrioventricular valve keeps blood flowing in one direction. (2)
questions.solution:
Opens when pressure in the atrium is higher than in the ventricle [B1]
Closes when ventricle pressure exceeds atrium, preventing backflow (tendons stop it inverting). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how semilunar valves prevent backflow of blood into the ventricles. (2)
hints: Pressure in the artery vs ventricle.
questions.solution:
Open when ventricle pressure is higher than in the artery [B1]
Close when artery pressure exceeds ventricle pressure (diastole), preventing backflow. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why veins have valves but arteries (apart from at the heart) do not. (2)
questions.solution:
Blood pressure in veins is low, so there's a risk of backflow [B1]
Arteries have high pressure, so blood keeps flowing forward. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how tissue fluid is formed and returned to the blood. (3)
hints: Hydrostatic pressure at the arterial end.
Water potential at the venous end.
questions.solution:
High hydrostatic pressure at the arterial end forces fluid out of capillaries [B1]
Proteins remain, lowering the water potential of the blood [B1]
At the venous end water returns by osmosis; excess drains into the lymph. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why high blood pressure can cause tissue fluid to build up (oedema). (3)
questions.solution:
Higher hydrostatic pressure in capillaries [B1]
More fluid forced out at the arterial end [B1]
Less returned at the venous end / lymph can't drain it all, so fluid accumulates. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the advantage of the Bohr effect during intense exercise. (2)
questions.solution:
Higher CO₂ / lower pH reduces haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen [B1]
More oxygen unloaded to respiring muscles. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin. (2)
hints: Where does the fetus get oxygen?
questions.solution:
Fetal haemoglobin must load oxygen from the mother's blood in the placenta [B1]
Where pO₂ is lower, so a higher affinity allows oxygen transfer. [B1]

questions.prompt: Animals living at high altitude have haemoglobin with a higher affinity for oxygen. Explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Lower pO₂ at altitude [B1]
Higher affinity means haemoglobin is still saturated in the lungs. [B1]

questions.prompt: A hormone (EPO) increases the proportion of blood made up of red cells. Heart attacks result from reduced glucose and oxygen delivery to heart muscle. Suggest how overuse of EPO could increase the risk of a heart attack. (2)
questions.solution:
More red cells make blood more viscous / thicker [B1]
Increased risk of clots in coronary arteries, reducing oxygen and glucose supply to heart muscle. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how atheroma formation can lead to a heart attack. (2)
questions.solution:
Atheroma narrows coronary arteries / can rupture, causing a clot (thrombosis) [B1]
Less oxygen to heart muscle, so cells die (myocardial infarction). [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two risk factors for cardiovascular disease and explain one. (2)
questions.solution:
Two from: smoking; high blood pressure; high LDL / cholesterol; obesity; inactivity [B1]
E.g. high blood pressure damages artery lining, increasing atheroma formation. [B1]

questions.prompt: A chemical binds to haemoglobin and reduces its affinity for oxygen. Describe where its dissociation curve would lie compared with the normal curve. (1)
hints: Lower affinity — less saturated at each pO₂.
questions.solution: To the right of (below) the normal curve. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe where the dissociation curve of myoglobin lies compared with haemoglobin, and why. (1)
questions.solution: To the left — myoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the effect of increased carbon dioxide on the haemoglobin dissociation curve. (1)
questions.solution: Shifts it to the right (lower affinity). [B1]

questions.prompt: A chemical in red blood cells reduces haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen. Suggest and explain a situation in which this would benefit a person. (2)
hints: When do tissues need more oxygen?
questions.solution:
At high altitude / during exercise / anaemia [B1]
More oxygen unloaded to respiring tissues. [B1]

questions.prompt: Small mammals have haemoglobin with a lower affinity for oxygen than large mammals. Explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Small mammals have a larger SA : V ratio, lose heat faster, so higher metabolic rate [B1]
Lower affinity unloads more oxygen for respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Lugworms live in burrows with low oxygen. Explain why their haemoglobin has a high affinity for oxygen. (2)
questions.solution:
Little oxygen in the environment [B1]
High affinity lets haemoglobin load oxygen at low pO₂. [B1]

category: Organisms exchange substances with their environment

questions.prompt: A ring of bark, including the phloem, was removed from a tree trunk. After some weeks, the trunk swelled just above the ring and the tissue there had a high sucrose concentration. Explain how this supports the idea that phloem transports sugars. (2)
hints: Which direction were sugars moving from the leaves?
questions.solution:
Phloem removed, so sucrose cannot move down past the ring [B1]
Sucrose accumulates above the ring (causing swelling). [B1]

questions.prompt: A leaf was supplied with carbon dioxide containing radioactive ¹⁴C. One hour later, radioactivity was detected in the phloem of the stem and in the roots. Explain these results. (2)
hints: What is CO₂ used to make in the leaf?
questions.solution:
¹⁴CO₂ used in photosynthesis to make (radioactive) sugars / sucrose [B1]
Sucrose translocated in the phloem from the leaf (source) to the roots (sink). [B1]

questions.prompt: An aphid's mouthparts were cut off while feeding on a stem, leaving them inserted into a sieve tube. Sap kept flowing out of the cut mouthparts. Explain how this supports the mass flow hypothesis. (2)
hints: What does the sap flowing out show about the contents of the sieve tube?
What does mass flow depend on?
questions.solution:
Sap is under (hydrostatic) pressure in the sieve tubes [B1]
Mass flow depends on a pressure gradient pushing sap from source to sink. [B1]

questions.prompt: Plants were treated with chemical X, which damages phloem. Transpiration rate (mean ± SD) was 2.3 ± 0.4 g h⁻¹ in treated plants and 2.5 ± 0.5 g h⁻¹ in untreated plants. Explain how these data support the idea that chemical X did not affect the xylem. (2)
hints: Is the difference between the means large?
questions.solution:
Means are similar and the standard deviations overlap [B1]
So no significant difference — water is still transported through the xylem. [B1]

questions.prompt: Coloured dye was added to the water around the roots of two plants: one with its phloem damaged and one untreated. In both, dye reached the leaves after 20 minutes. Explain what this shows. (2)
hints: Which tissue carries water up the plant?
questions.solution:
Dye is carried in the xylem (with the transpiration stream) [B1]
Same time in both, so xylem still working / not damaged. [B1]

questions.prompt: A ring of bark was removed from a branch. The leaves above the ring did not wilt. Explain why. (2)
hints: Is the xylem part of the bark?
What do leaves need to stay turgid?
questions.solution:
Xylem is deeper in the stem / not removed with the bark [B1]
So water still reaches the leaves, keeping cells turgid. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Scientists measured magnesium ion concentration in old and young leaves of plants. In some plants the phloem in the leaf stalks of old leaves was killed with steam. The table shows the results.

Use the data to make conclusions about how magnesium ions move in the plant. (4)
hints: Compare old leaves with and without working phloem.
Where would Mg²⁺ go if it could leave old leaves?
questions.solution:
Old leaves accumulate more Mg²⁺ when their phloem is killed, so Mg²⁺ normally leaves old leaves in the phloem [B1]
Young leaves receive less when phloem is blocked, so they normally get Mg²⁺ from old leaves via the phloem [B1]
Mg²⁺ is redistributed / mobile (old → young leaves) [B1]
Young leaves still contain some Mg²⁺, so some arrives another way, e.g. in the xylem from the roots. [B1]
questions.table:
Leaves | Untreated | Phloem killed
Old | 20 | 32
Young | 30 | 14

questions.prompt: Radioactive phosphate was supplied to the roots of a plant. After 6 hours, radioactivity was found in the xylem of the stem. After 24 hours, it was found in the phloem and in young leaves at the shoot tip. Use these results to describe how phosphate moves through the plant. (4)
hints: What is the first tissue it travels in?
Which tissue carries things to growing regions (sinks)?
questions.solution:
Phosphate absorbed by roots and transported up in the xylem (transpiration stream) [B1]
Later moved into the phloem [B1]
Phloem carries it to sinks / growing regions such as young leaves [B1]
So phosphate is redistributed / can move both up and down the plant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Calcium ion concentration in old leaves increases over time, while young leaves stay low in calcium. Killing the phloem has no effect on calcium distribution. Calcium deficiency symptoms appear first in young leaves. Use this information to explain how calcium moves in plants. (4)
hints: Which leaves lose most water by transpiration?
questions.solution:
Calcium is moved only in the xylem / transpiration stream [B1]
It is not transported (redistributed) in the phloem [B1]
Old (large) leaves transpire more, so receive and accumulate more calcium [B1]
Calcium cannot move from old to young leaves, so deficiency shows in young leaves. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one adaptation of the leaves of a xerophytic plant and explain how it reduces water loss. (2)
hints: Think about the cuticle, stomata or leaf shape.
Link the feature to evaporation or the water potential gradient.
questions.solution:
Feature, e.g. thick waxy cuticle / sunken stomata / hairs / rolled leaves / fewer stomata [B1]
Matching explanation, e.g. less evaporation / traps moist air so a smaller water potential gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Marram grass leaves roll up in dry conditions, with their stomata on the inside. Explain how this reduces water loss. (2)
hints: What builds up inside the rolled leaf?
How does that affect the diffusion gradient?
questions.solution:
Traps humid / moist air around the stomata [B1]
Reduces the water potential gradient, so less water lost by transpiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Cacti have spines instead of broad leaves. Explain how this helps them survive in deserts. (2)
hints: What is the surface area of a spine compared with a leaf?
Where does photosynthesis take place instead?
questions.solution:
Spines have a small surface area, so less water lost by transpiration [B1]
Photosynthesis takes place in the (green) stem instead. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a plant's stomata close when it is short of water. (2)
hints: What is lost through open stomata?
What would happen if this continued?
questions.solution:
Reduces water loss by transpiration [B1]
Prevents the plant losing turgor / wilting / dehydrating. [B1]

questions.prompt: Plants grown in high CO₂ concentrations develop fewer stomata. A newspaper claimed this will make crops more drought-tolerant as CO₂ levels rise. Evaluate this claim. (4)
hints: How does stomatal density affect water loss?
What else changes as CO₂ rises?
questions.solution:
Fewer stomata means less transpiration / water loss, supporting the claim [B1]
Enough CO₂ can still enter because its concentration is higher [B1]
But rising temperatures with climate change could increase transpiration [B1]
Stomata may be larger / open for longer; only some species studied / lab not field conditions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Mean transpiration rate (± SD) was 1.2 ± 0.3 g h⁻¹ for a hairy-leaved species and 1.6 ± 0.5 g h⁻¹ for a smooth-leaved species. Evaluate the claim that leaf hairs reduce transpiration. (4)
hints: Are the two species identical apart from hairs?
questions.solution:
Hairy species has a lower mean, consistent with hairs trapping moist air / reducing the water potential gradient [B1]
SD ranges overlap, so the difference may not be significant [B1]
Two different species — other differences (stomatal number, leaf area, cuticle) could explain it [B1]
Need a statistical test / more data. [B1]

questions.prompt: The transpiration rate of a tree rises from early morning to early afternoon, then falls in the evening. Explain these changes. (4)
hints: What happens to stomata as light increases?
How do temperature and humidity change over the day?
questions.solution:
Light increases, so stomata open [B1]
Temperature rises, so faster evaporation / diffusion of water vapour [B1]
Humidity falls, so steeper water potential gradient [B1]
In the evening light falls, stomata close and it is cooler, so transpiration falls. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why transpiration rate increases in windy conditions. (4)
hints: What builds up around the leaf on a still day?
What does wind do to it?
questions.solution:
Wind removes water vapour from around the stomata [B1]
Maintains a steep water potential gradient [B1]
So faster diffusion of water vapour out of the leaf [B1]
More water pulled up the xylem (cohesion–tension). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why transpiration rate falls when the air is very humid. (4)
hints: Compare water potential inside the leaf and outside.
questions.solution:
Humid air has a high water potential [B1]
Smaller water potential gradient between air spaces in the leaf and outside [B1]
Slower diffusion of water vapour out of the stomata [B1]
So less water is pulled up the xylem. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe evidence that supports the mass flow hypothesis of translocation, and evidence that does not. (5)
hints: Think about ringing, aphids and radioactive tracers.
questions.solution:
For: removing a ring of phloem causes sugars to build up above the ring [B1]
For: aphid stylets show phloem sap is under pressure [B1]
For: radioactive tracers show sugars move from source to sink [B1]
Against: sugars travel to different sinks at different rates / in different directions at once [B1]
Against: sieve plates would slow mass flow / translocation stops if companion cell respiration is inhibited (active process). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how water moves from the roots to the leaves of a plant through the xylem. (5)
hints: What property of water keeps the column together?
questions.solution:
Water evaporates from leaf cells and diffuses out through stomata (transpiration) [B1]
Lowers water potential in leaf cells, so water moves out of the xylem into them [B1]
Water molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds (cohesion) [B1]
So a continuous column of water is pulled up the xylem under tension [B1]
Adhesion of water to xylem walls also helps. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the structure and function of xylem and phloem. (5)
hints: What does each carry, and in which direction?
questions.solution:
Xylem carries water and mineral ions; phloem carries organic substances (sucrose, amino acids) [B1]
Xylem flow is upwards only; phloem in both directions (source to sink) [B1]
Xylem vessels are dead, hollow tubes with no end walls; phloem sieve tubes are living with sieve plates [B1]
Xylem walls strengthened with lignin [B1]
Phloem has companion cells with many mitochondria (for active loading). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why xylem vessels having no end walls is important for water transport. (3)
questions.solution:
Forms a continuous tube [B1]
So an unbroken column of water can be pulled up (cohesion maintained) [B1]
Less resistance to flow. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why lignin in the walls of xylem vessels is important. (3)
hints: Water in xylem is under tension.
What would happen to an unsupported tube?
questions.solution:
Strengthens / supports the walls [B1]
Water in the xylem is under tension (negative pressure) [B1]
So vessels do not collapse inwards. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an air bubble in a xylem vessel stops water moving up that vessel. (3)
hints: Can tension be transmitted across a gap?
questions.solution:
Breaks the continuous column of water [B1]
Cohesion between water molecules is lost at the bubble [B1]
So tension / transpiration pull cannot be transmitted. [B1]

questions.prompt: Guard cells actively take up potassium ions when stomata open. Explain how this opens the stomata. (4)
hints: What do K⁺ ions do to water potential?
What happens to the guard cells?
questions.solution:
K⁺ ions actively transported into guard cells (using ATP) [B1]
Water potential of the guard cells is lowered [B1]
Water enters by osmosis [B1]
Guard cells become turgid, opening the pore. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how sucrose is loaded into the phloem at a source. (4)
hints: What does the companion cell pump out?
questions.solution:
H⁺ ions are actively pumped out of companion cells using ATP [B1]
H⁺ diffuses back in through co-transporter proteins, carrying sucrose [B1]
Sucrose concentration in the companion cell rises [B1]
Sucrose moves into the sieve tube (through plasmodesmata / by diffusion). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the mass flow hypothesis explains the movement of sucrose from a source to a sink. (4)
hints: What happens to water potential in the sieve tube at the source?
questions.solution:
Sucrose loaded at the source lowers the water potential of the sieve tube [B1]
Water enters from the xylem by osmosis, raising hydrostatic pressure [B1]
At the sink, sucrose is removed, so water leaves and pressure is lower [B1]
Pressure gradient pushes sap from source to sink. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why translocation in the phloem requires energy. (4)
questions.solution:
Sucrose is actively loaded at the source (H⁺ pumps use ATP) [B1]
Companion cells have many mitochondria producing ATP [B1]
Unloading at some sinks may also be active [B1]
Respiratory inhibitors stop translocation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the process that moves sugars from the leaves down a tree trunk. (1)
questions.solution: Translocation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why using a fan increases the rate of water uptake measured by a potometer. (3)
hints: What happens to the water vapour around the leaf?
questions.solution:
Air movement removes water vapour from around the leaf / stomata [B1]
Increases the water vapour potential gradient [B1]
So more transpiration, and more water is pulled up (cohesion-tension). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one reason why the rate of water uptake measured by a potometer may not equal the rate of water loss by the whole plant. (1)
questions.solution: Some water is used in photosynthesis / to keep cells turgid / the cut shoot is not a whole plant with roots. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the process by which water moves up the xylem. (1)
questions.solution: Cohesion-tension. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one feature of xylem vessels that makes them suitable for transporting water. (1)
questions.solution: No end walls / continuous tube / lignin for support / pits for lateral movement. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how reduced aquaporin in root cells would affect water uptake by a plant. (3)
hints: How does water enter root cells?
questions.solution:
Less water enters cells by osmosis (symplast pathway) [B1]
At the endodermis, the Casparian strip forces water through membranes [B1]
So water uptake / transport to the xylem would decrease. [B1]

questions.prompt: In normal plants, the percentage of radioactive carbon remaining in a leaf fell after it was given ¹⁴CO₂ but never reached zero. Suggest two reasons. (2)
questions.solution:
Some carbon used to make structural molecules in the leaf (cellulose, proteins) / stored as starch [B1]
Some used in respiration in the leaf / sucrose still being made from stored starch. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how radioactive tracers can be used to show that sucrose is transported in the phloem. (2)
questions.solution:
Supply leaf with ¹⁴CO₂, which is incorporated into sugars by photosynthesis [B1]
Cut sections and use autoradiography — radioactivity found in phloem. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how ringing experiments provide evidence that sugars are transported in the phloem. (2)
questions.solution:
Remove a ring of bark (including phloem) but leave xylem [B1]
Tissue above the ring swells with sugars, showing phloem carries sugars downwards. [B1]

questions.prompt: Sucrose inhibits production and activity of rubisco. Use the table to explain how the factors contribute to the lower dry mass of modified (type A) plants. (4)
hints: Sucrose builds up in leaves — effect on rubisco?
questions.solution:
Low sucrose transport, so sucrose accumulates in leaves (22 vs 4 mmol m⁻²) [B1]
High sucrose inhibits rubisco, so lower rate of photosynthesis (4 vs 14) [B1]
Less sugar made for growth / less biomass [B1]
Less sucrose reaches roots, so less root growth (high shoot : root ratio), less water / mineral uptake. [B1]
questions.table:
Measure | Type A | Type B
Sucrose transport / µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ | 0.1 | 3.7
Leaf sucrose / mmol m⁻² | 22 | 4
Shoot to root dry mass | 6 to 1 | 2 to 1
Photosynthesis / µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ | 4 | 14

questions.prompt: Describe the mass flow hypothesis for translocation. (4)
questions.solution:
Sucrose actively loaded into phloem sieve tubes at the source (co-transport with H⁺) [B1]
Lowers water potential, so water enters by osmosis from xylem [B1]
Increases hydrostatic pressure, pushing sap towards the sink [B1]
At the sink sucrose is removed / used, so water leaves and pressure falls. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how sucrose is loaded into phloem companion cells and sieve tubes. (4)
questions.solution:
H⁺ ions actively pumped out of companion cells (ATP) [B1]
H⁺ diffuse back in through co-transport proteins, carrying sucrose [B1]
Sucrose then diffuses through plasmodesmata into sieve tube elements [B1]
Lowers water potential in the sieve tube. [B1]

category: Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

questions.prompt: Name the two types of molecule that make up a chromosome in a eukaryotic cell. (1)
hints: Eukaryotic DNA is wound around something.
The answer includes a type of protein.
questions.solution: DNA and histones / (histone) proteins (both needed). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the DNA in a eukaryotic chromosome is wound around histones. (1)
hints: How long is the DNA in one chromosome compared with the nucleus?
questions.solution: To package / condense very long DNA so it fits in the nucleus. [B1]

questions.prompt: A stain binds more strongly to some regions of a DNA molecule than others. Suggest one feature of the DNA that could differ between these regions. (1)
hints: DNA is made of four different bases.
questions.solution: Different base sequence / proportion of particular bases (e.g. more A–T pairs) / degree of coiling. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term allele. (1)
hints: Where are they found on a chromosome?
questions.solution: A different form / base sequence of a gene (found at the same locus). [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term locus. (1)
questions.solution: The position of a gene on a chromosome / DNA molecule. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two ways in which the DNA in a mitochondrion differs from the DNA in the nucleus of the same cell. (2)
hints: Mitochondria are thought to have come from bacteria.
questions.solution:
Mitochondrial DNA is circular, nuclear DNA is linear [B1]
Mitochondrial DNA is not associated with histones [B1]
Mitochondrial DNA is shorter / has fewer genes [B1]
Mitochondrial DNA has no introns. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Give two differences between a plasmid and the main chromosome in a bacterium. (2)
hints: Compare size and the number of genes.
Can one be passed to another bacterium?
questions.solution:
Plasmid is smaller / has fewer genes [B1]
Plasmid carries non-essential genes, e.g. antibiotic resistance [B1]
Plasmids can be transferred between bacteria [B1]
There may be many copies of a plasmid but only one chromosome. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Give two similarities between DNA in prokaryotic cells and DNA in eukaryotic cells. (2)
hints: Think about the structure of the molecule.
questions.solution:
Both made of nucleotides with deoxyribose / the same four bases [B1]
Both double helix / two strands held by hydrogen bonds [B1]
Both have phosphodiester bonds / sugar–phosphate backbone [B1]
Both use the same genetic code. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the semi-conservative replication of DNA. (3)
hints: Start with what happens to the hydrogen bonds.
questions.solution:
DNA helicase breaks hydrogen bonds between strands [B1]
Both strands act as templates [B1]
Free DNA nucleotides attach by complementary base pairing [B1]
DNA polymerase joins nucleotides (forming phosphodiester bonds) [B1]
Each new molecule has one original and one new strand. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Bacteria were grown on a medium with heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) for many generations, then moved to a medium with light nitrogen (¹⁴N) for one generation. Their DNA was then all of intermediate density. Explain how this supports semi-conservative replication, and predict the result after a second generation in ¹⁴N. (3)
hints: What does each new DNA molecule contain in semi-conservative replication?
What happens when an intermediate molecule replicates in ¹⁴N?
questions.solution:
Each new molecule has one ¹⁵N (old) strand and one ¹⁴N (new) strand, so intermediate density [B1]
Conservative replication would give heavy and light bands, not intermediate [B1]
After two generations: half intermediate, half light. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three differences between DNA replication and transcription. (3)
hints: How much of the DNA is copied in each?
questions.solution:
Replication copies both strands; transcription uses one template strand [B1]
DNA polymerase vs RNA polymerase [B1]
DNA nucleotides (deoxyribose, thymine) vs RNA nucleotides (ribose, uracil) [B1]
Whole molecule copied vs one gene. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Radioactive thymidine (a DNA nucleotide containing thymine) was added to dividing cells. Describe how it becomes part of the DNA and explain why it is only taken up by cells that are replicating their DNA. (5)
hints: Why would it not go into RNA?
questions.solution:
Helicase breaks hydrogen bonds / strands separate [B1]
Both strands act as templates [B1]
Labelled thymine nucleotides pair with adenine (complementary base pairing) [B1]
DNA polymerase joins them into the new strand [B1]
Each new DNA molecule has one labelled strand [B1]
Only used during DNA replication (S phase) — RNA contains uracil, not thymine. [B1]
Any 5 of these points — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: Cells replicated their DNA once in a medium containing a labelled nucleotide, then replicated it again in a medium without the label. Describe and explain the labelling of the two chromatids of each chromosome after the second replication. (5)
hints: After the first round, how many strands of each DNA molecule are labelled?
In the second round, what does each strand pair with?
questions.solution:
After the first replication each DNA molecule has one labelled and one unlabelled strand (semi-conservative) [B1]
In the second replication the strands separate and each acts as a template [B1]
New strands are made from unlabelled nucleotides [B1]
One molecule has a labelled strand + unlabelled strand; the other is completely unlabelled [B1]
So each chromosome has one labelled and one unlabelled chromatid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of DNA helicase in DNA replication. (2)
hints: Why do the strands need to separate?
questions.solution:
Breaks hydrogen bonds between complementary bases [B1]
Unwinds / separates the two strands so each can act as a template. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of complementary base pairing in DNA replication. (2)
hints: What does this mean for the new molecules?
questions.solution:
Free nucleotides pair with template bases (A with T, C with G) by hydrogen bonds [B1]
So the new strands are exact copies / the new DNA molecules are identical. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three differences between the DNA in a chloroplast and the DNA in the nucleus of the same plant cell. (3)
hints: Think about shape, proteins and length.
questions.solution:
Chloroplast DNA is circular; nuclear DNA is linear [B1]
Chloroplast DNA not associated with histones [B1]
Chloroplast DNA is shorter / has fewer genes [B1]
Chloroplast DNA has no introns. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Bacteria grown on ¹⁵N were moved to ¹⁴N. After one generation, all the DNA was of intermediate density. Explain why this rules out conservative replication, and describe the result after two generations that would distinguish semi-conservative from dispersive replication. (3)
hints: What would conservative replication give after one generation?
Semi-conservative after two generations gives two bands; dispersive gives…?
questions.solution:
Conservative would give one heavy and one light band, not intermediate [B1]
After two generations, semi-conservative gives two bands: intermediate and light [B1]
Dispersive would give a single band between intermediate and light. [B1]

questions.prompt: Predict the DNA bands that would be seen after one and after two generations in ¹⁴N if DNA replicated conservatively. (3)
hints: In conservative replication, the original molecule stays intact.
Each new molecule is made entirely of new nucleotides.
questions.solution:
Generation 1: half heavy (¹⁵N) and half light (¹⁴N) [B1]
Generation 2: one quarter heavy, three quarters light [B1]
No intermediate band at any stage. [B1]

questions.prompt: Bacteria with all-¹⁵N DNA were grown for three generations in ¹⁴N. Assuming semi-conservative replication, what proportion of DNA molecules would contain any ¹⁵N? Explain. (3)
hints: The two original ¹⁵N strands are never broken up.
How many molecules after three generations?
questions.solution:
After 3 generations there are 8 molecules [B1]
Only 2 contain an original ¹⁵N strand (intermediate) [B1]
So 25% (1/4) contain ¹⁵N; 75% are light. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a eukaryotic chromosome and how it differs from the DNA of a prokaryote. (6)
hints: What is eukaryotic DNA wound around?
Shape and number of molecules in prokaryotes.
questions.solution:
Eukaryotic chromosome: one long linear DNA molecule [B1]
Wound around histone proteins [B1]
Coiled / condensed further [B1]
Genes at specific loci; chromosomes found in homologous pairs [B1]
Prokaryotic DNA is circular and not associated with histones [B1]
Prokaryotes may also have plasmids; DNA is shorter. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a chromosome at metaphase of mitosis. (6)
questions.solution:
Two sister chromatids [B1]
Joined at a centromere [B1]
Each chromatid is one DNA molecule (identical copies) [B1]
DNA wound around histones [B1]
Tightly coiled / condensed [B1]
Genes found at the same loci on both chromatids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how DNA polymerase joins DNA nucleotides together. (2)
hints: Which bond forms, between which parts?
questions.solution:
Condensation reactions (releasing water) [B1]
Forming phosphodiester bonds between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the deoxyribose of the next. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the 3′ end of a growing DNA strand. (4)
hints: What group is at the 3′ end?
What is the enzyme's active site complementary to?
questions.solution:
The 3′ end has a free OH group on the deoxyribose [B1]
The phosphate of a new nucleotide forms a bond with this 3′ OH [B1]
DNA polymerase's active site is complementary to the 3′ end only [B1]
So the new strand grows in the 5′ → 3′ direction. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why, during DNA replication, the two new strands are built in opposite directions. (4)
hints: How are the two template strands arranged?
Which direction can DNA polymerase work in?
questions.solution:
The two template strands are antiparallel [B1]
DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the 5′ → 3′ direction (to the 3′ end) [B1]
So the new strands grow in opposite directions [B1]
One strand is made continuously, the other in short fragments. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the DNA content per cell doubles during interphase. (3)
questions.solution:
DNA replicates (in S phase) [B1]
Semi-conservative replication makes two copies of each DNA molecule [B1]
Each chromosome now has two identical sister chromatids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two enzymes involved in semi-conservative replication of DNA. (2)
questions.solution:
DNA helicase [B1]
DNA polymerase. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of DNA helicase and DNA polymerase in DNA replication. (2)
questions.solution:
Helicase breaks hydrogen bonds between bases, unwinding / separating strands [B1]
DNA polymerase joins adjacent nucleotides by condensation, forming phosphodiester bonds. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why DNA replication is described as semi-conservative. (2)
hints: What happens to each original strand?
What is in each new molecule?
questions.solution:
Each original strand acts as a template [B1]
Each new molecule contains one original strand and one new strand. [B1]

category: Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

questions.prompt: Describe the role of transfer RNA (tRNA) in translation. (3)
hints: Each tRNA has two important regions — what is attached at each end?
Start with: each tRNA carries a specific amino acid…
questions.solution:
tRNA carries / binds a specific amino acid [B1]
Has an anticodon that is complementary to a codon on mRNA [B1]
Brings the amino acid to the ribosome (in the correct sequence) [B1]
Two tRNAs held at the ribosome so the amino acids can be joined by a peptide bond [B1]
tRNA is released (without its amino acid) and can collect another amino acid. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to an mRNA codon. It brings its amino acid to the ribosome, where two tRNAs are held so their amino acids can be joined by a peptide bond. The tRNA is then released to collect another amino acid. (Any 3 points.)

questions.prompt: Describe how pre-mRNA is produced from a gene in a eukaryotic cell. Do not include splicing in your answer. (3)
hints: Think about what has to happen to the DNA double helix first.
Start with: hydrogen bonds between the two DNA strands are broken…
questions.solution:
Hydrogen bonds between DNA strands broken / DNA helicase separates strands [B1]
Only one strand acts as a template [B1]
Free RNA nucleotides line up by complementary base pairing (uracil pairs with adenine) [B1]
RNA polymerase joins adjacent nucleotides [B1]
Forming phosphodiester bonds. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
DNA helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds so the strands separate; one strand is used as a template. Free RNA nucleotides align by complementary base pairing (U with A), and RNA polymerase joins them with phosphodiester bonds to form pre-mRNA. (Any 3 points.)

questions.prompt: Describe how a peptide bond is formed between two amino acids at a ribosome, and what then happens to the first tRNA molecule and the ribosome. (3)
hints: What type of reaction joins two monomers?
Which two groups on the amino acids react?
questions.solution:
Two tRNAs (with amino acids) are held at the ribosome [B1]
Condensation reaction (releasing water) [B1]
Between the amine group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of the other [B1]
Uses energy from ATP (hydrolysis) [B1]
First tRNA released and ribosome moves along mRNA to the next codon. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Two tRNAs bound to adjacent codons are held in the ribosome. A condensation reaction joins the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amine group of the other, using energy from ATP. The first tRNA is released and the ribosome moves one codon along the mRNA. (Any 3 points.)

questions.prompt:
A section of mRNA has the base sequence

A U G G C A U U C G A C

Give the base sequence of the DNA template strand it was transcribed from. (1)
hints: In DNA, which base pairs with U on the RNA?
questions.solution:
T A C C G T A A G C T G [B1]

Model answer:
Pair each base: A→T, U→A, G→C, C→G.
DNA template: TAC CGT AAG CTG

questions.prompt:
Three mRNA codons are

C C A   G U U   A C G

Give the base sequences of the three tRNA anticodons that bind to these codons. (1)
hints: tRNA is RNA, so it contains U, not T.
questions.solution:
GGU  CAA  UGC [B1]

Model answer:
Complementary pairing (RNA to RNA): CCA→GGU, GUU→CAA, ACG→UGC.

questions.prompt:
A DNA template strand has the base sequence

T A C G G A C T T A A G

Give the base sequence of the mRNA transcribed from this strand. (1)
hints: mRNA is complementary to the template strand.
Remember A in DNA pairs with U in RNA.
questions.solution:
A U G C C U G A A U U C [B1]

Model answer:
T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C.
mRNA: AUG CCU GAA UUC

questions.prompt: Two different proteins are produced in a eukaryotic cell from the same gene. Explain how this is possible. (2)
hints: Think about what happens to pre-mRNA before translation.
Not every exon has to be kept.
questions.solution:
Pre-mRNA is spliced / introns removed [B1]
Different exons can be kept or removed (alternative splicing), giving different mRNA and so different amino acid sequences. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why mRNA in a bacterium can be translated immediately after it is transcribed, whereas mRNA in a eukaryotic cell cannot. (2)
hints: What do eukaryotic genes contain that prokaryotic genes do not?
Where does translation happen relative to the DNA in each cell type?
questions.solution:
Prokaryotic genes do not contain introns, so no splicing is needed [B1]
Eukaryotic pre-mRNA must be spliced (introns removed) / leave the nucleus before translation. [B1]

questions.prompt: A eukaryotic gene is 3600 bases long. The polypeptide it codes for contains 450 amino acids. Use this information to explain why the gene contains far more bases than are needed to code for the polypeptide. (2)
hints: How many bases code for one amino acid?
questions.solution:
450 amino acids need only 1350 bases (+3 for the stop codon) / 3 bases per amino acid [B1]
The rest is non-coding DNA / introns, which are removed by splicing. [B1]

Model answer:
Each amino acid is coded for by a triplet, so 450 × 3 = 1350 bases (plus a stop codon). The remaining bases are introns / non-coding sequences, removed from pre-mRNA by splicing.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the genetic code being degenerate. Use an example from the table in your answer. (2)
hints: Look for an amino acid with more than one codon.
How many codons code for alanine?
questions.solution:
More than one codon / base triplet codes for the same amino acid [B1]
e.g. GCU, GCC and GCA all code for Ala. [B1]
questions.table:
mRNA codon | Amino acid
GCU | Ala
GCC | Ala
GCA | Ala
UGG | Trp
AUG | Met
GAA | Glu
GAG | Glu
CAU | His

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the genetic code being (i) universal and (ii) non-overlapping. (2)
hints: (ii) Think about how many triplets each base belongs to.
questions.solution:
(i) The same triplets code for the same amino acids in (almost) all organisms [B1]
(ii) Each base is part of only one triplet / triplets are read one after another. [B1]

questions.prompt: A polypeptide contains 312 amino acids. What is the minimum number of bases in the gene that codes for it? (1)
hints: Each amino acid is coded for by a triplet.
This is the minimum, so ignore introns.
questions.solution: 936 (accept 939, including a stop codon). [B1]

questions.prompt: A polypeptide contains 250 amino acids. How many bases code for it in the mRNA, including the stop codon? (1)
hints: The stop codon is three more bases.
questions.solution:
753 [B1]

Model answer:
250 × 3 = 750, + 3 for the stop codon = 753.

questions.prompt: The exons of a gene contain 2730 bases, not counting the stop codon. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide? (1)
hints: Each amino acid needs three bases.

questions.prompt: A gene is 9600 bases long. Its mature mRNA is 1500 bases long. The polypeptide it codes for has 480 amino acids. Explain the differences between these numbers. (3)
hints: Why is the mRNA so much shorter than the gene?
questions.solution:
Gene contains introns, which are removed by splicing, so mRNA is shorter [B1]
480 amino acids need 1440 bases (plus 3 for the stop codon) [B1]
Remaining mRNA bases are not translated (non-coding regions). [B1]

questions.prompt:
Complete the passage with the correct terms.

A gene is transcribed to make (1) ________. This is spliced to remove (2) ________. The mRNA leaves the nucleus through a (3) ________ and attaches to a (4) ________. tRNA molecules with complementary (5) ________ bring amino acids, which are joined by (6) ________ bonds. (3)
hints: Think through transcription, splicing, then translation.
The tRNA region that pairs with a codon is the…
questions.solution:
(1) pre-mRNA; (2) introns; (3) nuclear pore; (4) ribosome; (5) anticodons; (6) peptide. [B3]
6 correct = 3 marks; 4–5 correct = 2; 2–3 correct = 1.

questions.prompt: Explain how two different polypeptides can be made from one gene, and why the mature mRNA is shorter than the gene. (3)
hints: Must the same exons always be kept?
questions.solution:
Introns (non-coding sequences) are removed from pre-mRNA by splicing, so mRNA is shorter [B1]
Different exons can be kept or removed (alternative splicing) [B1]
Giving different mRNAs, so different amino acid sequences / polypeptides. [B1]

questions.prompt: Radioactive uridine (an RNA nucleotide containing uracil) was given to cells. Explain why it labels RNA but not DNA, and describe where the label is found first and later. (5)
hints: Where is RNA made and where does mRNA go?
questions.solution:
RNA contains uracil (and ribose); DNA contains thymine (and deoxyribose) [B1]
RNA polymerase uses RNA nucleotides; DNA polymerase does not [B1]
Transcription occurs in the nucleus, so label appears there first [B1]
mRNA leaves through nuclear pores [B1]
So label later appears in the cytoplasm / at ribosomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of RNA polymerase in transcription. (2)
hints: What does it use as a guide?
questions.solution:
Joins RNA nucleotides together / forms phosphodiester bonds [B1]
Along the template strand of DNA, forming pre-mRNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three differences between mRNA and tRNA. (3)
hints: Which one carries an amino acid?
questions.solution:
mRNA is linear; tRNA is folded (clover-leaf) [B1]
tRNA has hydrogen bonds between some base pairs; mRNA does not [B1]
tRNA has an amino acid binding site; mRNA does not [B1]
tRNA has an anticodon; mRNA has codons [B1]
mRNA is longer / length varies; tRNA is short. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by an exon and an intron. (2)
hints: Which one stays in the mature mRNA?
questions.solution:
Exon: coding sequence that is kept in the mature mRNA [B1]
Intron: non-coding sequence that is removed by splicing. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe transcription in a prokaryote and explain how producing mRNA differs in a eukaryote. (5)
hints: Start with the DNA strands separating.
What extra step happens in eukaryotes?
questions.solution:
Hydrogen bonds broken and DNA strands separate; one strand is the template [B1]
Free RNA nucleotides align by complementary base pairing (U with A) [B1]
RNA polymerase joins them by phosphodiester bonds [B1]
In prokaryotes mRNA is used directly (no introns) [B1]
In eukaryotes pre-mRNA is spliced to remove introns, then mRNA leaves the nucleus through nuclear pores. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare and contrast DNA replication and transcription. (5)
hints: Think about similarities first: what do both use?
Then compare templates, enzymes, nucleotides and products.
questions.solution:
Both: strands separate / hydrogen bonds broken, complementary base pairing, phosphodiester bonds form [B1]
Replication uses both strands as templates; transcription uses one [B1]
DNA polymerase vs RNA polymerase [B1]
DNA nucleotides (thymine, deoxyribose) vs RNA nucleotides (uracil, ribose) [B1]
Replication copies whole DNA; transcription copies one gene / produces single-stranded mRNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structures of mRNA and tRNA and explain how each is suited to its role. (5)
hints: What does mRNA carry and where?
What features let tRNA bring the right amino acid?
questions.solution:
mRNA is a single linear strand with codons (triplets) carrying the gene's sequence [B1]
mRNA is small enough to leave the nucleus through pores / is broken down after use [B1]
tRNA is folded into a clover-leaf shape held by hydrogen bonds [B1]
tRNA has an anticodon complementary to an mRNA codon [B1]
tRNA has a binding site for a specific amino acid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of mRNA, tRNA, ribosomes and ATP in translation. (6)
questions.solution:
mRNA carries the sequence of codons; attaches to a ribosome [B1]
Ribosome moves along mRNA, holding two tRNAs at a time [B1]
tRNA anticodon binds to the complementary codon [B1]
tRNA carries a specific amino acid [B1]
Peptide bond forms between adjacent amino acids (condensation) [B1]
ATP provides energy for peptide bond formation / attaching amino acids to tRNA [B1]
Continues until a stop codon is reached. [B1]
Any 6 of these points — max 6 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how the base sequence of a gene determines the primary structure of a polypeptide. (6)
hints: How many bases code for one amino acid?
Follow it through transcription and translation.
questions.solution:
Sequence of base triplets in DNA codes for amino acids [B1]
Transcription makes mRNA with complementary codons [B1]
mRNA attaches to a ribosome; codons read in sequence [B1]
tRNA with complementary anticodon brings the specific amino acid [B1]
Order of codons determines order of amino acids [B1]
Amino acids joined by peptide bonds. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how tRNA molecules make sure amino acids are joined in the correct order during translation. (3)
hints: What does its anticodon pair with?
questions.solution:
Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid [B1]
Its anticodon is complementary to a specific mRNA codon [B1]
Codons are read in sequence, so amino acids are brought in the order coded by the mRNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the roles of ATP in translation. (3)
hints: What needs energy to attach to tRNA?
Which bond forms between amino acids?
questions.solution:
Provides energy to attach amino acids to tRNA [B1]
Provides energy for peptide bond formation [B1]
ATP is produced by respiration (mitochondria). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a ribosome moves along mRNA as a polypeptide grows. (3)
hints: How many tRNAs does the ribosome hold at once?
What happens to the first tRNA?
questions.solution:
Ribosome holds two codons / two tRNAs at a time [B1]
Peptide bond forms between their amino acids [B1]
First tRNA is released and the ribosome moves along one codon; repeats until a stop codon. [B1]

questions.prompt: A DNA template triplet is TAC. Give the mRNA codon transcribed from it. A mutation changes the mRNA codon to AUA — give the mutated DNA template triplet. (2)
hints: mRNA is complementary to the template, with U instead of T.
Work backwards for the mutated codon.
questions.solution:
mRNA codon: AUG [B1]
Mutated DNA template triplet: TAT. [B1]

questions.prompt: A tRNA has the anticodon UCC. Give the mRNA codon it binds to and the DNA template triplet that codes for that codon. (2)
hints: The DNA template is complementary to the codon.
questions.solution:
mRNA codon: AGG [B1]
DNA template triplet: TCC. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three features of a tRNA molecule and explain the function of each. (3)
hints: Where does the amino acid attach?
questions.solution:
Anticodon — pairs with a complementary codon on mRNA [B1]
Amino acid binding site — carries a specific amino acid [B1]
Folded clover-leaf shape held by hydrogen bonds — gives a specific shape to fit the ribosome / enzyme that loads amino acid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three differences between producing mRNA in a eukaryotic cell and in a prokaryotic cell. (3)
questions.solution:
Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is spliced to remove introns; prokaryotic mRNA is not [B1]
Eukaryotic transcription in the nucleus; prokaryotic in the cytoplasm [B1]
Eukaryotic mRNA must leave through nuclear pores; prokaryotic mRNA can be translated straight away. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three differences between transcription and translation. (3)
hints: What is made, and which bonds form?
questions.solution:
Transcription in the nucleus; translation at ribosomes in the cytoplasm [B1]
Transcription uses RNA polymerase; translation uses ribosomes and tRNA [B1]
Transcription makes mRNA (phosphodiester bonds); translation makes a polypeptide (peptide bonds). [B1]
