questions.prompt: Use the table. Give the amino acid sequence coded for by the mRNA AUG CCA GGA. (1)
hints: Look each up in the table.
questions.solution: Met – Pro – Gly. [B1]
questions.table:
mRNA codon | Amino acid
AUG | Met
UUU | Phe
UUC | Phe
CGG | Arg

UAC | Tyr

questions.prompt: Use the table. Give the amino acid sequence coded for by the mRNA UAC GCG UUU. (1)
questions.solution: Tyr – Ala – Phe. [B1]
questions.table:

AUG | Met
UUU | Phe
UUC | Phe
CGG | Arg
AGG | Arg
GCG | Ala
GGG | Gly
GGA | Gly
CCA | Pro
UAC | Tyr
UAG | Stop

questions.prompt: Use the table. A DNA template strand has the sequence TAC GGT. Give the amino acids coded for. (1)
questions.solution: mRNA AUG CCA: Met – Pro. [B1]
questions.table:
mRNA codon | Amino acid
AUG | Met
UUU | Phe
UUC | Phe
CGG | Arg

questions.prompt: What is removed from pre-mRNA to form mature mRNA? (1)
questions.solution: Introns. [B1]

questions.prompt: Where in a eukaryotic cell does splicing of pre-mRNA take place? (1)
questions.solution: In the nucleus. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the process that removes introns and joins exons in pre-mRNA. (1)
hints: It's a word for joining pieces.
questions.solution: Splicing. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why RNA polymerase only joins RNA nucleotides that are complementary to the template strand. (2)
hints: How are nucleotides held in place on the template?
When does RNA polymerase join them?
questions.solution:
Free nucleotides first pair with template bases by hydrogen bonds (complementary base pairing) [B1]
RNA polymerase then joins the nucleotides held in place. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the base sequence of mRNA is the same as the coding (non-template) strand of DNA, except that it contains uracil. (2)
hints: mRNA is complementary to which strand?
The two DNA strands are complementary to each other.
questions.solution:
mRNA is complementary to the template strand [B1]
The coding strand is also complementary to the template strand, so mRNA has the same sequence (with U in place of T). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the sequence of codons on mRNA is translated into a polypeptide at a ribosome. (6)
hints: What attaches to the mRNA first?
questions.solution:
mRNA attaches to a ribosome [B1]
tRNA with an anticodon complementary to the start codon binds [B1]
tRNA carries a specific amino acid [B1]
Ribosome holds two tRNAs; a peptide bond forms between their amino acids (condensation, using ATP) [B1]
Ribosome moves along to the next codon and the first tRNA is released [B1]
Continues until a stop codon is reached. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare protein synthesis in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. (6)
hints: What extra steps happen in eukaryotes?
questions.solution:
Both: transcription makes mRNA; translation uses ribosomes, tRNA and ATP [B1]
Same genetic code [B1]
Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes; eukaryotes 80S (in cytoplasm) [B1]
Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is spliced; prokaryotic mRNA is not [B1]
Eukaryotic mRNA leaves the nucleus; in prokaryotes translation can begin during transcription [B1]
Eukaryotic proteins may be modified in the RER / Golgi. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a ribosome and explain its roles in translation. (6)
hints: What is a ribosome made of?
How many tRNAs does it hold?
questions.solution:
Made of rRNA and protein [B1]
Two subunits (large and small) [B1]
Binds mRNA and moves along it codon by codon [B1]
Holds two tRNA molecules at a time [B1]
Catalyses peptide bond formation between amino acids [B1]
70S in prokaryotes, 80S in the eukaryotic cytoplasm. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of DNA helicase, RNA polymerase and splicing in producing mature mRNA in a eukaryotic cell. (6)
hints: What must happen to the DNA first?
questions.solution:
DNA helicase breaks hydrogen bonds, separating the strands [B1]
One strand acts as the template [B1]
Free RNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases (U with A) [B1]
RNA polymerase joins them by phosphodiester bonds, forming pre-mRNA [B1]
Splicing removes introns and joins exons [B1]
Mature mRNA leaves the nucleus through nuclear pores. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how mRNA is produced in the nucleus and explain how its sequence relates to the gene. (6)
hints: How is the base sequence complementary?
questions.solution:
Hydrogen bonds between DNA strands broken; strands separate [B1]
One strand acts as the template [B1]
RNA nucleotides align by complementary base pairing — A with U, T with A, C with G [B1]
RNA polymerase joins them into pre-mRNA [B1]
pre-mRNA has the same base sequence as the coding strand (with U for T) [B1]
Introns removed by splicing to give mRNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a mutation in an intron could change the protein produced from a gene. (2)
hints: Introns are removed — but where are the splice sites?
questions.solution:
Could change splice sites, so exons are spliced differently [B1]
Different mRNA and amino acid sequence / protein. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutation in mitochondrial DNA changes one base in a tRNA anticodon. Suggest how this leads to a non-functional protein. (3)
hints: What does the anticodon pair with?
questions.solution:
Anticodon no longer complementary to the right codon / pairs with a different codon [B1]
Wrong amino acid placed in the polypeptide / amino acid not added [B1]
Changes primary and tertiary structure, so non-functional protein. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of tRNA in translation. (3)
hints: How does it find the codon?
questions.solution:
tRNA carries a specific amino acid [B1]
Anticodon pairs with the complementary codon on mRNA at the ribosome [B1]
Brings amino acids in the correct order; peptide bonds form (using ATP). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two differences between tRNA and mRNA. (3)
questions.solution:
tRNA is clover-leaf shaped; mRNA is linear [B1]
tRNA has hydrogen bonds between base pairs; mRNA doesn't [B1]
tRNA has an amino acid binding site and anticodon; mRNA has codons. [B1]

category: Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

questions.prompt: Explain how meiosis produces genetically different gametes. (4)
hints: One happens between homologous chromosomes in prophase I.
questions.solution:
Crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes [B1]
Exchanges alleles / produces new combinations of alleles [B1]
Independent segregation of homologous chromosomes (in meiosis I) [B1]
Random arrangement on the equator, so gametes get different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two differences between mitosis and meiosis. Explain why it is important that meiosis halves the chromosome number. (4)
hints: Compare number of divisions and the type of cells produced.
What happens when two gametes fuse?
questions.solution:
Meiosis has two divisions; mitosis has one [B1]
Meiosis produces haploid cells; mitosis produces diploid cells / meiosis produces genetically different cells; mitosis identical [B1]
Halving means fertilisation restores the diploid number [B1]
So the chromosome number stays constant from generation to generation. [B1]

Model answer:
2 differences (1 mark each) + 2 marks for the explanation.

questions.prompt:
A cell has a diploid number of 8.

(i) How many chromosomes are in each cell at the end of meiosis I, and how many chromatids does each chromosome have?
(ii) How many chromosomes are in each cell at the end of meiosis II, and how many chromatids does each chromosome have?
(iii) How many different combinations of chromosomes are possible in the gametes from independent segregation alone? (4)
hints: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis II separates chromatids.
Number of combinations = 2ⁿ, where n is the haploid number.
questions.solution:
(i) 4 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids [B1]
(ii) 4 chromosomes, each with 1 chromatid [B1]
(iii) 2⁴ [B1]
= 16. [B1]

Model answer:
(i) Homologous pairs separate → 4 chromosomes, each still 2 chromatids.
(ii) Chromatids separate → 4 chromosomes of 1 chromatid.
(iii) Haploid number 4 → 2⁴ = 16 combinations.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a diploid cell? (1)
questions.solution: A cell containing two sets of chromosomes / chromosomes in homologous pairs (2n). [B1]

questions.prompt:
A cell has a diploid number of 4 (two homologous pairs). Each chromosome has two chromatids at the start of meiosis.

State how many chromosomes and chromatids each cell contains (i) at the end of meiosis I and (ii) at the end of meiosis II. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 2 chromosomes, 4 chromatids [B1]
(ii) 2 chromosomes, each a single chromatid (2 in total). [B1]

questions.prompt: In the human life cycle, state the type of cell division that (i) produces gametes and (ii) allows a zygote to grow into an adult. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Meiosis [B1]
(ii) Mitosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: A moss plant has haploid cells and produces gametes. Explain why the gametes are made by mitosis rather than meiosis. (2)
hints: What would meiosis do to the chromosome number?
Does a haploid cell have homologous pairs?
questions.solution:
The plant is already haploid / has no homologous pairs to separate [B1]
Mitosis keeps the haploid number (meiosis would halve it again). [B1]

questions.prompt: A diploid fern plant produces haploid spores. Name the type of cell division involved and explain your answer. (2)
hints: Which division halves the chromosome number?
What does it do to genetic variation?
questions.solution:
Meiosis [B1]
Because it halves the chromosome number from diploid to haploid (producing genetically different spores). [B1]

questions.prompt: A horse (64 chromosomes) and a donkey (62 chromosomes) can produce a mule, but mules are infertile. Explain why. (2)
hints: How many chromosomes does a mule have?
What must chromosomes do in meiosis I?
questions.solution:
Mule has 63 chromosomes / an odd number, so chromosomes cannot all form homologous pairs [B1]
So meiosis fails and no viable gametes are produced. [B1]

questions.prompt: State whether each of the following happens in mitosis, meiosis or both: (i) crossing over, (ii) separation of sister chromatids, (iii) DNA replication before division, (iv) independent segregation of homologous chromosomes. (2)
hints: Sister chromatids separate in mitosis and meiosis II.
questions.solution:
(i) meiosis; (ii) both; (iii) both; (iv) meiosis. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2–3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Explain how crossing over increases genetic variation. (4)
questions.solution:
In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes pair up [B1]
Non-sister chromatids break and rejoin at chiasmata [B1]
Exchanging sections of DNA / alleles [B1]
Producing new combinations of alleles on chromatids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how independent segregation and random fertilisation increase genetic variation. (4)
hints: How do homologous pairs line up?
questions.solution:
Homologous pairs line up randomly on the equator in meiosis I [B1]
So each gamete gets a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes [B1]
Fertilisation is random — any gamete can fuse with any other [B1]
So many different combinations of alleles in offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. Calculate the number of different chromosome combinations in gametes from independent segregation alone, and the number of combinations in a zygote from random fertilisation of two such gametes. Explain your answers. (4)
hints: For the zygote, multiply the possibilities from each parent.
questions.solution:
Each pair can line up two ways, independently [M1]
Gametes: 2²³ = 8 388 608 combinations [M1]
Zygote: (2²³)² = about 7.0 × 10¹³ combinations [M1]
Crossing over increases variation even further. [A1]

questions.prompt: Describe the behaviour of chromosomes during prophase I and anaphase I of meiosis. (4)
hints: What pairs up in prophase I?
questions.solution:
Prophase I: homologous chromosomes pair up (bivalents) [B1]
Crossing over at chiasmata between non-sister chromatids [B1]
Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate (not sister chromatids) [B1]
Pulled to opposite poles by spindle fibres. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare anaphase of mitosis with anaphase I of meiosis. (4)
hints: What is similar about the mechanism?
questions.solution:
Both: spindle fibres pull chromosome material to opposite poles [B1]
Mitosis: centromeres divide and sister chromatids separate [B1]
Meiosis I: homologous chromosomes separate; centromeres do not divide [B1]
Each pole in meiosis I receives one of each pair (haploid); in mitosis a full set. [B1]

questions.prompt: A cell contains 6 units of DNA at the start of interphase. Give the DNA content of: one cell at the end of interphase; each daughter cell after mitosis; each cell at the end of meiosis II. (3)
hints: Mitosis halves it once; meiosis halves it twice.
questions.solution:
End of interphase: 12 [B1]
After mitosis: 6 [B1]
End of meiosis II: 3. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the DNA content of a cell halves twice during meiosis, but the chromosome number halves only once. (3)
questions.solution:
Meiosis I: homologous chromosomes separate, so chromosome number and DNA both halve [B1]
Meiosis II: sister chromatids separate, so DNA halves again [B1]
But each separated chromatid becomes a chromosome, so chromosome number stays the same in meiosis II. [B1]

questions.prompt: At the end of interphase, a cell contains 20 units of DNA. Give the DNA content at the start of interphase, at the end of meiosis I and at the end of meiosis II. (3)
questions.solution:
Start of interphase: 10 [B1]
End of meiosis I: 10 [B1]
End of meiosis II: 5. [B1]

questions.prompt: A cell with 6 chromosomes (3 homologous pairs) completes meiosis I. Describe the chromosomes in one of the cells produced. (1)
questions.solution: 3 chromosomes — one from each homologous pair — each still made of two chromatids. [B1]

questions.prompt: A cell has a diploid number of 8. How many chromosomes and chromatids are in each cell at the end of meiosis I? (1)
hints: Each chromosome still has two chromatids.
questions.solution: 4 chromosomes, 8 chromatids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why each cell at the end of meiosis I contains only one chromosome from each homologous pair. (1)
hints: Where does each member of a pair go?
questions.solution: Homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I and move to opposite poles. [B1]

questions.prompt: Put these stages of meiosis in order: prophase I, anaphase II, metaphase I, telophase I, metaphase II. (1)
hints: Within each division: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.
questions.solution: Prophase I, metaphase I, telophase I, metaphase II, anaphase II. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the DNA content per cell halves at the end of meiosis I. (3)
questions.solution:
Homologous chromosomes separate (in anaphase I) [B1]
One chromosome of each pair goes to each new cell [B1]
Each chromosome still has two chromatids, but there are half as many chromosomes per cell. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the DNA content per cell halves at the end of meiosis II. (3)
questions.solution:
Centromeres divide [B1]
Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles [B1]
Each new cell receives one chromatid of each chromosome. [B1]

questions.prompt: What happens to the DNA content per cell when two gametes fuse at fertilisation? (1)
questions.solution: It doubles (back to the diploid amount). [B1]

questions.prompt: What happens to the chromosome number at fertilisation? (1)
questions.solution: Doubles from haploid to diploid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two events in meiosis that produce genetic variation. (2)
hints: One involves how pairs line up.
questions.solution:
Crossing over [B1]
Independent segregation of homologous chromosomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how random fertilisation increases genetic variation. (2)
questions.solution:
Any male gamete can fuse with any female gamete [B1]
So a huge number of different allele combinations are possible in offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two ways meiosis produces genetic variation. (2)
questions.solution:
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes exchanges alleles [B1]
Independent segregation of homologous chromosomes gives different combinations. [B1]

questions.prompt: A cell has the genotype Aa. After meiosis I, one daughter cell receives the chromosome carrying A. Which allele does the other daughter cell receive, and why? (1)
questions.solution: a — homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis I, so each cell gets one of the pair. [B1]

questions.prompt: A cell is AaBb with genes on different chromosomes. Give all the possible allele combinations in the gametes. (1)
questions.solution: AB, Ab, aB, ab. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the number of possible combinations of chromosomes in human gametes from independent segregation alone. (1)
questions.solution: 2²³ (about 8.4 million). [B1]

questions.prompt:
After meiosis I, a cell contained a chromosome with alleles A and a on its two chromatids. Which process produced this combination?

Choose one answer.

A  Anaphase
B  Crossing over
C  Independent segregation
D  Semi-conservative replication (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which process separates sister chromatids?

Choose one answer.

A  Prophase I
B  Metaphase I
C  Anaphase I
D  Anaphase II (1)
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt:
In which stage do homologous chromosomes pair up?

Choose one answer.

A  Prophase I
B  Metaphase II
C  Anaphase I
D  Telophase II (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

category: Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

questions.prompt: Some bacteria secrete an enzyme called β-lactamase, which breaks down penicillin. Suggest and explain one advantage to the bacteria of secreting this enzyme into their surroundings. (2)
hints: Where does penicillin act — inside or at the surface of the bacterium?
What happens to bacteria that are not killed?
questions.solution:
Penicillin is broken down before it can reach / damage the cell wall [B1]
So the bacteria (and nearby bacteria) survive and reproduce / are resistant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Tuberculosis is treated with four different antibiotics taken together. Explain why using several antibiotics at once reduces the chance of antibiotic resistance developing. (3)
hints: How does resistance arise in the first place?
What is the chance of one bacterium being resistant to all four?
questions.solution:
Resistance arises by random mutation [B1]
A bacterium resistant to one antibiotic is (likely to be) killed by another [B1]
Very low probability of one bacterium having mutations for resistance to all the antibiotics [B1]
So resistant bacteria do not survive and reproduce / resistance allele frequency does not increase. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Explain why patients are told to complete the full course of antibiotics even when they feel better. (3)
hints: Which bacteria are left after a few days?
Use the language of natural selection.
questions.solution:
The most susceptible bacteria are killed first; some (more resistant) bacteria survive [B1]
If treatment stops, survivors reproduce [B1]
Passing on the resistance allele [B1]
So the frequency of resistance increases in the population. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Some farmers add antibiotics to animal feed. Explain how this could lead to human infections that are difficult to treat. (3)
hints: The antibiotic is a selection pressure.
How can resistance pass between different species of bacteria?
questions.solution:
A mutation gives some bacteria resistance [B1]
Antibiotic acts as a selection pressure — resistant bacteria survive and reproduce [B1]
Resistance allele frequency increases [B1]
Resistance (on plasmids) passed to other / pathogenic bacteria (horizontal transmission) that infect humans. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: In a polluted area, the proportion of dark-coloured peppered moths rose from 5% to 90% over 50 years. Use your knowledge of directional selection to explain this change. (3)
hints: Where did the dark colour come from?
Why did dark moths survive better?
questions.solution:
Dark colour arose by mutation / variation in colour [B1]
Dark moths better camouflaged on soot-darkened trees, so less predation [B1]
Survive and reproduce, passing on the allele for dark colour [B1]
Frequency of the dark allele increases over generations. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: When myxoma virus was introduced to kill rabbits, most died. Over several years, the proportion of rabbits resistant to the virus increased. Explain this change. (3)
hints: Did any rabbits already have resistance?
Use the steps of natural selection.
questions.solution:
Some rabbits had an allele for resistance (variation from mutation) [B1]
Resistant rabbits survived infection and reproduced [B1]
Passing on the resistance allele [B1]
Frequency of the allele increased in the population. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Plant breeders allowed only the tallest 10% of plants to breed each generation. Over several generations, mean height increased. Explain why this is an example of directional selection and how the change happens. (3)
hints: Which end of the range is favoured?
What happens to the alleles for tallness?
questions.solution:
Selection favours one extreme of the range (tall plants) [B1]
Only tall plants reproduce, passing on alleles for tallness [B1]
Frequency of these alleles increases, so the mean shifts each generation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Birds that lay very large clutches cannot feed all their chicks, and birds that lay very small clutches produce few offspring. Explain how stabilising selection affects clutch size. (3)
hints: Which clutch size leaves the most surviving offspring?
questions.solution:
Intermediate clutch sizes produce the most surviving offspring [B1]
Extremes are selected against [B1]
Alleles for intermediate clutch size are passed on more [B1]
Range / standard deviation decreases; mean stays the same. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between stabilising selection and directional selection, in terms of which individuals are favoured and the effect on the mean and standard deviation. (3)
questions.solution:
Stabilising: individuals with average / intermediate phenotype favoured, extremes selected against [B1]
Stabilising: mean stays the same, standard deviation decreases [B1]
Directional: one extreme favoured (often after an environmental change), so the mean shifts in that direction. [B1]

questions.prompt: On a windy hillside, tall plants of one species are often blown over and very short plants are shaded out. Explain how this affects plant height in the population over many generations. (3)
hints: Which type of selection is this?
questions.solution:
Intermediate-height plants survive and reproduce most [B1]
Alleles for intermediate height passed on (stabilising selection) [B1]
Mean height stays similar but the range / variation decreases. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA are more common in hospitals than in the community. (3)
hints: What does an antibiotic do as a selection pressure?
questions.solution:
Antibiotics are used heavily in hospitals, creating a strong selection pressure [B1]
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, so become common [B1]
Many patients are ill / have weakened immunity and are close together, so infection spreads easily. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how antibiotic resistance can spread from one species of bacteria to another. (3)
hints: Where are resistance genes often found?
How can that DNA move between bacteria?
questions.solution:
Resistance allele / gene is often on a plasmid [B1]
Plasmid copied and transferred by conjugation (horizontal gene transmission) [B1]
Recipient bacterium becomes resistant and passes it on when it divides. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest three ways of slowing the development of antibiotic resistance. (3)
questions.solution:
Only prescribe antibiotics when necessary / not for viral infections [B1]
Patients complete the full course [B1]
Good hygiene (hand washing) to stop resistant bacteria spreading [B1]
Avoid routine use in farming / rotate antibiotics. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why prescribing antibiotics for colds can increase antibiotic resistance. (1)
hints: What do the antibiotics do to bacteria already in the body?
questions.solution: Exposes bacteria in the body to antibiotic unnecessarily, selecting for resistant bacteria. [B1]

questions.prompt: The sickle-cell allele is common in parts of Africa where malaria is common. People with one copy of the allele (heterozygotes) are resistant to malaria. Explain why the allele is common there. (4)
questions.solution:
Heterozygotes are more likely to survive malaria than people without the allele [B1]
So they are more likely to reproduce [B1]
And pass on the sickle-cell allele [B1]
So the allele frequency stays high (even though homozygotes are selected against). [B1]

questions.prompt: An allele that lets adults keep digesting lactose is common in populations with a long history of dairy farming. Explain why. (4)
hints: Where did the allele come from?
What advantage does it give where milk is available?
questions.solution:
Allele arose by mutation [B1]
Where milk is available, adults who can digest lactose get more nutrition / are healthier [B1]
So they survive and reproduce more, passing on the allele [B1]
Allele frequency increased over generations. [B1]

questions.prompt: An allele that gives resistance to a disease is rare in populations where the disease has never been present. Explain why. (4)
hints: Could the allele have a cost?
questions.solution:
No selection pressure from the disease, so the allele gives no advantage [B1]
Carriers are no more likely to survive and reproduce [B1]
Allele frequency does not increase [B1]
It may even be selected against if it has a disadvantage / lost by chance (genetic drift). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why infections with MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) increased after methicillin became widely used. (3)
hints: What did methicillin do to non-resistant bacteria?
questions.solution:
Random mutation gave some bacteria resistance [B1]
Methicillin killed non-resistant bacteria (selection pressure) [B1]
Resistant bacteria survived and reproduced, so the allele frequency increased. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why patients in intensive care units are at high risk of infection by antibiotic-resistant bacteria. (3)
hints: What is their immune system like?
How much antibiotic is used there?
questions.solution:
Patients are very ill / have weakened immune systems [B1]
Invasive procedures (tubes, catheters) give bacteria entry points [B1]
Heavy antibiotic use selects for resistant strains. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how hand washing in hospitals reduces the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. (3)
hints: How do bacteria move between patients?
questions.solution:
Bacteria are carried between patients on hands [B1]
Washing removes / kills bacteria on hands [B1]
So fewer resistant bacteria are transmitted and fewer infections occur. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define genetic diversity. (1)
questions.solution: The number of different alleles of genes in a population. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one event that can reduce the genetic diversity of a population. (1)
hints: What happens if a population becomes very small?
What about a few individuals starting a new population?
questions.solution: Genetic bottleneck / founder effect / selective breeding. [B1]

questions.prompt: In species A, 120 of 400 genes studied had more than one allele (polymorphic). In species B, 90 of 200 genes were polymorphic. Use calculations to explain which species has greater genetic diversity. (2)
questions.solution:
A: 30% polymorphic; B: 45% [M1]
Species B has a greater proportion of genes with more than one allele, so greater genetic diversity. [A1]

questions.prompt: Population 1 had 15 alleles across 10 genes studied. Population 2 had 28 alleles across 20 genes. Use calculations to explain which population has greater genetic diversity. (2)
hints: Find the mean number of alleles per gene.
questions.solution:
Population 1: 1.5 alleles per gene; population 2: 1.4 [M1]
Population 1 has more alleles per gene, so slightly greater genetic diversity. [A1]

questions.prompt: For the same five genes, a rare breed of sheep had 6 alleles and a wild population had 20 alleles. Use calculations to compare their genetic diversity and suggest a reason. (2)
questions.solution:
Rare breed 1.2 alleles per gene; wild 4.0 per gene [M1]
Rare breed much less diverse — selective breeding / small population (inbreeding). [A1]

questions.prompt: The allele for Huntington's disease is dominant and harmful, but has not been removed by natural selection. Explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Symptoms usually appear after people have had children [B1]
So the allele has already been passed on — no selection against it. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a harmful recessive allele can remain in a population for many generations. (2)
hints: Can selection act on hidden alleles?
questions.solution:
Carried by heterozygotes, who show no harmful phenotype [B1]
So the allele is not selected against in carriers. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the sickle-cell allele remains common in regions with malaria even though homozygotes are ill. (2)
hints: Which genotype is protected from malaria?
questions.solution:
Heterozygotes are resistant to malaria, so survive and reproduce more [B1]
Heterozygote advantage keeps the allele frequency high. [B1]

questions.prompt: Populations with a long history of eating starchy food tend to have more copies of the gene for salivary amylase. Describe how this could have arisen by natural selection. (4)
hints: Where did extra copies come from?
questions.solution:
Extra copies arose by mutation (gene duplication) [B1]
More amylase lets people digest starch more effectively / get more energy [B1]
These people were more likely to survive and reproduce [B1]
Passing on the allele, so its frequency increased over generations. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how resistance to a pesticide can become common in an insect population. (4)
questions.solution:
Random mutation produces a resistance allele [B1]
Pesticide kills non-resistant insects (selection pressure) [B1]
Resistant insects survive and reproduce, passing on the allele [B1]
Allele frequency increases over generations. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how dark skin could have become common in human populations living in regions with high UV levels. (4)
questions.solution:
Mutations produced alleles for more melanin / darker skin [B1]
Dark skin protects against UV damage (e.g. skin cancer / breakdown of folate) [B1]
People with dark skin more likely to survive and reproduce [B1]
Alleles passed on and their frequency increased. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an advantageous dominant allele spreads through a population faster than an advantageous recessive allele. (2)
hints: Is a dominant allele expressed in heterozygotes?
Can selection act on hidden alleles?
questions.solution:
Dominant allele is expressed in heterozygotes, so selection acts on it immediately [B1]
Recessive allele is hidden in heterozygotes and only selected in homozygotes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an advantageous recessive allele spreads slowly when it is rare. (2)
hints: Where are most copies when it's rare?
questions.solution:
When rare, almost all copies are in heterozygotes [B1]
Not expressed, so give no advantage — few homozygotes for selection to act on. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why allele frequencies change faster when the selection pressure is strong. (2)
hints: How different is survival between phenotypes?
questions.solution:
Bigger difference in survival / reproduction between phenotypes [B1]
So more of the advantageous allele is passed on each generation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two factors that could cause variation in skin colour between individuals of a lizard species. (2)
questions.solution:
Genetic variation (different alleles / mutations / meiosis) [B1]
Environmental factors, e.g. temperature, light, diet, surface lived on. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why mutation is the original source of new alleles. (2)
questions.solution:
Mutation changes the base sequence of DNA [B1]
Creating a new version of the gene — a new allele. [B1]

questions.prompt: Lizards that are active in the day can change skin colour to match the surfaces they rest on. Explain the advantage. (2)
hints: How does survival link to reproduction?
questions.solution:
Camouflage so less likely to be seen / eaten by predators [B1]
So more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on alleles. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the advantage to a lizard of having dark skin in a cool environment. (2)
questions.solution:
Dark skin absorbs more heat, raising body temperature [B1]
So enzymes work faster / more active to find food and escape predators. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the difference between behavioural, physiological and anatomical adaptations, giving one example of a behavioural one. (2)
hints: What an organism does, how it works, what it looks like.
questions.solution:
Behavioural = how it acts (e.g. basking in sun); physiological = processes inside the body; anatomical = structure [B1]
They all increase chance of survival / reproduction. [B1]

questions.prompt: The frequency of an insecticide-resistance allele rose from 0.05 to 0.6 over five years of spraying, then fell after spraying stopped. Suggest an explanation. (4)
questions.solution:
Resistance allele arose by mutation [B1]
Insecticide is a selection pressure — mosquitoes with the allele survive and reproduce [B1]
Pass on the allele, so frequency increases over generations [B1]
After spraying stopped, the allele gives no advantage / may be a disadvantage, so frequency falls. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how antibiotic resistance becomes more common in a population of bacteria. (4)
hints: Where does the allele come from?
questions.solution:
Mutation produces an allele for resistance [B1]
Antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria [B1]
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the allele (also horizontal gene transfer via plasmids) [B1]
Frequency of the allele increases — directional selection. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why rotating different insecticides can slow the development of resistance. (4)
hints: Is resistance to one insecticide usually resistance to all?
questions.solution:
Resistance alleles are usually specific to one insecticide [B1]
Changing insecticides kills insects resistant to the previous one [B1]
Selection pressure for any one allele is reduced [B1]
So frequency of each resistance allele rises less. [B1]

questions.prompt: Large-brained female fish are better at identifying predators, and only they choose brightly coloured males. Suggest and explain the advantage to the population of these females choosing bright males. (3)
hints: Bright males are more visible — how do they survive?
questions.solution:
Bright males that survive must be good at avoiding predators (fit) [B1]
Offspring inherit alleles for survival / large brains [B1]
So more offspring survive and reproduce, and advantageous alleles increase in the population. [B1]

questions.prompt: Male peacocks have large tail feathers that make them more visible to predators. Explain why this feature has been selected for. (3)
questions.solution:
Females prefer males with large tails [B1]
Those males mate more and pass on their alleles [B1]
Reproductive advantage outweighs the survival disadvantage. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how courtship behaviour helps animals to reproduce successfully. (3)
questions.solution:
Recognise members of the same species, so offspring are fertile [B1]
Identify a mate that is sexually mature / fertile [B1]
Synchronise mating / form a pair bond. [B1]

questions.prompt: A group of viruses previously infected only one species of frog but can now infect several species. Suggest and explain how. (2)
hints: Which protein binds to host cells?
questions.solution:
Mutation in the viral genome changes the attachment protein [B1]
Now complementary to receptors on cells of other species, and these viruses are selected / reproduce. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a new strain of influenza can arise to which people have no immunity. (2)
questions.solution:
Mutation changes the viral antigen (antigenic variability) [B1]
Memory cells / antibodies no longer complementary, so no immunity. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why viruses evolve quickly. (2)
questions.solution:
Short generation time / reproduce in large numbers [B1]
High mutation rate (especially RNA viruses), so lots of variation for selection. [B1]

questions.prompt: Slow-growing, shade-tolerant plants have poisonous chemicals in their mature leaves. Suggest how this benefits them. (2)
questions.solution:
Deters herbivores from eating leaves [B1]
Slow growth means lost leaves are hard to replace, so they keep more leaves for photosynthesis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how toxins in plants could become more common in a population over many generations. (2)
questions.solution:
Plants with more toxin are eaten less, so survive and reproduce more [B1]
Pass on alleles for toxin production, so their frequency increases. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest a disadvantage to a plant of producing large amounts of toxic chemicals. (2)
questions.solution:
Uses energy / resources (e.g. nitrogen) to make them [B1]
So less available for growth / reproduction. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a population of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic. (2)
questions.solution:
Random mutation produces an allele for resistance [B1]
Bacteria with it survive antibiotic treatment and reproduce, passing on the allele. [B1]

questions.prompt: A recessive genetic disease is far more common on a group of isolated islands than worldwide. Suggest and explain one reason. (2)
questions.solution:
Founder effect — the original small population carried the allele by chance [B1]
Isolation / inbreeding means carriers are more likely to have children together, so more homozygous recessive. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by genetic drift and why it has a greater effect in small populations. (2)
questions.solution:
Random changes in allele frequency due to chance [B1]
In small populations, chance events change frequencies by a larger proportion. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a genetic bottleneck reduces genetic diversity. (2)
questions.solution:
A large fall in population size [B1]
Many alleles lost, so few alleles in the gene pool when it recovers. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how both genes and environment can affect a phenotype, with an example. (2)
questions.solution:
Genotype determines the potential [B1]
Environment affects whether it is reached, e.g. height depends on genes and diet. [B1]

category: Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

questions.prompt: Using appearance, species P and Q were placed in the same genus and species R in a different genus. Later DNA comparisons showed that R and Q have more similar base sequences than P and Q. Suggest what this shows about the evolutionary relationships of these species. (2)
hints: Which pair shares the most recent common ancestor?
Why might P and Q look alike if they aren't closest relatives?
questions.solution:
R and Q are most closely related / share the most recent common ancestor [B1]
Similar appearance of P and Q is due to similar environments / convergent evolution, not close relationship. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why classification based on DNA base sequences is more reliable than classification based on observable features. (2)
hints: What can affect observable features apart from genes?
questions.solution:
Observable features can be affected by the environment / similar features can evolve separately (convergent evolution) [B1]
DNA base sequence directly reflects genetic relatedness / more differences can be compared. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two populations of birds look very different but can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Suggest what this tells you about their classification, and explain why they look different. (2)
hints: What is the definition of a species?
What causes variation within a species?
questions.solution:
They are the same species (able to produce fertile offspring) [B1]
Differences due to (genetic) variation within the species / different alleles / environment. [B1]

questions.prompt: List the eight taxonomic ranks in order, starting with domain. (1)
hints: There are eight ranks in the hierarchy.
A common mnemonic is 'Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup'.
questions.solution: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. [B1]

questions.prompt:
The grey wolf is classified as follows: Domain Eukarya, Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order ________, Family Canidae, Genus ________, Species lupus.

Complete the two missing names. (1)
hints: The genus is the first word of the binomial name for the dog family.
questions.solution: Carnivora and Canis (both needed). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the three domains used to classify living organisms. (1)
hints: One contains all organisms with a nucleus.
Prokaryotes are split into two domains.
questions.solution: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya (all three needed). [B1]

questions.prompt: The domestic cat is Felis catus and the wildcat is Felis silvestris. Name the lowest taxon that both species belong to. (1)
hints: Look at the first word of each name.
The first word of a binomial is…
questions.solution: Genus. [B1]

questions.prompt: A plant was renamed from Aster novae-angliae to Symphyotrichum novae-angliae. Which taxon was changed? (1)
hints: Which part of the name changed?
The first part of a binomial name refers to…
questions.solution: Genus. [B1]

questions.prompt: What do the two parts of a binomial name represent? (1)
questions.solution: Genus (first part) and species (second part). [B1]

questions.prompt: The brown bear is Ursus arctos, the polar bear is Ursus maritimus and the giant panda is Ailuropoda melanoleuca. What do these names suggest about the evolutionary relationships of the three species? (2)
hints: What does sharing a genus suggest about ancestry?
questions.solution:
Brown and polar bears are in the same genus, so more closely related / share a more recent common ancestor [B1]
Giant panda is in a different genus, so less closely related to them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Quercus robur and Quercus petraea are two oak species. They can occasionally interbreed, but the hybrids have reduced fertility. Explain why they are classified as separate species but in the same genus. (2)
hints: What does being in the same genus suggest?
questions.solution:
They do not produce (fully) fertile offspring, so are different species [B1]
Same genus because they are closely related / share a recent common ancestor. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two species are in the same family but different genera. A third species is in the same genus as one of them. Explain which two species are most closely related. (2)
hints: Which is the smaller group: family or genus?
Smaller shared group = more recent common ancestor.
questions.solution:
The two in the same genus are most closely related [B1]
Genus is a smaller / lower taxon than family, so they share a more recent common ancestor. [B1]

questions.prompt: DNA similarity between three species is: A–B 92%, A–C 70%, B–C 71%. Which two species are most closely related? (1)
hints: Highest similarity = most recent common ancestor.
questions.solution: A and B. [B1]

questions.prompt: DNA similarity between three species is: P–Q 45%, P–R 80%, Q–R 47%. Which species diverged first from the other two? (1)
hints: The odd one out branched off first.

questions.prompt: The number of amino acid differences in cytochrome c compared with humans is: chimpanzee 0, dog 11, yeast 44. Which organism is least closely related to humans? (1)
questions.solution: Yeast. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two populations of a lizard have 92% similarity in a non-coding DNA sequence. Individuals within one population vary between 90% and 95% similarity. Do these data support classifying the two populations as separate species? Explain. (2)
hints: Is the between-population value outside the within-population range?
How else could you test whether they are one species?
questions.solution:
No: 92% is within the range found within one population, so the difference could be normal variation [B1]
Need other evidence, e.g. whether they can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a phylogenetic tree based on one gene may differ from a tree based on whole genomes. (2)
hints: How much information does one gene give?
Do all genes change at the same rate?
questions.solution:
One gene is a small sample of the DNA, so less reliable [B1]
Genes evolve at different rates / one gene may be under selection. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why scientists often compare non-coding DNA, rather than coding DNA, to work out relationships between closely related species. (2)
hints: Are mutations in non-coding DNA usually harmful?
questions.solution:
Mutations in non-coding DNA are not selected against (do not affect proteins) [B1]
So they accumulate faster, giving more differences to compare. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two populations of deer live on separate islands and look different, but are classified as the same species. Suggest why. (1)
hints: What is the definition of a species?
What would happen if they met?
questions.solution: They could still interbreed to produce fertile offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Dog breeds look very different from each other but are all one species. Explain why. (1)
hints: What can different breeds do together?
questions.solution: Different breeds can interbreed and produce fertile offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt:
A phylogenetic tree of a parasite shows that strains in South America are most closely related to strains in Europe, and European strains are most closely related to strains in Africa. Which route of spread is most likely?

Choose one answer.

A  Africa → Europe → South America
B  South America → Europe → Africa
C  Africa → South America → Europe
D  Europe → Africa → South America (1)
hints: The oldest, most diverse strains are at the origin.
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
A lizard species lives on the mainland and on islands A, B and C. Island A lizards are most similar to the mainland population, island B to island A, and island C to island B. Which order of colonisation is most likely?

Choose one answer.

A  Mainland → C → B → A
B  Mainland → B → A → C
C  Mainland → A → B → C
D  Mainland → A → C → B (1)
hints: Each new population is founded from the closest relative.
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which statement about phylogenetic trees is correct?

Choose one answer.

A  Species at the tips of longer branches are more advanced
B  Each branch point represents a common ancestor
C  Species next to each other on the page are always most closely related
D  Trees show the order in which species were discovered (1)
hints: Do trees show which species is 'more advanced'?
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt: Bacteria were once classified mainly by cell shape (rods, spheres or spirals). Evaluate this method. (3)
hints: Does similar shape mean close relationship?
questions.solution:
Advantage: shape is easy to see with an optical microscope [B1]
Limitation: unrelated bacteria can have the same shape [B1]
Shape may change with conditions / DNA comparisons give a more accurate picture of relationships. [B1]

questions.prompt: Evaluate the use of Gram staining (which reflects cell wall structure) to classify bacteria. (3)
hints: Does it reflect a real structural difference?
questions.solution:
Advantage: reflects a real difference in wall structure; quick and cheap [B1]
Limitation: only divides bacteria into two groups — cannot identify species [B1]
Some bacteria stain variably / unrelated bacteria may stain the same way. [B1]

questions.prompt: Evaluate classifying birds using beak shape. (3)
hints: What does beak shape relate to?
Could unrelated birds have similar beaks?
questions.solution:
Advantage: easy to observe and measure [B1]
Limitation: beak shape reflects diet, so unrelated birds with similar diets may have similar beaks (convergent evolution) [B1]
Variation within a species / DNA evidence is more reliable. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why some species have recently been moved into different genera. (1)
hints: What new evidence is available now?
questions.solution: New DNA / genome sequence evidence shows different evolutionary relationships. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why classification systems change over time. (1)
hints: Does scientific knowledge stay the same?
questions.solution: New evidence / technology (e.g. DNA sequencing) changes our understanding of relationships. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the three-domain system replaced the five-kingdom system of classification. (1)
hints: What did molecular evidence show about archaea and bacteria?
Were they as similar as once thought?
questions.solution: Molecular evidence (e.g. rRNA sequences) showed archaea are very different from bacteria. [B1]

questions.prompt: Complete the classification of humans: Domain Eukarya, Kingdom ______, Phylum Chordata, Class ______, Order Primates, Family Hominidae, Genus ______, Species sapiens. (2)
hints: Humans feed their young on milk.
questions.solution:
Animalia; Mammalia; Homo. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: The English oak is in the kingdom Plantae and the genus Quercus. Its species name is robur. Give its domain and its binomial name. (2)
questions.solution:
Domain: Eukarya [B1]
Binomial: Quercus robur. [B1]

questions.prompt: Put these taxa in order from largest to smallest: family, class, genus, kingdom, order, phylum. (2)
hints: Remember the mnemonic for the ranks.
questions.solution:
Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus. [B1]
Fully correct = 2 marks; one pair swapped = 1 mark. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how comparing amino acid sequences of a protein can show how closely related two species are. (3)
questions.solution:
Amino acid sequence is determined by the base sequence of DNA [B1]
Compare sequences of the same protein [B1]
Fewer differences means more closely related / more recent common ancestor. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how immunological comparisons can be used to show how closely related species are. (3)
questions.solution:
Antibodies raised against a protein from one species [B1]
Mixed with the same protein from another species [B1]
More precipitate means more similar protein, so more closely related. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the technique used to compare the base sequences of a gene in different species to determine relatedness. (1)
questions.solution: DNA sequencing. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name a protein-based method used to compare relatedness of species. (1)
questions.solution: Comparing amino acid sequences / immunological comparison. [B1]

questions.prompt: A journalist claimed that recently evolved shade-tolerant plant groups have higher concentrations of toxins. Data for six groups show two recently evolved groups with toxin concentrations above the mean for all plants and one below; of three older groups, two are below and one above. Do the data support the claim? Justify your answer. (2)
questions.solution:
Partly — most recently evolved groups are above the mean [B1]
But not all, and an older group is also above; only six groups / no statistics. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a phylogenetic tree shows which species are most closely related. (2)
questions.solution:
Species that branch from a more recent common ancestor are more closely related [B1]
Shorter branch distances / branch points closer to the tips. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two types of evidence used to build phylogenetic trees. (2)
questions.solution:
DNA base sequences / mRNA [B1]
Amino acid sequences / immunological comparisons / fossils. [B1]

questions.prompt: How many genera are represented by Chrysolina graminis, Gastrophysa viridula and Chrysolina herbacea? (1)
Panthera leo, Panthera tigris and Felis catus — how many genera are represented? (1)
List the taxonomic hierarchy from domain to species. (1)
questions.solution: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. [B1]

category: Genetic information, variation and relationships between organisms

questions.prompt: Explain why comparing DNA base sequences can give more information about relationships than comparing the amino acid sequences of proteins. (3)
hints: Does all DNA code for amino acids?
questions.solution:
Genetic code is degenerate — different triplets can code for the same amino acid [B1]
So some base changes / mutations do not change the amino acid sequence but are detected in DNA [B1]
Non-coding DNA / introns can also be compared. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how comparing the amino acid sequence of a protein can be used to find out how closely related two species are. (3)
hints: The same protein must be compared.
questions.solution:
Use the same protein from both species [B1]
Determine / compare the sequence of amino acids [B1]
Count the number of differences [B1]
Fewer differences = more closely related / more recent common ancestor. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: Describe how immunological comparisons can be used to find out how closely related two species are. (3)
hints: Antibodies are made against a protein from one species.
What is measured when they are mixed with another species' protein?
questions.solution:
Protein from species A injected into an animal (e.g. rabbit), which makes antibodies against it [B1]
Serum / antibodies mixed with the same protein from species B [B1]
Amount of precipitate / antibody binding measured [B1]
More precipitate = more similar protein = more closely related. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

Model answer:
Any 3 points.

questions.prompt: What does an index of diversity measure? (1)
hints: It uses two kinds of information.
questions.solution: The relationship between the number of species and the number of individuals in each species (in a community). [B1]

questions.prompt: Students used pitfall traps to sample invertebrates. Suggest one thing they should do to make the sampling ethical, and one thing to make sure the organisms are identified accurately. (2)
hints: How do you work out what species something is?
questions.solution:
Ethical: check traps regularly / release animals unharmed where caught / no preservative [B1]
Accurate identification: use an identification key / photograph / identify with a hand lens or expert. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two ethical considerations when sampling organisms from a rocky-shore rock pool. (2)
questions.solution:
Return organisms to where they were found / alive [B1]
Minimise disturbance to the habitat, e.g. replace rocks [B1]
Keep organisms in sea water / don't remove too many. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: A student placed five quadrats in places on a lawn where she could see lots of daisies, and counted the daisies. Suggest and explain two improvements to her method. (2)
questions.solution:
Place quadrats randomly (e.g. random number coordinates), to avoid bias [B1]
Use more quadrats, so results are representative / a reliable mean can be calculated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Students estimated the percentage cover of moss by eye, using one 1 m² quadrat on each of two lawns. Suggest and explain two improvements. (2)
hints: One quadrat may not be typical.
questions.solution:
Use a gridded quadrat / point quadrat, so cover is measured more objectively / accurately [B1]
Use more quadrats placed randomly on each lawn, so results are representative. [B1]

questions.prompt: The index of diversity is d = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1). State what N and n represent. (1)
hints: One is a total, one is per species.
questions.solution: N = total number of organisms of all species; n = number of organisms of each species. [B1]

questions.prompt: A sample contained 10 individuals of species A, 5 of species B and 5 of species C. Calculate the index of diversity using d = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1). (1)
What information does an index of diversity take into account that species richness does not? (1)
hints: Species richness is just a count of species.
What else does the index use?
questions.solution: The number of individuals of each species (abundance). [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two ways students could make sure their samples of invertebrates from a stream are representative. (2)
questions.solution:
Sample at random sites / along the whole stream [B1]
Take many samples [B1]
Use the same method / time for each kick sample. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Give two ways students could make sure a sample of tree species in a woodland is representative. (2)
hints: How do you avoid choosing sites yourself?
Does one quadrat cover a wood?
questions.solution:
Use random coordinates / random number generator [B1]
Use a large number of sampling points / quadrats across the whole wood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a large sample size gives a more representative estimate of biodiversity. (2)
hints: How does sample size affect the influence of unusual results?
Which species might a small sample miss?
questions.solution:
Reduces the effect of chance / anomalous samples [B1]
More likely to include rare species / gives a more reliable mean. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why removing hedgerows from farmland reduces the diversity of birds. (1)
hints: What do hedges provide for birds?
questions.solution: Fewer habitats / nesting sites / food sources. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why growing a single crop over a large area (monoculture) reduces insect diversity. (1)
hints: How many types of plant are available?
Different insects need different food plants.
questions.solution: Only one plant species, so few food sources / habitats / niches. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why leaving the edges of fields unsprayed with herbicide increases biodiversity. (1)
questions.solution: Wild plants survive, providing food / habitats for insects and other animals. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one advantage and one disadvantage to a farmer of leaving strips of land around fields uncultivated. Explain each. (2)
hints: Which animals might live in the strips?
questions.solution:
Advantage: habitat for predators of pests / pollinators, so less pesticide needed / higher yield [B1]
Disadvantage: less land for crops, so lower yield / income (or weeds spread). [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a farmer using pesticides. Explain each. (2)
hints: What do pesticides do for yield?
questions.solution:
Advantage: kills pests, so less crop damage / higher yield [B1]
Disadvantage: kills non-target species, reducing biodiversity / pests may become resistant / cost. [B1]

questions.prompt: A farmer replaces hedges with wire fences. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of this to the farmer. Explain each. (2)
questions.solution:
Advantage: more land for crops / less maintenance, so higher yield [B1]
Disadvantage: loss of habitat for pest predators / more soil erosion by wind, so may reduce yield. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why percentage cover, rather than number of individuals, is used to record grass species in a quadrat. (1)
hints: Can you easily tell where one grass plant ends?
questions.solution: It is difficult to tell individual grass plants apart / count them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why biomass, rather than number of individuals, can be a better measure of how much each plant species contributes to a community. (1)
hints: Are all plants the same size?
A tree and a seedling both count as 'one'.
questions.solution: Individuals vary greatly in size, so numbers don't reflect how much of the community each species makes up. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest and explain why biodiversity is lower in a field that has been ploughed and sprayed with herbicide than in a nearby meadow. (2)
hints: What does herbicide do to wild plants?
questions.solution:
Herbicide kills wild plant species, so fewer food sources / habitats [B1]
Ploughing destroys habitats / soil organisms, so fewer species survive. [B1]

questions.prompt: When a field stops being farmed, the diversity of soil fungi recovers only slowly. Suggest two reasons. (2)
hints: Where must new fungi come from?
Could farming chemicals remain in the soil?
questions.solution:
Spores must spread in from other areas / few fungi left to recolonise [B1]
Residues of fertiliser / fungicide remain / soil structure has been damaged. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why two communities with the same species richness can have different indices of diversity. (1)
hints: What else does the index include?
Think about how evenly individuals are spread among species.
questions.solution: The number of individuals in each species differs between the communities. [B1]

questions.prompt: Community A has 4 species with 25 individuals each. Community B has 4 species with 97, 1, 1 and 1 individuals. Which has the higher index of diversity? (1)
questions.solution: Community A. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define species richness. (1)
questions.solution: The number of different species in a community. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why pitfall traps were placed in several different parts of a woodland. (1)
hints: Is the woodland the same everywhere?
questions.solution: Different species live in different microhabitats, so the sample is more representative. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why insect samples were collected at different times of day. (1)
hints: Are all insects active at the same time?
questions.solution: Different species are active at different times of day. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a biodiversity survey was repeated throughout a year. (1)
hints: Do numbers stay the same all year?
questions.solution: Abundance of species changes with the seasons. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how removing hedgerows to make larger fields reduces biodiversity on farmland. (2)
hints: Biodiversity = number of species and their abundance.
questions.solution:
Fewer habitats / niches / food sources [B1]
So fewer species (lower species diversity). [B1]

questions.prompt: Tropical rainforests have many plant species arranged in several layers. Explain why this leads to high animal biodiversity. (3)
hints: What do plants provide for animals?
questions.solution:
Many plant species provide many different food sources [B1]
Many habitats / layers, so many niches [B1]
So many animal species can coexist (less competition). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why replacing a rainforest with a single crop (monoculture) reduces animal biodiversity. (3)
questions.solution:
Only one plant species, so fewer food sources [B1]
Fewer habitats / niches [B1]
So fewer animal species can survive / pesticides kill others. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how an index of diversity takes account of both the number of species and the number of individuals. (3)
hints: What does a high value mean?
questions.solution:
N is the total number of organisms; n the number of each species [B1]
Index increases with more species and with more even numbers of each [B1]
High index means high diversity / more stable community. [B1]

questions.prompt: Use the formula d = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1) to calculate the index of diversity for the plant species counts in the table. (2)
questions.table:
Species | Number
A | 5
B | 12
C | 8
D | 3
E | 2

questions.prompt: Use d = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1) to calculate the index of diversity for the counts in the table. (2)
questions.table:
Species | Number
A | 10
B | 10
C | 6
D | 4

questions.prompt: Use d = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1) to calculate the index of diversity for the counts in the table. (2)
questions.table:
Species | Number
A | 15
B | 3
C | 2
D | 20

questions.prompt: Explain why an index of diversity gives more information than species richness. (3)
hints: Does richness consider numbers of each species?
questions.solution:
Species richness is only the number of species [B1]
Index also takes into account the number of individuals of each species [B1]
So shows whether one species dominates / evenness. [B1]

questions.prompt: For a fish survey, N = 400 and Σn(n − 1) = 19 950. Calculate the index of diversity d = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1). (1)
N = 250 and Σn(n − 1) = 12 450. Calculate d. (1)
N = 120 and Σn(n − 1) = 3570. Calculate d. (1)
Describe and explain how a year could have the highest species richness but the lowest index of diversity. (2)
questions.solution:
Many species present, but most individuals belong to one / a few species [B1]
Index accounts for the number of individuals of each species, so dominance lowers d. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two sites each have 5 species and 100 individuals. At site A each species has 20 individuals; at site B one species has 96. Explain which has the higher index of diversity. (2)
questions.solution:
Site A [B1]
Individuals evenly spread, so Σn(n − 1) is smaller and d is larger. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an index of diversity is more useful than species richness for comparing communities. (2)
questions.solution:
Index takes into account the number of individuals of each species as well as number of species [B1]
Shows evenness / whether one species dominates. [B1]

questions.prompt:
The number of bird species breeding in a woodland was counted each year. Which statement correctly describes species richness of this woodland?

Choose one answer.

A  The number of all species in the woodland
B  The number of species and habitats
C  The number of animal and plant species
D  The number of bird species breeding in the woodland (1)
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which is the definition of species richness?

Choose one answer.

A  The number of different species in a community
B  The number of individuals of each species
C  The index of diversity
D  The total biomass (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which measure takes account of both species and individuals?

Choose one answer.

A  Species richness
B  Population size
C  Index of diversity
D  Carrying capacity (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how protecting a woodland might increase bird diversity over time. (4)
questions.solution:
No logging / disturbance allows succession, with more trees and layers [B1]
More habitats / niches [B1]
More food sources (insects, seeds) [B1]
So more bird species can breed there. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three ways in which human activities reduce biodiversity. (3)
questions.solution:
Deforestation / habitat destruction [B1]
Pollution / pesticides / eutrophication [B1]
Monoculture / hedgerow removal / overfishing / climate change. [B1]

category: Energy transfers in and between organisms

questions.prompt: Explain why a plant that closes its stomata on a hot day grows more slowly. (2)
questions.solution:
Less carbon dioxide diffuses in [B1]
So less photosynthesis / fewer sugars for growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: Most plants open their stomata in the light and close them in the dark. Explain the advantage of this. (2)
hints: What is lost through open stomata?
questions.solution:
CO₂ is only needed for photosynthesis in the light, so stomata open to let it in [B1]
Closing in the dark reduces water loss when no CO₂ is needed. [B1]

questions.prompt: A scientist claims that crop plants bred to have more stomata will photosynthesise faster. Evaluate this claim. (4)
hints: Is CO₂ always the limiting factor?
questions.solution:
More stomata let more CO₂ in, which could increase photosynthesis [B1]
But only if CO₂ is the limiting factor — light or temperature may limit instead [B1]
More stomata also increase water loss, which could cause stomata to close / wilting [B1]
Needs testing with data from real crops / yields. [B1]

questions.prompt: Magnesium-deficient plants have yellow leaves and grow slowly. Explain why. (3)
hints: Link it to the light-dependent reaction and growth.
questions.solution:
Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll [B1]
Less chlorophyll, so less light absorbed / less light-dependent reaction (less ATP and NADPH) [B1]
Less light-independent reaction / less glucose for respiration and growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: Plants grown without nitrate grow slowly. Explain why. (3)
hints: Why are these needed for growth?
questions.solution:
Nitrate needed to make amino acids / proteins (including enzymes) [B1]
Also needed for nucleotides / DNA / ATP / chlorophyll [B1]
So less protein synthesis / cell division / photosynthesis — slower growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: Electron micrographs show that chloroplasts from stressed plants have fewer and smaller grana. Suggest why these plants grow more slowly. (3)
hints: What is on the thylakoid membranes?
Which stage of photosynthesis needs them?
questions.solution:
Less thylakoid membrane, so less chlorophyll / fewer electron carriers [B1]
Less light-dependent reaction, so less ATP and reduced NADP [B1]
Less light-independent reaction, so less sugar for growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the rate of photosynthesis of an alpine population and a lowland population of the same plant species at two temperatures. Use the data to show how each population is adapted. (4)
hints: Which population photosynthesises faster in the cold?
What determines how photosynthesis responds to temperature?
questions.solution:
Alpine plants photosynthesise faster at 10 °C; lowland plants faster at 25 °C [B1]
Alpine plants' enzymes (e.g. rubisco) work better / have a lower optimum temperature [B1]
Alpine plants may have more unsaturated fatty acids, keeping membranes fluid in the cold [B1]
So each makes more sugar for growth in its own environment. [B1]
questions.table:
Population | Rate at 10 °C | Rate at 25 °C
Alpine | 14 | 16
Lowland | 6 | 24

questions.prompt: Name the stacks of thylakoids found in a chloroplast. (1)
questions.solution: Grana. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the fluid that surrounds the thylakoids in a chloroplast. (1)
questions.solution: Stroma. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the insoluble storage structures often seen in the stroma of chloroplasts. (1)
questions.solution: Starch grains. [B1]

questions.prompt: Chloroplasts in a mutant plant have no grana. Predict the effect on photosynthesis and justify your prediction. (2)
hints: Which stage of photosynthesis happens there?
questions.solution:
Photosynthesis would be reduced [B1]
Less thylakoid membrane / chlorophyll, so less light-dependent reaction (less ATP and reduced NADP). [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutant plant has half the normal number of chloroplasts in each palisade cell. Predict the effect on photosynthesis and justify. (2)
questions.solution:
Photosynthesis would be reduced (especially in low light) [B1]
Less chlorophyll, so less light absorbed for the light-dependent reaction. [B1]

questions.prompt: The thylakoid membranes of a mutant plant lack ATP synthase. Predict the effect on photosynthesis and justify. (2)
questions.solution:
No ATP produced in the light-dependent reaction [B1]
So the light-independent reaction stops (ATP needed to reduce GP and regenerate RuBP). [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutant plant has half the chlorophyll of a normal plant but a higher rate of photosynthesis. Suggest explanations for these results. (3)
hints: Is chlorophyll always the limiting factor?
How might light reach deeper cells?
questions.solution:
Chlorophyll / light absorption is not the limiting factor in the normal plant (e.g. CO₂ or enzymes limit) [B1]
Less chlorophyll in upper cells lets more light reach lower cells in the leaf [B1]
The mutant may have more rubisco / other enzymes or more stomata. [B1]
questions.table:
Plant | Chlorophyll / µg cm⁻³ | Rate of photosynthesis / a.u.
Normal | 40 | 10
Mutant | 20 | 12

questions.prompt: Plants growing in shade have a higher proportion of chlorophyll b than plants in full sun. Suggest an explanation. (3)
hints: Do chlorophyll a and b absorb the same wavelengths?
questions.solution:
Chlorophyll b absorbs different wavelengths from chlorophyll a [B1]
So a wider range of wavelengths is absorbed [B1]
Helps absorb more of the limited light (wavelengths that pass through the canopy) in shade. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how chromatography could show that a mutant plant lacks chlorophyll b. (3)
hints: How are pigments extracted and separated?
How do you compare the plants?
questions.solution:
Grind leaves with solvent to extract pigments; spot onto chromatography paper [B1]
Run with a solvent; pigments separate by solubility / Rf value [B1]
Compare with a normal plant: the spot with chlorophyll b's Rf value is missing in the mutant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Leaves were supplied with ¹⁴CO₂. Name the process by which the leaves turn it into sugars. (1)
questions.solution: Photosynthesis. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an investigation using chloroplasts and DCPIP, one tube contained chloroplasts and DCPIP kept in the dark. Explain the purpose of this tube. (2)
hints: What does the dark tube rule out?
questions.solution:
Shows that light is needed for DCPIP to be decolourised [B1]
So the change is due to the light-dependent reaction. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an investigation using chloroplasts and DCPIP, one tube contained DCPIP but no chloroplasts and was kept in the light. Explain the purpose of this tube. (2)
hints: What does the control rule out?
questions.solution:
Shows that light alone does not decolourise DCPIP [B1]
So the change in other tubes is due to the chloroplasts. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an investigation using chloroplasts and DCPIP, one tube contained boiled chloroplasts in the light. Explain the purpose of this tube. (2)
hints: What does boiling do to chloroplast proteins?
questions.solution:
Boiling denatures enzymes / proteins in the chloroplasts [B1]
Shows that functioning chloroplasts are needed for the colour change. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why DCPIP is decolourised faster when chloroplasts are kept in bright light than in dim light. (2)
hints: What does light do to chlorophyll?
questions.solution:
More light means more photoionisation of chlorophyll / more electrons released [B1]
DCPIP accepts the electrons, so is reduced (decolourised) faster. [B1]

questions.prompt: A chemical blocks the transfer of electrons from chlorophyll to the electron transfer chain. Explain why DCPIP stays blue when chloroplasts are treated with it. (2)
questions.solution:
Electrons do not reach the electron transfer chain / DCPIP [B1]
So DCPIP is not reduced and stays blue. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what DCPIP replaces in the light-dependent reaction when used in this investigation. (2)
hints: What normally accepts electrons at the end of the chain?
What happens to DCPIP when it accepts electrons?
questions.solution:
DCPIP acts as the electron acceptor instead of NADP [B1]
It is reduced, changing from blue to colourless. [B1]

questions.prompt: A herbicide inhibits an enzyme of the Calvin cycle. Explain how this slows weed growth. (2)
hints: What does the Calvin cycle produce?
questions.solution:
Less GP converted to triose phosphate, so less glucose / sugars made [B1]
Less respiratory substrate / fewer organic molecules for growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: A herbicide destroys chlorophyll. Explain how this slows weed growth. (2)
hints: Which products of the light-dependent reaction are needed?
questions.solution:
Less light absorbed, so less ATP and reduced NADP made [B1]
Less light-independent reaction, so less sugar for growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: A herbicide blocks ATP synthase in chloroplasts. Explain how this slows plant growth. (2)
questions.solution:
No ATP made in the light-dependent reaction [B1]
So the light-independent reaction cannot reduce GP / regenerate RuBP — less sugar made. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the light-independent reaction stops when a plant is moved into the dark. (2)
hints: Which products of the light-dependent reaction are needed?
What do they do in the Calvin cycle?
questions.solution:
No ATP or reduced NADP produced in the dark [B1]
So GP cannot be reduced to triose phosphate / RuBP cannot be regenerated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the concentration of GP in chloroplasts rises when the light is switched off. (2)
questions.solution:
GP is still made from RuBP and CO₂ (for a while) [B1]
GP is not converted to triose phosphate because there is no ATP / reduced NADP, so it accumulates. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the concentration of RuBP in chloroplasts rises when the CO₂ supply is removed. (2)
hints: What does RuBP normally combine with?
questions.solution:
RuBP is not used up, because there is no CO₂ to combine with [B1]
RuBP is still regenerated from triose phosphate using ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: At high light intensity, increasing light further does not increase the rate of photosynthesis. Explain why the activity of rubisco may now limit the rate. (2)
hints: Is light still the limiting factor?
questions.solution:
Light is no longer limiting [B1]
Rate of CO₂ fixation (RuBP + CO₂ → GP) by rubisco limits production of GP / TP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why increasing carbon dioxide concentration can increase the rate of photosynthesis. (2)
questions.solution:
More CO₂ combines with RuBP (catalysed by rubisco) [B1]
So more GP and triose phosphate / glucose are produced. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how low temperature limits the rate of the light-independent reaction. (2)
questions.solution:
Enzymes such as rubisco have less kinetic energy [B1]
So fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form and CO₂ is fixed more slowly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Where in a chloroplast is ATP synthase located? (1)
hints: Where is the electron transfer chain?
questions.solution: Thylakoid membranes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Where in a chloroplast is chlorophyll found? (1)
questions.solution: Thylakoid membranes (grana). [B1]

questions.prompt: Where in a chloroplast does the Calvin cycle take place? (1)
questions.solution: Stroma. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the activity of rubisco, the activity of rubisco activase (an enzyme that activates rubisco) and the rate of photosynthesis at different temperatures, as percentages of their values at 25 °C. Evaluate the conclusion that high temperature reduces photosynthesis by affecting rubisco activase rather than rubisco itself. (4)
hints: Which enzyme's activity falls in line with photosynthesis?
What else could high temperature affect?
questions.solution:
Rubisco activity stays high (90% at 45 °C) while activase falls sharply (to 15%) [B1]
Fall in activase matches the fall in photosynthesis, supporting the conclusion [B1]
But this is a correlation — other factors (stomatal closure, membrane damage) could also reduce photosynthesis [B1]
Enzymes may have been tested in isolation, not in the leaf / no SD or repeats. [B1]
questions.table:
