Temperature / °C | Rubisco | Rubisco activase | Photosynthesis
25 | 100 | 100 | 100
35 | 98 | 60 | 70
45 | 90 | 15 | 25

questions.prompt: At 25 °C, 35 °C and 45 °C, rates of photosynthesis were 100%, 70% and 25% of maximum, and stomatal opening was 100%, 90% and 85%. Evaluate the conclusion that high temperature reduces photosynthesis mainly by closing stomata. (4)
hints: Compare the size of the two falls.
questions.solution:
Stomatal opening falls only a little (15%) while photosynthesis falls by 75% [B1]
So stomatal closure alone cannot explain most of the decrease — conclusion not well supported [B1]
Enzymes (e.g. rubisco / activase) may be denatured at high temperature [B1]
Correlation only / no SD or statistics. [B1]

questions.prompt: Plants given extra copies of the rubisco activase gene photosynthesised at 80% of their maximum rate at 40 °C, compared with 40% for normal plants. Evaluate the conclusion that rubisco activase limits photosynthesis at high temperature. (4)
hints: What does doubling the photosynthesis rate suggest?
questions.solution:
Extra activase doubled photosynthesis at 40 °C, supporting the idea that activase is limiting [B1]
Shows a cause-and-effect relationship because only activase was changed [B1]
But photosynthesis still did not reach 100%, so other factors also limit it [B1]
Need repeats / SD / statistics and more temperatures / species. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which list gives the products of the light-dependent reaction?

Choose one answer.

A  ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen
B  ATP, glucose and oxygen
C  GP, triose phosphate and RuBP
D  Carbon dioxide, water and light (1)
hints: Which are made on the thylakoids?
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which list gives the substances needed for the light-independent reaction?

Choose one answer.

A  Water, light and chlorophyll
B  Oxygen, ATP and glucose
C  ATP, reduced NADP and carbon dioxide
D  NADP, ADP and oxygen (1)
hints: Which products of the light-dependent reaction are used?
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
What replaces the electrons lost from chlorophyll in the light-dependent reaction?

Choose one answer.

A  Electrons from NADPH
B  Electrons from the photolysis of water
C  Electrons from glucose
D  Electrons from ATP (1)
hints: What molecule is split by light?
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe photolysis in the light-dependent reaction. (2)
hints: What are the products used for?
questions.solution:
Light energy splits water into H⁺ (protons), electrons and oxygen [B1]
Electrons replace those lost from chlorophyll (H⁺ used to reduce NADP; oxygen released). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how ATP is made in the light-dependent reaction. (2)
hints: What happens as electrons pass along the chain?
Which enzyme do protons flow through?
questions.solution:
Energy from electrons passing along the electron transfer chain pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid space [B1]
H⁺ diffuse back through ATP synthase, which joins ADP and Pi (chemiosmosis). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how NADP is reduced in the light-dependent reaction. (2)
hints: Where do the electrons come from?
Where do the H⁺ come from?
questions.solution:
Electrons from the end of the electron transfer chain [B1]
Combine with H⁺ (from photolysis) and NADP, forming reduced NADP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to extract photosynthetic pigments from leaves. (2)
hints: How do you break open the cells?
questions.solution:
Grind leaves with a solvent such as propanone (and sand) [B1]
Filter / decant to obtain the pigment solution. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest the advantage of a leaf containing chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b. (1)
hints: Do they absorb exactly the same wavelengths?
questions.solution: Absorb a wider range of wavelengths, so more light energy is used for photosynthesis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why most leaves look green. (1)
questions.solution: Green wavelengths are not absorbed but reflected. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of accessory pigments such as carotenoids. (1)
questions.solution: Absorb wavelengths that chlorophyll does not, and pass the energy to chlorophyll. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the five-carbon molecule that accepts CO₂ in the Calvin cycle and the enzyme that catalyses this reaction. (2)
hints: It's regenerated each turn of the cycle.
The most abundant enzyme on Earth.
questions.solution:
RuBP (ribulose bisphosphate) [B1]
Rubisco. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the two three-carbon molecules in the Calvin cycle. (2)
hints: One is formed when CO₂ combines with RuBP.
The other is formed by reducing it.
questions.solution:
Glycerate 3-phosphate (GP) [B1]
Triose phosphate (TP). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the three products of photolysis. (2)
questions.solution:
Protons (H⁺), electrons and oxygen. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Apart from respiration, give two uses of the sugars made in photosynthesis. (2)
hints: What structural molecule do plants make?
questions.solution: Two from: making cellulose (cell walls); starch for storage; sucrose for transport; amino acids / lipids / other organic molecules. [B2]

questions.prompt: Describe the light-dependent reaction of photosynthesis. (6)
hints: What happens to chlorophyll when light hits it?
How are ATP and reduced NADP made?
questions.solution:
Light energy excites electrons in chlorophyll, which are lost (photoionisation) [B1]
Electrons pass along the electron transfer chain in the thylakoid membrane [B1]
Energy released pumps protons into the thylakoid space [B1]
Protons diffuse back through ATP synthase, making ATP from ADP + Pi (chemiosmosis) [B1]
Photolysis of water produces protons, electrons and oxygen; electrons replace those lost by chlorophyll [B1]
Electrons and protons reduce NADP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how triose phosphate from the Calvin cycle is used to make other organic molecules in a plant. (6)
hints: How are lipids and amino acids made?
questions.solution:
Most triose phosphate is used to regenerate RuBP [B1]
Some is converted to glucose (hexose) [B1]
Glucose used to make sucrose, starch and cellulose [B1]
Triose phosphate converted to glycerol, and GP to fatty acids — for lipids [B1]
Amino acids made from GP / TP with nitrogen from nitrate [B1]
These are used for growth / proteins / membranes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the light-dependent and light-independent reactions of photosynthesis. (6)
hints: What are the inputs and outputs?
questions.solution:
Light-dependent: on thylakoid membranes; light-independent: in the stroma [B1]
Light-dependent needs light; light-independent doesn't directly need light [B1]
Light-dependent uses water and produces oxygen [B1]
Light-dependent produces ATP and reduced NADP [B1]
Light-independent uses ATP, reduced NADP and CO₂ [B1]
Light-independent produces triose phosphate and regenerates RuBP (enzyme-controlled, uses rubisco). [B1]

questions.prompt: The same pigment extract was run with two different solvents. Solvent X separated five pigments but solvent Y separated six. Explain why. (2)
hints: How does solubility affect how far a pigment moves?
What happens to two pigments with the same Rf value?
questions.solution:
Pigments have different solubilities in each solvent, so move different distances [B1]
In solvent X two pigments had the same / very similar Rf value, so they appeared as one spot. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why chloroplasts contain several different photosynthetic pigments rather than just one. (2)
hints: What happens to the energy they absorb?
questions.solution:
Different pigments absorb different wavelengths of light [B1]
So more of the light spectrum is used / more energy is transferred to the reaction centre for photosynthesis. [B1]

questions.prompt: A plant grown in the shade had more chlorophyll b relative to chlorophyll a than a plant grown in full sun. Suggest how this is an advantage to the shade plant. (2)
hints: Does chlorophyll b absorb the same wavelengths as chlorophyll a?
What light reaches the shade plant?
questions.solution:
Chlorophyll b absorbs wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs less well [B1]
So the shade plant absorbs more of the limited light / more light energy for the light-dependent reaction. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the percentage of light absorbed by a leaf and its rate of photosynthesis in different colours of light. State one conclusion about (i) percentage absorbed and rate, and (ii) colour of light and rate. (2)
hints: Which colours give the highest rates?
questions.solution:
(i) Higher percentage absorbed, higher rate of photosynthesis (positive correlation) [B1]
(ii) Rate highest in blue and red light, lowest in green. [B1]
questions.table:
Colour | Light absorbed / % | Rate / arbitrary units
Blue | 85 | 80
Green | 20 | 15
Yellow | 35 | 30
Red | 75 | 70

questions.prompt: Explain why leaves appear green. (2)
questions.solution:
Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light [B1]
Green light is reflected / transmitted to our eyes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis is low in green light. (2)
hints: How much green light is absorbed?
questions.solution:
Little green light is absorbed by chlorophyll [B1]
So less energy for photoionisation / fewer electrons excited, so less ATP and reduced NADP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the products of the light-dependent reaction are used to make triose phosphate. Do not describe the regeneration of RuBP. (3)
hints: What is made when CO₂ combines with RuBP?
questions.solution:
CO₂ combines with RuBP (rubisco) to form two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate (GP) [B1]
GP is reduced to triose phosphate [B1]
Using reduced NADP and energy from ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the concentration of GP rises and RuBP falls when a plant is moved from light into darkness. (3)
questions.solution:
Light-dependent reaction stops, so no ATP or reduced NADP [B1]
GP can't be reduced to TP, so GP accumulates (still made from RuBP + CO₂) [B1]
RuBP can't be regenerated (needs ATP), so RuBP falls. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the concentration of RuBP rises and GP falls when the carbon dioxide concentration around a plant is lowered. (3)
questions.solution:
Less CO₂ to combine with RuBP [B1]
So less GP formed, and GP still converted to TP, so GP falls [B1]
RuBP still regenerated from TP (ATP available), so RuBP accumulates. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why increasing the carbon dioxide concentration in a greenhouse can increase crop yield, but only up to a point. (2)
questions.solution:
More CO₂ combines with RuBP, so more GP / TP / sugars made [B1]
At high CO₂ another factor (light / temperature) becomes limiting. [B1]

questions.prompt: Chloroplasts were isolated from normal and mutant plants. Explain why the rate of oxygen production was measured to compare their photosynthesis. (2)
questions.solution:
Oxygen is produced in the light-dependent reaction (photolysis of water) [B1]
Rate of oxygen production indicates the rate of photosynthesis / easy to measure. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the rate of oxygen production by a whole leaf may underestimate its rate of photosynthesis. (2)
questions.solution:
Some oxygen is used in respiration by the leaf [B1]
So only net oxygen release is measured. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a redox indicator such as DCPIP can be used to measure the rate of the light-dependent reaction in isolated chloroplasts. (2)
questions.solution:
DCPIP accepts electrons from the electron transfer chain and changes from blue to colourless [B1]
Faster colour change means faster light-dependent reaction (measure with a colorimeter). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis levels off at high light intensities. (4)
questions.solution:
At low intensities, light is the limiting factor [B1]
As intensity increases, another factor becomes limiting [B1]
Such as CO₂ concentration or temperature [B1]
Or the amount of rubisco / chlorophyll / rate of the light-independent reaction. [B1]

questions.prompt: Plants grown in shade have more chlorophyll per chloroplast than those grown in bright light. Explain the advantages of this. (4)
questions.solution:
Shade has lower light intensity [B1]
More chlorophyll absorbs more of the available light [B1]
More photoionisation / more ATP and reduced NADP [B1]
Maintains a higher rate of photosynthesis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how reduced aquaporin in leaf cells could reduce the rate of photosynthesis. (3)
hints: Can CO₂ enter the chloroplast easily?
questions.solution:
Less CO₂ diffuses into cells / chloroplasts [B1]
Less CO₂ combines with RuBP, so less GP / TP made [B1]
Less water for photolysis / stomata may close. [B1]

questions.prompt: Very high light intensity can stop chlorophyll from releasing electrons. Suggest how this could explain lower CO₂ uptake by leaves in full sun around midday. (4)
hints: Products needed for the Calvin cycle.
questions.solution:
Fewer electrons released / less photoionisation, so fewer electrons pass along the electron transfer chain [B1]
Less ATP and reduced NADP produced [B1]
Less GP reduced to TP / RuBP not regenerated [B1]
So less CO₂ combined with RuBP / taken up (also stomata may close / high temperature). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why CO₂ uptake by a plant falls when the temperature is very high. (4)
questions.solution:
Enzymes such as rubisco denature [B1]
Less CO₂ fixed with RuBP [B1]
Stomata close to reduce water loss [B1]
Less CO₂ enters the leaf / photorespiration increases. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the effect of increasing light intensity on CO₂ uptake by a leaf from darkness to bright light. (4)
questions.solution:
In darkness, CO₂ is released (respiration only) [B1]
As light increases, photosynthesis increases until CO₂ uptake equals release (compensation point) [B1]
Then net CO₂ uptake increases as light is limiting [B1]
Levels off when another factor (CO₂, temperature) becomes limiting. [B1]

category: Energy transfers in and between organisms

questions.prompt: A germinating seed contains a store of starch. Suggest how this starch provides energy for the growing seedling. (2)
hints: Starch is too large to be used directly — what must happen to it?
What process releases energy from glucose?
questions.solution:
Starch is hydrolysed (by amylase) to maltose / glucose [B1]
Glucose is used in respiration to produce ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how triglycerides stored in adipose tissue provide energy for muscle cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Triglycerides hydrolysed (by lipase) into glycerol and fatty acids [B1]
These are respired / used in respiration to produce ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Muscle cells store glycogen. Explain how this glycogen provides energy for muscle contraction during exercise. (2)
hints: Two steps: break the store down, then make the energy currency.
What is the immediate energy source for contraction?
questions.solution:
Glycogen hydrolysed to glucose [B1]
Glucose respired (aerobically or anaerobically) producing ATP, which is hydrolysed to release energy for contraction. [B1]

questions.prompt: In glycolysis, glucose is phosphorylated using ATP. Explain why. (2)
hints: Is phosphorylated glucose more or less reactive?
What is needed to split it?
questions.solution:
Phosphate from ATP is added to glucose [B1]
Makes glucose more reactive / lowers activation energy so it can be split into triose phosphate. [B1]

questions.prompt: What are cristae? (1)
hints: They are found in an organelle used in respiration.
questions.solution: Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some time after leaves were given ¹⁴CO₂, radioactive CO₂ was released from the roots. Name the process that released it. (1)
hints: Which process breaks down sugars to release CO₂?
Roots do it all the time.
questions.solution: Respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: During long periods of exercise, muscles respire more fatty acids. Explain how transporting more fatty acids into mitochondria helps muscles keep contracting. (3)
hints: What are fatty acids broken into?
Which stage of respiration makes most ATP?
questions.solution:
Fatty acids are broken into acetyl groups that enter the Krebs cycle (as acetyl coenzyme A) [B1]
Producing more reduced NAD / FAD [B1]
So more ATP from oxidative phosphorylation (and glycogen is spared). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why lipids release more energy per gram than carbohydrates when respired. (3)
hints: Which bonds are lipids rich in?
questions.solution:
Lipids contain more C–H bonds / hydrogen per gram [B1]
More hydrogen to reduce NAD and FAD [B1]
So more ATP produced by oxidative phosphorylation. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug blocks transport of fatty acids into mitochondria. Suggest the effect on a muscle during a long period of exercise. (3)
hints: What must the muscle use instead?
What happens when that runs out?
questions.solution:
Fewer fatty acids respired [B1]
Muscle relies more on glucose / glycogen, which is used up faster [B1]
Less ATP later in exercise, so fatigue occurs sooner. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a respirometer containing germinating seeds and potassium hydroxide (which absorbs CO₂), the coloured liquid moved towards the seeds. Explain why. (2)
hints: What happens to the CO₂ produced?
questions.solution:
Oxygen is used in aerobic respiration and CO₂ produced is absorbed by the KOH [B1]
So gas volume / pressure in the tube decreases, pulling the liquid towards the seeds. [B1]

questions.prompt: Yeast respiring anaerobically was placed in a sealed tube attached to a capillary tube, with no CO₂ absorber. The coloured liquid moved away from the yeast. Explain why. (2)
hints: Is oxygen used in anaerobic respiration?
questions.solution:
Anaerobic respiration produces CO₂ without using oxygen [B1]
So gas volume increases and pushes the liquid away. [B1]

questions.prompt: Seeds respiring aerobically using glucose were placed in a respirometer without a CO₂ absorber. The liquid hardly moved. Explain why. (2)
hints: Compare oxygen used with CO₂ produced.
What is the RQ of glucose?
questions.solution:
For glucose, the volume of CO₂ produced equals the volume of O₂ used (RQ = 1) [B1]
So there is no net change in gas volume. [B1]

questions.prompt: Glucose solution was added to the dishes containing shoot segments. Explain why. (2)
hints: Can cut segments in the dark photosynthesise?
What do cells need for growth?
questions.solution:
Glucose is a respiratory substrate (segments cannot photosynthesise in the dark / are cut off from leaves) [B1]
Provides ATP for growth / cell elongation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Plant tissue cultures are grown on a medium containing sucrose. Explain why. (2)
hints: Can small pieces of tissue make enough sugar?
questions.solution:
Tissue cannot photosynthesise enough / has no leaves [B1]
Sucrose provides a source of energy (respiratory substrate) and carbon for growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol when oxygen is not available. (2)
questions.solution:
Oxidises reduced NAD, regenerating NAD [B1]
So glycolysis can continue, producing ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why anaerobic respiration produces much less ATP than aerobic respiration. (2)
questions.solution:
Only glycolysis occurs — no Krebs cycle or oxidative phosphorylation [B1]
So only 2 ATP (net) per glucose. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what happens to lactate after a period of intense exercise. (2)
questions.solution:
Lactate is carried to the liver [B1]
Converted back to pyruvate / glucose (using oxygen — oxygen debt). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how fat stores allow a hibernating animal to survive for months without eating. (3)
hints: What does respiring fat produce besides ATP?
questions.solution:
Fat is respired, releasing energy (ATP and heat) [B1]
Fat stores a lot of energy per gram [B1]
Respiring fat produces metabolic water; low metabolic rate makes stores last. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why hibernating animals let their body temperature fall. (3)
questions.solution:
Maintaining a high temperature needs a high rate of respiration [B1]
Lower temperature means less respiration / energy used [B1]
So fat stores last longer. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why respiring fat produces water. (3)
hints: What is the final electron acceptor?
questions.solution:
In oxidative phosphorylation, oxygen is the final electron acceptor [B1]
It combines with electrons and protons (H⁺) to form water [B1]
Fats contain many hydrogen atoms, so produce a lot of water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how uncoupling proteins in brown fat generate heat. (2)
hints: What do protons normally flow through?
questions.solution:
Protons flow back through uncoupling proteins instead of ATP synthase [B1]
So energy from the proton gradient is released as heat rather than used to make ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why respiration releases heat. (2)
hints: Is all energy transferred to ATP?
questions.solution:
Not all energy from respiratory substrate is transferred to ATP [B1]
The rest is released as heat. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons. Explain why people taking it feel hot. (2)
hints: What happens to the proton gradient?
questions.solution:
Protons leak back without passing through ATP synthase, so less ATP made [B1]
Energy released as heat (and more respiration occurs to try to make ATP). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the link reaction. (4)
hints: What is removed from pyruvate, and what is it joined to?
questions.solution:
Pyruvate is actively transported into the mitochondrial matrix [B1]
Pyruvate is oxidised to acetate — CO₂ removed (decarboxylation) [B1]
Hydrogen removed reduces NAD [B1]
Acetate combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl coenzyme A. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the Krebs cycle. (4)
hints: What does acetyl CoA combine with?
What is produced in each turn?
questions.solution:
Acetyl CoA combines with a 4-carbon molecule to form a 6-carbon molecule [B1]
Decarboxylation and dehydrogenation regenerate the 4-carbon molecule [B1]
Reduced NAD and reduced FAD produced [B1]
ATP produced by substrate-level phosphorylation and CO₂ released. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe oxidative phosphorylation. (4)
hints: Where do the electrons come from?
questions.solution:
Reduced NAD / FAD release hydrogen, which splits into protons and electrons [B1]
Electrons pass along the electron transfer chain, releasing energy [B1]
Energy used to pump protons into the intermembrane space; protons diffuse back through ATP synthase, making ATP (chemiosmosis) [B1]
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Cyanide inhibits the last carrier in the electron transfer chain. Explain why ATP production falls. (2)
hints: What happens to the proton gradient?
questions.solution:
Electrons cannot be passed to oxygen, so the electron transfer chain stops [B1]
No protons pumped / no proton gradient, so no ATP from oxidative phosphorylation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an inhibitor of a Krebs cycle enzyme reduces the amount of CO₂ released by a cell. (2)
hints: What happens if the cycle stops?
questions.solution:
Krebs cycle (and link reaction) stops / slows [B1]
So fewer decarboxylation reactions, releasing less CO₂. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why inhibiting the link reaction stops the Krebs cycle. (2)
hints: What does the link reaction produce?
Is it needed in the Krebs cycle?
questions.solution:
No acetyl coenzyme A is produced [B1]
So nothing to combine with the 4-carbon molecule — the Krebs cycle cannot continue. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which process occurs in aerobic respiration but not in anaerobic respiration?

Choose one answer.

A  Phosphorylation of glucose
B  Reduction of NAD
C  Oxidative phosphorylation
D  Production of pyruvate (1)
hints: Which stage needs oxygen as the final acceptor?
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which process occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration?

Choose one answer.

A  Glycolysis
B  The Krebs cycle
C  The link reaction
D  Oxidative phosphorylation (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
What is the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration?

Choose one answer.

A  NAD
B  Pyruvate
C  Carbon dioxide
D  Oxygen (1)
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why soda lime is placed in a respirometer used to measure oxygen uptake by germinating seeds. (3)
hints: What would that gas do to volume?
questions.solution:
Soda lime absorbs carbon dioxide released by the seeds [B1]
So CO₂ does not add to the gas volume [B1]
The volume change (and liquid movement) is due only to oxygen uptake. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the coloured liquid in a respirometer containing seeds moves more slowly at 10 °C than at 25 °C. (3)
hints: What controls the rate of respiration?
questions.solution:
Respiration is controlled by enzymes [B1]
At lower temperature enzymes have less kinetic energy, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes [B1]
Less oxygen used per minute, so the liquid moves more slowly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a respirometer containing boiled (dead) seeds is used alongside one with living seeds. (3)
hints: What can change gas volume apart from respiration?
What does the dead-seed tube show?
questions.solution:
Dead seeds don't respire [B1]
Any change is due to temperature / pressure changes [B1]
So it can be used to correct the results — showing changes in the test tube are due to respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a respirometer can be used to find the volume of carbon dioxide produced by respiring seeds. (3)
hints: Run it once with soda lime and once without.
questions.solution:
With soda lime: liquid movement measures oxygen uptake [B1]
Repeat with soda lime replaced by water (or an inert solid): movement measures O₂ uptake minus CO₂ released [B1]
Volume of CO₂ = O₂ uptake − net change in the second run. [B1]

questions.prompt: Seeds took up 2.4 cm³ of oxygen and released 1.7 cm³ of carbon dioxide. Calculate the respiratory quotient (RQ = CO₂ released ÷ O₂ taken up) and suggest which substrate was being respired. (3)
questions.solution:
1.7 ÷ 2.4 [M1]
RQ = 0.71 [M1]
Lipid is being respired. [A1]

questions.prompt: Germinating seeds had a respiratory quotient (RQ) of 1.0. Explain what this shows and why the liquid in a respirometer without CO₂ absorber would not move. (3)
questions.solution:
RQ of 1.0 shows carbohydrate (glucose) is being respired [B1]
Volume of CO₂ released equals volume of O₂ taken up [B1]
So there is no net change in gas volume. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how fatty acids can be used as a respiratory substrate. (3)
hints: Where do the products enter respiration?
questions.solution:
Lipids hydrolysed to glycerol and fatty acids [B1]
Fatty acids broken into 2-carbon fragments / acetyl coenzyme A [B1]
Enter the Krebs cycle, producing reduced NAD / FAD, so ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Complete the passage about glycolysis. 'Glycolysis takes place in the __1__ of the cell. Glucose is first __2__ using phosphate from ATP. Triose phosphate is then oxidised to form __3__, and NAD is converted to __4__.' (2)
hints: Glycolysis doesn't happen in an organelle.
questions.solution:
1 cytoplasm; 2 phosphorylated; 3 pyruvate; 4 reduced NAD. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Complete the passage about the link reaction. 'The link reaction occurs in the __1__ of the mitochondrion. Pyruvate is __2__, losing carbon dioxide, and combines with coenzyme A to form __3__. This enters the Krebs cycle by combining with a __4__-carbon molecule.' (2)
questions.solution:
1 matrix; 2 decarboxylated (and oxidised); 3 acetyl coenzyme A; 4 four. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Complete the passage. 'In the Krebs cycle, acetyl coenzyme A combines with __1__ to form a six-carbon compound. One turn of the cycle produces one molecule of __2__ by substrate-level phosphorylation, three of reduced NAD and one of reduced __3__. The cycle takes place in the __4__.' (2)
questions.solution:
1 oxaloacetate; 2 ATP; 3 FAD; 4 mitochondrial matrix. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Explain why six molecules of carbon dioxide are produced from the aerobic respiration of one molecule of glucose. (2)
questions.solution:
Glucose forms two pyruvate; each releases one CO₂ in the link reaction [B1]
Each acetyl group releases two CO₂ in the Krebs cycle, so 2 + 4 = 6. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the Krebs cycle turns twice for each molecule of glucose respired. (2)
hints: How many acetyl coenzyme A per glucose?
questions.solution:
One glucose gives two pyruvate, so two acetyl coenzyme A [B1]
Each acetyl coenzyme A enters one turn of the cycle. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the respiratory quotient (RQ) of glucose is 1.0. (2)
questions.solution:
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O [B1]
6 CO₂ ÷ 6 O₂ = 1.0. [B1]

questions.prompt: An inhibitor of the electron transfer chain was added to yeast. Explain why oxygen uptake fell, ATP production fell and ethanol was produced. (3)
hints: What is oxygen's role in the chain?
How is NAD regenerated without the chain?
questions.solution:
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, so with no electron flow, less oxygen is used [B1]
Less oxidative phosphorylation / chemiosmosis, so ATP only from glycolysis [B1]
Pyruvate is converted to ethanol to oxidise reduced NAD, regenerating NAD so glycolysis continues. [B1]

questions.prompt: A poison makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons. Explain why ATP production falls but oxygen uptake continues. (3)
hints: Does the chain still pass electrons?
questions.solution:
Protons leak back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase [B1]
So the proton gradient is lost / less ATP made by chemiosmosis [B1]
Electrons still flow along the chain to oxygen, so oxygen is still used (energy released as heat). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why lactate is produced in muscle during intense exercise, and why this allows ATP production to continue. (3)
questions.solution:
Not enough oxygen so the electron transfer chain stops / oxidative phosphorylation stops [B1]
Pyruvate is reduced to lactate, oxidising reduced NAD [B1]
NAD regenerated so glycolysis continues, producing 2 ATP per glucose. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a respirometer containing KOH, the coloured liquid moved towards the tube containing seeds. Explain why. (3)
hints: What happens to the CO₂ made?
questions.solution:
Seeds take up oxygen for aerobic respiration [B1]
CO₂ released is absorbed by KOH [B1]
So volume / pressure of gas in the seed tube decreases, pulling the liquid towards it. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a respirometer without KOH, the liquid did not move when germinating seeds respired glucose aerobically. Explain why. (3)
hints: What is the RQ of glucose?
questions.solution:
Volume of CO₂ released equals volume of O₂ taken up (RQ = 1) [B1]
No net change in gas volume / pressure [B1]
So no movement of the liquid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Yeast was placed in a respirometer without KOH under anaerobic conditions. Predict and explain the movement of the liquid. (3)
questions.solution:
No oxygen used in anaerobic respiration [B1]
Yeast produces CO₂ (with ethanol) [B1]
Gas volume increases, so the liquid moves away from the yeast tube. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mitochondrial disease affects skeletal muscle. Use your knowledge of respiration and muscle contraction to explain why it causes muscle weakness. (3)
questions.solution:
Less oxidative phosphorylation / Krebs cycle, so less ATP produced [B1]
Less ATP for myosin heads to move / detach and for calcium reuptake [B1]
So fewer cross-bridges / weaker contraction (and lactate builds up). [B1]

questions.prompt: Cyanide inhibits the final enzyme of the electron transfer chain. Explain why it is lethal. (3)
hints: What is the final electron acceptor?
questions.solution:
Electrons can't pass to oxygen, so the chain stops [B1]
No proton gradient / chemiosmosis, so little ATP [B1]
Not enough ATP for vital processes (e.g. heart muscle contraction). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cells with high energy demands, such as heart muscle, have many mitochondria with many cristae. (3)
questions.solution:
Cristae give a large surface area for the electron transfer chain / ATP synthase [B1]
More oxidative phosphorylation [B1]
More ATP for continuous contraction. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why blood lactate concentration is much higher than normal after exercise in people with a mitochondrial disease. (3)
questions.solution:
Less aerobic respiration / Krebs cycle / electron transfer chain works poorly [B1]
More anaerobic respiration to make ATP [B1]
Pyruvate converted to lactate (to regenerate NAD). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why trained athletes produce less lactate than untrained people during the same exercise. (3)
questions.solution:
More mitochondria / capillaries / myoglobin [B1]
More aerobic respiration [B1]
Less pyruvate converted to lactate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe what happens to lactate after exercise. (3)
questions.solution:
Lactate transported to the liver [B1]
Oxidised back to pyruvate [B1]
Converted to glucose / glycogen or respired aerobically. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest and explain one reason why having many faulty mitochondria slows enzyme-catalysed reactions in a cell. (2)
hints: What would be in short supply?
questions.solution:
Less ATP produced (oxidative phosphorylation) [B1]
So less ATP to phosphorylate substrates / for anabolic reactions / active transport. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cells with faulty mitochondria produce more lactate. (2)
questions.solution:
Less aerobic respiration (Krebs / electron transfer chain) [B1]
More pyruvate converted to lactate to regenerate NAD. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the electron transfer chain stops if the Krebs cycle stops. (2)
hints: What does the Krebs cycle provide?
questions.solution:
Krebs cycle provides reduced NAD / FAD [B1]
No electrons / protons supplied to the chain. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how endurance training could increase the maximum rate of oxygen uptake of muscles. (3)
questions.solution:
More mitochondria in muscle cells, so more aerobic respiration [B1]
More capillaries supply oxygen [B1]
More myoglobin / larger stroke volume. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Why can ATP only be made at a very high rate for a short time during maximum effort?

Choose one answer.

A  Glucose runs out within seconds
B  Phosphocreatine is used up quickly and lactate builds up
C  Oxygen cannot reach the mitochondria at all
D  ATP synthase is denatured (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which process makes ATP fastest without oxygen in muscle?

Choose one answer.

A  Phosphocreatine donating phosphate to ADP
B  Oxidative phosphorylation
C  Krebs cycle
D  Link reaction (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
How many ATP molecules are produced (net) by glycolysis of one glucose molecule?

Choose one answer.

A  1
B  2
C  4
D  38 (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why CO₂ production by yeast was slower in maltose solution than in glucose solution. (2)
questions.solution:
Maltose must first be hydrolysed into glucose (by maltase) before glycolysis [B1]
Fewer maltase enzymes / slower uptake of maltose, so less glucose available to respire. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why yeast produced no CO₂ when given lactose. (2)
questions.solution:
Yeast lacks the enzyme lactase / transport proteins for lactose [B1]
So lactose can't be hydrolysed into monosaccharides for respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why yeast produces CO₂ in both aerobic and anaerobic conditions. (2)
questions.solution:
Aerobic: CO₂ released in the link reaction and Krebs cycle [B1]
Anaerobic: pyruvate is decarboxylated to ethanal (then ethanol), releasing CO₂. [B1]

questions.prompt: In the link reaction, pyruvate (3C) is converted into an acetyl group. Name the molecules released or formed: the gas released, the coenzyme that is reduced, the reduced molecule formed and the compound acetyl combines with. (2)
questions.solution:
CO₂; NAD; reduced NAD; coenzyme A (forming acetyl coenzyme A). [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Describe the link reaction. (2)
questions.solution:
Pyruvate is decarboxylated (CO₂ removed) and oxidised (NAD reduced) in the mitochondrial matrix [B1]
Acetate combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl coenzyme A. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and why the link reaction can't occur without oxygen. (2)
questions.solution:
Pyruvate is actively transported into the matrix [B1]
Without oxygen, reduced NAD isn't reoxidised by the electron transfer chain, so no NAD is available. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug kills bacteria by blocking the movement of protons through ATP synthase. Explain how. (3)
questions.solution:
Protons can't diffuse through ATP synthase [B1]
So no / less ATP is made by oxidative phosphorylation / chemiosmosis [B1]
Not enough ATP for processes such as active transport / protein synthesis / DNA replication, so cells die. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe chemiosmosis in mitochondria. (3)
questions.solution:
Energy from electrons passing along the electron transfer chain pumps protons into the intermembrane space [B1]
Creates a proton (electrochemical) gradient [B1]
Protons diffuse back through ATP synthase, producing ATP from ADP + Pi. [B1]

questions.prompt: A poison blocks the final electron carrier in the electron transfer chain. Explain why ATP production falls. (3)
questions.solution:
Electrons can't pass to oxygen, so the chain stops [B1]
No energy released to pump protons, so no proton gradient [B1]
No chemiosmosis, so little ATP produced. [B1]

category: Energy transfers in and between organisms

questions.prompt: Explain why dry mass, rather than fresh mass, is used to measure biomass. (1)
hints: What varies a lot between samples of fresh tissue?
questions.solution: Water content varies (and contains no chemical energy), so dry mass is more reliable. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define net primary productivity (NPP). (2)
hints: What is lost before energy is stored?
questions.solution:
NPP = GPP minus respiratory losses (R) [B1]
The chemical energy stored in plant biomass available to the next trophic level / for growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the increase in dry mass of plants over time can be used to estimate net primary productivity. (2)
questions.solution:
Dry mass is biomass, which stores chemical energy [B1]
The increase is what remains after respiration, i.e. net production. [B1]

questions.prompt: A plant community has a GPP of 20 000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ and loses 12 000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ in respiration. Calculate its NPP. (2)
Suggest why the net primary productivity of plants growing at ground level in a mature forest is low. (2)
hints: How much light reaches the forest floor?
questions.solution:
Little light reaches the ground [B1]
So less photosynthesis / GPP, so NPP is low. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the NPP of a young forest increases as the trees grow. (2)
questions.solution:
Greater leaf area [B1]
More photosynthesis / GPP, so more energy stored as biomass. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the NPP of a mature forest may stop increasing. (2)
hints: What else increases as biomass grows?
questions.solution:
Respiratory losses increase with the large biomass (trunks, roots) [B1]
GPP is limited (e.g. by light), so NPP = GPP − R levels off. [B1]

questions.prompt: The NPP of grassland vegetation is 24 000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. Zebras eat 8% of it. Of the energy zebras eat, 60% is lost in faeces and urine and 37% in respiration. Calculate the energy stored in new zebra tissue. (2)
hints: What percentage of ingested energy is left for new tissue?
questions.solution:
Energy eaten = 1920 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹; 3% stored [M1]
57.6 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. [A1]

questions.prompt: Using N = I − (F + R), calculate the net production of a consumer that ingests 1500 kJ, loses 600 kJ in faeces and urine and 780 kJ in respiration. (2)
Producers in an ecosystem have an NPP of 20 000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. The net production of primary consumers is 1200 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer. (2)
hints: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100.

questions.prompt: Explain two features of a calorimeter that make sure the energy released by burning food heats the water. (2)
hints: How is the heat spread evenly?
questions.solution:
Insulated / closed container reduces heat loss to the surroundings [B1]
Water surrounds the combustion chamber / a stirrer distributes heat evenly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why oxygen is supplied to the combustion chamber of a calorimeter. (2)
questions.solution:
Ensures complete combustion of the sample [B1]
So all its chemical energy is released. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why burning food under a boiling tube of water underestimates its energy content. (2)
questions.solution:
Much heat is lost to the air / the tube [B1]
Combustion may be incomplete. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons why only a small percentage of the light falling on a plant is used in photosynthesis. (2)
questions.solution:
Some light is the wrong wavelength / reflected (e.g. green) [B1]
Some light misses chloroplasts / passes through the leaf [B1]
Other factors (CO₂, temperature) limit the rate. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why energy is lost between trophic levels. (2)
hints: Is all of an organism eaten?
What happens to energy used in respiration?
questions.solution:
Some parts are not eaten / not digested and lost in faeces [B1]
Energy lost as heat in respiration / in excretion (urine). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the net primary production of a plant is less than its gross primary production. (2)
hints: What do plants use some sugar for?
questions.solution:
Plants use some of the chemical energy they make in respiration [B1]
NPP = GPP − R. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give suitable units for (i) the biomass of plants in an area and (ii) net primary productivity. (2)
hints: Biomass is a mass per area.
Productivity is energy per area per time.
questions.solution:
(i) g m⁻² (or kg m⁻²) [B1]
(ii) kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ (energy per area per time). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the chemical energy stored in dry biomass can be estimated. (2)
questions.solution:
Burn a known mass of dry biomass in a calorimeter [B1]
Measure the temperature rise of a known volume of water and calculate the energy released. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which equation gives the net primary productivity (NPP) of plants?

Choose one answer.

A  NPP = GPP − R
B  NPP = GPP + R
C  NPP = R − GPP
D  NPP = GPP × R (1)
hints: Respiration is subtracted from the total.
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which calculation gives the efficiency of energy transfer between two trophic levels?

Choose one answer.

A  Energy in previous level ÷ energy in next level × 100
B  Energy in next level − energy in previous level
C  Energy in next level ÷ energy in previous level × 100
D  Energy lost ÷ energy gained (1)
hints: Next level divided by previous level.
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
Using I (energy ingested), F (energy lost in faeces and urine) and R (respiratory losses), which equation gives the net production (N) of a consumer?

Choose one answer.

A  N = I − F + R
B  N = I − (F + R)
C  N = I + F − R
D  N = (I − F) × R (1)
hints: Both F and R are losses.
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why more people can be fed from an area of land used to grow crops than from the same area used to rear cattle. (2)
hints: What happens to energy at each trophic level?
questions.solution:
Energy is lost at each trophic level (respiration / heat, faeces, parts not eaten) [B1]
Eating crops directly is a shorter food chain, so more energy reaches humans. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two ways farmers increase the efficiency of energy transfer in livestock. (2)
hints: How can respiratory losses be reduced?
questions.solution:
Restrict movement / keep animals warm, so less energy used in respiration / lost as heat [B1]
Give high-quality, easily digested food / slaughter young animals while growing fast. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels. (2)
hints: How much energy passes to each level?
questions.solution:
Most energy is lost at each transfer (only about 10% passed on) [B1]
Too little energy remains to support another population. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three reasons why the efficiency of energy transfer from secondary consumers to tertiary consumers is low. (3)
hints: Is all of the prey eaten?
questions.solution:
Not all of the prey is eaten (bones, fur) [B1]
Some is not digested / lost in faeces [B1]
Energy lost as heat in respiration / used for movement / lost in urine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the efficiency of energy transfer from producers to primary consumers is often lower than from primary to secondary consumers. (3)
hints: What makes plant material hard to digest?
questions.solution:
Plants contain cellulose / lignin that is hard to digest [B1]
So more energy is lost in faeces [B1]
Animal tissue has more protein / fat and is more easily digested, so more is absorbed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why mammals and birds have lower efficiency of energy transfer than reptiles or fish. (3)
hints: What is respiration used for in endotherms?
questions.solution:
Mammals and birds are endotherms / maintain a constant body temperature [B1]
So more food is respired to release heat [B1]
Less energy is left for growth / biomass to pass on. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why biomass is measured as dry mass rather than fresh mass. (2)
questions.solution:
Water content varies between samples / over time [B1]
Water contains no chemical energy / dry mass is more reliable for comparison. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one disadvantage of measuring dry mass, and explain how scientists get around it. (2)
hints: How could you avoid killing many?
questions.solution:
Organisms are killed [B1]
Use a small sample and scale up / use measurements from a representative sample. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why growing a crop above its optimum temperature can reduce the biomass produced. (2)
hints: What about enzymes such as rubisco?
questions.solution:
Rate of respiration increases more than photosynthesis / enzymes in photosynthesis denature [B1]
So less of the GPP is left as NPP / less sugar for growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why net primary production is always less than gross primary production. (2)
hints: What does the plant use some of its sugar for?
questions.solution:
Some of the chemical energy is used / lost in respiration [B1]
NPP = GPP − R, so only what remains is available for growth / consumers. [B1]

questions.prompt: Marsh plants have a high carbon use efficiency (CUE = NPP ÷ GPP). Explain what a high CUE means and the advantage. Do not refer to abiotic factors. (2)
hints: What's lost between GPP and NPP?
questions.solution:
Little of the GPP is used / lost in respiration [B1]
So more energy / biomass available for growth and reproduction / for consumers. [B1]

questions.prompt: A grassland has GPP of 25 000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ and respiratory losses of 15 000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. Calculate the NPP and the ratio NPP : GPP. (2)
questions.solution:
NPP = 10 000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ [M1]
Ratio = 0.4. [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why young growing forests have a higher NPP : GPP ratio than mature forests. (2)
questions.solution:
Mature trees have more non-photosynthetic biomass (wood) that respires [B1]
So a greater proportion of GPP is lost in respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Scientists were interested in the shoot-to-root ratio of a crop whose shoots are harvested. Explain why dry mass was an appropriate measure. (2)
questions.solution:
Water content of shoots and roots varies, so fresh mass is unreliable [B1]
Dry mass shows the actual biomass / organic matter produced. [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the shoot-to-root ratio for plants with shoot mass 9.81 g and root mass 1.61 g, and explain why a high ratio is useful for a crop harvested for its leaves. (2)
questions.solution:
9.81 ÷ 1.61 = 6.1 : 1 [M1]
More of the plant's biomass is in the harvested part. [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a plant with a very small root system may grow poorly in dry soil. (2)
questions.solution:
Smaller root surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions [B1]
So less water for photosynthesis / turgor, slowing growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: Shoot dry mass was 1.01 g (A), 9.81 g (B), 0.96 g (C) and 4.01 g (D). State which treatment gave the best commercial result and justify your answer. (2)
questions.solution:
B (live fungus + nitrate) [B1]
Highest shoot mass — about 2.4 times D and nearly 10 times A. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one further piece of information a farmer would need before using the best treatment commercially. (2)
questions.solution:
Cost of the fungus and fertiliser compared with the value of extra yield [B1]
Whether results are the same in field soil / other conditions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate how many times greater the shoot dry mass was with treatment D (4.01 g) than with treatment C (0.96 g), and what this shows. (2)
questions.solution:
4.01 ÷ 0.96 = 4.2 times [M1]
Living fungus greatly increases growth even with ammonium fertiliser. [A1]

category: Energy transfers in and between organisms

questions.prompt: Saprobiotic fungi secrete cellulase onto dead plant material. Suggest and explain one advantage to the fungus of secreting this enzyme rather than taking in whole pieces of plant material. (2)
hints: Can cellulose cross a cell membrane?
What do the products of digestion do next?
questions.solution:
Cellulose is too large to be absorbed / cross the membrane [B1]
Enzyme hydrolyses it to glucose (small, soluble), which can be absorbed and used in respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how increased nitrate uptake could increase plant growth. (1)
hints: Nitrogen is needed for which molecules?
questions.solution: Nitrate used to make amino acids / proteins / nucleic acids for growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how magnesium uptake helps plant growth. (1)
hints: Magnesium is part of which pigment?
questions.solution: Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll, so more photosynthesis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one use of phosphate in plants. (1)
hints: Think about molecules with phosphate groups.
questions.solution: Making ATP / nucleic acids (DNA, RNA) / phospholipids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in nodules on the roots of legumes. Suggest one benefit the bacteria gain. (1)
hints: What do plants make by photosynthesis?
questions.solution: Receive carbohydrates / sugars from the plant (and a protected habitat). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how legumes benefit from nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules. (1)
hints: What do the bacteria convert nitrogen gas into?
What does the plant use it for?
questions.solution: Bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonium / nitrogen compounds that the plant uses to make amino acids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how mycorrhizae (fungi associated with roots) benefit plants. (1)
hints: Which ions do they help absorb?
questions.solution: Increase surface area for uptake of water and mineral ions (especially phosphate). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest and explain how root nodules help legumes grow in soil that is low in nitrogen. (2)
hints: What do the bacteria in nodules do?
What does the plant use the product for?
questions.solution:
Bacteria in nodules fix nitrogen gas into ammonium / nitrogen compounds [B1]
Plant uses them to make amino acids / proteins / nucleic acids. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest and explain why carnivorous plants are often found in bogs. (2)
hints: Are bog soils rich in nitrate?
questions.solution:
Bog soils are low in nitrate / nutrients [B1]
Digesting insects gives the plant nitrogen (for proteins), giving it an advantage over other plants. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how saprobionts make nitrogen in dead organisms available to plants. (2)
hints: What does the next group of bacteria do?
questions.solution:
Saprobionts decompose proteins / nucleic acids, releasing ammonia (ammonification) [B1]
Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium into nitrates that plants absorb. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the mean dry biomass of plants grown with different masses of three fertilisers. Using all the information, evaluate the effect of the different fertilisers on plant growth. (5)
hints: Do any level off? What is missing from the data?
questions.solution:
All three fertilisers increase growth compared with none [B1]
Potassium nitrate gives the greatest growth and keeps increasing with mass [B1]
Ammonium sulfate levels off above 25 g (another factor limiting / possible toxicity or acidity) [B1]
Compost gives the smallest increase (nutrients released slowly by decomposition) [B1]
Limitations: no SD / statistics; fertilisers may contain different amounts of nitrogen; one species in pots, not a field. [B1]
questions.table:
Fertiliser / g | Potassium nitrate | Ammonium sulfate | Compost
0 | 0.6 | 0.6 | 0.6
12.5 | 2.0 | 1.8 | 1.0
25 | 3.5 | 2.4 | 1.4
37.5 | 4.5 | 2.5 | 1.8

questions.prompt: Evaluate the use of nitrogen-containing fertilisers on farmland, considering both crop yield and the environment. (5)
questions.solution:
Nitrogen is needed for amino acids / proteins / nucleic acids, so fertiliser increases yield [B1]
Above a certain amount, yield no longer increases (another factor limits), wasting money [B1]
Excess nitrate is leached into rivers and lakes [B1]
Causes eutrophication — algal blooms, decomposers use oxygen, fish die [B1]
Can reduce plant diversity by favouring fast-growing species. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the use of natural fertilisers (manure) and artificial fertilisers. (5)
hints: Which is more likely to be leached?
questions.solution:
Both supply mineral ions such as nitrate and phosphate, increasing yield [B1]
Artificial: known, precise composition, nutrients immediately available [B1]
Manure: nutrients released slowly as it decomposes, less leaching [B1]
Manure improves soil structure / adds organic matter [B1]
Artificial fertiliser more likely to be leached, causing eutrophication / costs more. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how fertiliser running off farmland into a lake can cause fish to die. (4)
hints: What do extra nitrates do to algae?
questions.solution:
Nitrates / phosphates cause rapid growth of algae (algal bloom) [B1]
Algae block light, so plants below die [B1]
Decomposers (saprobionts) increase and respire, using up oxygen [B1]
Fish die from lack of oxygen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why phosphate pollution causes algal blooms in lakes. (4)
hints: Is phosphate usually limiting in lakes?
What do algae need it for?
questions.solution:
Phosphate is often the limiting nutrient in fresh water [B1]
Algae need it for DNA / ATP / phospholipids [B1]
Extra phosphate removes this limit [B1]
So algae grow and reproduce rapidly, forming a bloom. [B1]

questions.prompt: Nitrate was added to cultures of bacteria and the activity of an enzyme was measured. The table shows the results. Evaluate the conclusion that nitrate inhibits the enzyme. (3)
hints: Does activity fall as nitrate increases?
Look at the nitrate remaining column.
questions.solution:
Activity falls as more nitrate is added, supporting the conclusion [B1]
Up to 30 µg cm⁻³ all the nitrate was used by the bacteria, but activity still fell, so the effect isn't simply due to nitrate left in the medium [B1]
Correlation only — nitrate might reduce production of the enzyme (gene expression) rather than inhibit it directly / no repeats or SD. [B1]
questions.table:
Nitrate added / µg cm⁻³ | Enzyme activity | Nitrate remaining / µg cm⁻³
0 | 50 | 0
10 | 35 | 0
20 | 20 | 0
30 | 5 | 0
40 | 0 | 5
50 | 0 | 12

questions.prompt: Explain why nitrogen fixation requires a large amount of ATP. (2)
hints: What bond holds a nitrogen molecule together?
questions.solution:
N₂ has a very strong triple bond [B1]
Breaking / reducing it needs a lot of energy from ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Root nodules of legumes contain leghaemoglobin, a protein that binds oxygen. Suggest why. (2)
hints: Which enzyme is damaged by oxygen?
But what do the bacteria still need?
questions.solution:
Nitrogenase is inhibited by oxygen, so leghaemoglobin keeps free oxygen concentration low [B1]
While still supplying oxygen for aerobic respiration to make ATP. [B1]

questions.prompt: Each year, a rock store containing 400 Tg of phosphorus releases 2% of its phosphorus to the soil, and a store in dead organic matter containing 150 Tg releases 8%. Calculate the difference in phosphorus supplied to the soil by the two stores each year. (2)
hints: Work out the mass supplied by each store.
questions.solution:
Rock: 400 × 0.02 = 8 Tg; organic matter: 150 × 0.08 = 12 Tg [M1]
Difference = 4 Tg. [A1]

questions.prompt: Each year a rock store of 2000 Tg of phosphorus releases 0.5% of its phosphorus to the soil, and a soil organic store of 300 Tg releases 5%. Calculate the difference in phosphorus supplied each year. (2)
questions.solution:
Rock: 2000 × 0.005 = 10 Tg; organic: 300 × 0.05 = 15 Tg [M1]
Difference = 5 Tg. [A1]

questions.prompt: A sediment store of 1200 Tg of phosphorus releases 1% to the soil each year and a store in living organisms of 80 Tg releases 20%. Calculate the difference in phosphorus supplied each year. (2)
hints: Subtract the smaller from the larger.
questions.solution:
Sediment: 1200 × 0.01 = 12 Tg; organisms: 80 × 0.20 = 16 Tg [M1]
Difference = 4 Tg. [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain how mycorrhizae and saprobionts each help to make nutrients available to plants, and why farmers might add mycorrhizal fungi to crops grown in poor soils. (5)
hints: What do saprobionts do to dead matter?
What does the plant give the fungus in return?
questions.solution:
Saprobionts secrete enzymes and digest dead organic matter (extracellular digestion) [B1]
Releasing ammonium / phosphate ions into the soil [B1]
Mycorrhizae are associations between fungi and plant roots [B1]
Fungal hyphae increase the surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions (e.g. phosphate) [B1]
Plant supplies the fungus with carbohydrates (mutualism) [B1]
So less fertiliser / irrigation is needed in poor soils. [B1]
Any 5 of these points — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: Rainforests have high rainfall and high mean temperatures. Explain how these two abiotic factors enable rapid recycling of nutrients. (2)
questions.solution:
High temperature: enzymes of saprobionts work fast / more kinetic energy, so faster decomposition [B1]
High rainfall: moist conditions for growth of microorganisms / dissolving nutrients for absorption. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why leaf litter decomposes slowly in cold, waterlogged soils. (2)
questions.solution:
Low temperature: enzymes work slowly / microorganisms less active [B1]
Waterlogged: little oxygen, so less aerobic respiration by decomposers / fewer nitrifying bacteria. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why farmers plough fields to aerate the soil. (2)
questions.solution:
Provides oxygen for nitrifying bacteria (aerobic), so more nitrate [B1]
Reduces anaerobic conditions, so fewer denitrifying bacteria / less nitrate lost. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of bacteria in recycling nitrogen-containing compounds from dead organic matter. (4)
hints: Then which make nitrite and nitrate?
questions.solution:
Saprobionts break down proteins / DNA / urea by extracellular digestion [B1]
Releasing ammonia / ammonium ions (ammonification) [B1]
Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrite [B1]
Then nitrite to nitrate, which plants absorb (needs oxygen). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of nitrogen-fixing and denitrifying bacteria in the nitrogen cycle. (4)
hints: Where do some nitrogen-fixing bacteria live?
questions.solution:
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonia / ammonium [B1]
Some live in root nodules of legumes (mutualism) [B1]
Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate back into nitrogen gas [B1]
In anaerobic / waterlogged conditions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how phosphorus is cycled in an ecosystem. (4)
hints: What releases it from dead matter?
questions.solution:
Phosphate ions released from rocks by weathering [B1]
Absorbed by plants (helped by mycorrhizae) and passed along food chains [B1]
Saprobionts break down dead organisms and waste, releasing phosphate ions [B1]
Some phosphate in sediments returns to rock over long periods / guano. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two nitrogen-containing biological molecules removed from a field when a crop is harvested. (2)
questions.solution: Two from: proteins / amino acids; DNA / RNA / nucleotides; ATP; chlorophyll; NAD / NADP. [B2]

questions.prompt: Give two biological molecules containing phosphorus that a plant needs phosphate ions to make. (2)
questions.solution: Two from: ATP / ADP; DNA / RNA / nucleotides; phospholipids; NADP; RuBP / GP / TP. [B2]

questions.prompt: Explain why farmers need to add fertilisers to fields where crops are harvested each year. (2)
hints: What happens to the minerals in the crop?
questions.solution:
Mineral ions are removed in the harvested crop and not returned by decomposition [B1]
So fertilisers replace nitrate / phosphate to maintain yield. [B1]

questions.prompt: Fertiliser use per hectare increased five-fold but the extra grain produced per kg of fertiliser fell from 15 kg to 5 kg. Evaluate the increased use of fertiliser. (2)
questions.solution:
Total grain yield increased, so more food produced [B1]
But diminishing returns — each kg gives less grain, so less cost-effective / more leaching and eutrophication. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how leaching of fertiliser into rivers can cause eutrophication. (2)
questions.solution:
Nitrate causes algal bloom, blocking light so plants below die [B1]
Saprobionts decompose them, respiring aerobically and using up oxygen, so fish die. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two advantages of using natural fertilisers (manure) compared with artificial fertilisers. (2)
questions.solution:
Released more slowly, so less leaching [B1]
Improves soil structure / organic matter / cheaper if available. [B1]

questions.prompt: Soil A (pH 6.9) converted ammonia quickly. Soil B (pH 4.3) converted it slowly. When soil B was adjusted to pH 6.9, it still converted ammonia slowly. Explain how this supports the idea that the soils contain different communities of nitrifying bacteria. (3)
hints: If it were just pH, what would happen when B was neutralised?
questions.solution:
If pH alone caused the difference, soil B at pH 6.9 should match soil A [B1]
It didn't, so pH isn't the only factor [B1]
Different species of bacteria (with enzymes adapted to different pH) are present. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why nitrification is slower in waterlogged soils. (3)
questions.solution:
Little oxygen in waterlogged soil [B1]
Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen (aerobic), so less ammonia converted to nitrite / nitrate [B1]
Denitrifying bacteria (anaerobic) convert nitrate to nitrogen gas. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the process of nitrification. (3)
questions.solution:
Ammonium ions oxidised to nitrite ions [B1]
Nitrite oxidised to nitrate ions [B1]
By nitrifying bacteria in aerobic conditions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of saprobionts in the nitrogen cycle. (2)
questions.solution:
Saprobionts feed on / break down dead organic matter and waste by extracellular digestion [B1]
Releasing ammonia / ammonium ions (ammonification). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of nitrifying bacteria in the nitrogen cycle. (2)
questions.solution:
Convert ammonium ions to nitrite [B1]
Then nitrite to nitrate (oxidation, needs oxygen). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules benefit both the bacteria and the plant. (2)
hints: What do the bacteria give the plant?
What does the plant give back?
questions.solution:
Bacteria convert nitrogen gas to ammonia / ammonium, which the plant uses to make amino acids / proteins [B1]
Plant provides carbohydrates / sugars to the bacteria (mutualism). [B1]

questions.prompt: Marsh soils are waterlogged and anaerobic. Explain why they have a high concentration of ammonium ions and low nitrite and nitrate. (2)
questions.solution:
Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen, so ammonium isn't converted to nitrite / nitrate [B1]
Denitrifying bacteria (anaerobic) convert any nitrate to nitrogen gas. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why legume plants can grow well in soils low in nitrate. (2)
questions.solution:
Root nodules contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria [B1]
They convert nitrogen gas into ammonium for the plant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why plants need nitrate. (2)
questions.solution:
To make amino acids / proteins [B1]
And nucleotides / DNA / ATP / chlorophyll. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one use of nitrate ions in plants. (1)
questions.solution: Make amino acids / proteins / nucleotides / DNA / chlorophyll. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a fungus living in association with plant roots could increase plant growth. (4)
questions.solution:
Fungal hyphae increase surface area for absorption [B1]
More water and mineral ions (e.g. nitrate, phosphate) taken up [B1]
More proteins / nucleic acids / chlorophyll made, so more growth [B1]
Plant provides fungus with sugars (mutualism). [B1]

category: Organisms respond to changes in their environments

questions.prompt: Describe how a rise in blood pressure is detected and leads to a decrease in heart rate. (4)
hints: Which part of the nervous system slows the heart?
questions.solution:
Baroreceptors (pressure receptors) in the aorta / carotid arteries detect the rise [B1]
More impulses sent to the medulla (cardiovascular centre) [B1]
More impulses along parasympathetic (vagus) neurones to the SAN [B1]
SAN frequency decreases, so heart rate falls. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a rise in blood carbon dioxide during exercise leads to an increase in heart rate. (4)
hints: What does CO₂ do to blood pH?
Which receptors detect it, and which nerves speed the heart?
questions.solution:
CO₂ lowers blood pH [B1]
Detected by chemoreceptors in the aorta / carotid arteries [B1]
More impulses to the medulla, then along sympathetic neurones to the SAN [B1]
SAN fires more frequently, increasing heart rate, so CO₂ is removed faster. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the SAN, AVN and Purkyne tissue coordinate a heartbeat. (4)
hints: Where does the wave of excitation start?
Why is there a delay before the ventricles contract?
questions.solution:
SAN sends a wave of electrical excitation across the atria, which contract [B1]
Non-conducting tissue stops it passing directly to the ventricles [B1]
AVN delays the impulse, so the atria finish contracting first [B1]
Bundle of His / Purkyne tissue carries it to the apex; ventricles contract from the base upwards. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why vision using rod cells has low visual acuity. (3)
hints: How many rods connect to one bipolar neurone?
Can the brain tell which rod was stimulated?
questions.solution:
Several rods connect to one bipolar neurone (retinal convergence) [B1]
Impulses from several rods are combined into one [B1]
So the brain cannot distinguish separate points of light close together. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why vision using cone cells has high visual acuity. (3)
questions.solution:
Each cone connects to its own bipolar neurone [B1]
So each sends a separate impulse to the brain [B1]
Brain can distinguish points of light close together. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why rod cells are more sensitive than cone cells in dim light. (3)
hints: What happens when several rods share a bipolar neurone?
How easily does rhodopsin break down?
questions.solution:
Several rods connect to one bipolar neurone — spatial summation [B1]
So the threshold is reached even when each rod receives little light [B1]
Rhodopsin is broken down by low light intensities. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how three types of cone cell allow us to see a range of colours. (3)
hints: What does each cone type contain?
How does the brain interpret colour?
questions.solution:
Three types of cone, each with a different pigment [B1]
Each absorbs a different range of wavelengths (red, green, blue) [B1]
Different colours stimulate different combinations of cones, which the brain interprets. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a person with no blue-sensitive cones cannot tell blue from yellow. (3)
hints: Which cones would respond to blue?
Do blue and yellow light give different signals?
questions.solution:
No pigment absorbing blue wavelengths [B1]
Blue and yellow light stimulate the remaining cones in a similar way [B1]
So the brain receives no difference in impulses. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why colour vision is poor in dim light. (3)
hints: What light intensity do cones need?
How many types of rod pigment are there?
questions.solution:
Cone pigment is only broken down by high light intensity [B1]
In dim light only rods work [B1]
Rods contain a single pigment, so give no colour information. [B1]

questions.prompt: Before testing the effect of IAA on shoot growth, the tips of the shoots were removed. Explain why. (2)
hints: What does the shoot tip produce?
Why would that be a problem?
questions.solution:
Shoot tips produce IAA (auxin) [B1]
Removing them means only the applied IAA affects growth. [B1]

questions.prompt: When testing the effect of IAA on shoot segments, all segments were cut from the same region of the shoot. Explain why. (2)
hints: Do all parts of a shoot respond the same way?
questions.solution:
Cells at different stages / regions respond differently to IAA [B1]
So differences in growth are due to IAA concentration only. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why many shoot segments were used for each concentration of IAA. (2)
hints: Do all segments grow the same?
What does a larger sample give?
questions.solution:
Segments vary in their growth [B1]
More segments give a more reliable mean / reduce the effect of anomalies. [B1]

questions.prompt: Shoot segments treated with IAA were kept in the dark. Explain why. (2)
hints: How does light affect IAA distribution?
questions.solution:
Light affects IAA distribution / causes phototropism [B1]
And photosynthesis would add sugar, another variable. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the mean change in length of shoot segments after 2 days in different IAA concentrations. Describe and explain the results, and suggest how roots would respond differently. (3)
hints: Describe the trend up to 10 ppm and after.
Are roots more or less sensitive?
questions.solution:
Growth increases with IAA concentration up to 10 ppm, then decreases at 100 ppm [B1]
IAA stimulates cell elongation (loosening cell walls); very high concentrations inhibit growth [B1]
Roots are more sensitive — their growth would be inhibited at much lower concentrations. [B1]
questions.table:
IAA / ppm | Mean change in length / mm
0.0001 | 0.1
0.01 | 0.6
1 | 2.2
10 | 3.5
100 | 2.0

questions.prompt: Explain how IAA causes a shoot to bend towards light coming from one side. (3)
hints: What does IAA do to shoot cells?
questions.solution:
IAA moves to the shaded side of the shoot [B1]
IAA stimulates cell elongation in shoots [B1]
Shaded side elongates more, so the shoot bends towards the light. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how IAA causes a root growing horizontally to bend downwards. (3)
hints: Where does IAA accumulate under gravity?
What does IAA do to root cells?
questions.solution:
IAA accumulates on the lower side of the root [B1]
In roots, IAA inhibits cell elongation [B1]
So the upper side elongates more and the root bends downwards. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest and explain why damage to autonomic neurones could cause an abnormal heart rate. (3)
hints: Which neurones carry signals from the medulla to the SAN?
What would happen if they were damaged?
questions.solution:
Sympathetic and parasympathetic neurones carry impulses from the medulla to the SAN [B1]
Damage disrupts these impulses [B1]
So heart rate cannot be increased / decreased appropriately (irregular). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the effect on resting heart rate of cutting the vagus (parasympathetic) nerve to the heart. (3)
hints: What does the vagus nerve normally do?
What would the SAN do on its own?
questions.solution:
Parasympathetic impulses normally slow the SAN [B1]
Without them the SAN fires at its own, faster intrinsic rate [B1]
So resting heart rate increases. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a heart can continue to beat after the nerves to it have been cut (e.g. after a transplant). (3)
questions.solution:
Cardiac muscle is myogenic — contraction starts in the heart itself [B1]
The SAN generates waves of electrical excitation [B1]
Nerves only change the rate, they don't start the beat. [B1]

questions.prompt: The iris contains circular muscles and radial muscles. Suggest and explain how these muscles widen the pupil in dim light. (2)
hints: Which muscle pulls the pupil open?
What must the other muscle do?
questions.solution:
Radial muscles contract, pulling the iris outwards [B1]
Circular muscles relax, so the pupil widens. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the iris needs two sets of muscles that work antagonistically. (2)
questions.solution:
Muscles can only contract / pull, not push [B1]
So one set is needed to reverse the effect of the other (constrict vs dilate). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the pathway that leads to the pupil getting smaller in bright light. (2)
questions.solution:
Light detected by photoreceptors in the retina; impulses along sensory neurones to the brain [B1]
Impulses along motor (parasympathetic) neurones cause circular muscles to contract. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why we see most detail when we look directly at an object. (3)
questions.solution:
Image is focused on the fovea, which has a high density of cones [B1]
Each cone connects to its own bipolar neurone [B1]
So separate impulses reach the brain and points close together can be distinguished. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why peripheral vision shows little detail but is good at detecting dim light. (3)
hints: Which receptors are in the periphery?
questions.solution:
Periphery of the retina has mainly rods [B1]
Several rods connect to one bipolar neurone (convergence), so summation lets dim light reach threshold [B1]
But the brain cannot tell which rod was stimulated — low acuity. [B1]

questions.prompt: Birds of prey have about five times as many cones per mm² in their fovea as humans. Explain how this lets them see prey from a great height. (3)
hints: More cones in the same area means what?
questions.solution:
More cones per unit area, each connected to its own bipolar neurone [B1]
So more separate impulses from a small image [B1]
Brain can distinguish finer detail / small objects far away. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how having many rod cells helps a nocturnal animal see at night. (3)
questions.solution:
Rods are sensitive to low light intensity [B1]
Several rods connect to one bipolar neurone [B1]
Generator potentials summate, so threshold is reached in dim light and impulses are sent to the brain. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why it takes several minutes to see clearly after moving from bright light into a dark room. (3)
hints: What happens to rhodopsin in bright light?
What must happen in the dark?
questions.solution:
Bright light breaks down (bleaches) rhodopsin in rods [B1]
Rhodopsin must be resynthesised before rods can respond [B1]
This takes time (and ATP), so dim-light vision returns gradually. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a faint star is easier to see when you look slightly to one side of it. (3)
hints: Where does the image fall when you look to the side?
questions.solution:
Image falls on the periphery of the retina, where there are many rods [B1]
Several rods connect to one bipolar neurone [B1]
Summation means the dim light reaches threshold. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the nervous system decreases heart rate when an animal's rate of respiration falls. (4)
hints: What happens to blood CO₂ and pH?
questions.solution:
Less CO₂ produced, so blood pH rises [B1]
Detected by chemoreceptors in the aorta / carotid arteries [B1]
Fewer impulses to the medulla / more impulses along the parasympathetic (vagus) nerve to the SAN [B1]
SAN fires less often, so heart rate falls. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how heart rate increases at the start of exercise. (4)
hints: Which division of the nervous system speeds the heart?
questions.solution:
Increased respiration raises CO₂ / lowers blood pH [B1]
Detected by chemoreceptors (also pressure receptors) [B1]
More impulses from the medulla along sympathetic neurones to the SAN [B1]
SAN fires more frequently, increasing heart rate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the roles of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems in controlling heart rate. (4)
questions.solution:
Both are part of the autonomic nervous system and connect the medulla to the SAN [B1]
Sympathetic impulses increase the frequency of SAN impulses — heart rate rises [B1]
Parasympathetic impulses decrease SAN frequency — heart rate falls [B1]
Balance between them is controlled by the cardiovascular centre in the medulla. [B1]

questions.prompt: A block of agar containing IAA was placed on one side of the cut tip of a shoot, in the dark. The shoot bent away from the side with the block. Explain this. (3)
hints: What does IAA do to shoot cells?
questions.solution:
IAA diffuses from the block down that side of the shoot [B1]
IAA stimulates cell elongation in shoots [B1]
Cells on that side elongate more, so the shoot bends away from the block. [B1]

questions.prompt: A shoot tip was covered with a foil cap and lit from one side. The shoot grew straight up. Explain this. (3)
questions.solution:
The tip detects light / produces IAA [B1]
With the tip covered, no light reaches it, so IAA is not redistributed to one side [B1]
Elongation is even on all sides, so the shoot grows straight. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some roots bend away from light. Explain how IAA could cause this. (3)
hints: What does IAA do to root cells?
questions.solution:
IAA moves to the shaded side [B1]
In roots, IAA inhibits cell elongation [B1]
So the lit side elongates more and the root bends away from the light. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a bioassay using shoot curvature and a calibration curve could be used to compare the IAA concentration in extracts from two plant species. (5)
hints: How do you make the calibration curve?
questions.solution:
Place agar blocks containing known IAA concentrations on one side of decapitated shoots [B1]
Measure the angle of curvature after a set time [B1]
Plot a calibration curve of curvature against IAA concentration [B1]
Repeat with agar blocks soaked in each extract and read concentrations from the curve [B1]
Control: same species / age of shoots, block size, time, temperature, kept in the dark. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to investigate the effect of IAA concentration on root growth. (5)
hints: How do you get a range of concentrations?
What do you measure and control?
questions.solution:
