Make a range of IAA concentrations by serial dilution (with a 0 control) [B1]
Place germinated seeds / root tips in each concentration [B1]
Measure root length at the start and after a set time [B1]
Use several roots per concentration and calculate the mean [B1]
Control temperature, light, volume of solution, seed species / age. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to investigate the effect of light from one side on the growth of shoots. (5)
hints: How do you measure the response?
questions.solution:
Grow seedlings in the dark, then expose them to light from one side [B1]
Control seedlings lit evenly from above (or kept in the dark) [B1]
Measure the angle of curvature after a set time [B1]
Use many seedlings and calculate the mean [B1]
Control light intensity, temperature, species, age and water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Shoot tips were placed on agar blocks, then the blocks were placed on decapitated shoots. Curvature: tip kept in light 18°; tip kept in dark 18°; tip lit from one side on a split block — shaded half 12°, lit half 6°. Give two conclusions. (2)
hints: Compare the two halves of the split block.
questions.solution:
Light does not affect the total amount of IAA produced [B1]
Light from one side causes IAA to move to the shaded side. [B1]

questions.prompt: Shoots with tips curved 20° towards light; shoots without tips curved 0°; shoots without tips but with an IAA block on one side curved 15°. Give two conclusions. (2)
hints: What does removing the tip show?
questions.solution:
The tip is needed for the response / produces the growth substance [B1]
IAA causes curvature (can replace the tip). [B1]

questions.prompt: Root growth was 10 mm with no IAA, 8 mm at 0.1 mg dm⁻³, 4 mm at 1 mg dm⁻³ and 1 mm at 10 mg dm⁻³. Give two conclusions. (2)
hints: Does IAA stimulate or inhibit root growth?
questions.solution:
IAA inhibits root growth [B1]
Higher IAA concentrations cause more inhibition. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the percentage of maximum absorption of light at 600 nm by the three types of cone cell in the human retina. Use it to explain how a person sees light of 600 nm as orange. (3)
hints: How does the brain interpret the combination?
questions.solution:
Red-sensitive cones are stimulated a lot and green-sensitive cones a little [B1]
Blue-sensitive cones not stimulated [B1]
Brain interprets this combination / ratio of impulses from cones as orange. [B1]
questions.table:
Cone type | Absorption at 600 nm / %
Blue-sensitive | 0
Green-sensitive | 30
Red-sensitive | 75

questions.prompt: The table shows the percentage of maximum absorption at 570 nm by each type of cone cell. Use it to explain how light of 570 nm is seen as yellow. (3)
hints: Compare the green and red cones.
Each cone type connects to its own bipolar neurone.
questions.solution:
Red- and green-sensitive cones are both strongly stimulated (90% and 60%) [B1]
Blue-sensitive cones not stimulated [B1]
Separate impulses from each cone type / the brain combines them and interprets this ratio as yellow. [B1]
questions.table:
Cone type | Absorption at 570 nm / %
Blue-sensitive | 0
Green-sensitive | 60
Red-sensitive | 90

questions.prompt: A person lacks working red-sensitive cones. The table shows absorption by their cones at two wavelengths. Explain why this person cannot tell 560 nm and 620 nm light apart if the brightness is adjusted. (3)
hints: How many cone types respond to each wavelength?
Is the ratio of stimulation different?
questions.solution:
At both wavelengths only the green-sensitive cones are stimulated [B1]
No other cone type gives a different ratio of impulses to compare [B1]
So the brain receives the same pattern / only intensity differs, which can be matched by changing brightness. [B1]
questions.table:
Cone type | Absorption at 560 nm / % | Absorption at 620 nm / %
Blue-sensitive | 0 | 0
Green-sensitive | 80 | 25

questions.prompt:
Which arrangement in the retina gives the highest sensitivity to dim light?

Choose one answer.

A  One photoreceptor connected to one neurone, spatial summation
B  One photoreceptor connected to one neurone, temporal summation
C  Several photoreceptors connected to one neurone, spatial summation
D  Several photoreceptors connected to several neurones, no summation (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which arrangement in the retina gives the highest visual acuity?

Choose one answer.

A  One cone connected to one bipolar neurone
B  Several cones connected to one bipolar neurone
C  Several rods connected to one bipolar neurone
D  One rod connected to several bipolar neurones (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which statement about rod cells is correct?

Choose one answer.

A  They contain iodopsin and give colour vision
B  They contain rhodopsin and several share one bipolar neurone
C  They give high visual acuity
D  They are concentrated in the fovea (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt: Increased muscle activity raises the concentration of carbon dioxide in the blood. Describe and explain how this increases heart rate. (4)
hints: Which nerve carries impulses to the SAN?
questions.solution:
Chemoreceptors in the aorta / carotid arteries detect the fall in blood pH [B1]
Send more impulses to the medulla / cardiac control centre [B1]
More impulses along sympathetic nerves to the SAN [B1]
SAN sends waves of excitation more often, so heart rate increases. [B1]

questions.prompt: When blood pressure rises above normal, heart rate falls. Describe and explain how. (4)
hints: Which nervous system slows the heart?
questions.solution:
Baroreceptors in the aorta / carotid arteries detect the rise [B1]
Send more impulses to the medulla [B1]
More impulses along parasympathetic (vagus) nerves to the SAN [B1]
SAN sends waves of excitation less often, so heart rate decreases. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a heartbeat is initiated and coordinated. (4)
hints: Why is there a delay at the AVN?
questions.solution:
SAN sends a wave of electrical activity across the atria, causing atrial systole [B1]
Non-conducting tissue stops the wave reaching the ventricles directly [B1]
AVN delays then passes impulses down the bundle of His / Purkyne fibres [B1]
Ventricles contract from the apex upwards. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe myogenic stimulation of the heart and how contraction of the atria and ventricles is coordinated. Do not include the role of the autonomic nervous system. (5)
hints: Why does the AVN delay the impulse?
questions.solution:
Heartbeat initiated by the heart muscle itself — the sinoatrial node (SAN) [B1]
SAN sends a wave of electrical activity over the atria, so they contract [B1]
Non-conducting tissue prevents the wave passing directly to the ventricles [B1]
AVN delays, then passes the wave down the bundle of His [B1]
Purkyne tissue carries it through the ventricle walls, so ventricles contract from the apex upwards after the atria have emptied. [B1]

questions.prompt: IAA loosens plant cell walls. The table shows the effect of IAA concentration on cell-wall plasticity and mean stem growth. Explain the relationship. (2)
questions.solution:
As IAA increases, cell walls become more plastic and stem growth increases [B1]
More plastic walls allow cells to elongate as they take in water. [B1]
questions.table:
IAA / mol dm⁻³ | Plasticity / arbitrary units | Mean growth / mm
10⁻⁸ | 1.0 | 2.0
10⁻⁷ | 1.6 | 3.1
10⁻⁶ | 2.4 | 4.4
10⁻⁵ | 3.0 | 5.6

questions.prompt: Explain how IAA causes a shoot to bend towards light. (2)
questions.solution:
IAA moves to the shaded side of the shoot [B1]
Cells on the shaded side elongate more, so the shoot bends towards light. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how IAA causes a root to grow downwards (positive gravitropism). (2)
hints: What does IAA do in roots?
questions.solution:
IAA accumulates on the lower side of the root [B1]
In roots IAA inhibits cell elongation, so the upper side grows more and the root bends down. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how an increase in blood carbon dioxide concentration leads to an increase in heart rate. (2)
questions.solution:
Chemoreceptors detect fall in pH and send more impulses to the medulla [B1]
More impulses along sympathetic nerves to the SAN, increasing heart rate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Atropine binds to acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane but doesn't activate them. The parasympathetic nerves to the heart release acetylcholine. Explain how atropine increases heart rate in people with a very slow heart rate. (3)
hints: What does the parasympathetic system do to the SAN?
questions.solution:
Atropine blocks acetylcholine binding to receptors on the SAN [B1]
So parasympathetic (vagus) nerve impulses have less effect [B1]
Less inhibition of the SAN, so it sends waves of excitation more frequently. [B1]

questions.prompt: Beta-blocker drugs block receptors for noradrenaline on the SAN. Explain how they lower heart rate. (3)
hints: What does it do to the SAN?
questions.solution:
Sympathetic nerves release noradrenaline to speed up the SAN [B1]
Beta-blockers stop noradrenaline binding [B1]
So less stimulation of the SAN and fewer waves of excitation / lower heart rate. [B1]

questions.prompt: After 10 minutes there were 15 shrimps in the darkest section and 3 in the brightest. Name the type of behaviour shown and suggest an advantage. (2)
hints: Directional movement towards/away from a stimulus.
Who might see them in bright light?
questions.solution:
Negative phototaxis [B1]
Avoid predators / stay hidden under stones / avoid drying out. [B1]

questions.prompt: Woodlice move faster and turn less in dry conditions. Name this type of behaviour and explain its advantage. (2)
questions.solution:
Kinesis [B1]
They spend less time in dry areas and more in humid areas, so less water loss. [B1]

questions.prompt: Distinguish between taxis and kinesis. (2)
questions.solution:
Taxis is a directional movement towards or away from a stimulus [B1]
Kinesis is a non-directional change in speed / rate of turning in response to the intensity of a stimulus. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the membrane potential at the end of a Pacinian corpuscle (P) with different pressures. Explain how pressure produces these changes. (3)
questions.solution:
Pressure deforms the lamellae / stretch-mediated sodium ion channels [B1]
Channels open and sodium ions diffuse in [B1]
Greater pressure opens more channels, so a larger generator potential. [B1]
questions.table:
Pressure | Potential at P / mV
None | −70
Light | −50
Medium | +30
Heavy | +40

questions.prompt: Explain why a Pacinian corpuscle responds to pressure but not to light or heat. (3)
hints: What sort of channels does it have?
questions.solution:
Receptors are specific to one type of stimulus [B1]
Pacinian corpuscle has stretch-mediated sodium channels [B1]
Only deformation of the membrane (mechanical pressure) opens them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a generator potential in a receptor leads to an action potential in a sensory neurone. (3)
questions.solution:
Stimulus causes depolarisation — generator potential [B1]
If the generator potential reaches threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open [B1]
An action potential is produced (all-or-nothing); larger stimuli give a higher frequency. [B1]

questions.prompt: Caffeine stimulates the sympathetic nervous system. Suggest how caffeine could explain an increase in heart rate 60 minutes after a drink. (2)
hints: Which nerves speed up the heart?
questions.solution:
More impulses along sympathetic nerves to the SAN [B1]
SAN sends waves of excitation more frequently, raising heart rate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why heart rate takes some time to rise after a caffeinated drink. (2)
questions.solution:
Caffeine must be absorbed from the gut into the blood [B1]
And transported to its site of action (brain / heart) before it has an effect. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the medulla controls heart rate. (2)
questions.solution:
Medulla sends impulses along sympathetic nerves to increase the SAN rate [B1]
And along parasympathetic (vagus) nerves to decrease it. [B1]

questions.prompt: Beetles released in the centre of an area with a light on one side all moved directly away from the light. Name this behaviour and give one advantage. (2)
questions.solution:
Negative phototaxis [B1]
Move to dark places so less likely to be seen by predators / avoid drying out. [B1]

questions.prompt: Flatworms move towards food placed at one end of a dish. Name this behaviour and give one advantage. (2)
questions.solution:
Positive chemotaxis [B1]
Find food sources. [B1]

questions.prompt: Plant shoots grow towards light. Name this response and give one advantage. (2)
questions.solution:
Positive phototropism [B1]
More light for photosynthesis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the structures in a Pacinian corpuscle: the layers of connective tissue around the nerve ending, the type of ion channel in the neurone membrane, and the neurone that carries impulses to the CNS. (2)
questions.solution:
Lamellae; stretch-mediated sodium ion channels; sensory neurone. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Describe how a Pacinian corpuscle produces a generator potential when pressure is applied. (2)
questions.solution:
Pressure deforms lamellae and stretch-mediated sodium channels open [B1]
Sodium ions diffuse in, producing a generator potential. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a Pacinian corpuscle only responds to mechanical pressure. (2)
questions.solution:
Receptors are specific to one stimulus [B1]
Only mechanical deformation opens its stretch-mediated sodium channels. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how applying pressure to a Pacinian corpuscle produces a generator potential. (3)
questions.solution:
Pressure deforms the lamellae / stretches the membrane [B1]
Stretch-mediated sodium ion channels open [B1]
Sodium ions diffuse into the neurone, depolarising the membrane (generator potential). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how light falling on a rod cell leads to a generator potential in a bipolar neurone. (3)
questions.solution:
Light breaks down rhodopsin (to opsin and retinal) [B1]
This changes the permeability of the rod cell membrane / alters neurotransmitter release [B1]
Bipolar neurone is depolarised, producing a generator potential. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a stronger pressure on a Pacinian corpuscle leads to a higher frequency of action potentials in the sensory neurone. (3)
questions.solution:
More deformation, so more stretch-mediated sodium channels open [B1]
Larger generator potential [B1]
Threshold reached more often, so more frequent action potentials. [B1]

category: Organisms respond to changes in their environments

questions.prompt: A drug inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Explain how this affects transmission at cholinergic synapses. (3)
hints: What happens if ACh stays in the cleft?
questions.solution:
ACh is not broken down, so it stays in the synaptic cleft longer [B1]
More ACh binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane [B1]
More Na⁺ channels open, so depolarisation / action potentials are more likely. [B1]

questions.prompt: Curare blocks acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. Explain how this affects synaptic transmission. (3)
hints: What happens to the Na⁺ channels?
questions.solution:
ACh cannot bind to the receptors [B1]
Na⁺ channels don't open, so no depolarisation [B1]
No action potential in the postsynaptic neurone / muscle (paralysis). [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug increases the amount of acetylcholine released from the presynaptic neurone. Explain how this affects synaptic transmission. (3)
hints: What is needed to reach threshold?
questions.solution:
More ACh diffuses across and binds to receptors [B1]
More Na⁺ enters the postsynaptic neurone [B1]
Threshold is reached more easily, so action potentials are more likely. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how acetylcholine causes depolarisation of a postsynaptic membrane. (3)
questions.solution:
ACh diffuses across the synaptic cleft [B1]
Binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane [B1]
Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ diffuses in and the membrane depolarises (action potential if threshold reached). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the events in the presynaptic neurone that lead to the release of neurotransmitter. (3)
hints: What happens when an action potential arrives?
questions.solution:
Action potential arrives and Ca²⁺ channels open [B1]
Ca²⁺ diffuses into the presynaptic knob [B1]
Vesicles move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing neurotransmitter by exocytosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how acetylcholine is removed from the synaptic cleft and why this is important. (3)
questions.solution:
Acetylcholinesterase hydrolyses ACh [B1]
Products diffuse back to the presynaptic neurone and are recycled [B1]
Prevents continuous stimulation / allows new impulses to be transmitted. [B1]

questions.prompt: Nicotine has a similar shape to acetylcholine. Explain how it can stimulate postsynaptic neurones. (2)
questions.solution:
Binds to ACh receptors (complementary shape) [B1]
Opens Na⁺ channels, causing depolarisation. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug resembles a neurotransmitter and binds to its receptor but does not open the ion channel. Explain how it reduces synaptic transmission. (2)
questions.solution:
Drug blocks the receptor, so the neurotransmitter cannot bind [B1]
Fewer Na⁺ channels open, so less depolarisation. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug reduces the entry of Ca²⁺ ions into presynaptic neurones in pain pathways. Explain how this reduces pain. (2)
questions.solution:
Less Ca²⁺ entry, so fewer vesicles fuse and less neurotransmitter is released [B1]
Fewer action potentials in postsynaptic neurones carrying pain signals. [B1]

questions.prompt: A neurotransmitter opens K⁺ channels in a postsynaptic membrane. Explain how this inhibits the postsynaptic neurone. (3)
hints: What happens to the membrane potential?
questions.solution:
K⁺ diffuses out of the neurone [B1]
Inside becomes more negative — hyperpolarisation [B1]
More Na⁺ needed to reach threshold, so action potentials less likely. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain spatial summation at a synapse. (3)
questions.solution:
Several presynaptic neurones release neurotransmitter onto the same postsynaptic neurone [B1]
Their effects add together [B1]
Enough to reach threshold and produce an action potential. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain temporal summation at a synapse. (3)
hints: One neurone — how often does it fire?
questions.solution:
One presynaptic neurone releases neurotransmitter several times in quick succession [B1]
Neurotransmitter builds up in the cleft [B1]
Combined effect reaches threshold, triggering an action potential. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how myelination increases the speed of conduction of nerve impulses. (3)
hints: Where can depolarisation occur in a myelinated axon?
questions.solution:
Myelin insulates the axon, so depolarisation occurs only at nodes of Ranvier [B1]
Impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction) [B1]
So fewer depolarisations are needed and the impulse travels faster. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how damage to the myelin sheath of motor neurones can cause muscle weakness. (3)
questions.solution:
Depolarisation can't jump between nodes / occurs along the whole membrane or leaks [B1]
Impulses slow down or fail to reach threshold [B1]
Fewer / no impulses reach the muscle, so it does not contract properly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the diameter of an axon affects the speed of conduction. (3)
hints: How easily do ions move along a wide axon?
questions.solution:
Wider axons have less resistance to the flow of ions along the axon [B1]
Less leakage of ions [B1]
So depolarisation spreads further / faster — faster conduction. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a nerve impulse is transmitted across a neuromuscular junction. (5)
hints: What enters the presynaptic knob when an action potential arrives?
What happens at the muscle membrane?
questions.solution:
Action potential arrives; calcium ion channels open and Ca²⁺ diffuses into the presynaptic neurone [B1]
Vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing acetylcholine by exocytosis [B1]
ACh diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the muscle membrane [B1]
Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ diffuses in [B1]
Depolarisation of the muscle membrane triggers an action potential / contraction. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how an action potential is propagated along an unmyelinated axon. (5)
hints: What happens to sodium channels in the next section?
questions.solution:
Depolarisation: Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ diffuses in [B1]
Local currents of Na⁺ cause the next section of membrane to depolarise [B1]
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open there, so the action potential moves along [B1]
Behind it, K⁺ channels open and K⁺ diffuses out (repolarisation) [B1]
Refractory period stops the impulse moving backwards. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a resting potential is established and maintained in a neurone. (5)
questions.solution:
Sodium–potassium pump actively transports 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in (using ATP) [B1]
Membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than Na⁺ (more K⁺ channels open) [B1]
K⁺ diffuses out, Na⁺ cannot easily diffuse back in [B1]
Inside of the axon becomes negative relative to outside [B1]
Resting potential about −70 mV. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the sodium–potassium pump helps to establish the resting potential. (3)
hints: How many ions does it move each way?
questions.solution:
Actively transports 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, using ATP [B1]
Creates concentration gradients of Na⁺ and K⁺ across the membrane [B1]
More positive ions leave than enter, contributing to the inside being negative. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the axon membrane is more permeable to potassium ions than sodium ions at rest, and how this affects the resting potential. (3)
hints: Which channels are open at rest?
questions.solution:
More K⁺ channels are open; voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are closed [B1]
K⁺ diffuses out down its concentration gradient [B1]
Inside becomes more negative relative to outside (about −70 mV). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a neurone at rest is described as polarised. (3)
hints: Is there a potential difference across the membrane?
questions.solution:
There is a potential difference across the membrane [B1]
Inside is negative relative to outside (about −70 mV) [B1]
Due to unequal distribution of Na⁺ and K⁺ ions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why impulses travel slowly along non-myelinated axons. (3)
questions.solution:
Depolarisation must occur along the whole length of the membrane [B1]
Each section must depolarise in turn [B1]
This takes more time than saltatory conduction. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the distance between nodes of Ranvier affects the speed of conduction in a myelinated axon. (3)
questions.solution:
Depolarisation only occurs at nodes; the impulse jumps between them (saltatory conduction) [B1]
Longer distances between nodes mean fewer depolarisations along the axon [B1]
So conduction is faster. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of Schwann cells in nerve impulse conduction. (3)
questions.solution:
Schwann cells wrap around the axon, forming the myelin sheath [B1]
Myelin is an electrical insulator, preventing depolarisation [B1]
Depolarisation only at nodes of Ranvier, so impulses jump (saltatory conduction) and are faster. [B1]

questions.prompt: Ouabain inhibits the sodium–potassium pump. Explain why the resting potential of a neurone treated with ouabain gradually disappears. (3)
hints: What happens to ions without it?
questions.solution:
Na⁺ and K⁺ are no longer pumped [B1]
Ions leak / diffuse down their gradients (Na⁺ in, K⁺ out) [B1]
Concentration gradients are lost, so the potential difference falls to zero. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a neurone deprived of oxygen soon cannot conduct impulses. (3)
hints: What does the sodium–potassium pump need?
Can action potentials form without ion gradients?
questions.solution:
No aerobic respiration, so little ATP [B1]
Sodium–potassium pump stops, so ion gradients / resting potential are lost [B1]
So no action potentials can be generated. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug opens extra potassium ion channels in a neurone membrane. Explain why it becomes harder to generate an action potential. (3)
hints: What happens to the membrane potential?
questions.solution:
More K⁺ diffuses out of the neurone [B1]
Membrane becomes hyperpolarised (more negative) [B1]
More Na⁺ must enter to reach threshold, so action potentials are less likely. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why transmission across a cholinergic synapse can only occur in one direction. (2)
questions.solution:
Vesicles of acetylcholine are only in the presynaptic neurone [B1]
ACh receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of the refractory period in a neurone. (2)
hints: What does that mean for impulses?
questions.solution:
Na⁺ channels cannot reopen, so a new action potential cannot be produced immediately [B1]
Ensures impulses travel in one direction / are discrete / limits impulse frequency. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an action potential travels in only one direction along an axon. (2)
hints: What state is the membrane behind the action potential in?
questions.solution:
The region behind the action potential is in its refractory period [B1]
Na⁺ channels there cannot open, so depolarisation only spreads forwards. [B1]

questions.prompt: Repeated stimulation of one presynaptic neurone eventually causes an action potential in the postsynaptic neurone, but a single stimulus does not. Name and explain this. (2)
questions.solution:
Temporal summation [B1]
Neurotransmitter builds up from repeated release until threshold is reached. [B1]

questions.prompt: Stimulating three presynaptic neurones together triggers an action potential, but stimulating any one alone does not. Name and explain this. (2)
questions.solution:
Spatial summation [B1]
Neurotransmitter from several neurones together is enough to reach threshold. [B1]

questions.prompt: A single stimulus causes a small depolarisation of the postsynaptic membrane, but no action potential. Explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Not enough neurotransmitter released / too few Na⁺ channels open [B1]
So depolarisation does not reach threshold. [B1]

questions.prompt: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions. Explain why this weakens muscle contraction. (2)
hints: What happens to the muscle membrane?
questions.solution:
Fewer receptors for ACh to bind to, so fewer Na⁺ channels open [B1]
Less depolarisation of the muscle membrane / fewer action potentials, so weaker contraction. [B1]

questions.prompt: Curare blocks acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Explain why curare causes paralysis. (2)
questions.solution:
ACh cannot bind to receptors, so Na⁺ channels don't open [B1]
No action potential in the muscle, so it cannot contract. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a drug that inhibits acetylcholinesterase helps people with myasthenia gravis. (3)
hints: What happens to ACh in the cleft?
How does more ACh help with fewer receptors?
questions.solution:
ACh is not broken down, so stays in the cleft longer / builds up [B1]
More ACh binds to the remaining receptors [B1]
More Na⁺ channels open, so threshold is reached and the muscle contracts. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some insecticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Explain why they kill insects. (3)
questions.solution:
ACh is not broken down, so accumulates in the synaptic cleft [B1]
Postsynaptic membranes / muscles are continuously stimulated [B1]
Causing spasms / paralysis (e.g. of breathing muscles) and death. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how increasing the amount of ACh released could overcome partial blocking of ACh receptors. (3)
hints: What happens to the chance of ACh finding a free receptor?
questions.solution:
More ACh in the cleft, so more binds to the remaining unblocked receptors [B1]
More Na⁺ channels open [B1]
Depolarisation reaches threshold, triggering an action potential. [B1]

questions.prompt: Glutamate is the neurotransmitter at synapses carrying pain impulses. A drug blocks the voltage-gated calcium ion channels in the presynaptic membrane of these synapses. Explain how this drug reduces pain. Transmission at these synapses works in the same way as at a cholinergic synapse. (5)
hints: What normally happens when an action potential reaches the presynaptic knob?
questions.solution:
Action potential arrives but calcium ions can't diffuse into the presynaptic neurone [B1]
So vesicles don't move to / fuse with the presynaptic membrane [B1]
Less / no glutamate released by exocytosis [B1]
Less glutamate diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane [B1]
Fewer sodium ion channels open, so no depolarisation / threshold not reached [B1]
No action potential in the postsynaptic neurone, so pain impulses don't reach the brain. [B1]
Any 5 of these points — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: A drug inhibits the enzyme acetylcholinesterase at cholinergic synapses. Explain how this drug affects transmission across the synapse. (5)
hints: What happens if acetylcholine stays bound?
questions.solution:
Acetylcholine is not hydrolysed / broken down in the synaptic cleft [B1]
Acetylcholine stays bound to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane [B1]
Sodium ion channels stay open, so sodium ions keep diffusing in [B1]
Postsynaptic membrane remains depolarised / repeated action potentials [B1]
Acetylcholine isn't recycled (choline and ethanoic acid not returned) / continuous stimulation, e.g. of muscles. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug has a similar shape to a neurotransmitter and binds to its receptors without opening them. Explain how this drug prevents transmission at the synapse. (5)
hints: What does the drug compete with?
What does the neurotransmitter normally cause on the postsynaptic membrane?
questions.solution:
Drug is complementary to / binds to the receptor site [B1]
So fewer neurotransmitter molecules can bind to receptors (competitive) [B1]
Sodium ion channels don't open [B1]
Less sodium ion influx so the postsynaptic membrane isn't depolarised / threshold not reached [B1]
No action potential generated in the postsynaptic neurone. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug made of a short polypeptide acts on synapses in the spinal cord. Suggest two reasons why it is injected into the fluid around the spinal cord rather than taken as a tablet. (2)
hints: What happens to polypeptides in the gut?
Can it reach the spinal cord from the blood?
questions.solution:
Polypeptide would be digested / hydrolysed by proteases (peptidases) in the gut [B1]
It is delivered directly to the site of action / too large to be absorbed or cross into the nervous tissue from the blood / lower dose needed / fewer side-effects elsewhere. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug that acts on the brain is a large, water-soluble polypeptide. Suggest two reasons why it might have little effect when given by injection into a vein. (2)
hints: Can large charged molecules cross membranes?
What enzymes are in the blood or tissues?
questions.solution:
Large / water-soluble (polar) so it can't diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer to reach the brain tissue [B1]
It may be broken down by enzymes (peptidases) before reaching its target / diluted in the blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name four structures found at a neuromuscular junction: the structure that stores acetylcholine, the organelle that supplies ATP in the axon terminal, the gap between neurone and muscle, and the membrane of the muscle fibre. (2)
hints: Neurotransmitter is stored in small membrane-bound sacs.
The muscle cell membrane has a special name.
questions.solution:
Synaptic vesicle; mitochondrion; synaptic cleft; sarcolemma. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Give two differences between a neuromuscular junction and a cholinergic synapse between two neurones. (2)
hints: Is a neuromuscular junction always excitatory?
questions.solution: Two from: NMJ is only excitatory (synapse may be inhibitory); NMJ connects motor neurone to muscle (synapse neurone to neurone); NMJ action potential always triggers a response / no summation needed; NMJ postsynaptic membrane has clefts with more receptors / acetylcholinesterase. [B2]

questions.prompt: Name the structures at a synapse: the receptors for acetylcholine are found on the __1__ membrane; the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine is __2__; ions entering the presynaptic knob to trigger exocytosis are __3__ ions; the products of acetylcholine breakdown that are recycled are choline and __4__. (2)
hints: Receptors are on the receiving cell.
questions.solution:
1 postsynaptic; 2 acetylcholinesterase; 3 calcium; 4 ethanoic acid. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Explain how hyperpolarisation of a postsynaptic membrane at an inhibitory synapse inhibits transmission of nerve impulses. (2)
hints: How far is the membrane from threshold?
How much sodium entry is needed?
questions.solution:
Inside becomes more negative, so more sodium ions need to enter to depolarise [B1]
Threshold is less likely to be reached, so fewer / no action potentials. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how an inhibitory synapse causes hyperpolarisation of the postsynaptic membrane. (2)
questions.solution:
Neurotransmitter opens chloride ion channels (chloride ions diffuse in) and potassium ion channels (potassium ions diffuse out) [B1]
So the inside becomes more negative than the resting potential. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by spatial summation at a synapse. (2)
questions.solution:
Several presynaptic neurones release neurotransmitter onto one postsynaptic neurone [B1]
The combined effect reaches threshold and triggers an action potential. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the parts of a myelinated motor neurone: the part containing the nucleus, the cells that form the myelin sheath, the gaps in the myelin, and the long process carrying impulses away from the cell body. (2)
hints: Myelin is made by special cells.
The gaps are named after a scientist.
questions.solution:
Cell body; Schwann cells; nodes of Ranvier; axon. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Give the function of (i) the myelin sheath and (ii) dendrites. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Insulates the axon, allowing saltatory conduction / faster impulses [B1]
(ii) Receive impulses from other neurones / carry impulses towards the cell body. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two differences between a sensory neurone and a motor neurone. (2)
questions.solution:
Sensory carries impulses from receptors to the CNS; motor from the CNS to effectors [B1]
Sensory cell body is part-way along the axon / in the dorsal root ganglion; motor cell body is at the end, in the CNS. [B1]

questions.prompt: A condition destroys myelin in the brain. Explain why it can increase reflex response times. (3)
hints: How do impulses travel in myelinated neurones?
questions.solution:
Without myelin there's no saltatory conduction / impulses can't jump between nodes [B1]
Depolarisation must occur along the whole length of the axon [B1]
So impulses travel more slowly, increasing response time. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how axon diameter and temperature affect the speed of conduction of nerve impulses. (3)
hints: What happens to diffusion when warm?
questions.solution:
Larger diameter gives less resistance / less leakage of ions, so faster [B1]
Higher temperature increases rate of diffusion of ions, so faster [B1]
Up to a point — at high temperatures proteins (channels, pumps) denature. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a myelinated axon conducts impulses faster than a non-myelinated axon of the same diameter. (3)
hints: Where does depolarisation happen in myelinated axons?
questions.solution:
Myelin insulates, so depolarisation only at nodes of Ranvier [B1]
Impulse jumps from node to node — saltatory conduction [B1]
Fewer depolarisations needed along the axon, so faster. [B1]

questions.prompt: Nicotine mimics acetylcholine and binds to its receptors at some synapses. Explain how this affects the postsynaptic neurone. (3)
questions.solution:
Nicotine is complementary to the receptors and binds to them [B1]
Sodium ion channels open, sodium ions diffuse in [B1]
Depolarisation / action potential in the postsynaptic neurone even without acetylcholine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the resting potential of −70 mV is maintained in a sensory neurone. (2)
hints: What does the sodium–potassium pump do?
questions.solution:
Sodium–potassium pump actively transports 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in [B1]
Membrane more permeable to K⁺ (more K⁺ channels open), so K⁺ diffuses out, inside negative. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the inside of an axon is negative compared with the outside at rest. (2)
questions.solution:
More positive ions pumped out than in (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) [B1]
K⁺ diffuses out through open channels; membrane less permeable to Na⁺. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug blocks the sodium–potassium pump. Suggest the effect on the resting potential and explain why. (2)
hints: What would happen to the ion gradients?
questions.solution:
Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients run down / ions not actively transported [B1]
Resting potential lost / becomes less negative, so action potentials can't be produced. [B1]

questions.prompt: Further along the sensory neurone (at Q) the potential was −70 mV with light pressure and +40 mV with both medium and heavy pressure. Explain why it was the same for medium and heavy pressure. (2)
questions.solution:
Action potentials are all-or-nothing [B1]
Once threshold is reached, all action potentials are the same size. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the nervous system distinguishes between a weak and a strong stimulus if all action potentials are the same size. (2)
questions.solution:
Stronger stimulus gives a higher frequency of action potentials [B1]
And may stimulate more receptors / neurones. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why light pressure produced no action potential at Q. (2)
questions.solution:
Generator potential didn't reach the threshold [B1]
So voltage-gated sodium channels didn't open / no action potential. [B1]

questions.prompt: In multiple sclerosis, myelin is lost from some neurones. Explain how this slows responses to stimuli. (2)
questions.solution:
No saltatory conduction / impulse can't jump between nodes of Ranvier [B1]
Depolarisation occurs along the whole axon, so slower conduction. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the refractory period and its importance. (2)
hints: Can another action potential occur immediately?
questions.solution:
Period after an action potential when sodium channels are closed / can't open [B1]
Ensures impulses travel in one direction / are discrete / limits frequency. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the events of depolarisation and repolarisation during an action potential. (2)
questions.solution:
Depolarisation: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ diffuses in, inside becomes positive [B1]
Repolarisation: Na⁺ channels close, K⁺ channels open and K⁺ diffuses out. [B1]

questions.prompt: An insecticide binds to sodium ion channels in insect neurones and keeps them open. Explain how this kills insects. (2)
questions.solution:
Sodium ions keep diffusing in, so the membrane stays depolarised / can't repolarise [B1]
No further action potentials / continuous impulses, so paralysis (of breathing muscles). [B1]

questions.prompt: Some insecticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Explain how this kills insects. (2)
questions.solution:
Acetylcholine isn't broken down, so stays bound to receptors [B1]
Continuous stimulation / depolarisation of muscles, causing spasms / paralysis. [B1]

questions.prompt: A toxin blocks voltage-gated sodium channels. Explain its effect on nerve impulses. (2)
questions.solution:
Sodium ions can't diffuse into the axon [B1]
No depolarisation, so no action potentials — paralysis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the arrival of a nerve impulse at a presynaptic knob causes the release of neurotransmitter. (3)
hints: Which channels open when the knob depolarises?
questions.solution:
Depolarisation opens voltage-gated calcium ion channels [B1]
Calcium ions diffuse into the presynaptic knob [B1]
Vesicles move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing neurotransmitter by exocytosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe what happens to acetylcholine after it is released into the synaptic cleft at a cholinergic synapse. (3)
questions.solution:
Diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane [B1]
Hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase into choline and ethanoic acid [B1]
Products diffuse back into the presynaptic knob and are used to resynthesise acetylcholine (using ATP). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why transmission across a cholinergic synapse is unidirectional. (3)
questions.solution:
Neurotransmitter is only in vesicles in the presynaptic knob / only released from the presynaptic membrane [B1]
Receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane [B1]
So impulses can only pass from presynaptic to postsynaptic neurone. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest and explain one advantage of mitochondria moving close to the presynaptic membrane when nerve impulses arrive. (2)
hints: What needs ATP at the synapse?
questions.solution:
ATP supplied close to where it's needed [B1]
For exocytosis / vesicle movement / resynthesis of neurotransmitter / pumping calcium ions out. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a presynaptic knob contains many mitochondria. (2)
questions.solution:
Lots of ATP needed [B1]
For synthesis of neurotransmitter / exocytosis / active transport to restore ion gradients. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why repeated stimulation of a synapse can cause it to stop transmitting impulses (synaptic fatigue). (2)
hints: Can it be resynthesised fast enough?
questions.solution:
Neurotransmitter is used up faster than it can be resynthesised [B1]
So not enough is released to reach threshold in the postsynaptic neurone. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student's estimate of nerve impulse speed was much lower than the published value of 76 m s⁻¹. Suggest three reasons. (3)
questions.solution:
Time taken for transmission across synapses (diffusion of neurotransmitter) [B1]
Time for processing in the brain / muscle contraction [B1]
Some neurones may be non-myelinated / narrower / pathway length estimated inaccurately. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why reflex actions are faster than voluntary responses. (3)
questions.solution:
Reflex arc involves only a few neurones / synapses [B1]
Doesn't involve conscious processing in the brain [B1]
So less time for transmission. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain three factors that increase the speed of conduction along an axon. (3)
questions.solution:
Myelination — saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier [B1]
Larger axon diameter — less resistance [B1]
Higher temperature — faster diffusion of ions (up to a point). [B1]

questions.prompt: Light pressure produced a small depolarisation but no action potential in a sensory neurone; heavier pressure produced an action potential of +40 mV. Use this to explain the all-or-nothing principle. (2)
questions.solution:
Below threshold, no action potential is produced [B1]
Once threshold is reached, an action potential is always the same size, whatever the stimulus strength. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two different strong stimuli both produced action potentials of +40 mV in the same neurone. Explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Action potentials are all-or-nothing — once threshold is reached they are the same size [B1]
Stimulus strength is shown by frequency of action potentials, not size. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the threshold of a neurone. (2)
questions.solution:
The minimum level of depolarisation (about −55 mV) needed to trigger an action potential [B1]
At which voltage-gated sodium channels open. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the period after an action potential when a new action potential cannot be produced. (1)
questions.solution: Refractory period. [B1]

questions.prompt: During which phase of an action potential do voltage-gated potassium channels open? (1)
questions.solution: Repolarisation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the phase of an action potential when the membrane potential becomes more negative than the resting potential. (1)
questions.solution: Hyperpolarisation. [B1]

category: Organisms respond to changes in their environments

questions.prompt: Muscle fibres from endurance-trained athletes stain more strongly for a Krebs cycle enzyme than fibres from untrained people. Suggest why. (1)
hints: Where does the Krebs cycle happen?
questions.solution: More mitochondria / more of the enzyme in trained fibres. [B1]

questions.prompt: Slow-twitch muscle fibres stain more strongly than fast-twitch fibres for succinate dehydrogenase (a Krebs cycle enzyme). Suggest why. (1)
hints: Which fibres rely on aerobic respiration?
questions.solution: Slow-twitch fibres have more mitochondria for aerobic respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why slow-twitch muscle fibres appear red. (1)
hints: Which protein stores oxygen in muscle?
questions.solution: They contain lots of myoglobin (and a rich blood supply). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why slow-twitch muscle fibres are suited to endurance activities. (3)
hints: Which type of respiration do they use?
questions.solution:
Many mitochondria, so lots of aerobic respiration and ATP [B1]
Myoglobin stores oxygen / rich capillary supply [B1]
Little lactate produced, so they fatigue slowly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why fast-twitch muscle fibres fatigue quickly. (3)
hints: Which respiration do they rely on?
questions.solution:
Rely on anaerobic respiration / glycolysis [B1]
Lactate builds up [B1]
Few mitochondria / little myoglobin / poor capillary supply. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how endurance training increases the time before muscles become fatigued. (3)
hints: What changes in the muscle fibres?
What does this do to respiration?
questions.solution:
More mitochondria / capillaries / myoglobin [B1]
More aerobic respiration, so more ATP [B1]
Less anaerobic respiration, so less lactate. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the force of contraction of isolated muscle fibres at three temperatures, at normal pH and at lowered pH, as a percentage of maximum. Evaluate the conclusion that lower pH reduces the force of muscle contraction. (4)
hints: Is force lower at low pH at every temperature?
How big is the effect at body temperature?
questions.solution:
Force is lower at low pH at all temperatures, supporting the conclusion [B1]
The effect gets smaller as temperature increases (25% at 12 °C, only 5% at 32 °C) [B1]
So at body temperature the effect may be small [B1]
Isolated fibres not whole muscles / no SD or statistics / limited species. [B1]
questions.table:
Temperature / °C | Normal pH | Low pH
12 | 80 | 55
22 | 90 | 75
32 | 95 | 90

questions.prompt: During exhausting exercise, blood lactate concentration rose from 1 to 12 mmol dm⁻³ and power output fell by 30%. Evaluate the conclusion that lactate causes muscle fatigue. (4)
hints: What else happens during intense exercise?
questions.solution:
Lactate rose as power fell, consistent with the conclusion [B1]
But this is a correlation — other changes (e.g. low pH, phosphate build-up, glycogen depletion) may cause fatigue [B1]
Lactate is in the blood, not measured in the muscle [B1]
Need experiments changing lactate alone / more data and statistics. [B1]

questions.prompt: Athletes taking a creatine supplement improved their sprint time by 2% compared with a placebo group. Creatine helps regenerate ATP from phosphocreatine. Evaluate the claim that creatine improves sprint performance. (4)
questions.solution:
Supports the claim — sprint performance improved [B1]
Plausible mechanism: more phosphocreatine regenerates ATP faster during short, intense exercise [B1]
But no information on sample size, SD or significance — 2% may be due to chance [B1]
Was the trial double-blind? Effects on other types of exercise unknown. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of calcium ions in muscle contraction. (3)
hints: Where are calcium ions released from?
questions.solution:
Calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum [B1]
Bind to troponin, causing tropomyosin to move [B1]
Exposing myosin-binding sites on actin, so cross-bridges form. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a muscle contracts less forcefully if less calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. (3)
questions.solution:
Fewer calcium ions bind to troponin [B1]
So fewer tropomyosin molecules move, exposing fewer binding sites on actin [B1]
Fewer actin–myosin cross-bridges form, so less force. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the roles of ATP in muscle contraction. (3)
hints: What happens to calcium after contraction?
questions.solution:
ATP hydrolysed by ATPase on the myosin head [B1]
Energy allows the myosin head to detach from actin and return to its original position (recocking) [B1]
ATP used to actively transport calcium ions back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the I band and H zone shorten when a muscle contracts, but the A band stays the same length. (3)
hints: What does the A band represent?
questions.solution:
Actin filaments slide over myosin towards the centre of the sarcomere [B1]
I band (actin only) and H zone (myosin only) get shorter as overlap increases [B1]
A band is the length of the myosin filaments, which don't change length. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a sarcomere. (3)
questions.solution:
Section of a myofibril between two Z lines [B1]
Thin actin filaments attached to the Z lines [B1]
Thick myosin filaments in the centre (A band), held at the M line. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a myofibril has a pattern of dark and light bands. (3)
hints: Which filaments are in the dark band?
Which are in the light band?
questions.solution:
Dark A bands contain thick myosin filaments (and overlapping actin) [B1]
Light I bands contain only thin actin filaments [B1]
H zone in the middle of the A band contains only myosin, so is lighter. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of ATP in muscle contraction. (2)
hints: What happens to the myosin head?
questions.solution:
Hydrolysis of ATP releases energy to move the myosin head (power stroke) / ATP binding detaches myosin from actin [B1]
Energy for active transport of calcium ions back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of calcium ions in muscle contraction. (2)
hints: What blocks the binding sites on actin?
questions.solution:
Calcium ions bind to tropomyosin (troponin) and cause it to move, exposing binding sites on actin [B1]
Calcium ions activate ATPase (ATP hydrolysis). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of phosphocreatine in muscle. (2)
hints: What does it give to ADP?
questions.solution:
Phosphocreatine provides a phosphate to regenerate ATP from ADP [B1]
Without needing oxygen, so it supports short bursts of intense activity. [B1]

questions.prompt: Creatine supplements help in short, intense exercise. Carbohydrate loading helps in prolonged exercise. Describe and explain how each improves performance, referring to fast and slow muscle fibres. (5)
hints: Which fibres are used in sprints?
questions.solution:
Creatine increases phosphocreatine stores in fast fibres [B1]
Phosphocreatine regenerates ATP anaerobically / quickly for short intense contractions [B1]
Carbohydrate loading increases glycogen stores in muscles [B1]
Slow fibres use aerobic respiration of glucose (from glycogen) for prolonged exercise [B1]
So fatigue / depletion of glycogen is delayed and ATP supply maintained. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the structure and properties of slow-twitch and fast-twitch muscle fibres. (5)
questions.solution:
Slow: many mitochondria; fast: fewer [B1]
Slow: lots of myoglobin (store oxygen) — red; fast: little [B1]
Slow: rich blood supply / many capillaries [B1]
Fast: more glycogen / phosphocreatine and thicker myosin filaments [B1]
Slow: aerobic, long periods, fatigue slowly; fast: anaerobic, short powerful contractions, fatigue quickly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a marathon runner's leg muscles contain a higher proportion of slow-twitch fibres than a sprinter's, and how these fibres are adapted. (5)
hints: What kind of respiration does a marathon need?
How is oxygen supplied and stored?
questions.solution:
Marathon needs prolonged contraction without fatigue [B1]
Slow fibres respire aerobically, producing a lot of ATP without lactate build-up [B1]
Many mitochondria for aerobic respiration [B1]
Myoglobin stores oxygen [B1]
Many capillaries supply oxygen and glucose. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the sequence of events after acetylcholine is released at a neuromuscular junction that leads to the release of calcium ions in the muscle fibre. (4)
hints: How does the depolarisation travel into the fibre?
questions.solution:
Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the sarcolemma [B1]
Sodium ion channels open and sodium ions diffuse in, depolarising the sarcolemma [B1]
Action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and down T-tubules [B1]
Calcium ion channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum open and calcium ions diffuse into the sarcoplasm. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe what happens in a myofibril after calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, up to the point where the myosin heads move actin. (4)
hints: What do calcium ions bind to?
What forms between actin and myosin?
questions.solution:
Calcium ions cause tropomyosin to move, exposing binding sites on actin [B1]
Myosin heads (with ADP attached) bind to actin, forming cross-bridges [B1]
Myosin heads change angle (power stroke), pulling actin along, releasing ADP [B1]
ATP binds and myosin detaches; ATP hydrolysis returns the head to its original position. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a muscle relaxes after the nerve impulses stop. (4)
questions.solution:
Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine, so the sarcolemma repolarises [B1]
Calcium ions actively transported back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum (using ATP) [B1]
Tropomyosin moves back and blocks binding sites on actin [B1]
Myosin can't bind, so no cross-bridges and filaments slide apart (by antagonistic muscle). [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which describes the changes in a sarcomere when a muscle contracts?

Choose one answer.

A  H-zone longer, I-band shorter, A-band same
B  H-zone shorter, I-band shorter, A-band same
C  H-zone shorter, I-band same, A-band shorter
D  H-zone same, I-band shorter, A-band shorter (1)
hints: The thick filaments don't change length.
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which band or zone of a sarcomere contains only actin filaments?

Choose one answer.

A  A-band
B  H-zone
C  I-band
D  M-line (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which band or zone of a sarcomere contains only myosin filaments?

Choose one answer.

A  I-band
B  H-zone
C  Z-line
D  A-band (1)
hints: In the middle of the A-band.
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt: Fast muscle fibres contain a higher concentration of glycogen than slow fibres. Explain how this relates to the properties of the two fibre types. (4)
hints: How much ATP does anaerobic respiration give per glucose?
questions.solution:
Fast fibres rely on anaerobic respiration / glycolysis [B1]
Which produces little ATP per glucose, so lots of glucose needed rapidly [B1]
Glycogen is hydrolysed to glucose for respiration [B1]
Slow fibres respire aerobically, getting more ATP per glucose, and use a steady supply of glucose / fatty acids from the blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Slow muscle fibres contain a lot of myoglobin and many mitochondria. Explain how these features relate to their function. (4)
questions.solution:
Myoglobin stores oxygen / has high affinity for oxygen [B1]
Releases oxygen for aerobic respiration when oxygen is low [B1]
Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration (Krebs, oxidative phosphorylation) [B1]
So a lot of ATP is made for sustained contraction without fatigue. [B1]

questions.prompt: Fast muscle fibres contain high concentrations of phosphocreatine and have fewer capillaries than slow fibres. Explain how these features relate to their function. (4)
hints: How fast does phosphocreatine regenerate ATP?
Do fast fibres need much oxygen?
questions.solution:
Phosphocreatine donates phosphate to ADP, regenerating ATP quickly / anaerobically [B1]
For short, powerful contractions [B1]
Fast fibres rely on anaerobic respiration so need less oxygen [B1]
So fewer capillaries are needed (but they fatigue quickly due to lactate). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of calcium ions and ATP in the contraction of a myofibril. (5)
hints: What do calcium ions do to tropomyosin?
What do ATP binding and hydrolysis do?
questions.solution:
Calcium ions diffuse into the myofibril from the sarcoplasmic reticulum [B1]
Calcium ions cause tropomyosin to move, exposing binding sites on actin [B1]
Myosin heads attach to actin, forming cross-bridges [B1]
Calcium ions activate ATPase / ATP hydrolysis releases energy for the myosin head to move (power stroke), pulling actin [B1]
ATP binding causes myosin to detach from actin [B1]
ATP used to pump calcium ions back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. [B1]
Any 5 of these points — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction and the evidence for it from changes in a sarcomere. (5)
questions.solution:
Myosin heads bind to actin and pull actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere [B1]
Filaments slide past each other — they don't shorten [B1]
Sarcomere / Z-lines move closer together [B1]
I-band and H-zone get shorter [B1]
A-band stays the same length (myosin doesn't change length). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why muscles work in antagonistic pairs and how a muscle fibre is adapted for contraction. (5)
hints: What structures are in the sarcoplasm?
questions.solution:
Muscles can only pull / contract, so one contracts while the other relaxes to move a bone back [B1]
Many mitochondria to supply ATP [B1]
Extensive sarcoplasmic reticulum storing calcium ions [B1]
T-tubules carry action potentials deep into the fibre [B1]
Many nuclei / multinucleate shared cytoplasm (sarcoplasm). [B1]

questions.prompt: Inside a presynaptic knob, myosin attached to a mitochondrion moves it along actin filaments towards the presynaptic membrane. Explain how myosin moves the mitochondrion. Do not refer to calcium ions or tropomyosin. (2)
hints: What does the myosin head bind to?
Where does the energy come from?
questions.solution:
Myosin head binds to actin and changes angle (power stroke), pulling along the actin [B1]
ATP hydrolysis provides energy to detach and re-cock the head, so it binds further along (repeated cycles). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why ATP is needed for a myosin head to detach from actin. (2)
hints: What binds to the myosin head?
questions.solution:
ATP binds to the myosin head, changing its shape so it detaches from actin (breaking the cross-bridge) [B1]
Hydrolysis of ATP then returns the head to its original position ready to rebind. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug activates an enzyme that increases the development of slow muscle fibres and aerobic respiration, even at rest. Explain why sports organisations ban athletes from taking it. Don't describe chemiosmosis. (4)
questions.solution:
More slow fibres / mitochondria, so more aerobic respiration [B1]
More ATP produced for sustained contraction / endurance [B1]
Less lactate / delayed fatigue [B1]
Gives an unfair advantage without training / possible health risks. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why anabolic steroids improve athletic performance and why they are banned. (4)
questions.solution:
Steroids increase protein synthesis, so bigger / stronger muscles [B1]
Faster recovery / more training possible [B1]
Unfair advantage over other athletes [B1]
Health risks (e.g. liver / heart damage). [B1]

questions.prompt: Creatine supplements increase phosphocreatine in muscles. Explain how this improves performance in sprints but not marathons. (4)
questions.solution:
Phosphocreatine regenerates ATP rapidly without oxygen [B1]
Fuels short, intense contraction of fast fibres [B1]
Stores are used in seconds [B1]
Marathons rely on aerobic respiration in slow fibres, not phosphocreatine. [B1]

category: Organisms respond to changes in their environments

questions.prompt: Explain why type II diabetes is often treated by changes to diet and exercise rather than insulin injections. (2)
hints: Do type II diabetics still make insulin?
How does exercise affect glucose uptake?
questions.solution:
In type II, insulin is often still produced but cells respond poorly, so extra insulin may not help [B1]
Diet reduces blood glucose rises; exercise increases glucose uptake / insulin sensitivity. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two differences between type I and type II diabetes. (2)
questions.solution:
Type I: no insulin produced (β cells destroyed, often autoimmune); type II: insulin produced but cells less responsive [B1]
Type I usually starts in childhood; type II linked to obesity / lifestyle / later onset. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two risks or problems of treating diabetes with a pancreas transplant. (2)
hints: What does the immune system do to foreign tissue?
How easy is it to find a donor?
questions.solution:
Rejection by the immune system / need for immunosuppressant drugs (infection risk) [B1]
Shortage of donors / risks of surgery. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which statement about glucagon is incorrect?

Choose one answer.

A  Glucagon binds to receptors on liver cells
B  Glucagon activates enzymes that convert glycogen to glucose
C  Glucagon is secreted by α cells of the pancreas
D  Glucagon increases the uptake of glucose by muscle cells (1)
hints: Which option would lower blood glucose?
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which statement about insulin is correct?

Choose one answer.

A  Insulin increases the number of glucose channel proteins in cell membranes
B  Insulin stimulates the breakdown of glycogen
C  Insulin is secreted by α cells
D  Insulin binds to receptors in the nucleus (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which statement about the action of adrenaline on liver cells is incorrect?

Choose one answer.

A  Adrenaline binds to receptors on the cell-surface membrane
B  Adrenaline activates adenylate cyclase, producing cAMP
C  cAMP activates protein kinase
D  Adrenaline enters the cell and binds directly to glycogen (1)
hints: Adrenaline is a hormone that binds to the cell surface.
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt: People with the same risk allele for type II diabetes differ in whether they develop the disease. Suggest and explain why. (2)
hints: Which lifestyle factors affect type II diabetes?
questions.solution:
Environmental factors such as diet / exercise / body mass differ [B1]
These affect insulin sensitivity, so only some people with the allele develop the disease. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a diuretic drug could lower blood pressure. (1)
hints: More water is lost in what?
questions.solution: More water lost in urine, so blood volume decreases. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a drug that blocks ADH receptors could lower blood pressure. (1)
questions.solution: Less water reabsorbed in the collecting duct, so more urine and lower blood volume. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a high-salt diet can raise blood pressure. (1)
hints: What does salt do to blood water potential?
What does the kidney do in response?
questions.solution: Lowers blood water potential, so more water is retained / reabsorbed, increasing blood volume. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the loop of Henle produces a low water potential in the medulla of the kidney. (3)
hints: What does the ascending limb pump out?
Is the ascending limb permeable to water?
questions.solution:
Cells of the ascending limb actively transport Na⁺ and Cl⁻ out into the medulla [B1]
The ascending limb is impermeable to water, so water cannot follow [B1]
Ions accumulate in the medulla, giving it a low water potential. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how ADH reduces the volume of urine produced. (3)
hints: What does it insert into membranes?
questions.solution:
ADH binds to receptors on cells of the collecting duct [B1]
More aquaporins are inserted into the cell membranes [B1]
More water is reabsorbed by osmosis into the medulla / blood, so a smaller volume of concentrated urine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why glucose appears in the urine of a person with untreated diabetes. (3)
questions.solution:
High blood glucose gives high glucose concentration in the filtrate [B1]
Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule by co-transport proteins [B1]
These become saturated, so not all glucose is reabsorbed and some stays in the urine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of glucagon in glycogenolysis. (2)
questions.solution:
Glucagon binds to receptors on liver cells [B1]
Activates enzymes that hydrolyse glycogen to glucose. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe gluconeogenesis. (2)
questions.solution:
Production of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources (e.g. glycerol, amino acids) [B1]
In the liver, stimulated by glucagon. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of insulin in glycogenesis. (2)
questions.solution:
Insulin activates enzymes that convert glucose into glycogen [B1]
In liver and muscle cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how insulin lowers blood glucose concentration. (2)
hints: What does insulin do to glucose transport proteins?
What happens to the glucose taken in?
questions.solution:
Insulin binds to receptors, causing more glucose channel proteins to be inserted into cell membranes, so more glucose is taken up [B1]
Activates enzymes converting glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why people with type II diabetes have high blood glucose even though they produce insulin. (2)
hints: How do their cells respond to insulin?
questions.solution:
Receptors / cells are less responsive to insulin [B1]
So fewer glucose channel proteins inserted / less glucose taken up and converted to glycogen. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how regular exercise helps lower blood glucose in people with type II diabetes. (2)
hints: What do muscles use during exercise?
questions.solution:
Muscles take up and respire more glucose [B1]
Exercise increases the number of glucose transport proteins / insulin sensitivity. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the second messenger model of adrenaline action on liver cells. (3)
questions.solution:
Adrenaline binds to receptors on the cell-surface membrane, activating adenylate cyclase [B1]
Adenylate cyclase converts ATP to cyclic AMP (cAMP) [B1]
cAMP activates protein kinase, which activates enzymes that break down glycogen to glucose. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a drug that blocks glucagon receptors could lower blood glucose. (3)
hints: What can glucagon no longer do?
questions.solution:
Glucagon cannot bind to its receptors on liver cells [B1]
Adenylate cyclase not activated, so less cAMP / protein kinase activity [B1]
Less glycogenolysis / gluconeogenesis, so less glucose released. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a drug that increases the breakdown of cAMP in liver cells would affect blood glucose. (3)
questions.solution:
Less cAMP in liver cells [B1]
Protein kinase less active, so fewer enzymes activated to break down glycogen [B1]
Less glucose released into the blood, so blood glucose falls. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why insulin receptors bind insulin but not glucagon. (2)
hints: What determines the receptor's binding site shape?
Are insulin and glucagon the same shape?
questions.solution:
The receptor's binding site has a specific tertiary structure [B1]
Complementary to insulin only; glucagon has a different shape. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why proteins are not normally found in urine. (2)
questions.solution:
Proteins are too large to pass through the basement membrane / pores of the glomerulus [B1]
So they are not filtered into the Bowman's capsule. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how long-term high blood pressure can cause protein to appear in the urine. (2)
hints: What could high pressure do to glomerular capillaries?
questions.solution:
Damages the glomerular capillaries / basement membrane [B1]
Larger gaps, so proteins can be filtered into the nephron. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why kidney failure leads to a build-up of urea in the blood. (2)
questions.solution:
Less blood is filtered in the glomeruli [B1]
So urea is not removed into the urine. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutation changes an amino acid in the binding site of the insulin receptor. Explain why insulin can no longer bind. (2)
hints: What does the amino acid sequence determine?
What must the binding site be?
questions.solution:
Changes the tertiary structure / shape of the binding site [B1]
Binding site is no longer complementary to insulin. [B1]

questions.prompt: Insulin from pigs differs from human insulin by one amino acid but works in humans. Suggest why. (2)
hints: Is the shape that binds the receptor changed?
questions.solution:
The difference is not in the part that binds the receptor / doesn't change the overall tertiary structure [B1]
So pig insulin is still complementary to human insulin receptors. [B1]

questions.prompt: Insulin binding to its receptor activates a pathway that makes vesicles containing glucose transport proteins fuse with the cell-surface membrane. Explain how a fault in this pathway can cause high blood glucose. (3)
hints: What happens if fewer transport proteins reach the membrane?
questions.solution:
Fewer glucose transport (channel) proteins inserted into the membrane [B1]
So less glucose is taken up by cells (and less converted to glycogen) [B1]
Blood glucose stays high — type II diabetes / insulin resistance. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why obesity is linked with type II diabetes. (3)
hints: What happens to cells' response to insulin?
What happens to β cells over time?
questions.solution:
Obesity is linked to cells becoming less responsive to insulin (insulin resistance) / fewer receptors [B1]
Less glucose taken up from the blood [B1]
β cells may produce less insulin over time, so blood glucose stays high. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why some people with type II diabetes eventually need insulin injections. (3)
hints: What happens to β cells after years of high demand?
questions.solution:
β cells are overworked / damaged over time [B1]
They produce less insulin [B1]
So diet / drugs alone can't control blood glucose and insulin must be given. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule. (3)
hints: How is the sodium gradient maintained?
questions.solution:
Na⁺ actively transported out of the epithelial cells into the blood [B1]
Glucose enters the cells from the filtrate by co-transport with Na⁺ [B1]
Glucose moves into the blood by facilitated diffusion; microvilli give a large surface area. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why people with untreated diabetes produce large volumes of urine. (3)
hints: What does glucose in the filtrate do to its water potential?
questions.solution:
Glucose remains in the filtrate (carriers saturated) [B1]
Lowers the water potential of the filtrate [B1]
Less water reabsorbed by osmosis, so more urine is produced. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the concentration of urea in the filtrate increases as it passes along the nephron. (3)
hints: What is reabsorbed from the filtrate?
questions.solution:
Water is reabsorbed from the filtrate [B1]
Most urea stays in the filtrate [B1]
So urea becomes more concentrated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Rats were fed either a normal diet (group A) or a high-fat diet (group B), then given a low dose of a drug that damages some β cells. The table shows the results (mean ± 2 SD). Group B rats still produced insulin. Evaluate whether group B rats are a good model of human type II diabetes. (5)
hints: Compare blood glucose and mass, using the ranges.
How does this compare with human type II diabetes?
questions.solution:
Group B has significantly higher blood glucose (ranges don't overlap) — hyperglycaemia, like diabetes [B1]
Group B is heavier, and a high-fat diet mirrors obesity / diet as a cause of type II [B1]
Insulin is still produced, as in type II (not type I) [B1]
But the drug damages β cells, which is more like type I / not the cause in humans [B1]
Rats are not humans / short study — long-term complications not tested. [B1]
questions.table:
Group | Mass / g | Blood glucose / mg dm⁻³
A | 220 ± 4 | 130 ± 8
B | 240 ± 6 | 380 ± 10

questions.prompt: In a mouse model of type I diabetes, the immune system destroys β cells. Blood glucose rose from 7 to 28 mmol dm⁻³ and insulin fell to near zero. Evaluate this model for testing new treatments for human type I diabetes. (5)
hints: Does the cause match human type I?
What are the limits of mouse models?
questions.solution:
Autoimmune destruction of β cells matches the cause of human type I [B1]
No insulin and very high glucose, as in untreated type I [B1]
So useful for testing treatments such as β-cell replacement [B1]
But mouse immune systems / metabolism differ from humans [B1]
Results must be confirmed in human trials. [B1]

questions.prompt: Mice fed a high-fat diet for 12 weeks became obese, had high blood glucose and high blood insulin. Evaluate using these mice to test a new drug for type II diabetes. (5)
hints: Do the features match type II?
questions.solution:
High glucose despite high insulin shows insulin resistance, as in type II [B1]
Obesity caused by diet mirrors a major human cause [B1]
Useful for testing drugs that increase insulin sensitivity [B1]
But mice differ from humans (metabolism, lifespan, genetics) [B1]
Need human trials to confirm safety and effectiveness. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why destroying all the β cells in rats makes them a model of type I rather than type II diabetes. (2)
questions.solution:
With no β cells no insulin is produced — this is type I [B1]
In type II insulin is still produced but cells respond poorly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why rats with no β cells could not be used to test a drug that increases cells' sensitivity to insulin. (2)
hints: Is there insulin to respond to?
questions.solution:
No insulin is produced [B1]
So increasing sensitivity to insulin would have no effect. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why damaging α cells as well as β cells would make an animal unsuitable for studying blood glucose control. (2)
questions.solution:
α cells make glucagon [B1]
Without glucagon, blood glucose could not be raised normally, so control would be very different from human diabetes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Where in the body are the osmoreceptors that detect blood water potential? (1)
questions.solution: Hypothalamus. [B1]

questions.prompt: Where is ADH produced? (1)
questions.solution: Hypothalamus. [B1]

questions.prompt: Which part of the nephron does ADH mainly act on? (1)
questions.solution: Collecting duct. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two signs of a person producing too much ADH. (2)
questions.solution:
Small volume of concentrated urine [B1]
Water retention / blood becomes dilute. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two signs or symptoms of dehydration. (2)
questions.solution:
Thirst [B1]
Small volume of dark / concentrated urine / headache / tiredness. [B1]

questions.prompt: People with a condition in which no ADH is produced show two main signs. Suggest what they are. (2)
hints: Without ADH, how much water is reabsorbed?
questions.solution:
Large volumes of dilute urine [B1]
Constant thirst. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the body responds when the water potential of the blood falls. (3)
questions.solution:
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the fall (they lose water) [B1]
More ADH released from the posterior pituitary [B1]
More aquaporins in collecting duct cells, so more water reabsorbed — smaller volume of concentrated urine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how ADH increases the permeability of collecting duct cells to water. (3)
hints: What happens to vesicles containing aquaporins?
questions.solution:
ADH binds to receptors on collecting duct cells [B1]
Activates a second messenger pathway (e.g. cAMP / phosphorylase) [B1]
Vesicles containing aquaporins fuse with the cell-surface membrane, adding water channels. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why drinking a large volume of water leads to production of dilute urine. (3)
hints: What happens to blood water potential?
questions.solution:
Blood water potential rises [B1]
Less ADH released [B1]
Fewer aquaporins, so less water reabsorbed — large volume of dilute urine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain three features of the cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule that allow rapid reabsorption of glucose into the blood. (3)
hints: Look at the membrane facing the lumen.
What provides the energy for co-transport?
questions.solution:
Microvilli give a large surface area [B1]
Many mitochondria provide ATP for active transport (of sodium ions out of the cell) [B1]
Many carrier / co-transport proteins in the membrane. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how glucose is reabsorbed from the filtrate in the proximal convoluted tubule. (3)
hints: Sodium ions are actively pumped first — where to?
What carries glucose in with sodium?
questions.solution:
Sodium ions actively transported out of the epithelial cells into the blood [B1]
This lowers the sodium ion concentration in the cell, so sodium ions diffuse in from the lumen via co-transport proteins, carrying glucose with them [B1]
Glucose then diffuses into the blood by facilitated diffusion. [B1]

questions.prompt: People with untreated diabetes often have glucose in their urine. Explain why. (3)
hints: Is there a limit to reabsorption?
questions.solution:
Blood glucose concentration is high, so more glucose is filtered [B1]
Co-transport proteins in the proximal tubule become saturated / all in use [B1]
So not all glucose is reabsorbed and some stays in the filtrate. [B1]

questions.prompt: ADH binds to receptors on cells in two parts of the nephron. Name these two parts. (1)
hints: Both are near the end of the nephron.
questions.solution: Distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of the brain that detects a fall in the water potential of the blood. (1)
questions.solution: Hypothalamus. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the gland that releases ADH into the blood. (1)
hints: It is attached to the hypothalamus.
questions.solution: Posterior pituitary gland. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest and explain why the receptors for ADH bind only ADH and not other hormones. (2)
hints: What determines the shape of the binding site?
questions.solution:
Receptor has a specific tertiary structure / shape [B1]
Only ADH has a complementary shape to bind to it. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why insulin affects liver and muscle cells but not red blood cells. (2)
hints: What must a cell have to respond to a hormone?
questions.solution:
Only target cells have insulin receptors on their cell-surface membranes [B1]
