Receptors are complementary to insulin; red blood cells lack them, so insulin can't bind. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutation changes the shape of the ADH receptor. Suggest and explain the effect on urine. (2)
questions.solution:
ADH can't bind (not complementary), so fewer aquaporins inserted into the membrane [B1]
Less water reabsorbed, so large volumes of dilute urine are produced. [B1]

questions.prompt: A fall in blood pressure stimulates the release of ADH. Give the location of the receptors that detect the fall in blood pressure, and explain how ADH helps to raise blood pressure. (3)
hints: Pressure receptors are in large arteries.
questions.solution:
Baroreceptors / pressure receptors in the aorta / carotid arteries (carotid sinus) [B1]
ADH makes the distal tubule and collecting duct more permeable to water (more aquaporins) [B1]
More water reabsorbed into the blood, so blood volume and pressure increase. [B1]

questions.prompt: After heavy sweating, a person produces a small volume of concentrated urine. Explain why. (3)
hints: What happens to blood water potential?
What detects it and what is released?
questions.solution:
Water potential of the blood falls, detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus [B1]
More ADH released from the posterior pituitary [B1]
Collecting duct more permeable to water (aquaporins), so more water reabsorbed and less, more concentrated urine. [B1]

questions.prompt: After drinking a large volume of water, a person produces a large volume of dilute urine. Explain how. (3)
questions.solution:
Water potential of the blood rises, detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus [B1]
Less ADH released by the posterior pituitary [B1]
Collecting duct less permeable / fewer aquaporins, so less water reabsorbed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why weight loss can be used to treat type II diabetes but not type I diabetes. (2)
hints: Do type I patients make insulin?
questions.solution:
Type I: no insulin produced (β cells destroyed), so weight loss can't restore it [B1]
Type II: linked to obesity / weight loss makes cells more responsive to insulin (receptors). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference in the cause of type I and type II diabetes. (2)
questions.solution:
Type I: autoimmune destruction of β cells, so insulin not produced [B1]
Type II: cells less responsive to insulin / receptors don't respond, or β cells produce less. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how insulin lowers blood glucose concentration. (2)
hints: What happens to glucose inside the cell?
questions.solution:
Insulin binds to receptors, more glucose channel proteins inserted so more glucose enters cells [B1]
Activates enzymes converting glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis) / increases respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the term for keeping the internal environment of the body within restricted limits. (1)
questions.solution: Homeostasis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the term for a response that brings a factor back towards its normal value. (1)
questions.solution: Negative feedback. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the term for a response that increases a change away from the normal value. (1)
questions.solution: Positive feedback. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a high blood glucose concentration can cause body cells to lose water. Do not refer to ADH or the kidneys. (2)
hints: What does glucose do to water potential?
questions.solution:
High glucose lowers the water potential of the blood / tissue fluid [B1]
Water leaves cells by osmosis down the water potential gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why it is important to keep blood glucose concentration from falling too low. (2)
hints: What do cells use glucose for?
Which organ depends on it most?
questions.solution:
Glucose is the respiratory substrate, so cells (especially brain) can't release enough energy / ATP [B1]
Low glucose raises blood water potential, so cells gain water by osmosis. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which is NOT a result of glucagon binding to liver cells?

Choose one answer.

A  Activation of protein kinase
B  Activation of cyclic AMP hydrolysis
C  Gluconeogenesis
D  Glycogenolysis (1)
hints: cAMP is made, not broken down.
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which is a result of adrenaline binding to receptors on liver cells?

Choose one answer.

A  Activation of adenylate cyclase
B  Glycogenesis
C  Inhibition of protein kinase
D  Uptake of glucose (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which process forms glucose from amino acids and glycerol?

Choose one answer.

A  Glycogenesis
B  Glycogenolysis
C  Gluconeogenesis
D  Glycolysis (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt: Blood pH is controlled as follows: when pH falls, chemoreceptors detect it and the respiratory centre increases breathing rate, removing more carbon dioxide so pH rises again. Use this example to outline the principles of negative feedback. (2)
questions.solution:
Receptors detect a change from the normal level (set point) [B1]
Effectors respond to reverse the change / return to normal. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why having separate mechanisms to raise and to lower a factor (e.g. insulin and glucagon) gives a greater degree of control. (2)
hints: Can one hormone push both ways?
questions.solution:
Each mechanism can actively move the level in one direction [B1]
So a faster response / more precise control, in both directions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between negative and positive feedback, with an example of positive feedback. (2)
questions.solution:
Negative feedback restores the normal level; positive feedback increases the change further [B1]
Example: opening of sodium channels during depolarisation / oxytocin in childbirth. [B1]

questions.prompt: Using the blood pH control system described (chemoreceptors detect falling pH; breathing rate increases to remove CO₂), describe and explain the changes in blood pH and ventilation rate during vigorous exercise. (2)
hints: What does CO₂ do to pH?
questions.solution:
More respiration produces more CO₂ (and lactate), so blood pH falls [B1]
Detected by chemoreceptors, so ventilation rate increases to remove CO₂ and pH returns towards normal. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the location of osmoreceptors in a mammal. (1)
questions.solution: Hypothalamus. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of the nephron where ultrafiltration occurs. (1)
questions.solution: Glomerulus / Bowman's capsule. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of the nephron that creates a low water potential in the medulla. (1)
questions.solution: Loop of Henle. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why osmoreceptor cells decrease in volume when a person is dehydrated. (2)
hints: What happens to blood water potential?
questions.solution:
Water potential of the blood falls / lower than in the cells [B1]
Water leaves the osmoreceptor cells by osmosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why osmoreceptor cells increase in volume after a person drinks a lot of water. (2)
questions.solution:
Blood water potential rises / higher than in the cells [B1]
Water enters the cells by osmosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the loop of Henle creates a low water potential in the medulla. (2)
questions.solution:
Sodium (and chloride) ions actively transported out of the ascending limb into the medulla [B1]
Ascending limb impermeable to water, so medulla has a low water potential. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain how increased ADH secretion affects the urine produced. (4)
questions.solution:
ADH binds to receptors on cells of the distal tubule / collecting duct [B1]
Vesicles containing aquaporins fuse with the membrane, making it more permeable to water [B1]
More water reabsorbed by osmosis into the blood (medulla has low water potential) [B1]
Smaller volume of more concentrated urine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the structure of the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule allows ultrafiltration. (4)
questions.solution:
Afferent arteriole wider than efferent, so high hydrostatic pressure [B1]
Fenestrated capillary endothelium (pores) [B1]
Basement membrane acts as a filter [B1]
Podocytes have gaps so filtrate passes into the capsule; large proteins / cells stay in blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why desert mammals have long loops of Henle. (4)
hints: What does a longer loop do to the medulla?
questions.solution:
Longer ascending limb pumps out more sodium ions [B1]
Lower water potential in the medulla [B1]
More water reabsorbed from the collecting duct by osmosis [B1]
So very concentrated urine, conserving water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Creatinine is a breakdown product of creatine in muscle. Apart from age and sex, give two factors that could affect blood creatinine concentration. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: muscle mass; exercise; diet (meat / creatine supplements); kidney disease; ethnicity. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why kidney failure leads to high blood urea concentration. (1)
questions.solution: Lower glomerular filtration rate, so less urea filtered out of the blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why glucose is not normally found in urine of a healthy person. (1)
questions.solution: All glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (by co-transport). [B1]

questions.prompt: Bone cells release a hormone that stimulates insulin secretion; insulin then stimulates the bone cells to release even more of the hormone. Explain why this is an example of positive feedback. (2)
hints: Does the response reduce or increase the original change?
questions.solution:
The hormone causes more insulin release, which causes more hormone release [B1]
So the change is amplified / increased rather than reversed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the control of blood glucose by insulin and glucagon is an example of negative feedback. (2)
questions.solution:
A rise in glucose causes insulin release, which lowers glucose; a fall causes glucagon release, which raises it [B1]
So the change is reversed and glucose returns to the normal level. [B1]

questions.prompt: During childbirth, contractions of the uterus stimulate release of the hormone oxytocin, which causes stronger contractions. Explain why this is positive feedback and why it doesn't continue indefinitely. (2)
hints: Does each response amplify the stimulus?
questions.solution:
Oxytocin increases contractions, which cause more oxytocin release — the change is amplified [B1]
It stops when the baby is born / stimulus is removed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how insulin binding to a cell increases its rate of respiration. (2)
hints: What does insulin cause to be added to the membrane?
questions.solution:
Insulin binding causes more glucose channel / carrier proteins to be inserted into the membrane [B1]
More glucose enters, so more respiratory substrate available. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how glucagon raises blood glucose using the second messenger model. (2)
questions.solution:
Glucagon binds to receptors, activating adenylate cyclase, which converts ATP to cAMP [B1]
cAMP activates protein kinase, which activates enzymes for glycogenolysis / gluconeogenesis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why muscle cells respond to insulin but not to glucagon. (2)
questions.solution:
Muscle cells have receptors complementary to insulin [B1]
But no glucagon receptors on their cell-surface membranes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how ultrafiltration happens in a glomerulus. (3)
hints: What layers does the filtrate pass through?
questions.solution:
Afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, giving high hydrostatic pressure [B1]
Small molecules (water, glucose, urea, ions) forced out through pores in the capillary endothelium and the basement membrane [B1]
Through gaps between podocytes into the Bowman's capsule; large proteins and blood cells stay in the blood. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule contains no red blood cells or large proteins. (3)
questions.solution:
The basement membrane acts as a filter [B1]
Red blood cells and large proteins are too big to pass through [B1]
So only small molecules are filtered. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a fall in blood pressure reduces the rate of glomerular filtration. (3)
questions.solution:
Filtration is driven by hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus [B1]
Lower blood pressure, lower hydrostatic pressure [B1]
So less fluid forced out into the Bowman's capsule. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which describes how glucose and water are reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule?

Choose one answer.

A  Glucose by osmosis; water by active transport
B  Glucose by co-transport with sodium ions; water by osmosis
C  Both by simple diffusion
D  Glucose by phagocytosis; water by facilitated diffusion (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which describes how sodium ions leave the ascending limb of the loop of Henle?

Choose one answer.

A  Osmosis
B  Simple diffusion
C  Co-transport with glucose
D  Active transport (1)
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which part of the nephron is impermeable to water?

Choose one answer.

A  Proximal convoluted tubule
B  Descending limb of the loop of Henle
C  Ascending limb of the loop of Henle
D  Collecting duct with ADH (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt: Across mammal species, those with a thicker kidney medulla produce more concentrated urine. Explain this pattern. (3)
hints: What does a longer loop do?
questions.solution:
Thicker medulla means longer loops of Henle [B1]
More sodium ions pumped out, giving a lower water potential in the medulla [B1]
More water reabsorbed by osmosis from the collecting duct, so more concentrated urine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Beavers live in water and have short loops of Henle. Explain how this relates to their environment. (3)
hints: Do they need to conserve water?
questions.solution:
Plenty of water available, so no need to conserve water [B1]
Short loop — smaller sodium ion gradient in the medulla [B1]
Less water reabsorbed, so large volumes of dilute urine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the counter-current multiplier in the loop of Henle maintains a water potential gradient in the medulla. (3)
questions.solution:
Sodium ions pumped out of ascending limb into the medulla; ascending limb impermeable to water [B1]
Water leaves the descending limb by osmosis, so filtrate becomes more concentrated going down [B1]
Flow in opposite directions maintains a gradient, lowest water potential at the bottom of the medulla. [B1]

questions.prompt: Use your knowledge of water potential to explain how a high sodium intake could increase blood volume and blood pressure. (3)
hints: Effect of sodium on water potential.
questions.solution:
High sodium lowers the water potential of the blood [B1]
Water moves into the blood from tissue fluid / cells by osmosis (and less water lost in urine) [B1]
Blood volume increases, raising blood pressure. [B1]

questions.prompt: For each part of the nephron — glomerulus, proximal convoluted tubule, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct — state which of these apply: has ADH receptors; water absorbed from filtrate; blood under high pressure; glucose absorbed from filtrate. (2)
hints: ADH acts late in the nephron.
questions.solution:
ADH receptors: DCT and collecting duct; water absorbed: PCT, DCT and collecting duct [B1]
High pressure: glomerulus; glucose absorbed: PCT only. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of the nephron where (i) ultrafiltration happens, and (ii) most glucose is reabsorbed. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Glomerulus / Bowman's capsule [B1]
(ii) Proximal convoluted tubule. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the function of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. (2)
questions.solution:
Reabsorb water by osmosis, controlled by ADH (via aquaporins) [B1]
Adjust ion / pH balance; collecting duct carries urine to the pelvis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why protein is normally absent from urine. (2)
questions.solution:
Proteins are too large to pass through the basement membrane in the glomerulus [B1]
So they aren't filtered (and any small ones are reabsorbed). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why protein in the urine is a sign of kidney damage. (2)
questions.solution:
Damage to the glomerulus / basement membrane [B1]
Lets large protein molecules through into the filtrate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why urea is present in urine but glucose is not. (2)
questions.solution:
Both are small, so both are filtered [B1]
All glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT, but most urea is not. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two treatments for kidney failure and give one advantage and one disadvantage of each. (5)
questions.solution:
Dialysis — blood passes alongside dialysis fluid across a partially permeable membrane, removing urea [B1]
Advantage: available without a donor; disadvantage: time-consuming, frequent sessions, diet restricted [B1]
Transplant — healthy kidney from a donor [B1]
Advantage: long-term / no regular dialysis [B1]
Disadvantage: needs a matching donor / immunosuppressants / risk of rejection. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define allele frequency. (1)
questions.solution: The proportion of a particular allele in a population's gene pool. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term genotype. (2)
questions.solution:
The genetic constitution of an organism [B1]
The alleles it has (for a particular gene). [B1]

questions.prompt: Define homozygous and heterozygous. (2)
questions.solution:
Homozygous: two identical alleles of a gene [B1]
Heterozygous: two different alleles of a gene. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define dominant allele and recessive allele. (2)
hints: Which is expressed in a heterozygote?
When is the recessive one seen?
questions.solution:
Dominant: always expressed in the phenotype, even with only one copy [B1]
Recessive: only expressed when two copies are present (no dominant allele). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of inheritance in which both alleles are expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote. (1)
hints: Think of roan cattle or AB blood group.
questions.solution: Codominance. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of inheritance in which a gene is carried on the X chromosome. (1)
questions.solution: Sex linkage. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of inheritance in which two genes on the same autosome tend to be inherited together. (1)
questions.solution: Autosomal linkage. [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a plant, gene A codes for an enzyme that converts a white precursor into a yellow pigment. Gene B codes for an enzyme that converts the yellow pigment into a red pigment. The recessive alleles a and b code for non-functional enzymes.

Give the flower colour of plants with genotypes AAbb and aaBB. (1)
hints: AAbb: can the first step happen? Can the second?
aaBB: is there any yellow pigment for enzyme B to work on?
questions.solution: AAbb yellow; aaBB white. [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a plant, gene A codes for an enzyme that converts a white precursor into a yellow pigment. Gene B codes for an enzyme that converts the yellow pigment into a red pigment. The recessive alleles a and b code for non-functional enzymes.

Give the flower colour of a plant with genotype AaBb, and explain. (1)
hints: Does it have at least one functional allele of each gene?
questions.solution: Red, because it has functional enzymes for both steps. [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a plant, gene A codes for an enzyme that converts a white precursor into a yellow pigment. Gene B codes for an enzyme that converts the yellow pigment into a red pigment. The recessive alleles a and b code for non-functional enzymes.

What is the expected ratio of red : yellow : white offspring from AaBb × AaBb? (1)
questions.solution: 9 red : 3 yellow : 4 white. [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a plant, gene A codes for an enzyme that converts a white precursor into a yellow pigment. Gene B codes for an enzyme that converts the yellow pigment into a red pigment. The recessive alleles a and b code for non-functional enzymes.

The genes are not linked. Give the genotypes, phenotypes and ratio of offspring from the cross aabb × AaBb. (3)
hints: The aabb parent only makes ab gametes.
The AaBb parent makes four types of gamete.
questions.solution:
Gametes: ab × AB, Ab, aB, ab [B1]
Offspring: AaBb red, Aabb yellow, aaBb white, aabb white [B1]
Ratio 1 red : 1 yellow : 2 white. [B1]

questions.prompt: In peas, round seed (R) is dominant to wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) is dominant to green (y). The genes are not linked. Give the genotypes, phenotypes and ratio of offspring from RrYy × rryy. (3)
hints: List the gametes from each parent.
questions.solution:
Gametes: RY, Ry, rY, ry × ry [B1]
RrYy round yellow; Rryy round green; rrYy wrinkled yellow; rryy wrinkled green [B1]
Ratio 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. [B1]

questions.prompt: Using the pea alleles R (round) / r (wrinkled) and Y (yellow) / y (green), give the expected phenotypes and ratio from RrYy × Rryy. (3)
hints: Do the genes one at a time: Rr × Rr and Yy × yy.
questions.solution:
Rr × Rr gives 3 round : 1 wrinkled; Yy × yy gives 1 yellow : 1 green [B1]
Combine the ratios [B1]
3 round yellow : 3 round green : 1 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green. [B1]

questions.prompt: DNA from 120 people was tested, giving 240 copies of the gene. Thirty mutant alleles were found, but only 29 people carried the mutation. Suggest an explanation. (2)
hints: How many copies of each gene does a person have?
How could 30 alleles be in 29 people?
questions.solution:
Each person is diploid, so has two copies — 240 alleles from 120 people [B1]
One person is homozygous (has two mutant alleles). [B1]

questions.prompt: Fifty people were tested, giving 100 alleles. Ten mutant alleles were found in ten different people. What does this suggest about their genotypes? Explain. (2)
hints: How many mutant alleles does each carrier have?
questions.solution:
Each person has two alleles, so 100 from 50 people [B1]
Each carrier has one mutant allele, so all ten are heterozygous. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why the numbers of offspring in a monohybrid cross may differ from the expected 3 : 1 ratio. (2)
questions.solution:
Fertilisation of gametes is random (chance) [B1]
Small sample size / some offspring die before being counted / lethal genotypes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a large number of offspring gives results closer to the expected ratio. (2)
hints: What is the role of chance?
questions.solution:
Fertilisation involves chance [B1]
Larger samples reduce the effect of chance on the ratio. [B1]

questions.prompt: A dihybrid cross gave far more offspring with the parental combinations of characteristics than a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio predicts. Suggest an explanation. (2)
questions.solution:
The genes are linked (on the same chromosome) [B1]
So alleles are inherited together unless crossing over separates them. [B1]

questions.prompt: In peas, tall (T) is dominant to dwarf (t) and round (R) is dominant to wrinkled (r). Give the genotype of a dwarf plant with wrinkled seeds. (1)
hints: Two recessive alleles of each gene.
questions.solution: ttrr. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a test cross, what genotype must the other parent have? (1)
hints: It must not hide any alleles.
questions.solution: Homozygous recessive (e.g. aabb). [B1]

questions.prompt: A fruit fly is heterozygous for grey body (G) and normal wings (N), with alleles G and N on one chromosome and g and n on its homologue. Write its genotype to show the linkage. (1)
hints: Show alleles on the same chromosome together.
questions.solution: GN/gn. [B1]

questions.prompt: A plant with genotype AaBb (alleles A and B on one chromosome, a and b on its homologue) was crossed with aabb. The offspring were: AB phenotype 420, ab 410, Ab 85, aB 85. Explain these results. (3)
hints: Where do the less common classes come from?
questions.solution:
Genes are linked (on the same chromosome) [B1]
Parental combinations (AB and ab) are most common because alleles are inherited together [B1]
Recombinant classes (Ab and aB) come from crossing over between the loci in prophase I — few because the loci are close. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why genes that are linked do not show independent segregation. (3)
questions.solution:
Linked genes are on the same chromosome [B1]
So their alleles move together into gametes in meiosis [B1]
They are only separated if crossing over occurs between them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why genes that are far apart on a chromosome produce more recombinant offspring than genes close together. (3)
hints: What is the chance of a chiasma between two loci?
questions.solution:
Crossing over occurs at chiasmata, which can form anywhere along the chromosome [B1]
The further apart the loci, the more likely a chiasma forms between them [B1]
So more recombinant gametes and offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: If the genes in a cross AaBb × aabb were on different chromosome pairs, what ratio of phenotypes would be expected, and how many of each in 1000 offspring? (2)
hints: Four gamete types in equal proportions.

questions.prompt: For a cross AaBb × AaBb with unlinked genes, give the expected phenotype ratio and the expected numbers out of 160 offspring. (2)
For a cross AaBb × aaBb with unlinked genes, give the expected phenotype ratio. (2)
questions.solution:
A_B_ : A_bb : aaB_ : aabb [B1]
3 : 1 : 3 : 1. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why haemophilia, a recessive X-linked condition, is more common in males than females. (2)
hints: How many X chromosomes does a male have?
What does a female need to show the condition?
questions.solution:
Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed [B1]
Females need two recessive alleles (one on each X). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a son cannot inherit an X-linked condition from his father. (2)
hints: Which sex chromosome does a father pass to his son?
Where does the son's X come from?
questions.solution:
A father passes his Y chromosome to his son [B1]
The son's X chromosome comes from his mother. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a woman who is a carrier for an X-linked condition has a 50% chance of passing the allele to each child. (2)
hints: How many X chromosomes does she have?
What fraction of her eggs carry the allele?
questions.solution:
She is heterozygous (one X with the allele, one without) [B1]
Half her eggs carry the allele (meiosis), so each child has a 50% chance. [B1]

questions.prompt: In fruit flies, grey body (G) is dominant to black (g) and red eyes (Xᴿ) are dominant to white (Xʳ), with eye colour sex-linked. Give the genotype of a black-bodied, white-eyed male. (1)
hints: Males have one X and a Y.
questions.solution: gg XʳY. [B1]

questions.prompt: Using G/g for body colour and Xᴿ/Xʳ for eye colour, give the genotype of a female heterozygous for both genes. (1)
hints: One of each allele for body colour.
questions.solution: Gg XᴿXʳ. [B1]

questions.prompt: Using G/g for body colour and Xᴿ/Xʳ for eye colour, give the genotype of a black-bodied female homozygous for red eyes. (1)
questions.solution: gg XᴿXᴿ. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two tall pea plants produce some dwarf offspring. What does this show about the tall allele? (1)
hints: Where did the dwarf allele come from?
It was hidden in the parents.
questions.solution: Tall is dominant (both parents are heterozygous). [B1]

questions.prompt: Two affected parents have an unaffected child. What does this show about the condition? (1)
hints: Could two recessive homozygotes have an unaffected child?
Parents must carry a hidden allele.
questions.solution: The condition is dominant (both parents are heterozygous). [B1]

questions.prompt: Two unaffected parents have an affected child. What does this show about the condition? (1)
hints: Where did the child's alleles come from?
questions.solution: The condition is recessive (both parents are carriers). [B1]

questions.prompt: A female with a recessive phenotype has a son with the dominant phenotype. Explain why the gene cannot be on the X chromosome. (2)
hints: Where does a son get his X chromosome?
What would the mother's X carry?
questions.solution:
A son's only X chromosome comes from his mother [B1]
If X-linked, she has two recessive alleles, so her son would have the recessive phenotype. [B1]

questions.prompt: A father with a condition passes it to his son. Explain why the gene cannot be on the X chromosome. (2)
hints: Which chromosome does a father pass to his son?
Where does the son's X come from?
questions.solution:
A father passes his Y chromosome, not his X, to his son [B1]
So the son did not inherit an X-linked allele from his father. [B1]

questions.prompt: A woman has an X-linked recessive condition. Explain why her father must also have the condition. (2)
hints: How many recessive alleles does she need?
Where does one of her X chromosomes come from?
questions.solution:
She must have two recessive alleles, one on each X chromosome [B1]
One X came from her father, whose only X carries the allele, so he is affected. [B1]

questions.prompt: In fruit flies, grey body (G) is dominant to black (g) and red eyes (Xᴿ) are dominant to white (Xʳ). A grey, red-eyed female heterozygous for both genes (Gg XᴿXʳ) is crossed with a black, white-eyed male (gg XʳY). Give the offspring phenotypes and their ratio (ignoring sex). (3)
hints: Gg × gg gives 1 : 1; XᴿXʳ × XʳY gives 1 red : 1 white.
questions.solution:
Body: 1 grey : 1 black; eyes: 1 red : 1 white [B1]
Phenotypes: grey red, grey white, black red, black white [B1]
Ratio 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. [B1]

questions.prompt: A woman who carries haemophilia (XᴴXʰ) has children with an unaffected man (XᴴY). Give the genotypes and phenotypes of the possible children and the expected ratio. (3)
hints: Sons get their X from their mother.
questions.solution:
Gametes: Xᴴ, Xʰ and Xᴴ, Y [B1]
XᴴXᴴ unaffected female; XᴴXʰ carrier female; XᴴY unaffected male; XʰY affected male [B1]
1 : 1 : 1 : 1. [B1]

questions.prompt: A colour-blind man (XᵇY) has children with a woman homozygous for normal vision (XᴮXᴮ). Give the genotypes and phenotypes of their children. (3)
questions.solution:
Gametes: Xᵇ, Y and Xᴮ [B1]
Daughters XᴮXᵇ — normal vision but carriers [B1]
Sons XᴮY — normal vision (none affected). [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two causes of variation in phenotype within a species other than mutation. (2)
questions.solution:
Genetic: crossing over / independent segregation / random fertilisation [B1]
Environmental factors, e.g. diet, climate, light. [B1]

questions.prompt: People with blood group AB have both A and B antigens on their red blood cells. Name the relationship between the Iᴬ and Iᴮ alleles. (1)
questions.solution: Codominance. [B1]

questions.prompt: In snapdragons, a red-flowered plant crossed with a white-flowered plant produces pink offspring. Name this relationship between the alleles. (1)
questions.solution: Codominance. [B1]

questions.prompt: What is the term for an allele whose effect is always seen in the phenotype when present? (1)
questions.solution: Dominant. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a plant, tall (T) is dominant to dwarf (t). Flower colour alleles Cᴿ (red) and Cᵂ (white) are codominant (CᴿCᵂ = pink). A tall, pink plant (TtCᴿCᵂ) is crossed with a dwarf, red plant (ttCᴿCᴿ). Give the offspring genotypes, phenotypes and ratio. (3)
questions.solution:
Gametes: TCᴿ, TCᵂ, tCᴿ, tCᵂ × tCᴿ [B1]
TtCᴿCᴿ tall red; TtCᴿCᵂ tall pink; ttCᴿCᴿ dwarf red; ttCᴿCᵂ dwarf pink [B1]
1 : 1 : 1 : 1. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two pink snapdragons (CᴿCᵂ) are crossed. Give the offspring genotypes, phenotypes and ratio. (3)
hints: Each parent makes Cᴿ and Cᵂ gametes.
questions.solution:
Gametes: Cᴿ, Cᵂ from each parent [B1]
CᴿCᴿ red, CᴿCᵂ pink, CᵂCᵂ white [B1]
1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. [B1]

questions.prompt: Using T (tall) / t (dwarf) and codominant Cᴿ (red) / Cᵂ (white), give the expected phenotype ratio from TtCᴿCᵂ × TtCᴿCᵂ. (3)
questions.solution:
Height 3 tall : 1 dwarf; colour 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white [B1]
Multiply the ratios [B1]
3 tall red : 6 tall pink : 3 tall white : 1 dwarf red : 2 dwarf pink : 1 dwarf white. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Where is a gene for a trait found only in males located?

Choose one answer.

A  Homologous region of the X chromosome
B  Non-homologous region of the Y chromosome
C  Non-homologous region of the X chromosome
D  An autosome (1)
hints: Which chromosome do only males have?
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which statement about an X-linked gene in a male is correct?

Choose one answer.

A  He has two copies of the gene
B  The gene is also found on his Y chromosome
C  He has only one copy, so a recessive allele is expressed
D  He passes it to all his sons (1)
hints: How many X chromosomes does a male have?
Is there a matching allele on the Y?
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
An X-linked mutation in a male is most likely to be on which part of the X chromosome?

Choose one answer.

A  Homologous region of the Y
B  Non-homologous region of the Y
C  Homologous region of the X
D  Non-homologous region of the X (1)
hints: Sex-linked genes have no partner on the Y.
Which region is unique to the X?
questions.solution: D [B1]

questions.prompt: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. Explain why it almost only affects boys. (2)
hints: How many X chromosomes do boys have?
questions.solution:
Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed [B1]
Females need two recessive alleles; usually have a normal allele that masks it. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a female can be a carrier of an X-linked recessive condition but a male cannot. (2)
hints: How many alleles does each sex have?
questions.solution:
Females have two X chromosomes, so can have one recessive and one dominant allele [B1]
Males have only one X — if they have the recessive allele they are affected. [B1]

questions.prompt: In cats, alleles for black and ginger fur are codominant and on the X chromosome. Tortoiseshell cats show both colours. Explain why tortoiseshell cats are almost always female. (2)
hints: How many X chromosomes are needed to carry both alleles?
questions.solution:
Tortoiseshell needs both alleles, one on each of two X chromosomes [B1]
Males have only one X, so can only carry one of the alleles. [B1]

questions.prompt:
In fruit flies, red eyes (Xᴿ) are dominant to white (Xʳ). A carrier female (XᴿXʳ) is crossed with a white-eyed male (XʳY). Which statement is correct?

Choose one answer.

A  All daughters have red eyes
B  Half the daughters and half the sons have white eyes
C  All sons have white eyes
D  No offspring have white eyes (1)
hints: Daughters get one X from each parent.
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
A homozygous red-eyed female fruit fly (XᴿXᴿ) is crossed with a white-eyed male (XʳY). Which statement is correct?

Choose one answer.

A  All offspring have red eyes
B  All sons have white eyes
C  Half the daughters have white eyes
D  All daughters have white eyes (1)
hints: What X can each daughter get from her mother?
Sons get their X from the mother.
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
A colour-blind woman (XᵇXᵇ) has children with a man with normal vision (XᴮY). Which statement is correct?

Choose one answer.

A  All children have normal vision
B  All daughters are colour-blind
C  All sons are colour-blind and all daughters are carriers
D  Half the sons are colour-blind (1)
hints: Sons get their X from their mother.
Daughters get one X from each parent.
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt: A fly heterozygous for grey body and long wings (with G and L on the same chromosome) was crossed with a black, short-winged fly (ggll). The offspring were: grey long 400; black short 390; grey short 5; black long 5. Explain these results. (3)
hints: Where do the rare classes come from?
questions.solution:
Genes are linked (on the same chromosome) [B1]
Parental combinations (grey long and black short) are most common because the alleles are inherited together [B1]
A few recombinants (grey short, black long) result from crossing over between the loci in meiosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: A cross between a fly heterozygous for two genes and a double homozygous recessive fly gave four phenotypes in a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio. Explain these results. (3)
hints: What ratio does a test cross of unlinked genes give?
How many gamete types does the heterozygote make?
questions.solution:
Genes are on different chromosomes (not linked) [B1]
Independent segregation in meiosis gives four types of gamete in equal numbers [B1]
Each fuses with the single gamete type from the recessive parent, giving a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio. [B1]

questions.prompt: A cross between a fly heterozygous for two genes and a double homozygous recessive fly produced only the two parental phenotypes, in equal numbers. Explain these results. (3)
questions.solution:
Genes are linked [B1]
So alleles are inherited together [B1]
Loci very close together, so no crossing over occurred between them (no recombinants). [B1]

questions.prompt: A woman with blood group O and a man with blood group AB have children. Give the possible genotypes of their children. (1)
questions.solution: IᴬIᴼ and IᴮIᴼ. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two parents with blood group A have a child with blood group O. Give the genotypes of the parents. (1)
questions.solution: Both IᴬIᴼ. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mother with blood group B and a father with blood group A have one child with group AB and one with group O. Give the parents' genotypes. (1)
hints: The O child needs an Iᴼ from each parent.
questions.solution: Mother IᴮIᴼ, father IᴬIᴼ. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two Rhesus-positive parents have a Rhesus-negative child. Explain what this shows about the Rhesus-positive allele. (2)
hints: Where did the child's alleles come from?
questions.solution:
Both parents must carry the negative allele (heterozygous) but show the positive phenotype [B1]
So the Rhesus-positive allele is dominant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why two Rhesus-negative parents can only have Rhesus-negative children. (2)
hints: What alleles can they pass on?
questions.solution:
Rhesus-negative is recessive, so both parents are homozygous recessive [B1]
They can only pass on the negative allele. [B1]

questions.prompt: A homozygous Rhesus-positive parent has children with a Rhesus-negative parent. Give the genotypes and phenotypes of their children. (2)
hints: What does each parent pass on?
questions.solution:
All children are Rr (heterozygous) [B1]
All are Rhesus-positive. [B1]

questions.prompt: Parents have genotypes IᴬIᴮ Rr and IᴼIᴼ Rr (R = Rhesus-positive, dominant). Calculate the probability that their next child is a daughter with blood group A who is Rhesus-positive. (2)
Two heterozygous Rhesus-positive parents (Rr × Rr) plan two children. Calculate the probability that both are Rhesus-negative. (2)
Parents have blood groups IᴬIᴼ and IᴮIᴼ. Calculate the probability that their next child is a son with blood group O. (2)

In cats, a gene on the X chromosome controls fur colour. A separate gene has a dominant allele F that prevents any pigment forming, giving white fur. Name this type of interaction between two genes. (1)
questions.solution: Epistasis. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a plant, flower colour depends on two genes. If the plant is homozygous recessive for gene A, the flowers are white whatever alleles of gene B are present. Name this type of gene interaction. (1)
questions.solution: (Recessive) epistasis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two alleles of a gene are both expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote. Name this type of inheritance. (1)
questions.solution: Codominance. [B1]

questions.prompt: The X-linked fur colour alleles Xᴳ (ginger) and Xᴮ (black) are codominant. The dominant allele F gives white fur. State the phenotype of a cat with the genotype XᴳXᴮff. (1)
hints: Does the cat have an F allele?
What do the two colour alleles together produce?
questions.solution: Tortoiseshell — patches of ginger and black, female. [B1]

questions.prompt: Using the same alleles (Xᴳ ginger, Xᴮ black, codominant; F dominant, gives white), state the phenotype of a cat with genotype XᴮY Ff. (1)
questions.solution: White (male). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why male cats are almost never tortoiseshell (ginger and black patches). (1)
hints: How many X chromosomes does a male have?
questions.solution: Males have only one X chromosome, so they can't carry both Xᴳ and Xᴮ. [B1]

questions.prompt: Using Xᴳ (ginger) and Xᴮ (black), codominant and X-linked, and F (white, dominant and epistatic) and f, give the genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring of the cross XᴮXᴮFf × XᴳYff, and the expected phenotype ratio. (3)
hints: Gametes: mother XᴮF, Xᴮf; father Xᴳf, Yf.
questions.solution:
Offspring genotypes: XᴮXᴳFf, XᴮXᴳff, XᴮYFf, XᴮYff [B1]
Phenotypes: white female, tortoiseshell female, white male, black male [B1]
Ratio 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 — i.e. 2 white : 1 tortoiseshell : 1 black. [B1]

questions.prompt: Using the same alleles, give the genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring of the cross XᴳXᴮff × XᴳYff, and the expected phenotype ratio. (3)
questions.solution:
Offspring genotypes: XᴳXᴳff, XᴳXᴮff, XᴳYff, XᴮYff [B1]
Phenotypes: ginger female, tortoiseshell female, ginger male, black male [B1]
Ratio 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. [B1]

questions.prompt: Using the same alleles, give the phenotypes of the offspring of the cross XᴳXᴮFf × XᴮYff, and the expected phenotype ratio. (3)
hints: Mother makes four types of gamete; father makes two.
Any offspring with F is white.
questions.solution:
Females: XᴳXᴮFf white, XᴳXᴮff tortoiseshell, XᴮXᴮFf white, XᴮXᴮff black [B1]
Males: XᴳYFf white, XᴳYff ginger, XᴮYFf white, XᴮYff black [B1]
Ratio 4 white : 2 black : 1 tortoiseshell : 1 ginger. [B1]

questions.prompt: In fruit flies, grey body (G) is dominant to black body (g). Explain how you could find out whether a grey-bodied fly is homozygous or heterozygous. (2)
hints: What fly would you cross it with?
questions.solution:
Cross with a black-bodied fly (gg) — a test cross [B1]
If any black offspring, it is heterozygous (Gg); if all grey (large sample), homozygous (GG). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a test cross uses a homozygous recessive organism. (2)
hints: What alleles does it pass on?
Can it hide the other parent's alleles?
questions.solution:
It only gives recessive alleles [B1]
So offspring phenotypes show which alleles the unknown parent passed on. [B1]

questions.prompt: A grey fly crossed with a black fly gave 48 grey and 52 black offspring. Explain what this shows about the grey parent. (2)
hints: Which parent gave the g alleles to black offspring?
questions.solution:
Black offspring are gg, so the grey parent must have passed on g [B1]
Grey parent is heterozygous Gg — the 1:1 ratio is as expected. [B1]

questions.prompt: A grey-bodied male fruit fly was crossed with a black-bodied female, and some of the female offspring were black-bodied. Explain how this shows the body-colour gene is not on the X chromosome. (1)
hints: If X-linked, which X do daughters get from the father?
questions.solution: If X-linked, all daughters would get the father's dominant Xᴳ and be grey, so black daughters show it isn't sex-linked. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why X-linked recessive conditions are more common in males than females. (1)
hints: How many X chromosomes do males have?
questions.solution: Males have one X chromosome (no allele on Y), so a single recessive allele is expressed. [B1]

questions.prompt: In fruit flies, white eye is X-linked recessive. A white-eyed female is crossed with a red-eyed male. Predict the eye colour of their sons. (1)
questions.solution: All sons white-eyed (they inherit Xʳ from the mother). [B1]

questions.prompt: In fruit flies, curly wings (R) is dominant to straight wings (r); RR is lethal in the embryo. Grey body (G) is dominant to black (g). Give the genotypes and phenotypes, and the ratio, of adult offspring from RrGg × Rrgg. (3)
hints: Wings: 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr, but RR dies.
questions.solution:
Surviving wing genotypes Rr : rr = 2 : 1; body Gg : gg = 1 : 1 [B1]
Phenotypes: curly grey (RrGg), curly black (Rrgg), straight grey (rrGg), straight black (rrgg) [B1]
Ratio 2 : 2 : 1 : 1. [B1]

questions.prompt: Using the same alleles (RR lethal), give the phenotypes and ratio of the adult offspring from RrGg × rrGg. (3)
questions.solution:
Wings Rr : rr = 1 : 1; body grey : black = 3 : 1 [B1]
Phenotypes: curly grey, curly black, straight grey, straight black [B1]
Ratio 3 : 1 : 3 : 1. [B1]

questions.prompt: Using the same alleles (RR lethal), give the genotypes, phenotypes and ratio of adult offspring from Rrgg × Rrgg. (3)
questions.solution:
Genotypes Rrgg and rrgg (RRgg die) [B1]
Curly black and straight black [B1]
Ratio 2 : 1. [B1]

questions.prompt: An autosomal recessive condition affects a family. Both parents are heterozygous. Calculate the probability that their next child will be a son with the condition. (1)
One parent is heterozygous for an autosomal recessive condition and the other is homozygous recessive. Calculate the probability that their next child is a son with the condition. (1)
Two parents are both heterozygous for an autosomal recessive condition. Calculate the probability that their first two children will both be affected. (1)
Explain what is meant by the term phenotype. (2)
questions.solution:
The observable characteristics of an organism [B1]
Result of interaction between the genotype and the environment. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the meanings of the terms genotype and allele. (2)
hints: One is a version of a gene.
questions.solution:
Genotype — the genetic constitution of an organism / alleles it has [B1]
Allele — a different version of a gene. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the meanings of the terms homozygous and heterozygous. (2)
questions.solution:
Homozygous — two identical alleles of a gene [B1]
Heterozygous — two different alleles of a gene. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons why the observed ratio of offspring phenotypes in a genetic cross may differ from the expected ratio. Do not refer to linkage. (2)
questions.solution:
Fertilisation of gametes is random / small sample size [B1]
Some genotypes may be lethal / die before counting; or epistasis. [B1]

questions.prompt: A dihybrid cross gives a 9 : 3 : 4 ratio instead of 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. Suggest an explanation. (2)
questions.solution:
Epistasis [B1]
One gene masks the expression of the other, so two classes have the same phenotype (3 + 1 = 4). [B1]

questions.prompt: A plant heterozygous for flower colour (purple dominant) and pollen shape (long dominant) was crossed with a red, round-pollen plant. The table shows the offspring. Explain the results. Include what autosomal linkage means and comment on the proportions of gametes. (3)
hints: Are the four classes in a 1:1:1:1 ratio?
questions.solution:
Genes are linked — on the same autosome (not sex chromosome) [B1]
So parental combinations of alleles are inherited together, giving mostly purple long and red round [B1]
Few recombinant gametes formed by crossing over, giving the small purple round and red long classes. [B1]
questions.table:

Red, round | 47.5
Purple, round | 2.1
Red, long | 1.8

questions.prompt: In a test cross of a fly heterozygous for body colour and wing shape, the results in the table were obtained. Explain what they show about the genes. (3)
questions.solution:
Genes are autosomally linked / on the same chromosome [B1]
Grey normal and black vestigial are the parental combinations, so most common [B1]
Grey vestigial and black normal are recombinants from crossing over, so fewer (18%). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why two linked genes that are far apart on a chromosome show more recombinant offspring than two genes close together. (3)
hints: Is it more likely between distant loci?
questions.solution:
Crossing over occurs at chiasmata at random points along chromatids [B1]
More likely to occur between loci far apart [B1]
So more recombinant gametes / offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two genes in fruit flies, for body colour and wing length, are linked. Explain what this means. (1)
questions.solution: The genes are on the same chromosome (autosome). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together. (1)
questions.solution: They stay together on one chromosome during meiosis unless separated by crossing over. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a sex-linked gene. (1)
questions.solution: A gene carried on a sex chromosome (usually the X). [B1]

questions.prompt: Flies homozygous for grey body and long wings were crossed with flies homozygous for black body and short wings; all offspring were grey with long wings (GgNn). These were test-crossed with black, short-winged flies. Use your knowledge of linkage to explain the results in the table. (4)
hints: Which combinations were in the original parents?
Where do the small classes come from?
questions.solution:
G and N are on one chromosome, g and n on the homologous chromosome (linked) [B1]
So most gametes from GgNn are GN or gn, giving many grey long and black short (parental types) [B1]
Crossing over during meiosis produces some Gn and gN gametes [B1]
Giving fewer grey short and black long (recombinants). [B1]

questions.prompt: In a plant, tall (T) and round seed (R) are dominant. A TtRr plant made from TTRR × ttrr parents was test-crossed with ttrr. Explain the results in the table. (4)
questions.solution:
Genes are linked: T with R and t with r on the same chromosomes [B1]
Most gametes are TR or tr, so tall round and short wrinkled are most common [B1]
Crossing over between the loci gives Tr and tR gametes [B1]
So a few tall wrinkled and short round offspring. [B1]
questions.table:

questions.prompt: A test cross of a heterozygous fly gave 450 grey normal, 440 black vestigial, 55 grey vestigial and 55 black normal. Calculate the percentage of recombinant offspring and explain what this shows. (4)
questions.solution:
Recombinants = 110 out of 1000 [B1]
= 11% [B1]
Genes are linked (far below the 50% expected if unlinked) [B1]
Recombinants formed by crossing over — low % suggests the genes are close together. [B1]

questions.prompt: State the ratio of phenotypes expected from a test cross of GgNn × ggnn if the two genes were NOT linked. (1)
State the ratio of phenotypes expected from a cross of GgNn × GgNn if the two genes were not linked. (1)
