Mitochondria are inherited only from the mother. Some forms of a muscle disease are caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA; others by recessive alleles in nuclear DNA. In couple A, the mother has the disease and all their children have it. In couple B, neither parent has the disease but one of their four children does. Explain these results. (4)
hints: What does every child get from the mother?
How can unaffected parents have an affected child?
questions.solution:
Couple A: mitochondrial mutation in the mother [B1]
All children inherit mitochondria (and mtDNA) from the mother's egg, so all affected [B1]
Couple B: nuclear recessive allele — both parents heterozygous carriers [B1]
Each child has a 1 in 4 chance of being homozygous recessive. [B1]

questions.prompt: A father has a disease caused by a mitochondrial DNA mutation. The mother does not. Explain whether their children are likely to inherit the disease. (4)
hints: Where do the zygote's mitochondria come from?
questions.solution:
Mitochondria in the zygote come from the egg (mother) [B1]
Sperm mitochondria don't enter / are destroyed [B1]
So children inherit the mother's mtDNA [B1]
Children won't inherit the disease. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a woman with a mitochondrial DNA mutation might have children with different severities of disease. (4)
hints: Does every mitochondrion carry the mutation?
questions.solution:
Cells contain many mitochondria, some normal, some mutant [B1]
Proportion of mutant mitochondria varies between eggs [B1]
Random distribution when cells divide [B1]
Higher proportion of mutant mitochondria means more severe disease. [B1]

questions.prompt: A woman's egg contains about 3 × 10⁵ mitochondria, many of them faulty. Scientists suggest replacing a healthy donor egg's nucleus with the woman's nucleus. Suggest how this prevents inheritance of the mitochondrial disease. (2)
questions.solution:
Mitochondria are inherited only from the egg cytoplasm [B1]
The child gets the woman's nuclear DNA but the donor's healthy mitochondria. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a disease caused by a mitochondrial DNA mutation shows a different inheritance pattern from a disease caused by a nuclear gene. (2)
hints: Where do the zygote's mitochondria come from?
questions.solution:
Mitochondria inherited only from the mother (egg cytoplasm) [B1]
So all children of an affected mother may be affected, none of an affected father — no Mendelian ratios. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why heterozygous squirrels with codominant alleles for fur colour have brown-black fur. (3)
questions.solution:
Codominant alleles are both expressed [B1]
Some receptors are normal and some are permanently active [B1]
So a mixture of pigments gives an intermediate colour. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a polygenic characteristic and give an example. (2)
questions.solution:
Controlled by many genes (at different loci) [B1]
Shows continuous variation, e.g. height / skin colour. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the lag, log and stationary phases of a bacterial growth curve. (3)
hints: Why is growth slow at first?
questions.solution:
Lag: bacteria adjust to conditions / make enzymes, so little division [B1]
Log: rapid binary fission — numbers double each generation, resources plentiful [B1]
Stationary: nutrients run out / waste builds up, so division rate equals death rate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how releasing large numbers of sterile male insects can reduce a pest population. (2)
hints: Who do wild females mate with?
questions.solution:
Wild females mate with sterile males [B1]
No offspring are produced, so the birth rate falls and the population decreases. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why far more sterile males than wild males are released in a sterile insect programme. (2)
hints: What increases the chance they choose a sterile male?
questions.solution:
Increases the probability that females mate with a sterile male [B1]
So fewer fertile matings and fewer offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why only male mosquitoes are released when using sterile insects to control a disease such as dengue. (2)
questions.solution:
Only females bite / transmit the virus [B1]
Releasing females would increase biting and disease transmission. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how mark–release–recapture could be used to estimate the size of a population of woodlice. (3)
hints: How is the first sample treated?
questions.solution:
Capture a sample, count and mark them (harmlessly, inconspicuously) [B1]
Release and allow time to mix with the population, then capture a second sample [B1]
Count marked individuals; population = (number in 1st sample × number in 2nd sample) ÷ number marked in 2nd sample. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a mark–release–recapture study, 60 beetles were marked and released. Later, 50 beetles were caught, of which 12 were marked. Estimate the population size. (3)
Give three assumptions made when using mark–release–recapture. (3)
hints: Think about movement in and out of the area.
questions.solution:
No immigration or emigration [B1]
No (or few) births and deaths between samples [B1]
Marking does not affect survival / chance of being caught [B1]
Marked individuals mix randomly with the population; marks are not lost. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Suggest why insects sterilised using radiation may be less successful at mating than wild males. (1)
questions.solution: Radiation damages other cells, so males are weaker / less competitive / less attractive to females. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why releasing sterile males may fail to control a pest on an island close to the mainland. (1)
hints: Can fertile insects arrive from elsewhere?
questions.solution: Fertile insects migrate in from the mainland. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why sterile males must be released repeatedly rather than once. (1)
hints: How long do released males live?
Are new wild adults still emerging?
questions.solution: Released males die / new wild adults keep emerging from eggs already laid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why control measures continued even after a pest population had fallen to very low numbers. (1)
questions.solution: To stop the population recovering from survivors / immigrants. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a population, 25% of plants show a recessive phenotype. Use the Hardy–Weinberg equations to calculate the percentage of plants that are heterozygous. (2)
In a population, 4% show a recessive phenotype. Calculate the percentage that are heterozygous. (2)
In a population, 64% show the dominant phenotype. Calculate the percentage that are heterozygous. (2)
In a sample of 80 people, 40 of the alleles for a gene were the dominant allele. Explain why there are 160 alleles in total and calculate the frequency of the dominant allele. (2)
questions.solution:
80 diploid people × 2 = 160 alleles [M1]
40 ÷ 160 = 0.25. [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why bacterial population sizes are usually plotted on a logarithmic scale. (1)
hints: Would they fit on a linear axis?
questions.solution: Numbers range over many orders of magnitude. [B1]

questions.prompt: What does a straight line on a graph of log (population) against time show? (1)
questions.solution: Exponential growth / a constant rate of doubling. [B1]

questions.prompt: On a log₁₀ scale, a population increases from 3 to 6. By how many times has the population increased? (1)
hints: Each unit on a log₁₀ scale is ×10.
questions.solution: 1000 times. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one reason for the death phase of a bacterial culture. (1)
questions.solution: Toxic waste products build up / nutrients run out. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a yeast population reaches a stationary phase. (1)
questions.solution: Glucose / nutrients become limiting (or ethanol accumulates), so birth rate equals death rate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why yeast in a sealed flask stops growing even though glucose remains. (1)
questions.solution: Ethanol accumulates to toxic concentrations. [B1]

questions.prompt: 1% of a population has a recessive condition. Use the Hardy–Weinberg equations to calculate the percentage who are heterozygous carriers. (2)
9% of a population has a recessive condition. Calculate the percentage who are carriers. (2)
1 in 2500 people has a recessive condition. Calculate the percentage who are carriers. (2)
91% of a population shows the dominant phenotype. Use the Hardy–Weinberg equations to calculate the percentage that are heterozygous. (2)
75% of a population shows the dominant phenotype. Calculate the percentage that are heterozygous. (2)
51% of a population shows the dominant phenotype. Calculate the percentage that are heterozygous. (2)
Describe how to estimate the population size of daisies in a field. (5)
hints: How do you avoid bias when placing quadrats?
How do you scale up to the whole field?
questions.solution:
Divide the field into a grid and use random numbers to give coordinates [B1]
Place quadrats at the coordinates [B1]
Count the daisies in each quadrat [B1]
Use a large number of quadrats and calculate the mean per quadrat [B1]
Multiply mean per quadrat by (area of field ÷ area of quadrat). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to estimate the number of snails in a garden. (5)
questions.solution:
Capture a sample of snails, count and mark them harmlessly [B1]
Release them and allow time to mix with the population [B1]
Capture a second sample and count marked and unmarked snails [B1]
Population = (number in first sample × number in second sample) ÷ number marked in second sample [B1]
Assume no migration / births / deaths and marks are not lost. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a population of plants with codominant red and white alleles, 16% of plants are red. Use the Hardy–Weinberg equations to calculate the percentage that are pink. (2)
In a population with codominant red and white alleles, 25% of plants are white. Calculate the percentage that are pink. (2)
In a population with codominant red and white alleles, 4% of plants are red. Calculate the percentage that are pink. (2)
Explain how mark–release–recapture estimates population size, and why the formula works. (4)
hints: What proportion of the second sample is marked?
questions.solution:
A first sample is caught, marked and released, then mixes with the population [B1]
A second sample is caught and the number marked counted [B1]
Proportion marked in the second sample is assumed to equal the proportion marked in the whole population [B1]
So population = (first sample × second sample) ÷ number marked in the second sample. [B1]

questions.prompt: 120 fish were caught, marked and released. Later, 150 fish were caught, of which 18 were marked. Estimate the population size and state two assumptions. (4)
hints: What must not change between samples?
questions.solution:
(120 × 150) ÷ 18 [M1]
1000 fish [M1]
Assume no migration / births / deaths between samples [M1]
Marked fish mix randomly and marks are not lost. [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain how breaking each of these assumptions would affect a mark–release–recapture estimate: marks rubbed off; marked animals more likely to be eaten. (4)
hints: How would each change the number of marked animals recaptured?
questions.solution:
Marks rubbed off: fewer marked animals recaptured (counted as unmarked) [B1]
So population is overestimated [B1]
Marked animals eaten more: fewer marked animals left to recapture [B1]
So population is also overestimated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why mark–release–recapture gives unreliable results in a very large lake. (1)
hints: Will marked fish mix through the whole lake?
questions.solution: Marked fish may not mix randomly through the whole population / very few are recaptured. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why mark–release–recapture is not used to estimate the population of a plant species. (1)
questions.solution: Plants don't move / can be counted directly using quadrats. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why mark–release–recapture would be unreliable if the population had many births during the study. (1)
hints: What happens to the proportion of marked animals?
questions.solution: Births add unmarked animals, lowering the proportion marked, so the population is overestimated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one precaution when fitting rings to birds in a mark–release–recapture study. (1)
hints: Could the ring affect the bird?
questions.solution: Ring must not affect the bird's ability to fly / feed / survive. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why marks on snails must be waterproof in a mark–release–recapture study. (1)
questions.solution: So marks are not lost, which would make the population overestimated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why marks used in mark–release–recapture should not be visible to predators. (1)
hints: Would marked animals be eaten more?
questions.solution: Marked animals would be eaten more, so fewer recaptured and population overestimated. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a population, the frequency of allele Iᴬ is 0.25 and Iᴮ is 0.10. What is the frequency of Iᴼ? (1)
For a gene with three alleles, p = 0.3 and r = 0.6. What is q? (1)
The frequency of allele Iᴼ is 0.7. What is the expected frequency of blood group O? (1)
Give two conditions that must be met for the Hardy–Weinberg principle to apply. (2)
questions.solution: Two from: large population; random mating; no mutation; no selection; no migration (immigration / emigration). [B2]

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons why allele frequencies in a small island population do not match Hardy–Weinberg predictions. (2)
hints: What has a big effect in small populations?
questions.solution:
Small population, so genetic drift changes allele frequencies by chance [B1]
Non-random mating / selection / founder effect. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why immigration can make observed blood group frequencies differ from those predicted by the Hardy–Weinberg principle. (2)
questions.solution:
Immigrants bring alleles at different frequencies into the population [B1]
So the assumption of no migration is broken and allele frequencies change. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a population of cats, 51% had white fur because they had at least one F allele. Use the Hardy–Weinberg equation to calculate the frequency of the f allele. (2)
hints: Non-white cats are ff, so q² = 1 − 0.51.

questions.prompt: In a population, 19% of cats had white fur (at least one dominant F allele). Calculate the frequency of the f allele. (2)
In a population, 75% of cats had white fur due to the dominant allele F. Calculate the frequency of the F allele. (2)
In a population of flies, 36% have a grey body (G, dominant). Calculate the percentage of the population that are heterozygous. (2)
In a population of flies, 51% have a grey body (G, dominant). Calculate the percentage that are heterozygous. (2)
In a population of flies, 75% have a grey body (G, dominant). Calculate the percentage that are heterozygous. (2)
In one year, the frequency of an insecticide-resistance allele in a mosquito population was 0.3. Calculate the frequency of heterozygotes. (2)
The frequency of a resistance allele was 0.15. Calculate the frequency of heterozygotes. (2)
The frequency of a resistance allele was 0.6. Calculate the frequency of heterozygotes. (2)
Describe and explain the phases of growth in a bacterial culture in a closed container. (4)
questions.solution:
Lag phase — bacteria adjusting / making enzymes [B1]
Log phase — rapid division as resources are plentiful [B1]
Stationary phase — births equal deaths as nutrients run out / waste builds up [B1]
Death phase — more die than are produced. [B1]

questions.prompt: In squirrels, fur colour is controlled by two codominant alleles: CᴳCᴳ grey, CᴳCᴮ brown-black, CᴮCᴮ black. A population of 50 squirrels contains 2 black squirrels. Use the Hardy–Weinberg equation to estimate the number of brown-black squirrels. (2)
Using the same alleles, a population of 100 squirrels contains 9 black squirrels. Estimate the number of brown-black squirrels. (2)
questions.solution:
q = 0.3, p = 0.7 [M1]
2pq = 0.42, so 42 squirrels. [A1]

questions.prompt: Using the same alleles, a population of 80 squirrels contains 5 black squirrels. Estimate the number of brown-black squirrels. (2)
A population of 50 squirrels has 28 grey (CᴳCᴳ), 20 brown-black (CᴳCᴮ) and 2 black (CᴮCᴮ). Without using Hardy–Weinberg, calculate the actual frequency of the Cᴳ allele. (1)
hints: Count Cᴳ alleles: 2 per grey, 1 per brown-black.

questions.prompt: 100 squirrels: 61 grey (CᴳCᴳ), 30 brown-black (CᴳCᴮ), 9 black (CᴮCᴮ). Calculate the actual frequency of Cᴳ. (1)
80 squirrels: 53 grey, 22 brown-black, 5 black. Calculate the actual frequency of the Cᴳ allele. (1)
In a mouse population, some mice have an autoimmune disease caused by a dominant allele. Would the Hardy–Weinberg principle apply? Explain. (2)
questions.solution:
No (probably not) [B1]
Disease may reduce survival / reproduction, so there's selection against the allele; mating may not be random / small population. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give four conditions needed for the Hardy–Weinberg principle to apply. (2)
questions.solution:
Large population; random mating [B1]
No mutation, no selection, no migration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the Hardy–Weinberg equation can be used to predict the frequency of carriers of a recessive allele. (2)
questions.solution:
Frequency of homozygous recessive (q²) can be counted, so q and p calculated [B1]
Carriers = 2pq, assuming the population is in equilibrium. [B1]

questions.prompt: A birth defect affects 1 in 700 births and has both genetic and environmental causes. Suggest two reasons the Hardy–Weinberg equation can't be used to estimate allele frequencies for it. (2)
questions.solution:
Not caused by a single gene with two alleles — many genes involved [B1]
Environment also affects the phenotype, so frequency of phenotype ≠ q² / selection against it. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two species of frog live in the same pond but breed at different times of year. Explain how this prevents them interbreeding. (2)
hints: What type of isolation is this?
questions.solution:
Temporal / seasonal reproductive isolation [B1]
Gametes are not released at the same time, so no fertilisation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two species of fruit fly have different courtship behaviours. Explain how this prevents them interbreeding. (2)
questions.solution:
Behavioural isolation [B1]
Females do not recognise / respond to the courtship of males of the other species, so they do not mate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a gene mutation can lead to evolution in a population. (4)
hints: What then happens through natural selection?
questions.solution:
Mutation produces a new allele [B1]
New allele may give an advantage [B1]
Individuals with it survive and reproduce more, passing it on [B1]
Allele frequency increases in the population over generations (evolution). [B1]

questions.prompt: Two populations have been separated for 10 000 years but are still the same species. What does this suggest? (1)
hints: Has enough genetic change built up?
questions.solution: Not enough genetic change has occurred for reproductive isolation / speciation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term gene pool. (1)
questions.solution: All the alleles of all the genes in a population. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term speciation. (1)
questions.solution: The formation of a new species from an existing one. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term genetic drift. (1)
questions.solution: A change in allele frequency due to chance (most significant in small populations). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how allopatric speciation occurs. (5)
hints: Why do their gene pools change differently?
questions.solution:
Populations become geographically isolated [B1]
No gene flow between them [B1]
Mutations produce different alleles in each population [B1]
Different selection pressures / environments, so different alleles are selected and allele frequencies change (plus genetic drift) [B1]
Eventually they are reproductively isolated — can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Apple maggot flies originally laid eggs only on hawthorn fruit. Some now lay eggs on apples, which ripen earlier, and mate on the fruit they hatch from. Suggest how sympatric speciation could occur. (5)
hints: How does mating on the host fruit isolate populations?
What does the different ripening time do?
questions.solution:
A mutation led some flies to prefer apples [B1]
Flies mate on their host fruit, and apples ripen earlier, so the two groups rarely meet / mate (reproductive isolation) [B1]
No gene flow between the groups [B1]
Different selection pressures on each host change allele frequencies [B1]
Eventually they cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring — new species. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how polyploidy can lead to the formation of a new plant species in a single generation. (5)
hints: What if chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis?
Could offspring breed with the parent species?
questions.solution:
Non-disjunction of a whole set of chromosomes produces diploid gametes [B1]
Fusion of two diploid gametes gives a tetraploid plant [B1]
Tetraploid crossed with the diploid parent gives triploid offspring [B1]
Triploids are sterile — chromosomes can't pair in meiosis [B1]
So the tetraploid is reproductively isolated: a new species (sympatric speciation). [B1]

questions.prompt: A rare disease allele is common in an isolated island population. Suggest and explain two reasons. (2)
hints: What happens to allele frequencies by chance in small populations?
questions.solution:
Founder effect: the few original settlers happened to carry the allele [B1]
Small population / inbreeding / genetic drift increases its frequency by chance. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how genetic drift can increase the frequency of an allele in a small population. (2)
questions.solution:
Chance events determine which individuals reproduce / which alleles are passed on [B1]
In a small population chance has a large effect on allele frequency. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a genetic bottleneck and how it affects genetic diversity. (2)
questions.solution:
Population is drastically reduced (e.g. by disaster) [B1]
Only the survivors' alleles remain, so genetic diversity is reduced. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a hare population, individuals vary in when they change coat colour. Explain how this variation could help the population survive as snow melts earlier. (4)
questions.solution:
Variation in moult timing is partly genetic (different alleles) [B1]
Hares that moult earlier are camouflaged when snow melts and survive predation [B1]
They reproduce and pass on their alleles [B1]
Frequency of alleles for earlier moulting increases, so the population adapts. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why populations with low genetic diversity are less likely to survive climate change. (4)
questions.solution:
Fewer different alleles in the population [B1]
Less likely that any individuals have alleles suited to new conditions [B1]
Natural selection has little variation to act on [B1]
So the population may not adapt and could become extinct. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how individuals moving between separate populations (gene flow) could help a population adapt to a changing environment. (4)
hints: What can selection then act on?
questions.solution:
Migrants bring new alleles into the population [B1]
Increases genetic diversity [B1]
Some new alleles may be advantageous in the new conditions [B1]
Selection increases their frequency, so the population adapts. [B1]

questions.prompt: In the past, falling water levels divided a large lake into several smaller lakes. Suggest and explain how this could have led to the formation of new fish species. (4)
hints: What happened to gene flow between the lakes?
questions.solution:
Populations became geographically isolated, so no gene flow [B1]
Different mutations / different selection pressures in each lake [B1]
Allele frequencies changed differently (and by genetic drift) [B1]
Eventually reproductively isolated, so new species formed (allopatric speciation). [B1]

questions.prompt: Fish of one species in a lake began feeding in different ways — some on the bottom, some in open water — and mating with fish feeding in the same area. Suggest how this could lead to sympatric speciation. (4)
hints: Do the two groups mate with each other?
What happens to their gene pools?
questions.solution:
Fish mate with those feeding in the same area, so there is reproductive isolation / little gene flow [B1]
Different selection pressures on each feeding group [B1]
Different alleles selected, so allele frequencies diverge [B1]
Eventually they cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: In some fish, females choose mates by their colour. Explain how female preference could lead to the formation of new species. (4)
hints: What happens if some females prefer red males and others blue?
questions.solution:
Females with different preferences mate only with males of a particular colour [B1]
Reproductive (behavioural) isolation between groups [B1]
No gene flow, so allele frequencies change independently [B1]
Eventually the groups become separate species. [B1]

questions.prompt: A large river formed across the range of a lemur species, separating it into two populations. Suggest how this could produce two separate species. (5)
questions.solution:
The river geographically isolates the two populations [B1]
No interbreeding / gene flow between them [B1]
Mutations produce new alleles in each population [B1]
Different selection pressures on each side, so different alleles selected / allele frequencies change (and genetic drift) [B1]
Eventually reproductively isolated — cannot produce fertile offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why species found on remote islands are often found nowhere else. (5)
hints: What happens once they are isolated?
questions.solution:
A few individuals colonised the island (founder effect), so allele frequencies differ from the mainland [B1]
Island population is geographically isolated — no gene flow [B1]
Different selection pressures on the island [B1]
Genetic drift is strong in small populations [B1]
Over time the population becomes a new species (allopatric speciation). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how scientists could find out whether two populations of lemurs are separate species. (5)
hints: What is the definition of a species?
questions.solution:
Test whether they can interbreed / produce fertile offspring [B1]
Compare DNA base sequences / mitochondrial DNA [B1]
Compare amino acid sequences of proteins / immunological tests [B1]
Compare behaviour, e.g. mating calls or courtship [B1]
Compare chromosome numbers / anatomy. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two related species of flower grow in the same mountains. Species A has pink flowers pollinated by bumblebees and grows at 1600–3000 m. Species B has red flowers pollinated by hummingbirds and grows up to 2000 m. Explain how these two species could have evolved from a common ancestor, using this information to justify your answer. (5)
hints: Their altitude ranges overlap — is this allopatric or sympatric?
questions.solution:
Sympatric speciation, because ranges overlap (1600–2000 m) [B1]
Mutation produced variation in flower colour [B1]
Different pollinators prefer different colours, so pollen carried only between similar flowers (reproductive isolation) [B1]
No gene flow between the two groups [B1]
Different alleles selected in each group, changing allele frequencies [B1]
Eventually they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring. [B1]
Any 5 of these points — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: A population of fish lived in a large lake. Falling water levels split the lake into two smaller lakes with different food sources. After many generations the fish in each lake could no longer interbreed. Explain how this happened. (5)
hints: What type of isolation is this?
questions.solution:
Allopatric speciation — populations geographically isolated [B1]
No gene flow between populations [B1]
Mutations produce different variation in each population [B1]
Different selection pressures (food) in each lake, so different alleles give an advantage and are passed on [B1]
Allele frequencies change in each population over many generations [B1]
Eventually they become reproductively isolated / can't produce fertile offspring — separate species. [B1]
Any 5 of these points — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: Two species of fruit fly live on the same trees. One species mates in the morning and the other in the evening. Explain how this difference could have led to the formation of two species from one. (5)
hints: What kind of isolation is different mating time?
questions.solution:
Sympatric speciation — same area [B1]
Mutation caused some flies to mate at a different time [B1]
So the groups became reproductively (temporally) isolated — no gene flow [B1]
Different mutations / selection in each group changed allele frequencies [B1]
Over time genetic differences meant they could no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Pale lizards live on walls and are active at night; dark lizards live on olive tree trunks and are active in the day. Mitochondrial genes show the day-active lizards form a distinct genetic group, but all are still one species. Evaluate the conclusion that disruptive selection is leading to sympatric speciation. (5)
hints: Do they live in the same area?
questions.solution:
Supports: two extreme forms (pale and dark) favoured — disruptive selection [B1]
Same area, so sympatric [B1]
Active at different times / different habitats, so may be reproductively isolated / little gene flow [B1]
Distinct genetic group suggests allele frequencies have diverged [B1]
Against: still one species / can interbreed; colour may be environmental (colour change) not genetic; mitochondrial genes are only inherited maternally / only some genes compared. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the differences between stabilising, directional and disruptive selection, giving an example of each. (5)
questions.solution:
Stabilising: average phenotype favoured, extremes selected against — e.g. human birth mass [B1]
Range narrows, mean stays the same [B1]
Directional: one extreme favoured, mean shifts — e.g. antibiotic resistance [B1]
Disruptive: both extremes favoured over the average [B1]
Can lead to two groups / speciation — e.g. beak sizes with two food types. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two populations of a bird are found on the same island. One feeds on large seeds, the other on small seeds, and they have different beak sizes. Explain how disruptive selection could lead to speciation. (5)
hints: Which beaks are at a disadvantage?
questions.solution:
Variation in beak size due to mutation / different alleles [B1]
Birds with medium beaks less efficient at both food sources, so less likely to survive [B1]
Birds with small and large beaks survive and reproduce, passing on alleles [B1]
Birds may mate only with similar birds, reducing gene flow (reproductive isolation) [B1]
Allele frequencies diverge until they can't interbreed to produce fertile offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how female mate choice could lead to sympatric speciation. (3)
questions.solution:
Females choose mates with particular features, so two groups mate only with each other (reproductive isolation) [B1]
No gene flow between the groups [B1]
Different allele frequencies, until they can no longer interbreed to give fertile offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a mutation causing a difference in flowering time could lead to sympatric speciation in plants. (3)
hints: Can plants that flower at different times cross?
questions.solution:
Plants flowering at different times can't pollinate each other (temporal isolation) [B1]
No gene flow between the groups [B1]
Mutations / selection change allele frequencies separately until they become separate species. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between allopatric and sympatric speciation. (3)
questions.solution:
Allopatric: populations separated geographically [B1]
Sympatric: in the same area, isolated reproductively (e.g. behaviour / timing) [B1]
Both lead to no gene flow and different allele frequencies. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Squirrels were introduced to the UK from North America in the 1870s. Black fur occurs in both places, and an identical mutation is found in a related species. Which conclusion is best supported?

Choose one answer.

A  The mutation arose in the UK after 1870
B  The mutation arose separately in each country
C  The mutation arose before the species separated from the related species
D  The mutation was caused by the UK climate (1)
hints: Same mutation in a related species.
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
A new allele is found in two isolated populations of the same species. Which is the most likely explanation?

Choose one answer.

A  The environment caused the same mutation in both
B  The allele was present before the populations were separated
C  The two populations interbreed
D  The allele is dominant (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which is the original source of all new alleles?

Choose one answer.

A  Mutation
B  Crossing over
C  Independent segregation
D  Random fertilisation (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term community. (1)
hints: How is it different from a population?
It includes more than one species.
questions.solution: All the populations of different species living in the same place at the same time. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term population. (1)
hints: How many species does it involve?
questions.solution: All the organisms of one species living in the same area at the same time. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a mark-release-recapture study of snails, explain why the mark must (i) not make the snails more visible to predators and (ii) not wash off in rain. (2)
hints: What happens to the number of marked snails if predators eat more of them?
How does a lost mark affect the recapture count?
questions.solution:
(i) More marked snails eaten, so fewer marked recaptured / population overestimated (and harms the snails) [B1]
(ii) Marked snails would be counted as unmarked, so population overestimated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Students marked 40 woodlice, released them, and caught a second sample 10 minutes later. Suggest and explain two improvements. (2)
hints: Have the marked woodlice had time to mix?
How could the estimate be made more reliable?
questions.solution:
Leave longer (e.g. 24 h) before recapture, so marked animals mix randomly with the population [B1]
Use larger samples / repeat, to give a more reliable estimate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the diversity of species on abandoned farmland usually increases over many years. (2)
hints: What process changes the community over time?
What do new plant species provide?
questions.solution:
Succession: new plant species colonise and change the conditions [B1]
More plant species provide more habitats / niches / food sources, so more animal species. [B1]

questions.prompt: Male fish exposed to an oestrogen-like chemical from sewage produce less sperm and court females less. Suggest and explain the effects on the fish population. (4)
hints: What happens to the number of successful matings?
What happens to the next generation?
questions.solution:
Fewer successful matings / less fertilisation [B1]
Fewer offspring produced [B1]
Population size decreases over generations [B1]
Fewer breeding individuals, so genetic diversity may fall. [B1]

questions.prompt: The pesticide DDT caused birds of prey to lay eggs with thin shells. Explain the effect on bird populations. (4)
hints: How does this affect birth rate?
questions.solution:
Thin shells break when parents sit on them [B1]
Fewer chicks hatch [B1]
Birth rate falls below death rate [B1]
Population decreases. [B1]

questions.prompt: Male frogs exposed to a pollutant called 50% less than unexposed males. Females prefer males that call more. Suggest and explain the effects on breeding in polluted habitats. (4)
hints: What happens to the alleles of exposed males?
questions.solution:
Exposed males are less likely to attract / be chosen by females [B1]
Fewer matings and fewer offspring [B1]
Lower reproductive success, so population may decline [B1]
If all males are exposed, fewer pairs breed overall. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one disadvantage of using insecticides, rather than sterile males, to control a pest. (1)
hints: Do insecticides only kill the pest?
questions.solution: Kill non-target species / pests may become resistant. [B1]

questions.prompt: A predator was introduced to control a pest. It later had to be reintroduced. Suggest why. (1)
hints: What happens to predators when prey becomes scarce?
questions.solution: Predator population declined / died out when the pest population fell (less food). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to estimate the mean number of dandelions per m² in a field. (3)
hints: How do you choose where quadrats go?
How do you convert to per m²?
questions.solution:
Use random coordinates (random number generator) to place quadrats [B1]
Count dandelions in each quadrat; use a large number of quadrats [B1]
Calculate the mean per quadrat and divide by quadrat area (if not 1 m²). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to estimate the percentage cover of a plant species using a gridded quadrat. (3)
hints: How many small squares does a gridded quadrat have?
questions.solution:
Place the quadrat at random positions [B1]
Count the number of squares (out of 100) in which the species is present / covers more than half [B1]
Repeat many times and calculate the mean percentage cover. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to investigate how plant cover changes from the sea to inland across a sand dune system. (3)
hints: Is random sampling suitable when there's a gradient?
What tool lays out the line?
questions.solution:
Lay a line / belt transect from the shore inland [B1]
Place quadrats at regular intervals along it [B1]
Record percentage cover of each species in each quadrat (repeat transects). [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the percentage cover of different plants on sand dunes of different ages. Explain why these data suggest that succession is occurring. (4)
hints: Which species are present early and which later?
questions.solution:
The community changes over time — different species dominate at different ages [B1]
Pioneer species (marram grass) colonise first and then decline [B1]
Each community changes the conditions (e.g. more soil / humus / nutrients, more shade), making it more suitable for later species [B1]
Trees eventually dominate (climax community). [B1]
questions.table:
Dune age / years | Marram grass % | Heather % | Shrubs % | Trees %
5 | 60 | 0 | 0 | 0
50 | 30 | 20 | 5 | 0
200 | 5 | 40 | 30 | 10
1000 | 0 | 10 | 25 | 60

questions.prompt: Describe how primary succession occurs on bare rock. (4)
questions.solution:
Pioneer species (e.g. lichens) colonise bare rock [B1]
They break down rock and die, adding organic matter to form a thin soil [B1]
Conditions become less hostile, so other species (mosses, grasses, then shrubs) colonise and outcompete earlier species [B1]
Eventually a stable climax community forms. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why biodiversity usually increases during succession. (4)
hints: What do more plant species provide?
questions.solution:
Conditions become less hostile / more soil and nutrients [B1]
More plant species can survive [B1]
More habitats / niches / food sources [B1]
So more animal species colonise (though diversity may fall slightly at climax). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why less light reaches the ground on older parts of a sand dune system. (1)
questions.solution: Taller plants / trees shade the ground. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why soil depth increases on older parts of a sand dune system. (1)
questions.solution: Organic matter (humus) from dead and decomposed plants builds up. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why pioneer species decline as succession proceeds. (1)
questions.solution: They are outcompeted by later species / conditions (e.g. shade) no longer suit them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how abandoned farmland can gradually become woodland. (4)
hints: How do they change conditions for later species?
questions.solution:
Pioneer species (e.g. grasses, annual weeds) colonise first [B1]
They change the conditions, e.g. adding organic matter / nutrients to the soil [B1]
Shrubs and then trees colonise and outcompete earlier species (e.g. by shading) [B1]
Eventually a stable climax community (woodland) develops. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how conservation managers prevent succession in order to maintain a heathland. (4)
hints: What would happen if heathland were left alone?
questions.solution:
Left alone, succession would turn heathland into woodland [B1]
Grazing / mowing / controlled burning removes shrubs and tree seedlings [B1]
This keeps the community at an earlier stage (plagioclimax) [B1]
Preserving habitats for species that depend on heathland. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a climax community and why it remains stable. (4)
hints: What is the final stage of succession?
Why don't new species take over?
questions.solution:
The final, stable community at the end of succession [B1]
Dominated by species best adapted to the conditions [B1]
These species do not change conditions in a way that favours others [B1]
So the community changes little over time (unless disturbed). [B1]

questions.prompt: Snowshoe hares turn white in winter. Suggest and explain how earlier snowmelt caused by climate change reduces their survival. (2)
hints: What colour is the ground after the snow melts?
questions.solution:
White hares on brown ground are easily seen [B1]
So more are caught by predators. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some birds time breeding by day length, but warmer springs make caterpillars appear earlier. Suggest how this affects the birds. (2)
hints: Do chicks hatch at the same time as food peaks?
questions.solution:
Chicks hatch after the peak in caterpillars (mismatch) [B1]
Less food for chicks, so fewer survive. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how rising sea temperatures can reduce coral populations. (2)
hints: What do corals rely on for food?
What happens to them at high temperature?
questions.solution:
High temperature causes corals to expel their photosynthetic algae (bleaching) [B1]
Less food / energy, so corals die. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to measure the percentage cover of seaweed from the low-tide line up a rocky shore. (3)
hints: How do you sample along a gradient?
questions.solution:
Lay a transect from the low-tide line up the shore [B1]
Place quadrats at regular intervals along it [B1]
Estimate percentage cover in each (e.g. count squares in a gridded quadrat); repeat transects. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to estimate the mean percentage cover of lichen on a large wall. (3)
hints: How do you choose where to place quadrats?
questions.solution:
Place gridded quadrats at random positions (random coordinates) [B1]
Count the squares containing lichen to give percentage cover [B1]
Use many quadrats and calculate the mean. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a point quadrat (a frame with pins) is used to estimate percentage cover. (3)
hints: What do you record for each pin?
How do you calculate the percentage?
questions.solution:
Place the frame at random positions and lower each pin [B1]
Record the species touched by each pin [B1]
Percentage cover = number of hits ÷ total number of pins × 100 (over many placements). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how succession can lead to a greater variety of animals in a habitat. (2)
hints: What happens to plant diversity and structure?
questions.solution:
More plant species and more complex structure develop [B1]
Providing more habitats / niches / food sources, so more animal species can live there. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a mature woodland supports more bird species than a young conifer plantation. (2)
questions.solution:
Mature woodland has more plant species and layers (canopy, shrubs, ground) [B1]
So more nesting sites / niches / types of food. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why species diversity sometimes falls slightly when a community reaches its climax. (2)
questions.solution:
A few dominant species (e.g. large trees) outcompete others [B1]
E.g. by shading, so some species that lived there earlier are lost. [B1]

questions.prompt: Soil eroded from deforested land washes into a lake. Explain how this could reduce fish populations. (4)
hints: What does soil do to the water clarity?
What does that do to producers?
questions.solution:
Water becomes cloudy (turbid), so less light reaches aquatic plants / algae [B1]
Less photosynthesis, so less food at the base of the food chain [B1]
Less oxygen produced [B1]
Sediment may also smother eggs / feeding areas, so fish populations fall. [B1]

questions.prompt: A model based on climate predicted that a lemur species could live in 20 000 km² of forest. The species actually occupies only 8 000 km², and the edge of its range follows a large river. Give three conclusions. (3)
hints: What fraction of suitable habitat is occupied?
questions.solution:
Species occupies only 40% of the climatically suitable area [B1]
The river may act as a barrier to dispersal [B1]
Other factors (biotic, e.g. competition / predation / food) must also limit its distribution. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two bird species have the same climatically suitable range, but one lives only above 1000 m and the other only below. Suggest three explanations. (3)
questions.solution:
Interspecific competition — each excludes the other from part of the range [B1]
Each is adapted to different conditions (e.g. temperature, food) at different altitudes [B1]
Different niches / resources at different altitudes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between abiotic and biotic factors and give an example of each that could limit the distribution of a species. (3)
questions.solution:
Abiotic factors are non-living, e.g. temperature, rainfall, light [B1]
Biotic factors are living, e.g. competition, predation, disease, food supply [B1]
Either type can make conditions unsuitable, limiting where a species is found. [B1]

questions.prompt: Complete the passage with the correct terms. 'The maximum population size an environment can support is its __1__. The role of a species within its habitat is its __2__. Non-living factors such as temperature are __3__ factors. All the populations of different species in a habitat form a __4__.' (2)
hints: Each gap is a key ecology term.
questions.solution:
1 carrying capacity; 2 niche; 3 abiotic; 4 community. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Complete the passage. 'All the organisms of one species in a habitat form a __1__. A community and the non-living components of its environment form an __2__. Living factors such as predation are __3__ factors. The gradual change in species in a community over time is called __4__.' (2)
hints: The last one is a process.
questions.solution:
1 population; 2 ecosystem; 3 biotic; 4 succession. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Complete the passage. 'The first species to colonise bare rock are called __1__ species. The final stable community is the __2__ community. Organisms that get energy by breaking down dead material are __3__. The place where an organism lives is its __4__.' (2)
questions.solution:
1 pioneer; 2 climax; 3 saprobionts (decomposers); 4 habitat. [B2]
4 correct = 2 marks; 2 or 3 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons for conserving tropical rainforests. (2)
hints: Think about the carbon cycle and human uses.
questions.solution: Two from: maintain biodiversity / habitats / prevent extinction; store carbon / reduce CO₂ in the atmosphere / climate change; source of medicines / food / timber; ecotourism / economic value; ethical reasons. [B2]

questions.prompt: Explain how conservation of a habitat may involve managing succession. (2)
hints: What would happen to a heathland if left alone?
questions.solution:
Succession would replace the habitat with a different (climax) community, losing the species that need it [B1]
Grazing / mowing / burning / coppicing stops succession at a particular stage. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you would estimate the number of weed plants of one species in a large field. (5)
hints: How do you choose where to sample?
questions.solution:
Divide the field into a grid using two long tape measures [B1]
Use random numbers / generator to choose coordinates [B1]
Place quadrats at the coordinates and count the plants in each [B1]
Use a large number of quadrats [B1]
Calculate the mean per quadrat and multiply by (field area ÷ quadrat area). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate how the abundance of a plant species changes from the edge of a woodland into an open field. (5)
hints: Random sampling won't show a gradient.
questions.solution:
Lay a tape from the woodland into the field (transect) [B1]
Place quadrats at regular intervals along it [B1]
Record percentage cover / number of plants in each quadrat [B1]
Repeat with several transects [B1]
Measure an abiotic factor (e.g. light intensity) at each point to relate to abundance. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how percentage cover can be used to estimate the abundance of a grass species, and explain why it is used instead of counting. (5)
hints: Can you count individual grass plants?
questions.solution:
Individual grass plants are hard to count (grow in clumps) [B1]
Place quadrats randomly (random coordinates) [B1]
Estimate % of quadrat area covered / use a point quadrat and count pins touching the species [B1]
Use many quadrats and calculate the mean percentage cover [B1]
Point frame: % cover = touches ÷ total pins × 100. [B1]

questions.prompt: A weed grows up to 2 m tall and absorbs large amounts of mineral ions. Explain why it reduces the growth of a crop, and name the type of competition. (3)
hints: Is the weed the same species as the crop?
questions.solution:
Shades crop, so less light for photosynthesis [B1]
Takes mineral ions (e.g. nitrate), so less for the crop to make proteins / nucleic acids [B1]
Interspecific competition. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a farmer sowing crop seeds too close together gets a lower yield per plant. (3)
hints: What do the crop plants compete for?
questions.solution:
Intraspecific competition [B1]
For light (shading), water and mineral ions [B1]
So less photosynthesis / growth per plant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how predator and prey populations both rise and fall in cycles. (3)
hints: What happens to predators when prey increase?
questions.solution:
More prey means more food, so predators increase [B1]
More predators eat more prey, so prey decreases [B1]
Less food for predators, so predators decrease, then prey rises again. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain two precautions needed to get a valid estimate of a lizard population by mark–release–recapture, and give the formula used. Do not refer to sample size. (3)
questions.solution:
Mark doesn't harm the animal / make it more visible to predators, so survival isn't affected [B1]
Leave enough time for marked animals to mix randomly with the population [B1]
Population = number in first sample × number in second sample ÷ number marked in second sample. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a mark–release–recapture study, 40 snails were marked and released. Later 50 were caught, of which 8 were marked. Estimate the population and state two assumptions. (3)
questions.solution:
40 × 50 ÷ 8 = 250 [B1]
No (or few) births, deaths, immigration or emigration [B1]
Marks don't come off / marked snails mix evenly. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a mark–release–recapture study, 60 beetles were marked. Later 45 were caught and 9 were marked. Estimate the population size and explain why the estimate would be too high if marks wore off. (3)
questions.solution:
60 × 45 ÷ 9 = 300 [B1]
If marks wore off, fewer marked would be recaptured [B1]
So the denominator is smaller and the estimate too large. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the process of secondary succession that regenerates a rainforest in an area that has been cleared. (4)
questions.solution:
Soil already present, so starts with colonising plants (e.g. grasses / shrubs) from seeds [B1]
Each stage changes the abiotic conditions (more humus, shade, nutrients) [B1]
Making conditions more suitable for other species, which outcompete the earlier ones [B1]
Biodiversity increases until a climax community (forest) is reached. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe primary succession on bare rock. (4)
questions.solution:
Pioneer species (e.g. lichens) colonise bare rock [B1]
They die and decompose, forming a thin soil / humus [B1]
Conditions change so other species (mosses, grasses, shrubs) can grow and outcompete earlier ones [B1]
Biodiversity increases until a climax community. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the features of pioneer species that allow them to colonise bare ground. (4)
hints: How do they survive the harsh conditions?
questions.solution:
Produce large numbers of seeds / spores dispersed by wind [B1]
Tolerate extreme conditions (drought, high light, low nutrients) [B1]
Some can fix nitrogen / photosynthesise / grow fast [B1]
Change conditions when they die (form soil). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two farming practices that would prevent a cleared rainforest area from regenerating by secondary succession. (2)
hints: What do animals do to young plants?
questions.solution: Two from: grazing by livestock; ploughing / tilling; using herbicides; burning; repeated mowing / harvesting. [B2]

questions.prompt: Explain why mowing a meadow every year maintains a high diversity of wildflowers. (2)
questions.solution:
Prevents succession to shrubs / woodland [B1]
So taller species don't shade out / outcompete the wildflowers. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two ways conservation of a habitat can be balanced with human needs. (2)
questions.solution: Two from: sustainable / selective logging with replanting; coppicing; protected areas / zones; ecotourism; fishing quotas. [B2]

questions.prompt: Outline a method to find the species richness of plants at a grassland site. (3)
hints: How do you choose sampling points?
questions.solution:
Use random coordinates (grid and random number generator) to place quadrats [B1]
Record / identify every different species in each quadrat [B1]
Use many quadrats until no new species are found; total number of species = richness. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why random sampling is used and how enough quadrats can be decided. (3)
questions.solution:
Random sampling avoids bias [B1]
Plot a running mean / cumulative species against number of quadrats [B1]
Enough when the mean levels off / no new species appear. [B1]

questions.prompt: Livestock and wild goats in mountains eat the same plants. Name the type of competition. (1)
questions.solution: Interspecific competition. [B1]

questions.prompt: Young trees in a forest compete for light. Name the type of competition. (1)
questions.solution: Intraspecific competition. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the maximum population size of a species that an environment can support. (1)
questions.solution: Carrying capacity. [B1]

questions.prompt: Farm animals compete with wild goats if they share the same habitat and eat similar food. The table shows how different each type of farm animal is from the wild goats in diet and habitat (0 = identical). Suggest and explain three actions farmers could take to balance conservation of the goats with keeping animals. (3)
questions.solution:
Keep yaks — their diet is identical but habitat very different (or cows, which differ in both) [B1]
Avoid horses, which share both diet and habitat, so compete most [B1]
Limit number of animals / keep them away from goat habitat / control extra feeding so populations don't grow too large. [B1]
questions.table:
Animal | Food difference | Habitat difference
Cow | 1.0 | 1.5
Horse | 0.5 | 0.0
Yak | 0.0 | 2.0

questions.prompt: Suggest and explain three ways farmers can conserve wildlife while keeping productive farmland. (3)
questions.solution:
Keep hedgerows / field margins to provide habitats and food [B1]
Reduce pesticide / fertiliser use to protect non-target species and water [B1]
Rotate crops / leave some land fallow / create ponds. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why conflict can arise between conservation and human needs, giving examples. (3)
questions.solution:
Land needed for farming / housing reduces habitats [B1]
Predators may kill livestock, so farmers want them removed [B1]
Local people rely on resources (timber, fishing) for income. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how heated water released into a river could affect fish populations. (4)
questions.solution:
Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen [B1]
Higher temperature increases fish metabolic rate / oxygen demand [B1]
Species with narrow temperature tolerance may die or move [B1]
Warm-tolerant species may increase — change in community / competition. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term population. (2)
questions.solution:
All the organisms of one species [B1]
Living in the same area at the same time. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the terms community and ecosystem. (2)
questions.solution:
Community — all the populations of different species in a habitat [B1]
Ecosystem — a community plus the non-living (abiotic) components. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the terms niche and habitat. (2)
questions.solution:
Niche — the role of a species in its habitat (all biotic and abiotic interactions) [B1]
Habitat — the place where an organism lives. [B1]

questions.prompt: A similarity index compared the bird community each year with the first year (1.0 = identical). It fell steadily over 20 years. Explain how this provides evidence of succession. (2)
questions.solution:
Species present gradually changed / were replaced over time [B1]
As conditions changed, new species colonised and others were outcompeted. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why animal communities change during plant succession. (2)
questions.solution:
New plant species provide different food and habitats / niches [B1]
So different animal species can colonise. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why biodiversity usually increases during succession. (2)
questions.solution:
Conditions become less hostile / more soil and nutrients [B1]
More habitats and niches, so more species. [B1]

questions.prompt: In the last 10 years of a study, the similarity index stayed fairly constant. Name this stage of succession and suggest why the index is not perfectly constant. (2)
questions.solution:
Climax community [B1]
Populations still fluctuate due to weather / migration / predation, or random sampling variation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the features of a climax community. (2)
questions.solution:
Stable / little change over time [B1]
Dominated by a few large species (e.g. trees) / high biodiversity / complex food webs. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a plagioclimax and give one example. (2)
questions.solution:
A community where succession is stopped by human activity before the climax [B1]
e.g. grassland grazed by sheep / mowed meadow / heather moorland managed by burning. [B1]

questions.prompt: Beetles feed and complete their life cycle on one plant species. Suggest two reasons for capturing the first sample at the same time each year, and one reason for identifying the beetles before marking them. (3)
questions.solution:
Adults present at that stage of the life cycle [B1]
Population not changing (no births / larvae emerging) between samples / comparable across years [B1]
Identify first because similar species are present, so only the target species is marked. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three assumptions made when using mark-release-recapture. (3)
questions.solution:
Marked individuals mix randomly with the population [B1]
No births, deaths, immigration or emigration between samples [B1]
Marks don't come off or affect survival. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why mark-release-recapture is not suitable for estimating the population of a plant species, and which method is used instead. (3)
questions.solution:
Plants don't move, so can't mix with the population [B1]
Use quadrats placed randomly [B1]
Count / estimate % cover and scale up. [B1]

questions.prompt: 300 beetles were marked and released. In the second sample, 180 were unmarked and 60 were marked. Estimate the population size. (2)
150 beetles were marked. In the second sample, 270 were unmarked and 30 marked. Estimate the population. (2)
220 beetles were marked. In the second sample, 165 were unmarked and 55 marked. Estimate the population. (2)
Ecologists captured insects from several sites on an island for a mark-release-recapture study. Explain how they should choose the sites. (2)
questions.solution:
Randomly, e.g. grid the island and use random number coordinates [B1]
To avoid bias / get a representative sample. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why systematic sampling along a transect is used instead of random sampling in some studies. (2)
questions.solution:
Used where an environmental factor changes across an area (e.g. from shore to dunes) [B1]
Shows how distribution changes along the gradient. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why several sites, rather than one, were used to capture insects for marking. (2)
questions.solution:
Insects may not be evenly distributed [B1]
Using several sites gives a more representative sample / marked insects spread through the population. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two assumptions made when using mark-release-recapture. (2)
questions.solution:
No births, deaths, immigration or emigration between samples [B1]
Marked individuals mix randomly / marks don't affect survival or come off. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why enough time must be left between release and recapture, but not too much. (2)
questions.solution:
Enough time for marked animals to mix with the population [B1]
Not so long that births / deaths / migration change the population. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why mark-release-recapture would overestimate the population if marked animals were more likely to be eaten. (2)
questions.solution:
Fewer marked animals in the second sample [B1]
Dividing by a smaller number gives a larger estimate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Insects were marked with a fluorescent powder that glows red under UV light. Suggest the advantages of this method. (2)
questions.solution:
Not visible in normal light, so doesn't increase predation [B1]
Easy to identify marked insects under UV / doesn't harm them / quick for many small insects. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two features of a good method for marking animals. (2)
questions.solution:
Doesn't harm the animal or make it more visible [B1]
Doesn't wash or rub off during the study. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest a disadvantage of marking snails with bright paint. (2)
questions.solution:
Paint may make snails more visible to predators (e.g. birds) [B1]
So fewer marked snails survive, affecting the estimate / paint may be toxic. [B1]

questions.prompt: 1200 marked insects were in the population. A day later, 450 insects were captured, of which 60 were marked. Estimate the population. (2)
800 marked insects were released. Of 300 later captured, 40 were marked. Estimate the population. (2)
2000 marked insects were released. Of 640 later captured, 160 were marked. Estimate the population. (2)
Population estimates rose each day after the first. Over 5 days, the number of marked insects caught fell from 78 to under 10. Suggest how the method could explain this. (2)
questions.solution:
Fluorescent powder may wear / rub off over time [B1]
So marked insects not recognised, fewer counted as marked, giving higher estimates. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why marked animals might avoid traps after being captured once, and how this affects the estimate. (2)
questions.solution:
Trap-shy — learned to avoid the traps [B1]
Fewer marked recaptured, so population is overestimated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why marked animals might be more likely to be recaptured, and how this affects the estimate. (2)
questions.solution:
Animals attracted to bait — trap-happy [B1]
More marked recaptured, so population is underestimated. [B1]

questions.prompt: A substitution mutation changes the codon GAA to GAG. Use the table to explain why this mutation may have no effect on the protein. (2)
hints: Which amino acids do GAA and GAG code for?
What feature of the genetic code does this show?
questions.solution:
GAG also codes for Glu / same amino acid because the code is degenerate [B1]
So the primary structure / amino acid sequence is unchanged. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an enzyme, a mutation that changes amino acid 150 from Leu to Ile has no effect on activity. A mutation that changes amino acid 72 from Cys to Ser stops the enzyme working. Suggest explanations for these results. (3)
hints: Leu and Ile have very similar R groups.
Which amino acid can form disulfide bridges?
questions.solution:
Leu and Ile have similar R groups, so the same bonds form and the tertiary structure is unchanged [B1]
Cys forms disulfide bridges but Ser cannot [B1]
Losing the disulfide bridge changes the tertiary structure / active site, so substrate no longer complementary. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a single base substitution in a gene could result in a non-functional enzyme. (3)
hints: Follow it through: codon → amino acid → structure → active site.
Which level of structure determines the active site's shape?
questions.solution:
Changes one codon, so a different amino acid / primary structure (or a premature stop codon) [B1]
Hydrogen / ionic / disulfide bonds form in different places, changing the tertiary structure [B1]
Active site changes shape, so substrate no longer complementary / no enzyme–substrate complexes. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutation changes an amino acid in the active site of an enzyme from Glu (negatively charged R group) to Lys (positively charged R group). Suggest why the enzyme's activity falls. (3)
hints: The substrate binds partly through charges.
Could the overall shape change too?
questions.solution:
Changes the charge in the active site [B1]
Substrate can no longer form ionic bonds / is repelled, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes [B1]
Ionic bonds in the protein change, altering the tertiary structure / shape of active site. [B1]

questions.prompt:
A cell with a diploid number of 6 undergoes meiosis. In meiosis I, one pair of homologous chromosomes fails to separate (non-disjunction). Meiosis II is normal.

How many chromosomes are in each of the four gametes? (2)
hints: Both chromosomes of one pair go into one cell after meiosis I.
questions.solution:
Two gametes have 4 chromosomes [B1]
Two gametes have 2 chromosomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how non-disjunction during meiosis can result in a zygote with three copies of one chromosome. (2)
questions.solution:
Homologous chromosomes / sister chromatids fail to separate, so one gamete gets an extra copy [B1]
Fertilised by a normal gamete, giving three copies (e.g. 47 chromosomes in humans). [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the possible effects on a polypeptide of a base substitution and a base deletion in a gene. (6)
hints: Why might a substitution have no effect?
questions.solution:
Substitution changes only one codon [B1]
May code for the same amino acid (code is degenerate), so no effect [B1]
Or one different amino acid, which may or may not change the tertiary structure [B1]
Deletion causes a frameshift — every codon after it changes [B1]
So many amino acids change / premature stop codon [B1]
Deletion is much more likely to produce a non-functional protein. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term gene mutation and describe how the rate of mutation can be increased. (4)
hints: A mutation is a change in what?
questions.solution:
Change in the base sequence of DNA (of a gene) [B1]
Mutations occur spontaneously during DNA replication [B1]
Mutagenic agents increase the rate [B1]
e.g. ionising radiation (X-rays), UV light, chemicals such as benzene / tar. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a mutation in a skin cell is not passed to a person's children, but a mutation in a cell that forms gametes may be. (4)
hints: Which cells pass DNA to the next generation?
What happens to the zygote's cells?
questions.solution:
Skin (body) cells are not involved in reproduction [B1]
Mutation in a gamete-forming cell can be in a gamete [B1]
Zygote formed from that gamete has the mutation [B1]
So it is in every cell of the offspring and can be inherited / selected. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutation replaces a cysteine with alanine in keratin, a structural protein in hair. The hair becomes weaker. Explain why. (2)
hints: What does that bond do for structure?
questions.solution:
Cysteine forms disulfide bridges; alanine cannot [B1]
Fewer strong bonds, so the structure is less stable / weaker. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutation replaces a charged amino acid on the surface of a protein with a non-polar one. The protein becomes less soluble. Explain why. (2)
hints: Charged R groups interact with what?
What do non-polar R groups do in water?
questions.solution:
Charged R group interacts with water, keeping the protein soluble [B1]
Non-polar R group is hydrophobic, so proteins stick together / clump. [B1]

questions.prompt: In collagen, every third amino acid is glycine, which has the smallest R group. A mutation replaces one glycine with a larger amino acid. Explain why this weakens collagen. (2)
hints: Why does collagen need a small R group?
What happens to the tight packing?
questions.solution:
Glycine's small R group lets the polypeptide chains pack / coil tightly together [B1]
Larger R group disrupts this packing / hydrogen bonding, weakening the structure. [B1]

questions.prompt: In the gene for haemoglobin, a DNA template triplet CTT is mutated to CAT. Give the mRNA codon before and after the mutation. (2)
hints: Pair each DNA base with its RNA partner.
T in DNA pairs with A in RNA.
questions.solution:
Before: GAA [B1]
After: GUA. [B1]

questions.prompt: After meiosis I, each cell of an organism contains 3 chromosomes. In meiosis II, the chromatids of one chromosome fail to separate in one of the two cells. How many chromosomes are in each of the four gametes? (2)
hints: In the abnormal cell, one gamete gets both chromatids.
questions.solution:
Two gametes have 3 chromosomes [B1]
One has 4 and one has 2. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why non-disjunction in meiosis I produces more abnormal gametes than non-disjunction in meiosis II. (2)
hints: In meiosis I, which cells inherit the error?
In meiosis II, does the other cell divide normally?
questions.solution:
Meiosis I: both cells formed are abnormal, so all four gametes are abnormal [B1]
Meiosis II: only one cell is affected, so two gametes are normal and two abnormal. [B1]

questions.prompt: Down syndrome is caused by having three copies of chromosome 21. Explain how this arises. (2)
hints: Which event in meiosis goes wrong?
questions.solution:
Non-disjunction: chromosome 21 (or its chromatids) fails to separate in meiosis, giving a gamete with two copies [B1]
Fertilised by a normal gamete, giving three copies / 47 chromosomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a mutation can change the amino acid sequence of an enzyme without affecting its activity. (2)
hints: Does the active site's shape change?
questions.solution:
Change is not in / near the active site, or the new amino acid has a similar R group [B1]
So the tertiary structure / active site shape is unchanged — substrate still complementary. [B1]

questions.prompt: Part of the mRNA for an enzyme's active site is UUU CGG GCG. A mutation changes it to UUU CGG GGG. Use the table to name the type of mutation, give the change in the DNA template strand, and explain the effect on the enzyme. (4)
hints: Compare the third codon base by base.
What amino acid does GGG code for?
questions.solution:
Substitution [B1]
DNA template base changes from G to C (template CGC → CCC) [B1]
Ala replaced by Gly in the active site [B1]
Different R group may change bonding / shape of the active site, so substrate may no longer be complementary. [B1]

Shorter polypeptide / missing part of the protein, so likely non-functional. [B1]

Deletion (of one base) [B1]
Frameshift — every codon after the mutation is changed [B1]
First amino acid still Phe (UUC), but Arg becomes Gly and later amino acids change [B1]
Polypeptide very different / likely non-functional. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of mutation that produces a gamete missing one chromosome and explain how it happens in meiosis. (3)
hints: Where does the missing chromosome go?
questions.solution:
Non-disjunction (chromosome mutation) [B1]
Homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II) fail to separate [B1]
Both go into one cell, so the other gamete has none of that chromosome. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how non-disjunction in meiosis II can produce a gamete with an extra chromosome. (3)
hints: What normally separates in anaphase II?
questions.solution:
Sister chromatids fail to separate in anaphase II [B1]
Both chromatids go to the same pole / cell [B1]
That gamete has one extra chromosome (n + 1). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how polyploidy can arise. (3)
hints: What if a whole set of chromosomes fails to separate?
questions.solution:
A whole set of chromosomes fails to separate during meiosis (or mitosis) [B1]
Producing a diploid gamete [B1]
Fusing with a haploid gamete gives a triploid, or with another diploid gamete gives a tetraploid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why RNA viruses produce new strains more rapidly than DNA-based organisms. (2)
hints: Do RNA-copying enzymes check for errors?
questions.solution:
Enzymes copying RNA (e.g. RNA polymerase / reverse transcriptase) have no proofreading [B1]
So more mutations occur, producing new variants quickly. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which statement about a deletion of one base in an exon is incorrect?

Choose one answer.

A  It causes a frameshift
B  It changes all the codons after the mutation
C  It changes only one amino acid
D  It may produce a premature stop codon (1)
hints: What happens to codons after the deletion?
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which statement about a substitution mutation is correct?

Choose one answer.

A  It always changes the amino acid
B  It may not change the amino acid because the code is degenerate
C  It causes a frameshift
D  It always produces a stop codon (1)
hints: Does a substitution shift the reading frame?
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which describes an inversion mutation?

Choose one answer.

A  A section of bases is reversed
B  An extra base is added
C  A base is removed
D  One base is replaced by another (1)
hints: Bases are not added or removed.
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt: In sickle cell disease, a substitution changes one amino acid in the β chain of haemoglobin from glutamic acid (charged) to valine (non-polar). Explain how this causes red blood cells to become sickle-shaped. (3)
hints: What happens to the primary structure?
How does a non-polar R group behave?
questions.solution:
One amino acid changed in the primary structure [B1]
Valine is hydrophobic, so haemoglobin molecules stick together (especially at low oxygen) [B1]
They form long fibres that distort the red blood cell into a sickle shape. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how deleting a single base early in the β-globin gene would affect the β polypeptide. (3)
hints: What does a deletion do to the reading frame?
questions.solution:
Frameshift — all codons after the deletion are changed [B1]
Many amino acids are different / a premature stop codon may form [B1]
So the β polypeptide is non-functional or not made. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a substitution in the third base of a codon often has no effect on the polypeptide. (3)
hints: Which base position varies most between codons for the same amino acid?
questions.solution:
The genetic code is degenerate [B1]
Codons for the same amino acid often differ only in the third base [B1]
So the amino acid / primary structure is unchanged. [B1]

questions.prompt: An inversion mutation in the gene for a blood-clotting protein produces a non-functional protein. The protein is not an enzyme. Explain how. (4)
hints: What happens to the base sequence?
How does this change the protein's shape?
questions.solution:
Inversion reverses a section of base sequence [B1]
So the sequence of codons / triplets changes, giving a different amino acid sequence (primary structure) [B1]
Changes the hydrogen / ionic / disulfide bonds, so a different tertiary structure [B1]
Protein can't bind to / interact with other clotting factors. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a substitution mutation may have no effect on a protein, but a deletion of one base usually has a large effect. (4)
questions.solution:
Substitution changes only one triplet; may code for the same amino acid (degenerate code) / similar amino acid [B1]
So the primary structure may be unchanged [B1]
Deletion causes a frameshift — every triplet after it changes [B1]
So many amino acids change, giving a different tertiary structure / non-functional protein. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a mutation that produces a stop codon early in a gene leads to a non-functional protein. (4)
hints: What does a stop codon do in translation?
questions.solution:
Mutation changes a triplet to a stop codon [B1]
Translation ends early, giving a shorter polypeptide [B1]
Missing amino acids, so different tertiary structure [B1]
Protein can't carry out its function. [B1]

questions.prompt: The normal allele codes for a sodium ion channel. Suggest how a mutant allele could give resistance to an insecticide that binds to the channel. (2)
questions.solution:
Mutation changes the amino acid sequence / tertiary structure of the channel [B1]
Insecticide can no longer bind (not complementary), so the channel closes normally. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how increased production of an enzyme could make an insect resistant to an insecticide. (2)
hints: What could the enzyme do to the insecticide?
questions.solution:
Enzyme breaks down / detoxifies the insecticide [B1]
More enzyme (gene duplication / more transcription) means insecticide removed before it acts. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the resistance allele may reduce the fitness of insects when the insecticide is absent. (2)
hints: Does the channel work as well?
questions.solution:
Altered channel may work less efficiently / slower nerve impulses [B1]
Or extra protein production uses energy, so reduced survival / reproduction. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a mutation in a gene for a membrane receptor could make a cancer cell resistant to a drug that binds to that receptor. (3)
questions.solution:
Mutation changes the base sequence and amino acid sequence [B1]
Changes the tertiary structure of the receptor [B1]
Drug no longer complementary / can't bind, so has no effect. [B1]

questions.prompt: In mitochondrial DNA, one group of people has thymine at a particular position and another has cytosine. Both DNA molecules are the same length. Name the most likely type of mutation. (1)
