questions.solution: Substitution. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutation causes all codons after it to be read differently, and the gene becomes one nucleotide shorter. Name the type of mutation. (1)
questions.solution: Deletion. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutation in a gene makes one triplet repeat many more times than usual. Name the type of mutation. (1)
questions.solution: Duplication / expansion of a triplet repeat. [B1]

questions.prompt: A protein of 250 amino acids is produced from an allele formed by a deletion of 15 base pairs from the original allele. Calculate the percentage reduction in protein length, to 3 significant figures. (2)
questions.solution:
5 amino acids lost; original = 255 [M1]
5 ÷ 255 × 100 = 1.96%. [A1]

questions.prompt: A protein of 412 amino acids is produced from an allele with a 36 base-pair deletion. Calculate the percentage reduction in protein length, to 3 significant figures. (2)
questions.solution:
12 amino acids lost; original = 424 [M1]
12 ÷ 424 × 100 = 2.83%. [A1]

questions.prompt: A protein of 180 amino acids is produced from an allele with a 9 base-pair deletion. Calculate the percentage reduction in protein length, to 3 significant figures. (2)
questions.solution:
3 amino acids lost; original = 183 [M1]
3 ÷ 183 × 100 = 1.64%. [A1]

questions.prompt: A receptor in skin cells normally switches on black pigment production only when a hormone binds to it; without the hormone, grey pigment is made. A deletion produces a receptor that has the same shape as the receptor with the hormone bound. Explain why squirrels homozygous for the deletion have black fur. (3)
questions.solution:
Deletion changes the amino acid sequence / tertiary structure of the receptor [B1]
Receptor is permanently in its active shape, even without the hormone [B1]
So black pigment is always produced. [B1]

questions.prompt: A deletion of three bases in a gene removes one amino acid but the protein still works. Explain why a single base deletion would usually have a larger effect. (3)
questions.solution:
Three-base deletion removes one codon, so the reading frame is unchanged [B1]
One-base deletion causes a frameshift [B1]
All following codons change, so many amino acids differ / a stop codon may appear — non-functional protein. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutated gene codes for a shorter polypeptide. Name one type of mutation that could cause this and explain how. (2)
questions.solution:
Substitution (or deletion/insertion causing frameshift) [B1]
Produces a premature stop codon, so translation ends early. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a deletion of one base can lead to a longer polypeptide. (2)
questions.solution:
Frameshift changes all following codons [B1]
The original stop codon may be lost, so translation continues further. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two mutagenic agents and explain how one increases the mutation rate. (2)
questions.solution:
UV / ionising radiation / X-rays; chemicals such as benzene / tar [B1]
e.g. radiation damages DNA bases, altering base pairing during replication. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some regions of a chromosome remain tightly coiled around histones. Suggest why genes in these regions are not expressed. (1)
hints: What enzyme needs to reach the DNA for a gene to be expressed?
Can it bind if the DNA is tightly packed?
questions.solution: RNA polymerase / transcription factors cannot access / bind to the DNA, so no transcription. [B1]

questions.prompt: Protein P is needed for cells to enter mitosis. Scientists used siRNA that binds to the mRNA for protein P. The table shows the results. Suggest explanations for these results. (3)
hints: What does siRNA do to the mRNA?
What does adding protein P back show?
questions.solution:
siRNA binds (complementary) to the mRNA, so it is broken down / not translated [B1]
No protein P made, so cells do not enter mitosis [B1]
Adding protein P restores mitosis, so it is the protein (not the mRNA) that is needed / effect is specific to P. [B1]
questions.table:
Treatment | % cells in mitosis
Control | 30
siRNA for P | 2
siRNA for P + protein P added | 28

questions.prompt: Explain how a mutation in a tumour suppressor gene can lead to a tumour. (3)
hints: What does the normal protein do?
What happens if it no longer works?
questions.solution:
Normal tumour suppressor protein slows cell division / causes apoptosis of damaged cells [B1]
Mutation produces a non-functional protein [B1]
So cells divide uncontrollably / rapidly, forming a tumour. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutation in a proto-oncogene produces an oncogene that is permanently switched on. Explain how this could lead to a tumour. (2)
hints: What does a proto-oncogene normally do?
What happens if it is always active?
questions.solution:
Proto-oncogene normally stimulates cell division; the oncogene stimulates it all the time [B1]
So cells divide rapidly / uncontrollably, forming a mass of cells (tumour). [B1]

questions.prompt: Some anti-cancer drugs stop DNA replication. Explain how this slows the growth of a tumour, and why these drugs also cause side effects. (2)
hints: Can cells divide without replicating DNA?
questions.solution:
Cells cannot replicate DNA so cannot divide, so the tumour stops growing [B1]
Healthy dividing cells (e.g. hair, gut lining) are also affected. [B1]

questions.prompt: Increased methylation of a tumour suppressor gene can lead to cancer. Explain how. (2)
hints: What does methylation do to transcription?
What does the tumour suppressor protein normally do?
questions.solution:
Methylation prevents transcription of the gene, so no tumour suppressor protein is made [B1]
So cell division is not slowed / cells divide uncontrollably. [B1]

questions.prompt: Chemotherapy drugs often cause hair loss. Suggest why. (2)
hints: Chemotherapy targets which kind of cells?
Are hair follicle cells like that?
questions.solution:
Drugs target rapidly dividing cells [B1]
Hair follicle cells also divide rapidly, so they are damaged too. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug stops cytokinesis and also causes cancer cells to die. The table shows cell growth relative to untreated cells after 72 hours; negative values mean there were fewer cells than at the start. Explain the results. (3)
hints: What happens to cell numbers as concentration increases?
Why would numbers fall below the starting number?
questions.solution:
Higher concentrations stop more cells completing division, so less growth [B1]
At high concentrations the drug also causes cell death (apoptosis) [B1]
When more cells die than divide, cell number falls below the starting number (negative values). [B1]
questions.table:
Drug / µmol dm⁻³ | Growth (proportion of control)
0 | 1.0
5 | 0.6
10 | 0.2
20 | −0.3

questions.prompt: A drug that blocks cell division was tested on cancer cells. Growth relative to control was 1.0 with no drug, 0.5 at 2 µM, 0.1 at 4 µM and 0.1 at 8 µM. Explain the results. (3)
hints: Why does growth fall as concentration rises?
questions.solution:
More drug blocks division in more cells, so less growth [B1]
Above 4 µM no further effect — all target molecules already inhibited [B1]
Remaining growth may be due to resistant cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Drug A slowed the growth of a tumour; drug B made the tumour shrink. Suggest an explanation for the difference. (3)
hints: Does stopping division make a tumour smaller?
questions.solution:
Drug A stops / slows cell division, so the tumour grows less [B1]
Drug B causes cell death (apoptosis) [B1]
Tumour shrinks when cells die faster than they divide. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how increasing transcription of the gene for an aquaporin could increase water uptake by a cell. (2)
questions.solution:
More mRNA, so more aquaporin proteins made (translation) and inserted into membranes [B1]
More channels for water, so faster osmosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a transcription factor could increase the production of a carrier protein. (2)
questions.solution:
Transcription factor binds to the promoter of the carrier gene [B1]
Stimulates RNA polymerase / transcription, so more mRNA and more carrier protein. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how siRNA targeting the mRNA for a carrier protein could slow fruit ripening. (2)
questions.solution:
siRNA is complementary to / binds the mRNA, which is broken down / not translated [B1]
Fewer carrier proteins, so less sugar transported into vacuoles. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a steroid hormone such as oestrogen stimulates the production of mRNA from a target gene. (6)
hints: How does oestrogen enter the cell?
questions.solution:
Oestrogen is lipid-soluble and diffuses through the cell-surface membrane [B1]
Binds to a receptor on a transcription factor [B1]
Changes the transcription factor's shape, activating it [B1]
Transcription factor enters the nucleus [B1]
Binds to the promoter of the target gene [B1]
Stimulates RNA polymerase to start transcription, producing mRNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how transcription factors can switch on genes in a differentiated cell. (2)
questions.solution:
Bind to the promoter region of target genes [B1]
Help RNA polymerase bind, so the genes are transcribed. [B1]

questions.prompt: All body cells contain the same genes. Explain why cells such as muscle and liver cells are different. (2)
hints: Are all genes expressed in every cell?
What controls which genes are expressed?
questions.solution:
Different genes are expressed / transcribed in different cells [B1]
Controlled by transcription factors / epigenetic silencing of some genes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells could be used to produce insulin-secreting cells. (2)
questions.solution:
iPS cells are pluripotent, so can differentiate into many cell types [B1]
Grown with specific factors so genes for β-cell function (e.g. insulin) are expressed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Diabetic mice given insulin-secreting cells made from iPS cells had blood glucose fall from 25 to 8 mmol dm⁻³ within 4 weeks; untreated diabetic mice stayed at 25; normal mice were at 7. Each group had 30 mice. Evaluate the use of iPS cells to treat type I diabetes in humans. (4)
hints: What are the limitations of moving from mice to humans?
questions.solution:
Glucose fell to near-normal levels, and controls show the effect was due to the treatment [B1]
Large groups (30) increase reliability [B1]
But mice are not humans / study was short — long-term effects (e.g. tumours) unknown [B1]
In type I diabetes the immune system may destroy the new β cells; iPS cells from the patient avoid rejection / fewer ethical issues than embryonic stem cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Evaluate the use of iPS cells compared with embryonic stem cells for treating disease. (4)
hints: Where do the cells come from?
Think about ethics, rejection and risks.
questions.solution:
iPS cells come from the patient's own cells, so no rejection [B1]
No embryos destroyed, so fewer ethical objections [B1]
But iPS cells may not be as versatile / reprogramming may be incomplete [B1]
Both carry a risk of uncontrolled division / tumours. [B1]

questions.prompt: Evaluate the use of adult stem cells from bone marrow to treat leukaemia. (4)
hints: What can bone-marrow stem cells become?
questions.solution:
Bone-marrow stem cells are multipotent — can form all blood cells, replacing cancerous ones [B1]
Using the patient's own or a matched donor's cells reduces rejection [B1]
Less ethically controversial than embryonic stem cells [B1]
But matched donors are hard to find / risk of graft rejection / limited to blood cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the amount of a particular mRNA in a cell indicates how strongly a gene is being expressed. (2)
hints: What does more mRNA lead to?
questions.solution:
mRNA is only produced when the gene is transcribed [B1]
More mRNA means more transcription / more protein can be translated. [B1]

questions.prompt: People with the same disease allele show symptoms at different ages. Suggest and explain one reason. (2)
hints: Is one gene the only factor?
questions.solution:
Other genes / environment (e.g. diet, lifestyle) / epigenetic changes affect expression [B1]
So the allele's effect appears earlier or later in different people. [B1]

questions.prompt: Identical twins with the same disease allele may develop the disease at different ages. Suggest and explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Different environments / lifestyles [B1]
Leading to different epigenetic changes (e.g. methylation) that alter gene expression. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how increased methylation of a tumour suppressor gene can lead to the development of a tumour. (3)
hints: What does methylation do to transcription?
What does the tumour suppressor protein normally do?
questions.solution:
Methyl groups added to the DNA (e.g. cytosine) of the gene / promoter [B1]
Prevents transcription factors binding, so the gene is not transcribed [B1]
No tumour suppressor protein, so cell division is not slowed / uncontrolled division. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how decreased methylation (hypomethylation) of an oncogene can lead to a tumour. (3)
hints: What normally keeps the gene switched off?
What does the oncogene's protein do?
questions.solution:
Less methylation means the oncogene is switched on / transcribed more [B1]
More protein that stimulates cell division [B1]
Cells divide rapidly / uncontrollably, forming a tumour. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how increased oestrogen concentration can increase the risk of breast cancer. (3)
hints: What does oestrogen bind to inside cells?
Which genes might it switch on?
questions.solution:
Oestrogen binds to receptors / activates transcription factors in breast cells [B1]
Stimulates transcription of genes that promote cell division (proto-oncogenes) [B1]
More cell division / uncontrolled division, so a tumour may develop. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a technique, an antibody against a transcription factor is used to pull down the transcription factor and anything attached to it from cell extracts. What will the DNA collected consist of? (1)
hints: Where does a transcription factor bind?
Only the bound DNA is collected.
questions.solution: The DNA fragments that the transcription factor was bound to (e.g. promoter regions). [B1]

questions.prompt: What part of a gene does a transcription factor bind to? (1)
questions.solution: The promoter (a specific base sequence). [B1]

questions.prompt: Why is DNA cut into small fragments before finding where a transcription factor binds? (1)
questions.solution: So only the short region bound by the transcription factor is isolated and can be identified. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how an RNA molecule complementary to an mRNA (antisense RNA) could reduce production of a protein. (1)
questions.solution: Binds to the mRNA, preventing translation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how siRNA prevents translation of a particular mRNA. (1)
questions.solution: Binds to complementary mRNA, which is then cut / broken down. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a molecule that binds to a gene's promoter could prevent its transcription. (1)
questions.solution: Stops RNA polymerase / transcription factors binding to the promoter. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a mutation in a gene's promoter region could increase expression of the gene. (2)
questions.solution:
Transcription factors / RNA polymerase bind more easily [B1]
So more transcription / more mRNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a mutation in the gene for a transcription factor could stop another gene being switched off. (2)
hints: What does the transcription factor control?
questions.solution:
Transcription factor stays active / binds permanently [B1]
So the target gene is transcribed continuously. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest and explain how a single-stranded DNA molecule complementary to an mRNA could reduce production of a harmful protein. (3)
questions.solution:
Base sequence complementary to the mRNA, so it binds to it [B1]
Prevents ribosomes binding / translation [B1]
The mRNA may be broken down, so less protein is made. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how RNA interference (RNAi) reduces expression of a gene. (3)
questions.solution:
Small interfering RNA (siRNA) associates with an enzyme / protein complex [B1]
siRNA binds to complementary mRNA [B1]
The mRNA is cut / broken down, so it is not translated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a drug that binds to the promoter of a gene could reduce the amount of protein made. (3)
hints: What normally binds to the promoter?
questions.solution:
Drug occupies the promoter region [B1]
Transcription factors / RNA polymerase cannot bind [B1]
Less transcription, so less mRNA and less protein. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug reduces production of a harmful protein in an inherited disease. Suggest two reasons why it is not a cure. (2)
hints: Is the faulty allele still there?
questions.solution:
The mutant allele is still present and still transcribed, so the drug must be taken continuously [B1]
Cells already damaged (e.g. neurones) are not replaced. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why treatment with siRNA must be repeated. (2)
hints: Does the gene keep being transcribed?
questions.solution:
siRNA is broken down over time [B1]
The gene keeps being transcribed, producing new mRNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how increased methylation of a mutant allele could delay the age at which symptoms of an inherited disease begin. (2)
hints: What does methylation do to transcription?
questions.solution:
Methylation reduces / prevents transcription of the mutant allele [B1]
So less harmful protein is produced and damage builds up more slowly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how acetylation of histones can increase gene expression. (2)
hints: What does acetylation do to how tightly DNA is wound?
questions.solution:
Acetylation loosens the association of DNA with histones (chromatin less condensed) [B1]
Transcription factors / RNA polymerase can bind, increasing transcription. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how environmental factors can change gene expression without changing the DNA base sequence. (2)
hints: Give an example of an environmental factor.
questions.solution:
Factors such as diet / stress / toxins cause epigenetic changes, e.g. DNA methylation or histone modification [B1]
These increase or decrease transcription of genes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why oestrogen can enter cells directly but insulin cannot. (2)
hints: What type of molecule is insulin?
questions.solution:
Oestrogen is lipid-soluble, so diffuses through the phospholipid bilayer [B1]
Insulin is a large, polar protein, so it cannot cross the bilayer and binds to surface receptors instead. [B1]

questions.prompt: Steroid hormones are carried in the blood bound to proteins. Suggest why. (2)
questions.solution:
Steroid hormones are hydrophobic / insoluble in water [B1]
So they are carried bound to proteins to be transported in the plasma. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why oestrogen only affects certain target cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Only target cells have receptors for oestrogen [B1]
The receptor's binding site has a shape complementary to oestrogen. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug has a shape similar to a hormone and binds to its receptor without activating it. Explain how this blocks the hormone's effect. (2)
questions.solution:
Drug binds to the receptor's binding site (competitively) [B1]
So the hormone cannot bind and the response is not triggered. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how oestrogen stimulates transcription of a target gene. (2)
hints: What does oestrogen bind to inside the cell?
Where does that complex then bind?
questions.solution:
Oestrogen binds to a receptor that is part of a transcription factor, changing its shape [B1]
The activated transcription factor binds to the promoter, so RNA polymerase can transcribe the gene. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a repressor protein can prevent transcription of a gene. (2)
questions.solution:
Binds to the promoter / DNA near the gene [B1]
Prevents RNA polymerase or transcription factors binding. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutation changes the DNA-binding region of a hormone receptor. Suggest the effect on expression of the target gene. (2)
hints: Can the receptor still bind the hormone?
questions.solution:
The hormone–receptor complex cannot bind to the promoter [B1]
So the target gene is not transcribed even when the hormone is present. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some cancers involve tumour suppressor genes silenced by histone deacetylation. Explain how a drug that inhibits histone deacetylase could treat these cancers. (3)
hints: What does acetylation do to chromatin?
What happens to the tumour suppressor genes?
questions.solution:
Histones remain acetylated, so chromatin stays less condensed [B1]
Transcription factors can access the tumour suppressor genes, which are transcribed [B1]
Tumour suppressor proteins slow cell division / cause apoptosis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how increased methylation can silence a tumour suppressor gene. (3)
questions.solution:
Methyl groups added to cytosine bases in the gene's promoter [B1]
Transcription factors / RNA polymerase cannot bind [B1]
Gene not transcribed, so no tumour suppressor protein. [B1]

questions.prompt: A drug that removes methyl groups from DNA helps only some patients with a type of cancer. Suggest why. (3)
hints: Are all cancers of this type caused by methylation?
What if the gene itself is mutated?
questions.solution:
In some patients the cancer is caused by methylation of tumour suppressor genes, which the drug reverses [B1]
In others, the tumour suppressor gene has a mutation, so removing methyl groups doesn't restore a working protein [B1]
Or other genes / oncogenes are involved. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two RNAi treatments, X and Y, were tested on cells infected with a virus. The table shows virus antigen concentration as a percentage of untreated cells (± 2 SD). Evaluate X and Y as possible treatments for the infection in humans. (5)
hints: Which is better early, which later?
questions.solution:
At 2 weeks X reduces antigen more than Y, but the ranges overlap (20–40 vs 35–55), so not clearly different [B1]
At 8 weeks Y keeps antigen lower; ranges don't overlap (32–48 vs 45–75), so Y is significantly better long-term [B1]
X's effect wears off [B1]
Neither removes the virus completely (still 40–60% of control) [B1]
Tested in cells, not humans — delivery, side effects and long-term safety unknown. [B1]

questions.prompt: An RNAi drug that silences a liver gene lowered LDL cholesterol by 50% after 6 months in 1500 patients, compared with 30% for a standard statin. The RNAi drug is injected twice a year; the statin is a daily tablet. Evaluate the RNAi drug. (5)
questions.solution:
Larger reduction in LDL (50% vs 30%) [B1]
Large sample (1500) makes results reliable [B1]
Only two injections a year — easier to keep to than daily tablets [B1]
But injection needed / cost unknown [B1]
Long-term side effects and effects on heart disease (not just LDL) unknown. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two antiviral drugs were tested in patients. Drug P reduced viral load by 90% but 20% of patients had side effects. Drug Q reduced viral load by 70% with side effects in 2%. Evaluate which drug should be used. (5)
questions.solution:
Drug P is more effective at reducing viral load [B1]
But many more patients have side effects [B1]
Drug Q is safer and still fairly effective [B1]
Choice may depend on severity of the infection / seriousness of the side effects [B1]
Need sample sizes / significance / long-term outcomes / resistance data. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why inheriting one faulty copy of a tumour suppressor gene greatly increases the risk of cancer. (3)
hints: How many working copies are left?
What if the remaining copy mutates?
questions.solution:
Only one functional copy remains in every cell [B1]
A mutation in that copy in any cell leaves no functional tumour suppressor protein [B1]
So that cell can divide uncontrollably, forming a tumour. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some tumour suppressor genes code for proteins that repair damaged DNA. Explain how mutations in these genes can lead to cancer. (3)
hints: What happens to DNA damage if it isn't repaired?
Which genes may then be affected?
questions.solution:
Faulty protein cannot repair DNA damage [B1]
Mutations accumulate, including in genes that control cell division (oncogenes / other tumour suppressors) [B1]
Leading to uncontrolled cell division / tumours. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why mutations in tumour suppressor genes usually need to affect both alleles to cause cancer, whereas a mutation in one allele of a proto-oncogene can be enough. (3)
hints: Can one working tumour suppressor allele do its job?
What does an oncogene allele do?
questions.solution:
One functional tumour suppressor allele still makes enough protein to control division, so both must be mutated [B1]
A mutated proto-oncogene (oncogene) is permanently switched on [B1]
So a single copy can stimulate uncontrolled division. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a drug with a similar shape to oestrogen can treat breast cancers that depend on oestrogen. (3)
questions.solution:
Drug binds to the oestrogen receptor (complementary shape) [B1]
Oestrogen cannot bind / the receptor is not activated [B1]
So genes that stimulate cell division are not transcribed — tumour growth slows. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why drugs that block oestrogen receptors don't work on breast cancers whose cells lack oestrogen receptors. (3)
hints: What does the drug act on?
questions.solution:
The drug works by binding to oestrogen receptors [B1]
These cells have no oestrogen receptors [B1]
Their growth is not oestrogen-dependent, so blocking oestrogen has no effect. [B1]

questions.prompt: Some drugs stop the body making oestrogen. Explain how this can treat oestrogen-dependent breast cancer. (3)
hints: Less oestrogen means fewer of what?
questions.solution:
Less oestrogen available to bind to receptors [B1]
Fewer transcription factors activated [B1]
Less transcription of genes promoting cell division, so the tumour grows more slowly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a raised blood level of a tumour marker does not always mean a person has cancer. (2)
hints: What else could raise the level?
questions.solution:
Other conditions (e.g. infection, inflammation, benign growths) can raise the marker [B1]
Levels vary naturally between people / with age. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a normal blood level of a tumour marker does not rule out cancer. (2)
hints: Do all cancers produce the marker?
questions.solution:
Some cancers do not produce the marker [B1]
Small / early tumours may not produce enough to raise the level. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a positive screening test for cancer is usually followed by further tests. (2)
questions.solution:
Screening tests can give false positives [B1]
Further tests (e.g. biopsy / scans) confirm whether cancer is present. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how a drug that inhibits DNA methyltransferase could reactivate a silenced tumour suppressor gene. (3)
hints: What does the enzyme normally do?
questions.solution:
Less methylation of the gene's promoter (new methyl groups not added) [B1]
Transcription factors / RNA polymerase can bind [B1]
Gene is transcribed, so tumour suppressor protein is made, slowing cell division. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one risk of using drugs that reverse epigenetic changes to treat cancer, and explain it. (3)
hints: Do the drugs act only on one gene?
Which other genes could be switched on?
questions.solution:
Drugs affect methylation of many genes, not just the target [B1]
Could switch on genes that should be silent, e.g. oncogenes [B1]
Also act on healthy cells, causing side effects. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why epigenetic changes can be reversed by drugs but gene mutations cannot. (3)
hints: Do epigenetic changes alter the base sequence?
questions.solution:
Epigenetic changes do not change the DNA base sequence [B1]
They are chemical tags (methyl groups, histone modifications) added / removed by enzymes [B1]
Drugs can alter these enzymes, but a mutation is a change in the sequence itself. [B1]

questions.prompt: The KRAS gene codes for a protein that relays signals stimulating cell division. Mutated KRAS is an oncogene. Suggest and explain how a mutation in KRAS could cause a tumour. (3)
hints: What happens to the protein if it is permanently 'on'?
Do the signals still need to be present?
questions.solution:
Mutation changes the base sequence, so a protein with a different tertiary structure is made [B1]
The protein is permanently active / always relays the signal, even without a signal [B1]
So cells divide rapidly and uncontrollably (mitosis), forming a tumour. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how mutation of a tumour suppressor gene can lead to the development of a tumour. (3)
hints: What does the normal protein do?
questions.solution:
Mutation changes the base sequence, so the protein is not made / is non-functional [B1]
Normally the protein slows cell division / causes apoptosis or DNA repair [B1]
So cell division is uncontrolled / cells with damaged DNA survive, forming a tumour. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how hypermethylation of a tumour suppressor gene can lead to cancer. (3)
questions.solution:
Methyl groups are added to the DNA (cytosine bases) of the gene [B1]
Transcription factors / RNA polymerase can't bind, so the gene isn't transcribed [B1]
Tumour suppressor protein isn't made, so cell division is uncontrolled. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the DNA sequence inserted with the spider gene so it is only expressed in the silk glands. (1)
questions.solution: A promoter (specific to silk-gland cells). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the proteins that bind to the promoter region to start transcription of a gene. (1)
questions.solution: Transcription factors. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of molecule that can bind to mRNA and cause it to be broken down, preventing translation. (1)
questions.solution: siRNA (small interfering RNA). [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why it was important that the spider silk gene was expressed only in the silk glands. (2)
hints: What if all cells made it?
questions.solution:
So the protein is secreted into the silk / can be collected [B1]
Production in other cells would waste energy / resources or harm the silkworm. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how increased methylation of tumour suppressor genes can lead to cancer. (3)
hints: What does methylation do to transcription?
What does the protein do normally?
questions.solution:
Methylation of DNA prevents transcription factors binding / prevents transcription [B1]
Tumour suppressor protein not made [B1]
So cell division is not slowed / uncontrolled cell division, forming a tumour. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how decreased methylation (hypomethylation) of an oncogene can lead to cancer. (3)
questions.solution:
Less methylation means the gene is transcribed more / switched on [B1]
More protein that stimulates cell division [B1]
Uncontrolled / rapid cell division — tumour. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how high oestrogen concentration can increase the risk of some breast cancers. (3)
questions.solution:
Oestrogen binds to receptors / transcription factor, activating it [B1]
Transcription factor binds to promoter of genes that cause cell division [B1]
Increased / uncontrolled cell division, forming a tumour. [B1]

questions.prompt: The ATM gene codes for a protein that detects DNA damage and stops the cell cycle until it's repaired. Predict the effects of a non-functional ATM gene. (3)
questions.solution:
DNA damage not detected / repaired [B1]
Cell cycle not stopped, so cells with mutations continue to divide [B1]
Mutations accumulate (e.g. in oncogenes / tumour suppressors), increasing risk of tumours. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two differences between benign and malignant tumours. (3)
questions.solution:
Benign grow slowly; malignant grow rapidly [B1]
Benign stay in one place / are encapsulated; malignant spread (metastasis) [B1]
Benign cells are differentiated / normal nuclei; malignant cells unspecialised / large nuclei. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mutation in a tumour suppressor gene is often recessive, but a mutation that creates an oncogene is dominant. Explain why. (3)
hints: One working copy of a tumour suppressor is enough?
questions.solution:
One normal tumour suppressor allele still produces enough protein to control division [B1]
Both alleles must be mutated for uncontrolled division [B1]
One oncogene allele is enough to keep stimulating division. [B1]

questions.prompt: Foreign DNA was inserted into poplar trees to reduce the expression of the aquaporin gene. Transgenic trees had about 15% of the normal level of aquaporin protein. What can you conclude about the foreign DNA? (3)
hints: How could DNA reduce protein production?
questions.solution:
The foreign DNA reduced the production of aquaporin (by 85%) [B1]
It may code for RNA that binds to the aquaporin mRNA (RNA interference) [B1]
So less mRNA translated / mRNA broken down, but not completely. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how siRNA can reduce the expression of a gene. (3)
questions.solution:
siRNA associates with proteins / enzyme [B1]
Binds to complementary bases on the target mRNA [B1]
mRNA is cut / broken down, so it isn't translated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how transcription of a gene can be stimulated by a transcription factor. (3)
questions.solution:
Transcription factor moves from the cytoplasm into the nucleus [B1]
Binds to the promoter region of the gene [B1]
Allows RNA polymerase to bind and start transcription. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the transgenic trees still produced some aquaporin. (1)
questions.solution: Not all the mRNA was broken down / other genes also code for aquaporin. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why an siRNA only affects one gene. (1)
questions.solution: It is complementary to the base sequence of only that gene's mRNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: A gene codes for a transcription factor that stimulates production of the surface protein targeted by a drug. In some patients a mutation makes this transcription factor non-functional, and the drug destroys fewer of their cancer cells. Suggest how the mutation causes this. (3)
hints: What does the transcription factor bind to?
Less protein on the surface means?
questions.solution:
Non-functional transcription factor can't bind to the promoter of the surface-protein gene [B1]
So less transcription / less protein made and placed on the cell surface [B1]
Fewer antibodies (drug) can bind, so fewer cancer cells destroyed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a mutation in a promoter region could increase the expression of a gene. (3)
questions.solution:
Promoter sequence changed [B1]
Transcription factors / RNA polymerase bind more easily [B1]
More transcription, more mRNA, more protein. [B1]

questions.prompt: Cells were treated with siRNA targeting the gene for protein X. On a gel, the band for protein X was large at 0 hours, smaller at 48 hours and absent at 72 hours; the band for a control protein stayed the same. Suggest how the siRNA produced these results. (3)
questions.solution:
siRNA binds to complementary mRNA for protein X, which is broken down [B1]
No new protein X translated; existing protein broken down over time, so band decreases [B1]
Control protein band unchanged — siRNA is specific / same amount of protein loaded. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a gene silenced by siRNA still has its DNA unchanged. (3)
questions.solution:
siRNA targets mRNA, not DNA [B1]
Acts after transcription [B1]
Translation prevented, so protein not made, but gene sequence is unchanged. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how siRNA could be used to treat a disease caused by a dominant harmful allele. (3)
hints: Can it be targeted to one allele?
questions.solution:
Design siRNA complementary to the mRNA of the harmful allele only [B1]
mRNA broken down, so harmful protein isn't made [B1]
Normal allele still expressed. [B1]

questions.prompt: The amount of mRNA for an enzyme was measured in bacterial cultures at different pH. Explain why this estimates expression of the gene but not growth of the population. (4)
hints: Does more mRNA mean more cells?
questions.solution:
mRNA is produced by transcription, so shows how much the gene is being expressed [B1]
But more mRNA could come from more transcription per cell or more cells [B1]
Number of cells not measured [B1]
mRNA may not all be translated, so not a direct measure of protein either. [B1]

questions.prompt: A non-coding control region of mitochondrial DNA stimulates synthesis of mitochondrial DNA and mRNA. Suggest two ways a mutation in this region could increase the activity of a mitochondrial enzyme. (2)
questions.solution:
More transcription, so more mRNA and more enzyme made [B1]
More mtDNA / more mitochondria, so more enzyme. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a mutation in a non-coding region of DNA can still affect the phenotype. (2)
questions.solution:
Non-coding regions include promoters / regulatory sequences [B1]
Mutation alters binding of transcription factors / RNA polymerase, changing how much protein is made. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a mutation in an intron usually has no effect on the protein produced. (2)
questions.solution:
Introns are removed from pre-mRNA during splicing [B1]
So they aren't translated into the amino acid sequence. [B1]

questions.prompt: Increased methylation of the promoter of a tumour suppressor gene is passed to daughter cells. An enzyme (DNMT) adds the methyl groups. A substance in green tea is a competitive inhibitor of DNMT. Suggest how it allows the tumour suppressor gene to be transcribed in daughter cells. (3)
hints: What happens to methylation in new DNA?
questions.solution:
Inhibitor binds to DNMT's active site, so less methylation of the promoter in new DNA [B1]
Transcription factors / RNA polymerase can bind to the promoter [B1]
Gene transcribed, mRNA made, tumour suppressor protein produced. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how acetylation of histones affects gene expression. (3)
questions.solution:
Acetylation loosens the association of DNA with histones / less condensed chromatin [B1]
Transcription factors and RNA polymerase can access the promoter [B1]
So the gene is transcribed (switched on). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by epigenetics and why epigenetic changes can be inherited by daughter cells. (3)
questions.solution:
Heritable changes in gene function without changes to the base sequence [B1]
Caused by changes in the environment (e.g. methylation / histone acetylation) [B1]
Tags are copied when DNA replicates / by enzymes, so daughter cells inherit them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Plants were given an extra gene that produces antisense mRNA complementary to the mRNA of the sucrose transporter gene. Explain how this reduces expression of the transporter gene. (4)
hints: Base pairing between the two mRNAs.
questions.solution:
Antisense mRNA is complementary to the sense mRNA [B1]
It binds to the sense mRNA by base pairing, forming double-stranded RNA [B1]
Ribosomes can't bind / tRNA can't bind, so it isn't translated [B1]
Less transporter protein made. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two ways gene expression can be controlled after transcription in eukaryotes. (4)
questions.solution:
Splicing of pre-mRNA — removing introns [B1]
Alternative splicing gives different proteins [B1]
RNA interference — siRNA binds to complementary mRNA [B1]
mRNA cut / broken down, so not translated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how oestrogen stimulates transcription of a target gene. (4)
questions.solution:
Oestrogen diffuses through the cell membrane (lipid-soluble) [B1]
Binds to a receptor on a transcription factor, changing its shape [B1]
Transcription factor can then bind to the promoter / DNA [B1]
Stimulates RNA polymerase to transcribe the gene. [B1]

questions.prompt: An enhancer in a transferred DNA fragment only stimulates the gene in the milk-producing glands of goats. Suggest two reasons why this is important. (2)
questions.solution:
The protein is secreted in milk, so it's easy to collect / purify [B1]
Not made in other tissues where it could harm the goat / waste resources. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how an enhancer region can increase transcription of a gene. (2)
questions.solution:
Specific transcription factors (activators) bind to the enhancer [B1]
Helps RNA polymerase bind to the promoter, increasing transcription. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how induced pluripotent stem cells are produced and one advantage over embryonic stem cells. (4)
questions.solution:
Adult (unipotent) body cells are taken [B1]
Genes for specific transcription factors are introduced / switched on [B1]
These reactivate genes, making cells pluripotent [B1]
Advantage: no embryo destroyed / patient's own cells so no rejection. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two proteins are only made by heart muscle cells: one forms gap junctions between them, and one is a transcription factor for heart genes. Suggest how these proteins could show that stem cells had become working heart muscle. (2)
questions.solution:
Gap-junction protein shows new cells can connect and contract in coordination with others [B1]
Transcription factor shows heart-specific genes are being expressed / cells have differentiated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cells with the same genes can differentiate into different cell types. (2)
questions.solution:
Different genes are switched on / off in different cells [B1]
So different proteins are made, giving different structures / functions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how scientists could confirm that new heart cells came from the injected stem cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Label stem cells with a fluorescent marker / marker gene [B1]
Look for the marker in new heart muscle cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: A gene involved in lip development can be methylated as a result of inflammation. Describe one effect methylation could have on the gene. (1)
questions.solution: Methylation prevents transcription factors binding, so the gene is not transcribed / switched off. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the effect of decreased acetylation of histones on gene expression. (1)
questions.solution: DNA binds more tightly to histones, so transcription factors can't access it — gene switched off. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one environmental factor that can cause epigenetic changes. (1)
questions.solution: Diet / stress / toxins / smoking / inflammation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the two-hit hypothesis applies to tumour suppressor genes in cancer. (3)
questions.solution:
Tumour suppressor genes are recessive — one working allele is enough [B1]
First hit: one allele mutated (inherited or acquired) [B1]
Second hit: other allele mutated / methylated — no functional protein, uncontrolled division. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the genome and the proteome of a cell. (2)
hints: One is about DNA, the other about proteins.
questions.solution:
Genome: the complete set of genes / DNA in a cell [B1]
Proteome: the full range of proteins that a cell is able to produce. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the proteome of a human cell contains more proteins than the number of genes in its genome. (2)
hints: Can one gene give more than one mRNA?
Can proteins be modified after translation?
questions.solution:
Alternative splicing — one gene can produce several different mRNAs / proteins [B1]
Proteins can be modified after translation (e.g. in the Golgi). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why sequencing the genome of a bacterium allows its proteome to be predicted, but this is much harder for humans. (2)
hints: What else is in human DNA?
questions.solution:
Bacteria have little non-coding DNA / no introns, so the base sequence translates directly [B1]
Human DNA contains introns, non-coding DNA and regulatory genes, and splicing varies. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term genome and give one use of sequencing a pathogen's genome. (2)
hints: Genome means the complete set of…
How could it help with vaccines?
questions.solution:
Genome: the complete set of genes / DNA in a cell or organism [B1]
Use: identify antigens for vaccines / track spread / compare relationships. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term proteome. (1)
hints: All the proteins a cell can make.
questions.solution: The full range of proteins a cell is able to produce. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the term genome. (1)
questions.solution: The complete set of genes / DNA in a cell. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why comparing whole genomes is useful for working out evolutionary relationships. (1)
questions.solution: Base sequences can be compared directly, giving very detailed evidence of relatedness. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how comparing mitochondrial genes can show that a group of lizards is genetically distinct, and how modern techniques make this comparison quick. (3)
questions.solution:
Compare the base sequences of the genes [B1]
More differences = less closely related / distinct group [B1]
DNA sequencing is now automated / high-throughput, so it is faster and cheaper. [B1]

questions.prompt: A bacterium has about 4.6 million base pairs and about 4000 genes. Explain why its proteome is easier to determine than that of a eukaryote. (2)
questions.solution:
Little non-coding DNA / no introns, so the genome translates directly to the proteome [B1]
Fewer genes / smaller genome / no alternative splicing. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why knowing the genome of a complex organism does not easily tell us its proteome. (2)
hints: Can one gene make several proteins?
questions.solution:
Lots of non-coding DNA / introns and regulatory genes [B1]
Alternative splicing means one gene can code for several proteins. [B1]

questions.prompt: Define the terms genome and proteome. (2)
questions.solution:
Genome — the complete set of genes / DNA in a cell [B1]
Proteome — the full range of proteins a cell is able to produce. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how determining the proteomes of disease-causing bacteria has helped protect people from infectious diseases. (2)
hints: Which proteins are on the surface?
What can they be used to make?
questions.solution:
Identifies antigens (surface proteins) [B1]
Used to develop vaccines / herd immunity. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how sequencing the genomes of pathogens helps identify new strains during an outbreak. (2)
questions.solution:
Compare base sequences to identify mutations / differences between strains [B1]
Rapid sequencing allows tracking spread / vaccines to be updated. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what VNTRs are and why they are useful in genetic fingerprinting. (4)
questions.solution:
Variable number tandem repeats — non-coding base sequences repeated next to each other [B1]
Number of repeats varies between individuals [B1]
Probability of two people having the same VNTR pattern is very low (except identical twins) [B1]
Inherited, so related people share more of the same VNTRs. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two techniques used to analyse viral DNA and show how related different viruses are. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: PCR; DNA sequencing; gel electrophoresis; restriction mapping / genetic fingerprinting; DNA hybridisation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how determining the genome of a virus could allow a vaccine to be developed. (2)
hints: Which genes code for surface proteins?
What is used in the vaccine?
questions.solution:
Identify genes for antigens / surface proteins [B1]
Produce these antigens (e.g. by genetic engineering) for use in a vaccine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Complete the definitions: the genome is the complete set of __ in a cell; the proteome is the full range of __ a cell can produce. (2)
questions.solution:
Genome — genes / DNA [B1]
Proteome — proteins. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the proteome of a human is larger than the number of genes. (2)
questions.solution:
Alternative splicing of pre-mRNA produces different mRNAs from one gene [B1]
Proteins can be modified after translation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why different cells in the same body have the same genome but different proteomes. (2)
questions.solution:
All cells have the same DNA [B1]
Different genes are switched on / expressed in different cell types. [B1]

questions.prompt: What are non-coding multiple repeats (VNTRs), and why are they useful in genetic fingerprinting? (2)
hints: Where are they found and what do they code for?
Is the number of repeats the same in everyone?
questions.solution:
Short base sequences repeated many times, found between genes (non-coding) [B1]
Number of repeats varies between individuals, giving a unique pattern. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one ethical objection to using embryonic stem cells in research. (1)
hints: Where do embryonic stem cells come from?
questions.solution: Embryos are destroyed (which some people believe have a right to life). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of reverse transcriptase when producing DNA from mRNA. (1)
questions.solution: Uses mRNA as a template to make complementary (c)DNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of a restriction endonuclease in gene technology. (1)
questions.solution: Cuts DNA at a specific recognition (base) sequence, often leaving sticky ends. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of DNA ligase in gene technology. (1)
questions.solution: Joins DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of primers in PCR. (1)
hints: What can't DNA polymerase do without them?
questions.solution: Bind to the start of the target sequence so DNA polymerase can attach and begin copying. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a heat-stable DNA polymerase is used in PCR. (1)
hints: What temperature is used to separate the strands?
What would happen to a normal enzyme?
questions.solution: It is not denatured by the high temperature (95 °C) used in each cycle. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why free nucleotides are added to a PCR mixture. (1)
hints: What are the new strands made from?
questions.solution: To be joined by DNA polymerase into new strands complementary to the templates. [B1]

questions.prompt: Before using RT-PCR to measure the mRNA for a gene, the sample is treated to remove DNA. Explain why. (2)
hints: What are you trying to measure?
questions.solution:
DNA in the sample would also be copied / amplified by PCR [B1]
So results would not reflect only the mRNA / how much the gene is expressed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why mRNA must be converted into cDNA before it can be amplified by PCR. (2)
hints: What template does DNA polymerase use?
questions.solution:
DNA polymerase copies DNA, not RNA [B1]
cDNA is a stable DNA copy of the mRNA that can be amplified. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the amount of PCR product stops increasing after many cycles. (1)
questions.solution: Primers / nucleotides are used up (or the enzyme loses activity). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the temperature is lowered to about 55 °C during each PCR cycle. (1)
questions.solution: So primers can anneal / bind to the single DNA strands. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the mixture is heated to 95 °C at the start of each PCR cycle. (1)
questions.solution: Breaks hydrogen bonds, separating the two DNA strands. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why several different primers are used to detect all strains of a virus with PCR. (2)
hints: Do strains have identical base sequences?
questions.solution:
Strains have different base sequences (viruses mutate rapidly) [B1]
A primer must be complementary to bind, so a variety is needed to detect all strains. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a DNA probe designed for one strain of a virus may not detect another strain. (2)
questions.solution:
Probe binds by complementary base pairing to a specific sequence [B1]
Another strain has a different base sequence, so the probe isn't complementary. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a DNA probe designed to detect a single-base substitution might also bind to the normal allele. (2)
hints: Does a probe need a perfect match to bind?
questions.solution:
The probe differs from the normal allele by only one base [B1]
So it is still mostly complementary and can hybridise to the normal allele. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a DNA probe can be used to detect a particular allele. (2)
questions.solution:
Single-stranded DNA complementary to part of the allele, labelled (fluorescent / radioactive) [B1]
Binds (hybridises) to the allele by base pairing, so the label shows it is present. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the DNA being tested must be made single-stranded before a DNA probe is used. (2)
hints: What holds the double helix together?
questions.solution:
The probe binds by complementary base pairing to exposed bases [B1]
Heating breaks the hydrogen bonds so the bases are available. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a gene is inserted into a plasmid. (2)
questions.solution:
Same restriction enzyme cuts the plasmid and the gene, producing complementary sticky ends [B1]
DNA ligase joins them, forming phosphodiester bonds. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the same restriction enzyme is used to cut both the plasmid and the DNA containing the gene. (2)
hints: What kind of ends does it make?
questions.solution:
It cuts at the same recognition sequence, producing complementary sticky ends [B1]
So the sticky ends of the gene and plasmid can base pair. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how marker genes are used to identify bacteria that have taken up a recombinant plasmid. (2)
hints: What extra gene is on the plasmid?
questions.solution:
Plasmid carries a marker gene, e.g. antibiotic resistance or a fluorescence gene [B1]
Grow bacteria on antibiotic (only transformed survive) or look for fluorescence. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how DNA fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis. (2)
questions.solution:
DNA is negatively charged (phosphate groups), so moves towards the positive electrode [B1]
Smaller fragments move further through the gel. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why DNA moves towards the positive electrode in gel electrophoresis, and why fragments of different lengths separate. (2)
hints: Which part of DNA is charged?
How does the gel affect movement?
questions.solution:
Phosphate groups give DNA a negative charge [B1]
The gel resists larger fragments more, so they move more slowly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells could be used to replace damaged retinal cells. (2)
hints: Where could iPS cells come from?
What would they be turned into?
questions.solution:
iPS cells made from the patient's own body (e.g. skin) cells [B1]
Differentiated into retinal / cone cells and transplanted into the eye. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how gene therapy could correct an inherited form of colour blindness. (2)
hints: What must be added to cone cells?
questions.solution:
A functional allele for the cone pigment is inserted into cone cells using a vector (e.g. a virus) [B1]
Cells then produce the correct pigment. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give advantages and disadvantages of gene therapy for treating cystic fibrosis. (3)
questions.solution:
Advantage: corrects the cause (adds a functional allele) rather than treating symptoms [B1]
Disadvantage: effect is temporary as lung cells are replaced, so treatment must be repeated [B1]
Disadvantage: immune response to the vector / allele may be inserted into the wrong place. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why gene therapy on gametes or embryos (germ-line therapy) is controversial. (3)
questions.solution:
The change is passed to all future generations [B1]
Long-term effects are unknown [B1]
Future generations cannot consent / concerns about 'designer babies'. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare somatic gene therapy with germ-line gene therapy. (3)
hints: Which cells are altered in each?
questions.solution:
Both insert a functional allele into cells [B1]
Somatic: body cells only — not inherited, may need repeating [B1]
Germ-line: gametes / embryo — inherited by all descendants, raising more ethical concerns. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a bone marrow transplant from a healthy donor can be an effective long-term treatment for sickle cell disease. (3)
hints: What do bone marrow stem cells produce?
How long do they keep doing this?
questions.solution:
Donor bone marrow contains stem cells with the normal haemoglobin allele [B1]
They divide and differentiate into red blood cells with normal haemoglobin [B1]
Stem cells keep dividing throughout life, so normal red cells are produced long-term. [B1]

questions.prompt: Before a bone marrow transplant for sickle cell disease, the patient's own bone marrow is destroyed. Explain why. (3)
hints: What do the patient's own stem cells make?
Could the patient's immune cells attack the donor cells?
questions.solution:
Removes stem cells producing faulty (sickle) red blood cells [B1]
Gives space for donor stem cells to establish [B1]
Destroys the patient's immune cells, reducing rejection of donor cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a gene therapy trial for sickle cell disease, the patient's own stem cells were given a normal β-globin allele. The percentage of normal haemoglobin in their blood was 30% at 3 months, 45% at 6 months, 46% at 12 months and 47% at 15 months. Evaluate the conclusion that this gene therapy will be more effective long-term than a bone marrow transplant from a donor. (3)
hints: How does 47% compare with a donor transplant?
questions.solution:
Level is stable from 6 to 15 months, suggesting modified stem cells keep producing normal haemoglobin [B1]
Uses the patient's own cells, so no rejection and no need for a matched donor [B1]
But only about 47% normal haemoglobin, less than a successful donor transplant / only one patient followed for 15 months — long-term effects unknown. [B1]

questions.prompt: Evaluate the use of viruses as vectors to deliver a normal allele in gene therapy. (3)
hints: How do viruses get genes into cells?
questions.solution:
Advantage: viruses efficiently enter cells and deliver DNA [B1]
Disadvantage: may trigger an immune response [B1]
Disadvantage: the allele may insert into the wrong place in the genome, disrupting other genes (e.g. causing cancer). [B1]

questions.prompt: Gene therapy using the patient's own cells corrected 40% of red blood cells in 10 patients after one year, with no rejection. A donor transplant can correct nearly all red cells but has a 10% risk of serious rejection. Evaluate which treatment is better. (3)
questions.solution:
Donor transplant is more effective (nearly all cells corrected) [B1]
Gene therapy is safer — no rejection and no need for a donor [B1]
Small sample / only one year of data, so long-term effectiveness and safety of gene therapy unknown. [B1]

questions.prompt: What is a primer, as used in PCR? (2)
hints: How long is it and is it single-stranded?
questions.solution:
Short, single-stranded piece of DNA [B1]
Complementary to the start of the target sequence, allowing DNA polymerase to bind. [B1]

questions.prompt: What are VNTRs? (2)
hints: What does the abbreviation stand for?
questions.solution:
Variable number tandem repeats — short non-coding base sequences repeated many times [B1]
The number of repeats varies between individuals. [B1]

questions.prompt: What is a DNA probe? (2)
questions.solution:
Short single-stranded DNA with a base sequence complementary to the target [B1]
Labelled (e.g. fluorescent or radioactive) so it can be detected. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how restriction enzymes cut DNA into fragments. (2)
questions.solution:
Cut at specific recognition sequences (often palindromic) [B1]
Hydrolyse phosphodiester bonds, leaving sticky or blunt ends. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why different restriction enzymes cut DNA at different sites. (2)
hints: What must the active site match?
questions.solution:
Each enzyme has an active site with a specific shape [B1]
Complementary only to one particular base sequence (recognition site). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why DNA fragments produced by the same restriction enzymes differ in length between individuals. (2)
questions.solution:
Base sequences differ, so recognition sites are in different positions [B1]
Different numbers of repeats (VNTRs) between sites. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why DNA is heated to about 95 °C before a DNA probe is added. (1)
questions.solution: Breaks hydrogen bonds, separating the strands so the probe can base-pair with exposed bases. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why DNA probes are labelled. (1)
hints: How would you know where it bound?
questions.solution: So the probe's location (and so the target sequence) can be detected. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why unbound probe is washed off before results are read. (1)
hints: Only bound probe should be seen.
questions.solution: So only probe that has hybridised to the target is detected (no false positive). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a DNA ladder is used to find the size of DNA fragments on an electrophoresis gel. (2)
questions.solution:
Ladder contains fragments of known sizes [B1]
Run alongside the samples — compare how far sample fragments moved with the ladder bands. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why smaller DNA fragments move further through a gel during electrophoresis. (2)
hints: What does the gel act like?
Which fragments get through more easily?
questions.solution:
The gel is a mesh / has small pores [B1]
Smaller fragments meet less resistance, so move faster and further. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why all samples on a gel are run at the same voltage and for the same time. (2)
hints: What affects how far fragments move?
questions.solution:
Distance moved depends on voltage and time [B1]
So distances can be compared fairly with the ladder / between samples. [B1]

questions.prompt: On a gel, volunteer A had bands at 250 and 400 base pairs, B at 535, C at 300, and D had no bands. Which volunteers had a fragment of either 250 or 535 base pairs? (1)
questions.solution: A and B. [B1]

questions.prompt: A child has DNA bands at 120 and 340 base pairs. The mother has bands at 120 and 500. Man X has bands at 340 and 600; man Y at 200 and 450. Which man could be the father? (1)
hints: Which band didn't come from the mother?
questions.solution: Man X. [B1]

questions.prompt: DNA from a crime scene gave bands at 150, 300 and 450 base pairs. Suspect 1 gave 150, 300 and 450; suspect 2 gave 150, 280 and 450. Which suspect's DNA matches? (1)
questions.solution: Suspect 1. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons why the effects of gene therapy may not be permanent. (2)
hints: Is the new gene inserted into the chromosomes?
questions.solution:
Treated cells die and are replaced by untreated cells [B1]
The inserted gene may not be integrated into the DNA / may be destroyed by an immune response. [B1]

questions.prompt: Mice with an inherited kidney disease were given stem cells. The table shows the percentage of mice with protein in their urine after 20 weeks (40 mice per group). Evaluate the use of stem cells to treat this disease in humans. (4)
hints: What are the limits of mouse data?
questions.solution:
Healthy (wild-type) stem cells reduced the percentage with proteinuria (97.5% → 68%), so they had some effect [B1]
Stem cells from diseased mice had no effect, showing healthy alleles are needed [B1]
But most treated mice still had proteinuria — not a cure / effect partial [B1]
Mice not humans / donor cells may be rejected / long-term safety unknown; large groups (40) increase reliability. [B1]
questions.table:
Group | % with protein in urine
Healthy mice | 0
Diseased, untreated | 97.5
Diseased + own stem cells | 100
Diseased + healthy stem cells | 68

questions.prompt: Mice with muscular dystrophy were injected with healthy muscle stem cells. After 8 weeks, 30% of muscle fibres produced the missing protein, compared with 2% in untreated mice. Evaluate this as a treatment for humans. (4)
hints: What else would you want to know?
questions.solution:
Large increase in fibres making the protein (2% → 30%), supporting the treatment [B1]
But 70% of fibres still lack it — muscle function may not be restored [B1]
Mice not humans / sample size and statistics not given [B1]
Risk of rejection of donor cells / long-term effects unknown. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a trial, gene therapy restored 50% of normal enzyme activity in 8 of 10 patients for at least two years. Evaluate this treatment. (4)
questions.solution:
Most patients (80%) responded, and the effect lasted at least two years [B1]
50% activity may be enough to reduce symptoms (heterozygotes are often unaffected) [B1]
But two patients did not respond / small sample (10) [B1]
Long-term safety unknown (e.g. vector inserting in wrong place, immune response). [B1]

questions.prompt: Female mice with a kidney disease were given stem cells from healthy male mice. Later, some cells in their kidneys contained a Y chromosome. Suggest how the stem cells reduced the disease. (2)
hints: Where must the Y-containing cells have come from?
What did the stem cells become?
questions.solution:
Donor stem cells moved to the kidney and differentiated into kidney (glomerular) cells [B1]
These have the normal allele, so produce functional protein and repair the glomeruli. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why finding a Y chromosome in the cells of a female recipient shows that donor cells colonised that tissue. (2)
hints: Do female cells contain a Y chromosome?
questions.solution:
Female cells have no Y chromosome [B1]
So any cell containing a Y must have come from the male donor. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how transplanted healthy stem cells could repair a tissue damaged by a genetic disease. (2)
hints: What can stem cells divide and become?
What do they contain that the patient's cells lack?
questions.solution:
Stem cells divide and differentiate into the specialised cells of that tissue [B1]
They contain the functional allele, so make the normal protein and replace damaged cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a gene for human growth hormone could be made from mRNA. (2)
hints: Which enzyme makes DNA from RNA?
questions.solution:
Extract the mRNA from cells that make growth hormone (pituitary cells) [B1]
Use reverse transcriptase to make cDNA (then DNA polymerase makes it double-stranded). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how restriction enzymes and DNA ligase are used to insert a gene into a plasmid. (2)
questions.solution:
The same restriction enzyme cuts the plasmid and the gene, producing complementary sticky ends [B1]
DNA ligase joins them by forming phosphodiester bonds. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why promoter and terminator regions are added to a gene before it is inserted into a host. (2)
questions.solution:
Promoter allows RNA polymerase (and transcription factors) to bind so transcription starts [B1]
Terminator stops transcription at the end of the gene. [B1]

questions.prompt: A gene was inserted into a fish embryo after the zygote had divided several times. Explain why some of this fish's offspring did not have the gene. (2)
hints: Do all cells of the fish contain the gene?
What about the cells that make gametes?
questions.solution:
Only some cells received the gene (the fish is a mosaic) [B1]
Some gametes come from cells without the gene, so offspring from them lack it. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why inserting a gene into a fertilised egg (zygote) means every cell of the animal will contain the gene. (2)
hints: How are all body cells produced?
questions.solution:
All cells are produced from the zygote by mitosis [B1]
So the gene is copied into every cell, including those producing gametes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why transgenic plants are often regenerated from a single transformed cell. (2)
hints: What would a plant grown from one cell contain?
Will the gene be passed on?
questions.solution:
Every cell of the plant comes from that one cell by mitosis, so all contain the gene [B1]
Including cells that form gametes, so the gene is inherited. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a haematopoietic stem cell transplant can treat leukaemia. (3)
hints: What happens to the patient's bone marrow first?
What do donor stem cells do?
questions.solution:
Patient's bone marrow is destroyed (chemotherapy / radiotherapy), removing cancerous cells [B1]
Donor haematopoietic stem cells divide and differentiate into healthy blood cells [B1]
A tissue-matched donor reduces rejection. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why haematopoietic stem cells are described as multipotent. (3)
hints: How many cell types can they become?
questions.solution:
They can differentiate into a limited range of cell types [B1]
All the types of blood cell (red cells, white cells, platelets) [B1]
Not all body cell types, unlike pluripotent stem cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a successful haematopoietic stem cell transplant can provide lifelong treatment. (3)
questions.solution:
Stem cells can self-renew by dividing [B1]
So they keep producing new stem cells and differentiated blood cells [B1]
Blood cells are replaced throughout life. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why DNA for gene therapy is sometimes packaged inside liposomes. (1)
questions.solution: Liposomes can fuse with cell membranes to deliver DNA, and protect it from being broken down by enzymes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the stages of one cycle of PCR, giving the approximate temperature of each. (4)
questions.solution:
Heat to about 95 °C to separate the DNA strands (break hydrogen bonds) [B1]
Cool to about 55 °C so primers anneal to the strands [B1]
Heat to about 72 °C; DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides [B1]
Producing two copies of the DNA from one. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why PCR needs primers, a heat-stable DNA polymerase and free nucleotides. (4)
hints: Why must the enzyme survive heat?
questions.solution:
Primers bind to the start of the target sequence, so DNA polymerase can attach [B1]
Primers define which section is copied [B1]
Heat-stable DNA polymerase isn't denatured at 95 °C [B1]
Free nucleotides are joined to form the new complementary strands. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how PCR is used in genetic fingerprinting. (4)
questions.solution:
A small DNA sample is amplified by PCR to give enough DNA [B1]
The regions copied are VNTRs, which vary between individuals [B1]
Fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis [B1]
Band patterns are compared — the more similar, the more likely the samples are from the same / related people. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the number of DNA molecules doubles in each cycle of PCR. (2)
hints: How many templates does each molecule provide?
questions.solution:
Each DNA molecule separates into two strands [B1]
Each strand acts as a template for a new complementary strand, giving two molecules. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a graph of the number of DNA molecules against number of PCR cycles levels off. (2)
questions.solution:
Primers / nucleotides are used up [B1]
So no more new strands can be made (DNA polymerase may also lose activity). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a DNA microarray could be used to screen a person's DNA for many known harmful mutations at once. (4)
hints: How is the person's DNA prepared?
What is attached to the array?
questions.solution:
DNA extracted (e.g. from saliva), amplified by PCR and labelled with fluorescent tags [B1]
Made single-stranded [B1]
Added to an array with probes for each known mutation; DNA hybridises to complementary probes [B1]
Washed, then fluorescence shows which mutations are present. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a DNA probe can be used to find out whether a person carries a particular mutant allele. (4)
questions.solution:
Probe is single-stranded DNA complementary to the mutant allele, labelled (fluorescent / radioactive) [B1]
Person's DNA is amplified by PCR and made single-stranded [B1]
Probe added; it hybridises only if the mutant allele is present [B1]
Unbound probe washed off; label detected shows the allele is present. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the benefits and drawbacks of screening people for inherited mutations that increase cancer risk. (4)
hints: What can people do if they know?
questions.solution:
Benefit: people at risk can have regular check-ups / preventive treatment, so cancer detected early [B1]
Benefit: family members can also be tested [B1]
Drawback: anxiety / not everyone with the mutation develops cancer [B1]
Drawback: possible discrimination (e.g. insurance) / privacy concerns. [B1]

questions.prompt: Short tandem repeats (STRs) are repeated sequences of 2–7 base pairs found throughout the genome. Describe how one STR could be cut out of a DNA sample. (2)
hints: Which enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences?
questions.solution:
Use restriction endonucleases [B1]
That cut at recognition sequences either side of the STR. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why different restriction endonucleases cut DNA at different base sequences. (2)
questions.solution:
Each enzyme has an active site with a specific shape [B1]
Only complementary to one specific recognition sequence. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how sticky ends are produced and why they are useful. (2)
hints: What can pair with sticky ends?
questions.solution:
Restriction enzymes make a staggered cut, leaving unpaired bases [B1]
Complementary sticky ends can join by base pairing (sealed by ligase), e.g. to insert DNA into a plasmid. [B1]

questions.prompt: To copy one STR by PCR, scientists must know the base sequences on either side of it. Explain why. (2)
hints: What short pieces of DNA start PCR?
questions.solution:
To make primers [B1]
Primers are complementary to / bind to the flanking sequences, so only the STR between them is copied. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of DNA polymerase in PCR and why the enzyme used comes from bacteria living in hot springs. (2)
hints: What temperature is reached in PCR?
questions.solution:
DNA polymerase joins nucleotides to form the new strand (from the primer) [B1]
It is thermostable — not denatured at the high temperature (about 95 °C) used to separate strands. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why PCR uses repeated cycles of 95 °C, 55 °C and 72 °C. (2)
hints: What happens to the hydrogen bonds at 95 °C?
questions.solution:
95 °C separates the strands (breaks hydrogen bonds); 55 °C lets primers anneal [B1]
72 °C is the optimum for DNA polymerase to join nucleotides. [B1]

questions.prompt: A double-stranded DNA fragment 16 base pairs long is copied by PCR for 30 cycles. Calculate the total number of base pairs present at the end, assuming every cycle doubles the DNA. (2)
questions.solution:
2³⁰ = 1.074 × 10⁹ molecules [M1]
× 16 = 1.72 × 10¹⁰ base pairs. [A1]

questions.prompt: One double-stranded DNA molecule 20 base pairs long is copied by PCR for 25 cycles. Calculate the total number of base pairs at the end. (2)
questions.solution:
2²⁵ = 3.36 × 10⁷ molecules [M1]
× 20 = 6.71 × 10⁸ base pairs. [A1]

questions.prompt: One double-stranded DNA molecule 8 base pairs long is copied by PCR for 40 cycles. Calculate the total number of base pairs at the end. (2)
questions.solution:
2⁴⁰ = 1.10 × 10¹² molecules [M1]
× 8 = 8.80 × 10¹² base pairs. [A1]

questions.prompt: The number of repeats in an STR varies between people. Give two features of STR fragments that allow them to be separated by gel electrophoresis. (2)
questions.solution:
DNA is negatively charged (phosphate groups), so it moves towards the positive electrode [B1]
Fragments differ in length / number of repeats, so smaller ones move further through the gel. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the DNA bands on an electrophoresis gel are made visible. (2)
questions.solution:
Add a labelled DNA probe (radioactive / fluorescent) or a stain [B1]
Probe binds to complementary bases, shown by X-ray film / UV light. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two uses of genetic fingerprinting. (2)
questions.solution: Two from: forensic science / matching suspects; paternity testing; plant and animal breeding to avoid inbreeding; medical diagnosis. [B2]

questions.prompt: A linear DNA molecule is 10 kb long. Enzyme 1 cuts it 3 kb from the left end; enzyme 2 cuts it 7 kb from the left end. Give the fragment sizes after digestion with (i) enzyme 1 only and (ii) both enzymes, and how many bands each shows on a gel. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 3 kb and 7 kb — two bands [B1]
(ii) 3 kb, 4 kb and 3 kb — two bands (3 kb and 4 kb). [B1]

questions.prompt: A linear DNA molecule is 12 kb long. Enzyme 1 cuts at 2 kb and 9 kb from the left end. Give the fragment sizes and explain which will move furthest in electrophoresis. (2)
questions.solution:
2 kb, 7 kb and 3 kb [B1]
2 kb moves furthest — smallest fragments move fastest through the gel. [B1]

questions.prompt: A linear DNA molecule of 8 kb is cut by an enzyme, giving fragments of 5 kb and 3 kb. A second enzyme cuts the 5 kb fragment into 1 kb and 4 kb. How many bands would a double digest show, and what are their sizes? (2)
questions.solution:
Fragments: 1 kb, 4 kb and 3 kb [B1]
Three bands. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how the sizes of DNA fragments on a gel could be determined. (2)
hints: What do you run alongside the samples?
questions.solution:
Run a DNA ladder / fragments of known size alongside [B1]
Compare the distance travelled by the samples with the known fragments. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why DNA fragments move through an electrophoresis gel and why they separate. (2)
questions.solution:
Phosphate groups make DNA negatively charged, so it moves to the positive electrode [B1]
Smaller fragments move more easily through the gel, so travel further. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why DNA samples are loaded into wells at the negative electrode end of the gel. (2)
hints: What would happen at the other end?
questions.solution:
DNA is negatively charged and moves towards the positive electrode [B1]
So fragments travel through / across the whole gel and separate. [B1]

questions.prompt: A circular plasmid has one site for enzyme 1 and one site for enzyme 2. How many fragments are produced when it is cut with both enzymes? (1)
hints: A circle cut once stays one piece.

questions.prompt: A circular plasmid has three restriction sites for one enzyme. How many fragments are produced? (1)
A linear DNA molecule has three restriction sites for one enzyme. How many fragments are produced? (1)
Describe how a restriction endonuclease and DNA ligase are used to insert a gene into a plasmid. (2)
questions.solution:
Same restriction enzyme cuts the plasmid and the gene, giving complementary sticky ends [B1]
DNA ligase joins the sugar-phosphate backbones (phosphodiester bonds). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why marker genes are inserted into plasmids along with the target gene. (2)
hints: Not all bacteria take up the plasmid.
How do you find those that did?
questions.solution:
To identify cells that have taken up the plasmid / recombinant DNA [B1]
E.g. antibiotic resistance or fluorescence genes — only transformed cells grow / glow. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a promoter and terminator region are added to a gene inserted into a plasmid. (2)
questions.solution:
Promoter allows RNA polymerase (transcription factors) to bind so the gene is transcribed [B1]
Terminator stops transcription at the end of the gene. [B1]
