questions.prompt: Explain how a functional gene can be delivered to cells using a harmless virus in gene therapy, and suggest why the treatment may not be permanent. (5)
hints: How does a virus get its DNA into cells?
What happens to cells over time?
questions.solution:
Functional allele inserted into the virus (vector) [B1]
Virus infects target cells and injects DNA [B1]
Gene is transcribed and translated, producing the functional protein [B1]
Treatment may wear off as the cells die / are replaced, or the DNA isn't passed on [B1]
Immune response to virus may prevent repeat treatment. [B1]

questions.prompt: What is a DNA probe? (2)
hints: Is it single or double stranded?
questions.solution:
Short, single-stranded DNA complementary to a specific base sequence (allele) [B1]
Labelled with a radioactive or fluorescent marker. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a DNA probe can be used to find out whether a person carries a specific mutated allele. (2)
hints: Is the DNA separated into single strands?
questions.solution:
DNA is heated to separate strands, probe added and binds (hybridises) to the complementary mutated allele [B1]
Detected by fluorescence / autoradiography — signal shows the allele is present. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two uses of genetic screening using DNA probes. (2)
questions.solution: Two from: identifying carriers of an inherited condition; prenatal / embryo testing; choosing drugs (personalised medicine); identifying alleles linked to cancer risk. [B2]

questions.prompt: A cystic fibrosis allele (f) has a deletion of 3 base pairs. A DNA region was copied and run on a gel: the normal allele (F) gives a 100 bp band and f gives a 97 bp band. Use the table to give each person's genotype and identify the child with cystic fibrosis. (3)
hints: Two bands means two different alleles.
Which person has only the 97 bp band?
questions.solution:
Parent 1: Ff; parent 2: Ff [B1]
Child 1: ff; child 2: FF [B1]
Child 1 has CF — only the shorter (97 bp) band, so homozygous for the deletion. [B1]
questions.table:
Person | 100 bp band | 97 bp band
Parent 1 | yes | yes
Parent 2 | yes | yes
Child 1 | no | yes
Child 2 | yes | no

questions.prompt: A disease allele (d) creates a restriction site. When cut, the normal allele D gives one 600 bp fragment and d gives fragments of 400 and 200 bp. Use the table to give the genotypes and identify any carriers. (3)
hints: d cuts into two smaller pieces.
questions.solution:
Person A: DD (600 only) [B1]
Person B: Dd (600, 400 and 200) — carrier [B1]
Person C: dd (400 and 200 only) — affected. [B1]
questions.table:
Person | 600 bp | 400 bp | 200 bp
A | yes | no | no
B | yes | yes | yes
C | no | yes | yes

questions.prompt: Two parents are both carriers of cystic fibrosis. Explain how genetic counselling and screening could help them. (3)
questions.solution:
Counsellor explains 1 in 4 (25%) chance of each child having CF [B1]
Embryos / fetus can be screened using DNA probes / PCR [B1]
Gives information on treatment options / support so they can make informed decisions. [B1]

questions.prompt: To make silkworms that produce spider silk, plasmids with the spider gene were injected into silkworm eggs rather than adults. Suggest why. (2)
hints: How many cells does an egg have?
Which cells divide to form all the others?
questions.solution:
Egg is a single cell (or few cells) [B1]
So all cells of the adult (including silk glands and gametes) will contain the gene / it is passed to offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why genes are inserted into embryos when making genetically modified animals. (2)
questions.solution:
All cells derived from the embryo by mitosis contain the gene [B1]
Including gametes, so the gene is inherited by offspring. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two ways in which DNA can be inserted into plant cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Using Agrobacterium (Ti plasmid) as a vector [B1]
Gene gun / electroporation / viral vector. [B1]

questions.prompt: A gene for a protein that glows green in UV light was inserted alongside the spider gene. Suggest why. (2)
hints: How do you know which eggs took up the plasmid?
questions.solution:
Marker gene shows which silkworms have taken up the plasmid / were transformed [B1]
Glows in UV, so they can be identified easily without harming them. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why using a fluorescent marker gene is often preferred to an antibiotic resistance marker. (2)
questions.solution:
Cells can be seen directly / quickly without being killed / replica plating [B1]
Avoids spreading antibiotic resistance genes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how replica plating with antibiotic resistance markers identifies bacteria containing a recombinant plasmid. (2)
questions.solution:
Gene inserted into one resistance gene, inactivating it [B1]
Bacteria that grow on one antibiotic but not the other (replica plate) contain the recombinant plasmid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two advantages of producing a protein in genetically modified animals rather than extracting it from the original organism. (2)
questions.solution:
Larger quantities can be produced [B1]
Cheaper / easier to collect / no need to harvest the original organism. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two ethical or environmental concerns about genetically modified animals. (2)
questions.solution:
Animal welfare — modification may cause suffering [B1]
GM animals could escape and interbreed with wild populations / unknown long-term effects. [B1]

questions.prompt: Only a small amount of mitochondrial DNA was extracted from a patient. Explain how enough DNA could be obtained and how sequencing could identify a mutation. (2)
questions.solution:
Use PCR to amplify the DNA [B1]
Sequence and compare with the normal (reference) base sequence. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why primers are needed in PCR. (2)
questions.solution:
DNA polymerase needs a starting point / binds to primer [B1]
Primers complementary to the ends of the target sequence, so only that region is copied. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two advantages of PCR over cloning DNA in bacteria. (2)
questions.solution:
Faster / automated [B1]
No living cells needed / less contamination / doesn't need restriction enzymes / ligase. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the foreign DNA was inserted with a marker gene. (1)
hints: How do you know which plants have it?
questions.solution: To identify which cells / plants have taken up the foreign DNA. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a radioactive DNA probe could be used to show that a sucrose transporter gene is present in DNA from leaf cells. Do not refer to PCR. (4)
questions.solution:
Extract DNA and cut with restriction enzymes [B1]
Separate fragments by gel electrophoresis; make single-stranded (heat / alkali) [B1]
Add radioactive probe complementary to part of the gene; it hybridises [B1]
Wash off excess probe and use X-ray film (autoradiography) to show where it bound. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a fluorescent DNA probe can be used to screen a patient for a specific mutated allele. (4)
questions.solution:
Probe is a short single-stranded DNA complementary to the mutated allele, with a fluorescent label [B1]
Patient's DNA is separated into single strands [B1]
Probe hybridises if the allele is present [B1]
Wash off unbound probe; fluorescence under UV shows the allele is present. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a gene can be isolated from a plant using mRNA. (4)
questions.solution:
Extract mRNA from cells where the gene is expressed [B1]
Use reverse transcriptase to make cDNA [B1]
Use DNA polymerase to make double-stranded DNA [B1]
No introns, so it can be expressed in bacteria. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why bacteria can use human DNA to make human proteins. (2)
questions.solution:
Genetic code is universal — same triplets code for the same amino acids [B1]
Transcription and translation mechanisms are similar. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cDNA (made from mRNA) rather than genomic DNA is used to make human proteins in bacteria. (2)
questions.solution:
Human genes contain introns [B1]
Bacteria can't remove introns, so cDNA (no introns) is used. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a gene can be cut out of human DNA using enzymes. (2)
questions.solution:
Restriction endonucleases cut at specific recognition sequences either side of the gene [B1]
Leaving sticky ends (staggered cuts). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest and explain one reason why bacteria may not produce a working version of every human protein. (1)
questions.solution: Bacteria lack a Golgi / can't modify proteins (e.g. add carbohydrate), so protein may not fold / function. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why yeast is sometimes used instead of bacteria to make human proteins. (1)
questions.solution: Yeast is eukaryotic, so can modify / fold proteins like human cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a human protein made in bacteria might need to be purified before use. (1)
questions.solution: To remove bacterial proteins / toxins that could cause an immune response. [B1]

questions.prompt: A DNA fragment for making a human protein in goat's milk contains a region that is stimulated by an enhancer and a region that codes for the protein. Name these two regions. (2)
questions.solution:
Promoter [B1]
Gene / coding region (for the human protein). [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two regions, other than the target gene, that must be added to a DNA fragment so that it is expressed in a transgenic organism. (2)
questions.solution:
Promoter [B1]
Terminator. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the enzymes used to (i) cut a plasmid and (ii) join a gene into it. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Restriction endonuclease [B1]
(ii) DNA ligase. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the purpose of a marker gene in a DNA fragment transferred into an organism. (1)
questions.solution: To identify cells / organisms that have taken up the fragment. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one example of a marker gene. (1)
questions.solution: Gene for green fluorescent protein / antibiotic resistance / an enzyme producing a coloured product. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why marker genes for antibiotic resistance are less used now. (1)
questions.solution: Risk of spreading antibiotic resistance genes to other bacteria. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two advantages of producing a human protein in goat's milk rather than extracting it from donated human blood. (2)
questions.solution:
Large amounts can be produced continuously [B1]
No risk of transmitting human infections (e.g. HIV) / doesn't rely on donors. [B1]

questions.prompt: A recessive disease that is usually fatal in early childhood can be caused by mutations in more than 75 genes and affects 1 in 40 000 people worldwide. Evaluate whether everyone should be screened for it. (3)
questions.solution:
For: identifies carriers so couples can make informed decisions / embryo testing [B1]
Against: rare, so very expensive to screen everyone for one rare disease [B1]
So many genes involved that a test may miss mutations / ethical issues and anxiety. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three ethical issues with genetic screening. (3)
questions.solution:
Discrimination, e.g. by insurers / employers [B1]
Could lead to termination of pregnancies — moral objections [B1]
Psychological stress / privacy of genetic data. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how genetic screening can help with personalised medicine. (3)
questions.solution:
Identifies alleles that affect how a person responds to drugs [B1]
Doctors can choose the most effective drug / dose [B1]
Fewer side-effects / less waste. [B1]

questions.prompt:
The first division of a zygote takes 30 hours. Each division after that takes 11 hours. After 96 hours the embryo has a total volume of 4.48 × 10⁻³ mm³.

Calculate the mean volume of one cell after 96 hours. Give your answer in standard form. (2)
hints: Work out how many divisions fit into 96 hours.
96 − 30 = 66 hours for later divisions; each division doubles cell number.
questions.solution:
Number of cells = 2⁷ = 128 [M1]
Mean volume = 3.5 × 10⁻⁵ mm³. [A1]

Model answer:
Later divisions: (96 − 30) ÷ 11 = 6, so 7 divisions in total.
Cells = 2⁷ = 128.
Mean volume = 4.48 × 10⁻³ ÷ 128 = 3.5 × 10⁻⁵ mm³.

questions.prompt:
A bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. Each bacterium has a volume of 1.5 µm³.

Starting with a single bacterium, calculate the total volume of all the bacteria after 4 hours. Give your answer in standard form. (2)
hints: How many 20-minute periods are there in 4 hours?
questions.solution:
2¹² = 4096 bacteria [M1]
Total volume = 6.1 × 10³ µm³ (accept 6.144 × 10³). [A1]

Model answer:
4 hours = 240 min → 240 ÷ 20 = 12 divisions.
2¹² = 4096 cells.
4096 × 1.5 = 6144 µm³ = 6.1 × 10³ µm³.

questions.prompt:
A culture contains 5.0 × 10³ animal cells. Every cell divides by mitosis once every 6 hours.

Calculate the number of cells after 2 days. Give your answer in standard form. (2)
hints: Multiply the starting number by 2 for each cycle.
questions.solution:
8 divisions / ×256 [M1]
1.28 × 10⁶ cells. [A1]

Model answer:
48 ÷ 6 = 8 divisions → 2⁸ = 256.
5.0 × 10³ × 256 = 1.28 × 10⁶ cells.

questions.prompt:
A rat with a mass of 250 g is given an antibiotic at a dose of 40 mg kg⁻¹ day⁻¹ for 5 days.

Calculate the total mass of antibiotic given. (2)
hints: Convert the rat's mass into kg first.
questions.solution:
Daily dose = 0.25 × 40 = 10 mg [M1]
Total = 50 mg. [A1]

Model answer:
250 g = 0.25 kg.
Daily dose = 0.25 × 40 = 10 mg.
Total = 10 × 5 = 50 mg.

questions.prompt:
A patient with a mass of 75 kg needs a single dose of antibiotic of 10 mg kg⁻¹. The antibiotic is supplied as 250 mg tablets.

Calculate how many tablets the patient should take. (2)
hints: Find the total mass needed first.
Then divide by the mass per tablet.
questions.solution:
Dose = 750 mg [M1]
3 tablets. [A1]

Model answer:
75 × 10 = 750 mg; 750 ÷ 250 = 3 tablets.

questions.prompt:
A mouse with a mass of 18 g is given a drug at a dose of 12 mg kg⁻¹.

Calculate the mass of drug given. Give your answer in µg. (2)

The number of bacteria in two groups of mice was recorded as log₁₀ values. Group X: 6.2. Group Y: 4.8.

Calculate the percentage by which the number of bacteria in group Y is lower than in group X. (2)

In a culture, log₁₀ (number of bacteria) fell from 7.5 to 7.2 after an antibiotic was added.

Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of bacteria. (2)
hints: Convert both log values into actual numbers.
Notice the difference in log values is 0.3.

questions.prompt:
Over 24 hours, log₁₀ (number of bacteria) in a culture increased from 3.0 to 5.5.

Calculate how many times larger the population was after 24 hours. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (2)

A student measured a rectangular leaf section. Length = 4.25 ± 0.15 cm. Width = 2.10 ± 0.08 cm.

Calculate the area of the section to an appropriate number of significant figures, and its percentage uncertainty. (3)
hints: Area = length × width; give it to the same number of s.f. as the data.
Percentage uncertainties add when you multiply.

questions.prompt:
A cell seen under a microscope is approximately rectangular. Length = 48 ± 2 µm. Width = 22 ± 2 µm.

Calculate the area of the cell to an appropriate number of significant figures, and its percentage uncertainty. (3)
hints: The data are given to 2 s.f.
questions.solution:
Area = 1.1 × 10³ µm² (2 s.f.) [M1]
% uncertainties: 4.2% and 9.1% [M1]
Total percentage uncertainty = 13%. [A1]

Model answer:
Area = 48 × 22 = 1056 → 1.1 × 10³ µm² (2 s.f.).
2 ÷ 48 × 100 = 4.17%; 2 ÷ 22 × 100 = 9.09%.
Total = 13.3% ≈ 13%.

questions.prompt:
An agar cube has sides of 1.50 ± 0.05 cm.

Calculate the volume of the cube to an appropriate number of significant figures, and its percentage uncertainty. (3)
hints: When a quantity is cubed, its percentage uncertainty is multiplied by 3.
questions.solution:
Volume = 3.38 cm³ (3 s.f.) [M1]
% uncertainty of side = 3.3% [M1]
Volume percentage uncertainty = 10%. [A1]

Model answer:
V = 1.50³ = 3.375 → 3.38 cm³.
0.05 ÷ 1.50 × 100 = 3.33%; × 3 = 10%.

questions.prompt:
A student's drawing of a cell is 50 mm long. The actual length of the cell is 25 µm.

Calculate the magnification of the drawing, and state what should be added to the drawing to show its size. (2)
hints: Convert both lengths to the same unit.
questions.solution:
× 2000 [M1]
Scale bar / the magnification. [A1]

Model answer:
50 mm = 50 000 µm. 50 000 ÷ 25 = × 2000. Add a scale bar (or state the magnification).

questions.prompt:
Potato tissue was cut into either one cube of side 20 mm, or eight cubes of side 10 mm (same total volume). Both were placed in the same sucrose solution. After 30 minutes, the single cube had lost 0.60 g and the eight small cubes together had lost 1.20 g.

Use calculations to decide whether the rate of mass loss per mm² of surface per minute was different for the two. (3)
hints: Surface area of a cube = 6 × side².
Rate = mass lost ÷ total surface area ÷ time.
questions.solution:
Surface areas: 2400 mm² and 4800 mm² [M1]
Rates: both 8.3 × 10⁻⁶ g mm⁻² min⁻¹ [M1]
No difference per unit area — the small cubes lost more only because of their larger total surface area. [A1]

Model answer:
Large cube: 6 × 20² = 2400 mm²; small cubes: 8 × 6 × 10² = 4800 mm².
0.60 ÷ 2400 ÷ 30 = 8.3 × 10⁻⁶ g mm⁻² min⁻¹
1.20 ÷ 4800 ÷ 30 = 8.3 × 10⁻⁶ g mm⁻² min⁻¹
Same rate per unit area.

questions.prompt:
A potato cylinder has a radius of 5.0 mm and a length of 40 mm. In 20 minutes it lost 0.12 g.

Calculate the rate of mass loss per mm² of surface per minute. Include both ends of the cylinder. Give your answer in standard form. (3)
hints: Curved surface area = 2πrl; each end = πr².

questions.prompt:
With an enzyme, 4.2 × 10⁶ substrate molecules react per minute. Without the enzyme, 1.4 × 10⁻² molecules react per minute.

Calculate how many times faster the reaction is with the enzyme. Give your answer in standard form. (2)
hints: Divide the rate with enzyme by the rate without.
When dividing powers of 10, subtract the indices.

questions.prompt:
Catalase breaks down 2.0 × 10⁷ molecules of hydrogen peroxide per second. Without catalase, 8.0 × 10⁻² molecules break down per second.

Calculate how many times faster the reaction is with catalase. Give your answer in standard form. (2)

An enzyme converts half of its substrate in 0.0050 s. Without the enzyme, the same reaction takes 2.4 × 10⁴ hours.

Calculate how many times faster the reaction is with the enzyme. Give your answer in standard form to 2 significant figures. (2)

The table shows the rate of an enzyme reaction at different substrate concentrations, with and without an inhibitor.

Calculate the rate without inhibitor at 2.5 mmol dm⁻³ as a percentage of the maximum rate with the inhibitor. (2)
hints: Find the right two numbers in the table first.
questions.table:
Substrate / mmol dm⁻³ | Rate without inhibitor | Rate with inhibitor
1.0 | 18 | 6
2.5 | 30 | 17
5.0 | 50 | 34
10.0 | 56 | 48

questions.prompt: Using the table, calculate the rate with inhibitor at 5.0 mmol dm⁻³ as a percentage of the maximum rate without inhibitor. (2)
hints: Maximum rate without inhibitor is the largest value in that column.
questions.table:
Substrate / mmol dm⁻³ | Rate without inhibitor | Rate with inhibitor
1.0 | 18 | 6
2.5 | 30 | 17
5.0 | 50 | 34
10.0 | 56 | 48

questions.prompt:
At a substrate concentration of 1.0 mmol dm⁻³, the rate of a reaction was 24 units without inhibitor and 9 units with inhibitor.

Calculate the percentage decrease in rate caused by the inhibitor. (2)

Blood is collected from animals at 12 cm³ per kg of body mass. A sheep has a mass of 70 kg and a rabbit 3 kg.

Calculate how many rabbits would be needed to give the same volume of blood as one sheep. (2)
hints: Find the blood volume from each animal.
You can't use part of a rabbit — round up.
questions.solution:
Sheep 840 cm³; rabbit 36 cm³ [M1]
840 ÷ 36 = 23.3, so 24 rabbits. [A1]

questions.prompt:
A 400 kg horse gives 13 cm³ of blood per kg. Plasma makes up 55% of blood, and the plasma contains 2.5 mg of antibody per cm³.

Calculate the mass of antibody obtained, in grams. (2)
hints: Blood volume first, then plasma volume.
questions.solution:
Blood = 5200 cm³; plasma = 2860 cm³ [M1]
2860 × 2.5 = 7150 mg = 7.15 g (accept 7.2 g). [A1]

questions.prompt:
A patient needs 120 mg of antibody. Antivenom contains 8 mg of antibody per cm³ and is supplied in 10 cm³ vials.

Calculate the number of vials needed. (2)
hints: Can you open part of a vial?

questions.prompt:
In a photograph taken at × 400, the image of a lipid droplet is 24 mm long. The ruler used can be read to ± 0.5 mm. Assume the magnification is exact.

Calculate the actual length of the droplet in µm and its uncertainty. (2)
hints: Convert mm to µm (× 1000) before dividing.
The uncertainty is divided by the magnification too.

questions.prompt:
In an electron micrograph at × 1500, a cell measures 36 mm. The ruler reading has an uncertainty of ± 0.5 mm.

Calculate the actual length of the cell in µm and its uncertainty. (2)

On a micrograph, a 10 µm scale bar measures 25 mm. The image of a mitochondrion is 40 mm long.

Calculate the magnification and the actual length of the mitochondrion. (2)
hints: Magnification = image size of bar ÷ real size of bar.
questions.solution:
Magnification = 25 000 ÷ 10 = × 2500 [M1]
Actual length = 40 000 ÷ 2500 = 16 µm. [A1]

questions.prompt:
A blood sample contains 4.0 × 10² virus particles per cm³. How many particles are in 250 mm³ of this blood?

Choose one answer.

A  1.0 × 10²
B  1.0 × 10⁵
C  1.6 × 10³
D  1.0 × 10¹ (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
Blood contains 3000 CD4 cells per mm³. How many CD4 cells is this per cm³?

Choose one answer.

A  3.0 × 10³
B  3.0 × 10⁴
C  3.0 × 10⁶
D  3.0 × 10⁹ (1)
hints: How many mm³ are in a cm³?
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
A culture contains 1.2 × 10⁴ bacteria per cm³. How many bacteria are in 5 mm³?

Choose one answer.

A  60
B  600
C  2.4 × 10³
D  6.0 × 10⁴ (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt: In a root-tip squash, 42 out of 600 cells were in a stage of mitosis. Calculate the mitotic index and state what it shows. (2)
hints: Mitotic index = cells in mitosis ÷ total cells (× 100).
What does a high value tell you?
questions.solution:
42 ÷ 600 × 100 = 7% (0.07) [M1]
Shows the proportion of cells dividing / how quickly the tissue is growing. [A1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to make 25 cm³ of 0.05 mol dm⁻³ sodium chloride solution from a 0.50 mol dm⁻³ stock solution. (2)
hints: The new solution is one tenth the concentration.
questions.solution:
2.5 cm³ of stock solution [M1]
Add 22.5 cm³ of distilled water (and mix). [A1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to make 50 cm³ of 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution from a 1.2 mol dm⁻³ stock solution. (2)
hints: A quarter of 50 cm³ is stock.
questions.solution:
12.5 cm³ of stock [M1]
+ 37.5 cm³ of distilled water. [A1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the mass of glucose (Mr = 180) needed to make 250 cm³ of a 0.1 mol dm⁻³ glucose solution. (2)
The table shows the water potential of some sucrose solutions. The relationship is linear. Calculate the concentration of sucrose with a water potential of −0.72 MPa. (2)
hints: How much does the water potential change per 0.05 mol dm⁻³?
−0.72 is halfway between which two values?
questions.solution:
Water potential = −4.8 × concentration [M1]
0.15 mol dm⁻³. [A1]
questions.table:
Sucrose / mol dm⁻³ | Water potential / MPa
0.05 | −0.24
0.10 | −0.48
0.20 | −0.96

questions.prompt: The relationship between concentration and water potential in the table is linear. Calculate the concentration that has a water potential of −1.04 MPa. (2)
hints: Find the change in water potential per 0.1 mol dm⁻³.
questions.solution:
Water potential = −2.6 × concentration [M1]
0.40 mol dm⁻³. [A1]
questions.table:
Concentration / mol dm⁻³ | Water potential / MPa
0.1 | −0.26
0.3 | −0.78
0.5 | −1.30

questions.prompt: A 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution has a water potential of −0.54 MPa, and a 0.4 mol dm⁻³ solution has −1.08 MPa. Assuming a linear relationship through the origin, calculate the water potential of a 0.25 mol dm⁻³ solution. (2)
hints: Find the water potential per mol dm⁻³.
questions.solution:
−2.7 MPa per mol dm⁻³ [M1]
−0.68 MPa (accept −0.675). [A1]

questions.prompt: A leaf has an area of 40 cm². Its area increases by 2.5% of its current area each day. Calculate its area after 3 days. (2)

A calibration curve for a colorimeter is a straight line through the origin, with an absorbance of 0.40 for 10 mmol dm⁻³ glucose. An unknown solution has an absorbance of 0.26. Calculate its glucose concentration. (2)
hints: Divide the unknown's absorbance by this.
questions.solution:
0.040 absorbance units per mmol dm⁻³ [M1]
6.5 mmol dm⁻³. [A1]

questions.prompt: A leaf's area was 52 cm² on day 4 and 61 cm² on day 10. Calculate the mean rate of growth and the percentage increase in area. (2)
Metabolic rate per kg of body mass can be estimated as 70 × M⁻⁰·²⁵, where M is body mass in kg. Calculate how many times greater the value is for a 0.025 kg mouse than for a 625 kg horse. (2)
questions.solution:
Mouse: 70 × 0.025⁻⁰·²⁵ = 176; horse: 70 × 625⁻⁰·²⁵ = 14 [M1]
About 12.6 times greater. [A1]

questions.prompt: Resting heart rate in mammals can be estimated as 241 × M⁻⁰·²⁵ beats per minute, where M is body mass in kg. Calculate the heart rate of a 16 kg dog and an 81 kg human, and how many times faster the dog's heart beats. (2)
questions.solution:
Dog 121 bpm (120.5); human 80 bpm (80.3) [M1]
1.5 times faster. [A1]

questions.prompt: Daily energy use of a mammal can be estimated as 63 × M⁰·⁷⁵ kJ, where M is body mass in kg. Calculate the daily energy use of a 16 kg animal, and its energy use per kg. (2)
questions.solution:
63 × 8 = 504 kJ per day [M1]
504 ÷ 16 = 31.5 kJ per kg per day. [A1]

questions.prompt: One cardiac cycle takes 0.75 s. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute. (1)
hints: How many 0.75 s cycles fit into 60 s?
questions.solution: 80 beats per minute. [B1]

questions.prompt: A person's heart rate is 72 beats per minute and their stroke volume is 70 cm³. Calculate their cardiac output in dm³ per minute. (1)
hints: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.
questions.solution: 5.04 dm³ per minute (5040 cm³). [B1]

questions.prompt: Four complete cardiac cycles take 2.4 s. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute. (1)
hints: Find the time for one cycle.
questions.solution: 100 beats per minute. [B1]

questions.prompt:
A solvent is made by mixing ethanol and water in the ratio 3 : 1. Which volumes make 80 cm³ of solvent?

Choose one answer.

A  53.3 cm³ ethanol, 26.7 cm³ water
B  60 cm³ ethanol, 20 cm³ water
C  75 cm³ ethanol, 25 cm³ water
D  70 cm³ ethanol, 10 cm³ water (1)
hints: How many parts are there altogether?
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
A solution is made from liquids X, Y and Z in the ratio 2 : 5 : 1. Which volumes make 40 cm³?

Choose one answer.

A  8, 20, 4 cm³
B  16, 20, 4 cm³
C  10, 25, 5 cm³
D  2, 5, 1 cm³ (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt:
A buffer and water are mixed in the ratio 9 : 1. Which volumes make 150 cm³?

Choose one answer.

A  135 cm³ buffer, 15 cm³ water
B  140 cm³ buffer, 10 cm³ water
C  90 cm³ buffer, 60 cm³ water
D  141 cm³ buffer, 9 cm³ water (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt: Without protein X, cells take 18 hours to reach the point where 25% are replicating DNA. With protein X they take 12 hours. Calculate the percentage decrease in time. (2)
A process took 40 minutes in control cells and 26 minutes in treated cells. Calculate the percentage decrease. (2)
The time for cells to complete the cell cycle increased from 15 hours to 24 hours after treatment. Calculate the percentage increase. (2)
At particulate concentrations of 10, 20 and 40 µg cm⁻³, the percentage of dead cells was 8, 16 and 40. Use a calculation to decide whether the relationship is linear (directly proportional). (2)
hints: Divide % dead cells by concentration for each point.
questions.solution:
Ratios: 0.8, 0.8 and 1.0 [M1]
Not constant, so not linear — doubling from 20 to 40 more than doubles cell death. [A1]

questions.prompt: At light intensities of 1, 2 and 4 units, the rate of photosynthesis was 5, 10 and 20 units. Use a calculation to show whether the relationship is directly proportional. (2)
hints: Is the answer always the same?
questions.solution:
Ratios are all 5 [M1]
Constant, so directly proportional (linear through the origin). [A1]

questions.prompt: At temperatures of 0, 5, 10 and 15 °C, the rate of a reaction was 2, 7, 12 and 17 units. Is the relationship linear? Is it directly proportional? Use the data to explain. (2)
hints: What is the increase in rate for each 5 °C?
Does the line go through zero?
questions.solution:
Rate increases by 5 for every 5 °C, so it is linear [M1]
Not directly proportional because rate is 2 (not 0) at 0 °C. [A1]

questions.prompt: A student counted stomata in three circular fields of view, each 0.40 mm in diameter: 18, 22 and 20. Calculate the mean number of stomata per mm². (2)
questions.solution:
Area = π × 0.20² = 0.126 mm²; mean count = 20 [M1]
20 ÷ 0.126 = 159 per mm². [A1]

questions.prompt: Stomata were counted in three square fields of view of side 0.25 mm: 12, 15 and 9. Calculate the mean number of stomata per mm². (2)
Stomata were counted in four circular fields of view of diameter 0.50 mm: 30, 26, 28 and 32. Calculate the mean stomatal density per mm². (2)
Mean stomatal density of a species fell from 280 per mm² in 1900 to 238 per mm² in 2000. Calculate the mean rate of change per 10-year period. (2)
questions.solution:
Change = −42 per mm² over 100 years [M1]
−4.2 per mm² per 10 years. [A1]

questions.prompt: Atmospheric CO₂ rose from 315 ppm in 1960 to 415 ppm in 2020. Calculate the mean rate of increase per 10 years. (2)
questions.solution:
100 ppm over 6 decades [M1]
16.7 ppm per 10 years. [A1]

questions.prompt: Stomatal density in a species fell by 15% from 300 per mm² over 75 years. Calculate the mean rate of decrease per 10 years. (2)
questions.solution:
Decrease = 45 per mm² [M1]
45 ÷ 7.5 = 6 per mm² per 10 years. [A1]

questions.prompt:
A bird has a mass of 0.040 kg and a lung volume of 3.2 cm³. A mouse has a mass of 0.020 kg and a lung volume of 0.30 cm³.

Calculate how many times greater the bird's lung volume per kg of body mass is, to an appropriate number of significant figures. Suggest one explanation for the difference. (3)
hints: Lung volume ÷ body mass for each animal.
Then divide the bird's value by the mouse's.
questions.solution:
Bird 80 cm³ kg⁻¹; mouse 15 cm³ kg⁻¹ [M1]
5.3 times (2 s.f.) [M1]
Birds fly, so have a higher metabolic / respiration rate and need more oxygen. [A1]

questions.prompt:
An athlete's heart has a mass of 400 g and body mass 80 kg. A non-athlete's heart has a mass of 300 g and body mass 75 kg.

Calculate how many times greater the athlete's heart mass per kg of body mass is, and suggest an explanation. (3)
hints: Heart mass ÷ body mass for each.
questions.solution:
Athlete 5.0 g kg⁻¹; non-athlete 4.0 g kg⁻¹ [M1]
1.25 times (accept 1.3) [M1]
Training enlarges the heart muscle / larger stroke volume to supply more oxygen. [A1]

questions.prompt:
A 2000 g tuna has a gill surface area of 6.0 × 10⁶ mm². A 500 g flounder has a gill area of 1.0 × 10⁵ mm².

Calculate how many times greater the tuna's gill area per gram is, and suggest an explanation. (3)
questions.solution:
Tuna 3000 mm² g⁻¹; flounder 200 mm² g⁻¹ [M1]
15 times [M1]
Tuna is a fast, active swimmer, so has a higher respiration rate / needs more oxygen. [A1]

questions.prompt: In control plants, the ratio of protein to chlorophyll is 8 : 1. Nutrient-deficient plants have 50% of the control protein and 20% of the control chlorophyll. Calculate the ratio of protein to chlorophyll in the deficient plants. (1)
hints: Multiply each side of the ratio by its percentage.

questions.prompt: The protein : chlorophyll ratio in control plants is 6 : 1. Treated plants have 30% of the control protein and 60% of the control chlorophyll. Calculate the ratio in treated plants. (1)

In sun leaves, the ratio of chlorophyll a to chlorophyll b is 3 : 1. Shade leaves contain the same amount of chlorophyll a but twice as much chlorophyll b. Calculate the ratio of chlorophyll a to b in shade leaves. (1)
hints: Keep a the same, double b.

questions.prompt: During anaphase, chromatids moved from 12 µm to 2 µm from the spindle pole in 4.5 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of movement in µm min⁻¹ to 3 decimal places. (2)
Chromosomes moved 8.4 µm in 6.0 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of movement in µm min⁻¹ to 3 decimal places. (2)
hints: Give 3 decimal places even if they are zeros.

questions.prompt: The distance between the two spindle poles increased from 18 µm to 30 µm in 7.0 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase in µm min⁻¹ to 3 decimal places. (2)
A mouse of mass 25 g is given a drug at 5 mg kg⁻¹. The drug solution contains 2 mg cm⁻³. Calculate the volume injected, in dm³, in standard form. (2)
A rat of mass 300 g is given 1.5 mg kg⁻¹ of an antibody. The solution contains 250 mg dm⁻³. Calculate the volume injected in dm³, in standard form. (2)
A 70 kg patient needs 10 mg kg⁻¹ of a drug supplied at 20 mg cm⁻³. Calculate the volume needed. (2)
A population of bacteria increased from 1.0 × 10⁴ to 8.0 × 10⁴ cells in 3 hours. Calculate the generation time. (2)
hints: Divide the time by the number of generations.
questions.solution:
8 = 2³, so 3 generations [M1]
Generation time = 1 hour. [A1]

questions.prompt: Using N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, calculate the generation time of bacteria that increased from 500 to 32 000 cells in 4 hours. (2)
A population increased from 2.0 × 10³ to 1.6 × 10⁶ cells in 6 hours. Using n = (log N − log N₀) ÷ log 2, calculate the generation time in minutes. (2)
questions.solution:
n = 9.64 generations [M1]
360 ÷ 9.64 = 37 minutes. [A1]

questions.prompt: The biomass of four plant species in an area was: A 10, B 20, C 30 and D 40 g m⁻². Calculate the index of diversity using d = 1 − Σ(n/N)². (2)
hints: Square each fraction n/N and add them up.

questions.prompt: A sample contained 25 individuals of each of four species. Calculate the index of diversity using d = 1 − Σ(n/N)². (2)
A sample contained 50 individuals of species A, 30 of B and 20 of C. Calculate the index of diversity using d = 1 − Σ(n/N)². (2)
A membrane channel has a circular cross-section with a diameter of 2.4 nm. Calculate its cross-sectional area in nm² to 1 decimal place. Use π = 3.14. (2)
A channel protein has a pore of diameter 0.80 nm. Calculate the cross-sectional area of the pore in nm² to 1 decimal place. Use π = 3.14. (2)
A nuclear pore has a radius of 3.5 nm. Calculate its cross-sectional area in nm² to 1 decimal place. Use π = 3.14. (2)

The risk of a trisomy pregnancy is 0.1% for mothers under 30 and 1.5% for mothers aged 40 or over. In one year there were 600 000 births to mothers under 30 and 30 000 to mothers aged 40 or over. A student concluded that most babies with trisomy are born to mothers aged 40 or over. Use calculations to show that this is not valid. (2)
hints: Work out the number of affected births in each group.
questions.solution:
Under 30: 600 cases; 40 and over: 450 cases [M1]
More affected babies are born to mothers under 30, because there are many more births in that group. [A1]

questions.prompt: Of 200 trisomy cases in mothers under 35, 70% were caused by errors in meiosis I. Of 400 cases in mothers over 35, 80% were from meiosis I. A student concluded that meiosis II errors decrease in older mothers. Use calculations to show why this conclusion needs care. (2)
hints: Find the number of meiosis II cases in each group.
questions.solution:
Meiosis II cases: 60 (under 35) and 80 (over 35) [M1]
The proportion falls but the number of meiosis II errors actually increases. [A1]

questions.prompt: The risk of a condition is 1 in 1250 for a 25-year-old mother and 1 in 100 for a 40-year-old mother. A student says the risk is 10 times greater at 40. Use a calculation to check this. (2)
hints: Turn each risk into a decimal or divide the denominators.
questions.solution:
0.0008 and 0.01 [M1]
12.5 times greater, so the student underestimates. [A1]

questions.prompt: Transpiration rate increased from 2.4 to 3.0 g h⁻¹. Calculate the percentage increase. (2)
Water uptake increased from 15 to 21 mm³ min⁻¹. Calculate the percentage increase. (2)
Transpiration rate fell from 3.6 to 2.7 g h⁻¹. Calculate the percentage decrease. (2)

A healthy gill filament has a surface area of 6.0 × 10³ µm² and a volume of 1.5 × 10⁴ µm³. A damaged filament has a surface area of 8.0 × 10³ µm² and a SA:V ratio of 0.20 : 1. Calculate the SA:V ratio of the healthy filament and the volume of the damaged filament, to 2 significant figures. (2)
questions.solution:
Healthy ratio = 0.40 : 1 [M1]
Damaged volume = 4.0 × 10⁴ µm³. [A1]

questions.prompt: A cell has a surface area of 2.4 × 10³ µm² and a volume of 8.0 × 10³ µm³. An enlarged cell has a volume of 2.7 × 10⁴ µm³ and a SA:V ratio of 0.15 : 1. Calculate the SA:V ratio of the first cell and the surface area of the enlarged cell, to 2 significant figures. (2)
questions.solution:
First cell ratio = 0.30 : 1 [M1]
Enlarged cell SA = 4.1 × 10³ µm². [A1]

questions.prompt: Treat a cell as a sphere. Calculate the SA:V ratio for a cell of radius 5 µm and a cell of radius 10 µm. (Sphere: SA = 4πr², V = 4/3πr³.) (2)
hints: For a sphere, SA:V simplifies to 3 ÷ r.
Or calculate each value and divide.
questions.solution:
Radius 5 µm: 0.60 : 1 [M1]
Radius 10 µm: 0.30 : 1. [A1]

questions.prompt: There are 250 million cases of a disease each year. 90% of cases are in Africa. Outside Africa, species X causes 50% of cases. Calculate the number of cases caused by species X each year (it does not occur in Africa). (1)
There were 400 000 deaths from a disease in one year; 67% were children under five. Calculate the number of deaths of children under five. (1)
There are 8.0 million cases of a bacterial disease each year; 15% are antibiotic-resistant, and 40% of resistant cases occur in one region. Calculate the number of resistant cases in that region. (1)
A circular well cut in agar has a diameter of 8 mm. Calculate the minimum depth needed to hold 100 mm³ of liquid. Use π = 3.14. (2)
A Petri dish has an internal diameter of 90 mm. It is filled with agar to a depth of 4 mm. Calculate the volume of agar in cm³. Use π = 3.14. (2)
A well in agar has a diameter of 5 mm and a depth of 4 mm. Calculate the maximum volume of liquid it can hold. Use π = 3.14. (2)
The image of a cell is 35 mm long. The actual cell is 7 µm long. Calculate the magnification. (2)
The image of a cell is 18 mm long at a magnification of × 1200. Calculate the actual length in µm. (2)
A bacterium is 1.5 µm long. Calculate the length of its image in mm at a magnification of × 12 000. (2)
hints: Convert µm to mm at the end.

questions.prompt: The concentration of a drug (Mr = 300) was increased from 2 µmol dm⁻³ to 10 µmol dm⁻³ in 0.01 dm³ of medium. Calculate the extra mass of drug added, in µg. (2)
A solution contains 50 µg cm⁻³ of a drug. Calculate the mass of drug in 0.02 dm³, in mg. (2)
A drug is used at 5 mg dm⁻³. Calculate the mass needed for 250 cm³ of solution, in µg. (2)
Four alveoli in a section viewed at × 40 had image diameters of 3.6, 4.0, 4.4 and 5.2 mm. Calculate the mean actual diameter in µm. (2)
hints: Find the mean image diameter first.
Convert to µm, then divide by 40.
questions.solution:
Mean image diameter = 4.3 mm = 4300 µm [M1]
4300 ÷ 40 = 107.5 µm (accept 108). [A1]

questions.prompt: Four cells viewed at × 100 had image lengths of 12, 15, 9 and 14 mm. Calculate their mean actual length in µm. (2)
hints: Convert to µm and divide by 100.

questions.prompt: Three nuclei viewed at × 400 had image diameters of 8, 10 and 12 mm. Calculate their mean actual diameter in µm. (2)
A ruler has 1 mm graduations. State the uncertainty of a single reading, and calculate the percentage error when measuring 8 mm. (2)
hints: Uncertainty is half the smallest division.

questions.prompt: An eyepiece graticule has divisions worth 2 µm. State the uncertainty of a reading and calculate the percentage error for a 20 µm measurement. (2)
A measuring cylinder has 2 cm³ graduations. State the uncertainty of a reading and calculate the percentage error for a volume of 25 cm³. (2)
An adult needs 10 000 kJ per day. Free sugars should provide no more than 10% of this. One biscuit provides 400 kJ from free sugar. How many biscuits would reach the limit? (1)
questions.solution: 2.5 biscuits. [B1]

questions.prompt: A teenager needs 9000 kJ per day; free sugars should be no more than 5% of this. A can of soft drink provides 600 kJ from sugar. What fraction of a can reaches the limit? (1)
questions.solution: 0.75 of a can. [B1]

questions.prompt: A child needs 8400 kJ per day; free sugars should be no more than 5% of this. One teaspoon of sugar provides 70 kJ. How many teaspoons reach the limit? (1)
questions.solution: 6 teaspoons. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the word equation for calculating magnification. (1)
hints: It uses image size and actual size.
Which one is divided by which?
questions.solution: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the word equation for calculating percentage change. (1)
questions.solution: Percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the word equation for calculating the mitotic index. (1)
hints: You count cells in a field of view.
questions.solution: Mitotic index = number of cells in mitosis ÷ total number of cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a root tip, 80% of cells were in interphase, 10% in prophase, 4% in metaphase, 2% in anaphase and 4% in telophase. The whole cell cycle takes 20 hours. Calculate the time spent in prophase and in metaphase, and explain your method. (3)
hints: The percentage of cells in a stage reflects the time spent in it.
questions.solution:
Proportion of cells in a stage = proportion of cycle time spent in it [M1]
Prophase: 0.10 × 20 = 2 hours [M1]
Metaphase: 0.04 × 20 = 0.8 hours (48 minutes). [A1]

questions.prompt: Ejection fraction (EF) = stroke volume ÷ volume of blood in the ventricle before contraction. A patient has 150 cm³ of blood in the ventricle and an EF of 0.30. A healthy person has 120 cm³ and an EF of 0.60. Calculate the percentage difference in the patient's stroke volume compared with the healthy person. (3)
questions.solution:
Patient SV = 45 cm³; healthy SV = 72 cm³ [M1]
(45 − 72) ÷ 72 × 100 [M1]
−37.5% (37.5% lower). [A1]

questions.prompt: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. A patient has a stroke volume of 50 cm³ and heart rate of 90 min⁻¹. A healthy person has 70 cm³ and 70 min⁻¹. Calculate the percentage difference in the patient's cardiac output compared with the healthy person. (3)
hints: Use the healthy value as the original.
questions.solution:
Patient 4500 cm³ min⁻¹; healthy 4900 cm³ min⁻¹ [M1]
(4500 − 4900) ÷ 4900 × 100 [M1]
−8.2%. [A1]

questions.prompt: Stroke volume fell from 72 cm³ (healthy) to 45 cm³ (disease). A student calculated the percentage change as (72 − 45) ÷ 45 × 100 = 60% decrease. Identify the error and give the correct answer. (3)
hints: Which value should you divide by?
The original value is the healthy one.
questions.solution:
Student divided by the new value instead of the original (healthy) value [M1]
Correct: (45 − 72) ÷ 72 × 100 [M1]
= −37.5% (37.5% decrease). [A1]

questions.prompt: In a group of 600 birds, 85% were seen singing. How many birds sang? (1)
In a population of 1200 male frogs, 2.5% made rasping calls. How many frogs made rasping calls? (1)
Of 400 male frogs, 60% made advertisement calls and 15% made aggressive calls (no frog made both). How many made either call? (1)
Three solutions are mixed in the ratio 4 : 1 : 1 to give 60 cm³. What volume of the second solution is used? (1)
questions.solution: 10 cm³. [B1]

questions.prompt: Three solutions are mixed in the ratio 7 : 2 : 1 to give 50 cm³. What volume of the second solution is used? (1)
questions.solution: 10 cm³. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two solutions are mixed in the ratio 5 : 3 to give 40 cm³. What volume of the second solution is used? (1)
questions.solution: 15 cm³. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mouse can run at 0.20 m s⁻¹ for 50 minutes before stopping. It has already run at this speed for 30 minutes. Calculate the extra distance it can cover. (2)
hints: How many more minutes can it run?
Convert to seconds, then distance = speed × time.

questions.prompt: A crab ran 360 m in 40 minutes at a constant speed. It can run at that speed for 70 minutes in total. Calculate its speed and the extra distance it could cover. (2)
questions.solution:
Speed = 360 ÷ 2400 = 0.15 m s⁻¹ [M1]
Extra distance = 0.15 × 1800 = 270 m. [A1]

questions.prompt: A lizard can sprint at 2.5 m s⁻¹ for a maximum of 12 s. It has already sprinted 20 m. Calculate how much further it can run. (2)
hints: Subtract what it has already run.
questions.solution:
Maximum = 2.5 × 12 = 30 m [M1]
Extra = 10 m. [A1]

questions.prompt: Each diploid stem cell in a testis divides by mitosis four times; every cell produced then undergoes meiosis to make four sperm. Calculate the minimum number of stem cells needed to produce 1.5 × 10⁷ sperm. Give your answer in standard form. (2)
questions.solution:
Each stem cell gives 64 sperm [M1]
1.5 × 10⁷ ÷ 64 = 2.3 × 10⁵ (234 375). [A1]

questions.prompt: Each cell in an anther undergoes meiosis to produce four pollen grains. A flower produces 2.4 × 10⁴ pollen grains. Calculate the minimum number of cells that underwent meiosis, in standard form. (2)

At a light intensity of 500 units, mutant chloroplasts grown in low light produced 42 µmol O₂ mg⁻¹ h⁻¹ and those grown in high light produced 66 µmol O₂ mg⁻¹ h⁻¹. Oxygen was collected for 15 minutes. Calculate the difference in oxygen produced per mg in 15 minutes. (2)
questions.solution:
66 − 42 = 24 µmol mg⁻¹ h⁻¹ [M1]
÷ 4 = 6 µmol mg⁻¹ in 15 minutes. [A1]

questions.prompt: Normal chloroplasts produced 35 µmol O₂ mg⁻¹ h⁻¹ and mutant chloroplasts produced 56 µmol O₂ mg⁻¹ h⁻¹. Calculate the percentage increase for the mutant. (2)
Chloroplasts produced 48 µmol O₂ mg⁻¹ h⁻¹. Calculate the oxygen produced by 2.5 mg of chloroplasts in 20 minutes. (2)
questions.solution:
48 ÷ 3 = 16 µmol mg⁻¹ in 20 min [M1]
× 2.5 = 40 µmol. [A1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the percentage of fat in the diet and deaths from a cancer per 100 000 people for ten countries. Describe how you would plot a suitable graph and justify your choice. (3)
hints: Which variable goes on the x-axis?
Are you looking for a relationship?
questions.solution:
Scatter graph — looking for a correlation between two continuous variables [B1]
Fat % on x-axis, deaths on y-axis with labels and units [B1]
Plot points (don't join) — a line of best fit can be added. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain when to use (i) a bar chart, (ii) a histogram, and (iii) a line graph. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Bar chart — categorical / discrete data [B1]
(ii) Histogram — frequency of continuous data in classes [B1]
(iii) Line graph — continuous independent variable / change over time. [B1]

questions.prompt: In 1970, farmers used 20 kg of fertiliser per hectare and each kg produced 15 kg of extra grain. In 2005, they used 100 kg per hectare and each kg produced 5 kg of extra grain. Calculate the difference in extra grain yield per hectare. (2)

Farmers used 30 kg of fertiliser per hectare with a response of 12 kg grain per kg, and later 120 kg per hectare with a response of 4 kg grain per kg. Calculate the difference in extra grain yield per hectare. (2)
questions.solution:
30 × 12 = 360 kg ha⁻¹; 120 × 4 = 480 kg ha⁻¹ [M1]
Difference = 120 kg ha⁻¹. [A1]

questions.prompt: Fertiliser use rose from 10 to 80 kg per hectare while the response fell from 20 to 6 kg grain per kg of fertiliser. Calculate the change in extra grain yield per hectare. (2)
questions.solution:
10 × 20 = 200 kg ha⁻¹; 80 × 6 = 480 kg ha⁻¹ [M1]
Increase of 280 kg ha⁻¹. [A1]

questions.solution:
Cell 904.3 µm³ − nucleus 113.0 µm³ = 791.3 µm³ [M1]
× 0.1 = 79 mitochondria. [A1]

questions.solution:
Volume = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ mm³, so 6 ÷ 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 24 000 per mm³ [M1]
× 200 = 4.8 × 10⁶ per mm³. [A1]

questions.prompt: A sample was diluted 100 times. The mean count was 9 cells per small square of 0.05 mm × 0.05 mm, depth 0.1 mm. Calculate the cells per mm³ in the original sample. (2)

Ammonia in soil A fell from 120 to 80 µg g⁻¹ in 2 days; in soil B it fell from 120 to 110 µg g⁻¹. Calculate the difference in the rate of ammonia breakdown, with units. (2)
questions.solution:
A: 40 ÷ 2 = 20; B: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 [M1]
Difference = 15 µg g⁻¹ day⁻¹. [A1]

questions.prompt: Ammonia in soil A fell from 150 to 90 µg g⁻¹ in 2 days; in soil B it fell from 150 to 138 µg g⁻¹. Calculate the difference in rate, with units. (2)

Difference = 24 µg g⁻¹ day⁻¹. [A1]

questions.prompt: Ammonia in soil A fell from 200 to 40 µg g⁻¹ in 4 days; in soil B it fell from 200 to 160 µg g⁻¹. Calculate the difference in rate, with units. (2)
questions.solution:
A: 40; B: 10 µg g⁻¹ day⁻¹ [M1]
Difference = 30 µg g⁻¹ day⁻¹. [A1]

The recommended maximum sodium intake is 2.4 g per day. Drug X: 250 mg tablets, max dose 0.5 g every 4 hours, each tablet contains 0.18 g sodium. Drug Y: 400 mg tablets, max dose 0.8 g every 8 hours, 0.5 g sodium per tablet. A journalist claims that taking either drug at the maximum dose exceeds the sodium limit. Is this true for both? Show your calculations. (2)
hints: Tablets per dose × doses per day.
questions.solution:
X: 2 tablets × 6 doses = 12 tablets × 0.18 = 2.16 g — below 2.4 g [M1]
Y: 2 tablets × 3 doses = 6 × 0.5 = 3.0 g — above; so only true for Y. [A1]

questions.prompt: The maximum sodium intake is 2.4 g per day. Drug P: 500 mg tablets, max 1.0 g every 4 hours, 0.1 g sodium per tablet. Drug Q: 200 mg tablets, max 0.6 g every 6 hours, 0.25 g sodium per tablet. Which drug would exceed the limit at maximum dose? (2)
questions.solution:
P: 2 × 6 = 12 tablets × 0.1 = 1.2 g [M1]
Q: 3 × 4 = 12 tablets × 0.25 = 3.0 g — only Q exceeds 2.4 g. [A1]

questions.prompt: Maximum sodium intake is 2.4 g per day. Drug M: 100 mg tablets, max 0.2 g every 3 hours, 0.16 g sodium per tablet. Drug N: 500 mg tablets, max 1.0 g every 12 hours, 0.55 g sodium per tablet. Which exceeds the limit? (2)
questions.solution:
M: 2 × 8 = 16 tablets × 0.16 = 2.56 g — exceeds [M1]
N: 2 × 2 = 4 tablets × 0.55 = 2.2 g — doesn't exceed. [A1]

During an exercise test, the ventilatory threshold is the first time breathed-out oxygen rises without an equivalent rise in carbon dioxide. Using the table, state the time this happened and the ratio of pO₂ : pCO₂ at that time. (2)
hints: Look for when pO₂ starts rising.
questions.solution:
At 60 s (pO₂ rises from 14.0 to 14.6 while pCO₂ only 4.9 to 5.0) [M1]
Ratio 14.6 : 5.0 = 2.92 : 1. [A1]

questions.prompt: Breathed-out pO₂ was 15.2 kPa and pCO₂ was 4.0 kPa. Calculate the ratio pO₂ : pCO₂ and explain what a rise in this ratio shows. (2)
hints: More oxygen left in exhaled air.
questions.solution:
15.2 ÷ 4.0 = 3.8 : 1 [M1]
A rise shows less oxygen taken up relative to CO₂ released / ventilation increasing more than gas exchange. [A1]

questions.prompt: Breathing rate was 15 breaths per minute and tidal volume 0.5 dm³. During exercise, breathing rate rose to 40 per minute and tidal volume to 2.0 dm³. Calculate the increase in pulmonary ventilation. (2)
questions.solution:
Rest: 7.5 dm³ min⁻¹; exercise: 80 dm³ min⁻¹ [M1]
Increase = 72.5 dm³ min⁻¹. [A1]

questions.solution:
Mean = 132 per 0.1 cm³ = 1320 per cm³ diluted [M1]

questions.prompt: Starting from one bacterium, how many generations are needed to produce at least 1.32 × 10⁸ cells, assuming none die? (1)

Bar chart — the groups are categories [B1]
Axes labelled: group on x, increase in thickness / cm × 10⁻³ on y, with suitable linear scale [B1]
Error bars drawn at ± 2 SD for each bar. [B1]

questions.solution:
About 95% of the data fall within ± 2 SD of the mean [B1]
Shows spread / variability [B1]
If bars don't overlap, the difference is likely significant. [B1]

Healthy females (15.6–21.4) and autoimmune females (13.7–19.7) overlap with healthy males [B1]
So none is clearly significantly different — a statistical test is needed. [B1]

questions.prompt: An island population of 60 000 has a genetic disease frequency of 1 in 2000. 70% of cases are caused by nuclear DNA mutations and 20% of those are in one gene. Estimate the number of people with the disease caused by a mutation in that gene, to the nearest whole number. (3)

questions.prompt:
Scientists tested herbicide X on barley (a crop) and fat hen (a weed). Leaf discs were placed in water or herbicide X, and ion leakage from the cells was measured (arbitrary units). Ion leakage shows membrane damage. A difference between two means greater than the least significant difference (LSD) is significant.

Evaluate the use of herbicide X to control fat hen in a barley crop. (4)

Limitation: only one concentration / only membrane damage measured, not plant death or crop yield / only one weed species. [B1]

Evaluate the claim that the drug lowers blood pressure. (4)
hints: What does P = 0.08 mean compared with 0.05?
Think about trial design — good features and limitations.

questions.prompt: The table shows the change in diversity of grassland communities on three islands over 30 years, for two measures. State whether the data show significant changes, giving reasons. (3)

questions.prompt: Explain what P ≤ 0.01 means and why scientists usually use 0.05 as a cut-off. (3)

0.05 means a 5% probability [B1]

So not significant — accept the null hypothesis [B1]
A real small change might not be detected with a small sample. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows the mean rate of movement of CO₂ and water in leaves of normal and transgenic trees with reduced aquaporin. Using only these data, evaluate the importance of aquaporin in the movement of CO₂ and water. (3)

Ranges of mean ± SD don't overlap (26–50 vs 5–25), suggesting a real difference [B1]
Use a t-test to determine whether the difference is significant. [B1]

questions.prompt: In group T, a scatter graph showed a positive correlation between percentage change in oxygen uptake and percentage change in mitochondrial enzyme activity. Evaluate the claim that having thymine at a particular mtDNA position increases exercise ability. (3)
questions.solution:

But correlation doesn't prove cause / no statistical test [B1]
Other genetic or lifestyle differences may be responsible; sample size unknown. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe what a correlation coefficient of +0.85 means and what further information you'd need to know if it is significant. (3)
questions.solution:
Strong positive correlation [B1]
Need to compare with the critical value for the number of data pairs [B1]
At P = 0.05 to decide whether it's significant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a study showing that people with a particular allele perform better in endurance sports does not prove the allele causes better performance. (3)
questions.solution:
Correlation does not mean causation [B1]
Other factors such as training, diet or other genes could be involved [B1]
May be a small / unrepresentative sample. [B1]

questions.prompt: Starfish were placed in a tank with a light at one end, and the number moving towards or away from the light was recorded. State a null hypothesis. (1)
questions.solution: There is no difference in the number of starfish moving towards and away from the light. [B1]

questions.prompt: Maggots were placed in a choice chamber with a dark and a light side. State a null hypothesis. (1)
questions.solution: There is no difference in the number of maggots in the light and dark sides. [B1]

questions.prompt: Woodlice were placed in a chamber with humid and dry sides. State a null hypothesis. (1)
questions.solution: Humidity has no effect on the distribution of woodlice. [B1]

Small numbers / tank, not reef, conditions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Fish were tested with two sounds. Use the table to evaluate the claim that both sounds repel fish. (3)

Only 50 fish / one species / tank conditions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Insects were offered two colours of light. Use the table to evaluate the claim that insects prefer blue to yellow light. (3)
questions.solution:

questions.prompt: Error bars on a bar chart show mean ± 2 standard deviations. Explain how they can be used to judge whether two means are different. (2)
questions.solution:
±2 SD includes about 95% of the data [B1]
If they don't overlap, the difference is likely to be significant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Mean percentage reduction in tumour volume was 45 ± 10% (± 2 SD) at 30 mg per week and 40 ± 12% at 20 mg per week. Which dose would you recommend, and why? (2)
questions.solution:
20 mg — ranges overlap, so no significant difference in effect [B1]
So the lower dose gives similar results with fewer side-effects / less cost. [B1]

questions.prompt: Drug A reduced tumour volume by 50 ± 6% and drug B by 25 ± 8% (± 2 SD). What can you conclude? (2)
questions.solution:
Ranges don't overlap (44–56 vs 17–33) [B1]
So drug A is significantly more effective. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a doctor might choose a lower dose of a drug even if a higher dose gives a slightly larger mean effect. (2)
questions.solution:
Difference may not be significant (overlapping error bars) [B1]
Higher doses may cause more side-effects / cost more. [B1]

questions.prompt: Twelve patients with arthritis were split into a drug group and a control group. Apart from age and general health, give two factors that should be considered when choosing patients. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: severity / stage of arthritis; same sex; other medication; weight / BMI; how long they've had the disease. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why a trial with only 12 patients may not give reliable results. (1)
questions.solution: Small sample not representative; individual variation / anomalies have a large effect. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why all patients in a drug trial were the same sex. (1)
questions.solution: Sex may affect the disease or response to the drug, so it's controlled. [B1]

questions.prompt: Pain scores (0–10) were recorded weekly for patients given a drug (R) or a placebo (S). Evaluate the conclusion that the drug reduces pain. (3)
questions.solution:
Group R pain fell from 9.7 to 5.1, more than group S (9.8 to 7.8), supporting the conclusion [B1]
But in week 3 group S was lower than R / both groups fell at first, suggesting a placebo effect [B1]
Pain scores are subjective / small sample / no statistical test / only 35 days. [B1]

questions.prompt: Mean joint swelling was recorded for patients on a drug or a placebo. Evaluate the conclusion that the drug reduces swelling. (3)
questions.solution:
Drug group fell from 4.2 to 2.1 cm (50%) vs placebo 4.1 to 3.6 cm [B1]
Larger reduction with drug supports the conclusion [B1]
But no SD / statistical test, so may not be significant; small study. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why scientists use a placebo group in a trial measuring pain. (3)
questions.solution:
Pain is subjective and may improve if patients expect it to (placebo effect) [B1]
Placebo group shows how much improvement happens without the drug [B1]
So the effect of the drug itself can be measured. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a study, each patient taking a high-sodium medicine was paired with a control patient taking a low-sodium version. Give two factors that should be the same within each pair and one that should differ. (2)
questions.solution:
Same: two from age; sex; BMI; medical condition / other medicines; smoking [B1]
Differ: sodium content of the medicine. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the advantage of using matched pairs in a medical study. (2)
questions.solution:
Reduces the effect of other variables (age, sex etc.) [B1]
So differences are more likely due to the factor being studied. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why very large numbers of patients are useful in an observational study of medicines. (2)
questions.solution:
Effects may be small / rare, so large numbers are needed to detect them [B1]
More representative / statistically significant results. [B1]

questions.prompt: A study found that adding a substance from green tea to cancer cells grown in a dish slowed their growth. A newspaper claimed green tea cures cancer. Suggest three reasons why the claim may be invalid. (3)
hints: Cells in a dish vs a person.
questions.solution:
Cells in vitro, not in a living person [B1]
Concentrations used may be far higher than could be reached by drinking tea / substance digested or not absorbed [B1]
Slowing growth isn't a cure / only one cell type / no statistical analysis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest three reasons why a study on mice showing a drug shrinks tumours does not prove it will work in humans. (3)
questions.solution:
Mice have different physiology / metabolism [B1]
Dose may not be safe / equivalent in humans [B1]
Tumours in mice may differ from human cancers; side-effects unknown. [B1]

questions.prompt: A study found people who eat more broccoli have lower cancer rates. Suggest three reasons why this doesn't prove broccoli prevents cancer. (3)
questions.solution:
Correlation, not causation [B1]
Broccoli eaters may have healthier lifestyles (exercise, less smoking) [B1]
Other factors such as genetics / sample size / self-reported diet. [B1]

questions.prompt: Normal male haematocrit is 47 ± 5%. Professional cyclists are allowed up to 50%. Give two reasons why this limit is not a valid way to detect EPO use. (2)
questions.solution:
Some people naturally have a haematocrit above 50% (within 47 ± 5) [B1]
Cheaters could use EPO and stay under 50% / altitude training raises it naturally. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a single blood test may not reliably show whether an athlete is using a performance-enhancing drug. (2)
questions.solution:
Drug may have been used earlier and cleared from the blood [B1]
Natural levels vary between people / over time, so a baseline is needed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why keeping a 'biological passport' of an athlete's blood values over time is better than a single limit. (2)
questions.solution:
Compares with the athlete's own normal values [B1]
Sudden unexplained changes can be detected. [B1]

questions.prompt: HIV binds to the CCR5 protein on helper T cells. Two HIV-positive patients received bone marrow stem cell transplants from donors whose cells lacked CCR5. Antiretroviral therapy was stopped 16 months later. 18 months after stopping, no HIV RNA was found in their plasma, no HIV DNA in their helper T cells and no CCR5 on these cells. Only about 59% of HIV-positive people can access antiretroviral therapy. Evaluate the use of stem cell transplants to treat HIV. (5)
hints: Did it work in these patients?
How many patients and how risky?
questions.solution:
Supports: no HIV detected after stopping therapy, so virus may be eliminated [B1]
Donor cells lacked CCR5 so HIV can't bind / infect new T cells [B1]
Could help people who can't access antiretroviral therapy [B1]
But only two patients / short follow-up — HIV might return or use another receptor [B1]
Transplants are risky (radiotherapy / chemotherapy, rejection), expensive and need matching donors lacking CCR5. [B1]

questions.prompt: A new HIV drug was given to 200 patients. After a year, viral load fell by 90% in 150 patients. Evaluate the drug as a treatment. (5)

25% didn't respond / may be resistant [B1]
No control / placebo group for comparison [B1]
Only one year — long-term effects / resistance unknown [B1]
Side-effects and cost not given. [B1]

questions.prompt: Two protein supplements were tested on muscle mass over 12 weeks. Group A gained 1.2 ± 0.8 kg and group B 1.5 ± 0.9 kg (mean ± SD). Evaluate the claim that supplement B is better. (3)
questions.solution:
B gained slightly more on average [B1]

Need a statistical test (t-test) / sample size / control group. [B1]

questions.prompt: A comparison of mean CO₂ uptake in sun and shade in the morning gave P greater than 0.5. What does this tell you? Use the terms probability and chance. (2)
hints: Accept or reject the null hypothesis?

questions.prompt: A t-test comparing two means gave P less than 0.01. What does this tell you? Use the terms probability and chance. (2)
questions.solution:
Probability the difference is due to chance is less than 1% [B1]
So the difference is significant — reject the null hypothesis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a P value of 0.06 is not considered significant even though the difference in means looks large. (2)
questions.solution:
Probability that the difference is due to chance is 6%, above the 5% threshold [B1]
Large spread / small sample may mean the difference could be due to chance. [B1]

questions.prompt: Fish were sampled each October for 29 years below a power station that releases heated water. Species richness and diversity varied but showed no clear trend. A journalist concluded heated water has no effect on fish communities. Explain why this may be invalid. (4)

Only sampled in October — effects may happen at other times (e.g. summer) [B1]
Fish may have already been affected before sampling started / other factors (pollution, fishing) changed [B1]
Sampling method / effort may vary; no statistical test of trend. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest how to design a study to test whether warm water released from a factory affects invertebrate diversity in a river. (4)

Sample upstream (control) and downstream of the outflow [B1]
Same method / net / time / area at each site, e.g. kick sampling [B1]
Repeat at different times of year and over several years [B1]
Calculate index of diversity and use a statistical test. [B1]

questions.prompt: Oestrogen increases the humoral response and decreases the cellular response in autoimmune mice, but has no effect in healthy mice. Oestrogen reduces the cellular response and prevents R — consistent with R being T-cell driven [B1]

Correlation only — no direct measurement of antibodies / T cells in patients; other effects of oestrogen possible. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why results from mouse studies of autoimmune disease might not apply to humans. (4)
questions.solution:
Mice have different immune systems / genes [B1]
Hormone levels and lifespans differ [B1]
Disease in mice may be induced and not identical to the human disease [B1]
Small samples / inbred strains lack human genetic variation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Joint stiffness was scored for 20 mice in each group and the median score was reported. Describe how the median is found. (1)

Highest dose gives lowest stiffness / largest reduction [B1]
But tested on mice, not humans [B1]

No statistical test / spread of scores / side-effects / only 6 weeks. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a new drug should be tested before it is given to patients. (5)
questions.solution:
Lab tests on cells / tissues [B1]
Tests on animals for safety / dosage [B1]
Phase 1: small group of healthy volunteers for safety [B1]
Phase 2/3: larger groups of patients, randomised, double-blind with placebo [B1]
Compare effectiveness and side-effects with existing treatments. [B1]

questions.solution:
Large sample — representative [B1]
Random allocation — avoids bias [B1]
Placebo / control group — comparison [B1]
Double blind — patients and doctors unaware of groups [B1]
Controlled variables e.g. age, sex, severity. [B1]

questions.prompt: In one protected woodland, the number of breeding bird species rose from 20 to 32 over 30 years. A student concluded that all woodlands should be protected to increase bird biodiversity. Evaluate this conclusion. (4)

Number of farms / sampling effort unknown [B1]

questions.solution: Interpolation estimates within the range of data; extrapolation estimates beyond it (less reliable). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why extrapolating a population growth curve may overestimate future population size. (1)
questions.solution: Growth may level off when resources become limiting (carrying capacity). [B1]

questions.prompt: An index of wildlife populations was set to 1.0 in 1970 and had fallen to 0.7 by 2005. A news headline claimed human activities are causing significant biodiversity decline. Suggest three reasons why this headline may not be valid. (3)

No evidence linking the decline to human activities (correlation / cause not shown) [B1]
Index based on a sample of species / populations, not all biodiversity / news graph may use a misleading scale. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a graph's y-axis that doesn't start at zero can be misleading. (3)
questions.solution:
Small changes appear much larger [B1]
Gives a false impression of the size of a trend [B1]
Readers should check axis values / scale. [B1]

questions.prompt: Underweight 5-day-old rats were fed high-protein milk (14 rats) or normal-protein milk (14 rats), then solid food from day 21. But rats, not humans — physiology / lifespan differ [B1]

questions.prompt: A study found that adults who ate high-protein diets had a higher rate of kidney disease. Evaluate the conclusion that high-protein diets cause kidney disease. (5)

Positive correlation between protein intake and kidney disease [B1]

Other factors — diabetes, blood pressure, obesity, age — may be responsible [B1]
Self-reported diet may be inaccurate [B1]
Sample size / statistical significance not given. [B1]

questions.prompt: The 'two-hit' model suggests a birth defect needs a genetic mutation plus an environmental factor. Drug-induced inflammation may not reflect natural environmental factors [B1]
Methylation measured, not the phenotype / effect on protein; only one gene / environmental factor tested. [B1]

Use several concentrations of the inflammation drug [B1]
Repeat / several cell lines / use a statistical test [B1]
Measure protein levels / mRNA to show expression changes / include a control without drug. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why trials of two drugs for a serious incurable lung disease had no control group. (1)

questions.prompt: Suggest how a trial without a placebo group could still compare a new treatment. (1)
questions.solution: Compare with an existing standard treatment / previous patients' data. [B1]

questions.solution: Patient welfare / safety comes first — they must give ongoing informed consent. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why median survival time is often used to compare treatments for serious diseases. (4)

Median isn't affected by extreme values [B1]
Can be calculated even if some patients are still alive at the end [B1]
Gives a fair comparison of typical outcomes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how to find the median survival time for a group of patients in a trial. (2)
questions.solution:

Median is the middle value (or mean of the two middle values). [B1]

questions.solution: So the only difference is the new drug, and its added effect can be measured. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why patients in a cancer trial are randomly allocated to groups. (1)
questions.solution: To avoid bias, so groups have similar characteristics. [B1]

So data support the claim [B1]
