So drug Y may be preferred unless the difference is significant / quality of life considered. [B1]
questions.table:
Drug | Median survival / months | Serious side-effects / %
Y | 13.5 | 12
Z | 14.2 | 32

questions.prompt: Explain why both survival time and tumour size are measured in cancer drug trials. (4)
questions.solution:
Survival time shows whether the drug prolongs life [B1]
Tumour size shows whether the drug acts on the cancer directly [B1]
A drug may shrink tumours without extending life (or vice versa) [B1]
Both together give a fuller picture of effectiveness. [B1]

questions.prompt: The table shows mean dry mass ± SD in grams per plant. Draw conclusions about (a) the effect of the living fungus and (b) nitrate vs ammonium fertiliser. (4)
hints: Compare A with B, C with D.
questions.solution:
Live fungus greatly increased root and shoot mass with both fertilisers (B vs A, D vs C) [B1]
Differences much larger than SDs, so likely significant [B1]
With fungus, nitrate gave more growth than ammonium (B vs D) [B1]
Without fungus, little difference between nitrate and ammonium (A vs C — SDs overlap). [B1]
questions.table:
Group | Root mass / g | Shoot mass / g
A killed + nitrate | 0.40 ± 0.05 | 1.01 ± 0.12
B live + nitrate | 1.61 ± 0.28 | 9.81 ± 0.33
C killed + ammonium | 0.34 ± 0.03 | 0.96 ± 0.26
D live + ammonium | 0.96 ± 0.18 | 4.01 ± 0.47

questions.prompt: Using the table of mean dry mass ± SD, explain how standard deviations help decide whether differences between groups are meaningful. (4)
questions.solution:
SD shows the spread of data around the mean [B1]
If means differ by much more than the SDs (e.g. shoot mass 9.81 ± 0.33 vs 1.01 ± 0.12), difference is likely real [B1]
If ranges overlap (e.g. A 1.01 ± 0.12 vs C 0.96 ± 0.26), difference is probably due to chance [B1]
A statistical test (t-test) is needed to confirm. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student investigated the effect of fertiliser concentration on the growth of bean plants. Give three environmental variables the student should keep the same. (2)
hints: Think about what a plant needs to photosynthesise.
Think about the soil and watering.
questions.solution:
Any three from: light intensity; temperature; volume of water given; carbon dioxide concentration; type / volume of soil; humidity. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: A student investigated the effect of temperature on the rate of respiration of yeast. Give three variables the student should keep the same. (2)
hints: Think about what the yeast is respiring.
Think about the solution the yeast is in.
questions.solution:
Any three from: concentration / volume of glucose; concentration / volume / mass of yeast; pH (buffer); time allowed to acclimatise; volume of solution. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: A student investigated the effect of temperature on the permeability of beetroot cell membranes. Give three variables the student should keep the same. (2)
hints: Think about the beetroot pieces themselves.
Think about the water they are placed in.
questions.solution:
Any three from: size / surface area of beetroot pieces; volume of water; time in water; same beetroot / age; rinsing method. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: In an investigation of beetroot membrane permeability, a student rinsed the beetroot pieces in water before the experiment and used the same volume of water in each tube. Give one reason for each of these steps. (2)
hints: What is on the surface of a freshly cut piece of beetroot?
How does volume affect the colour you measure?
questions.solution:
Rinsing removes pigment released from cells damaged by cutting [B1]
Same volume so the concentration / intensity of colour is comparable. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student placed agar cubes containing an indicator in acid to investigate diffusion. Suggest one reason for keeping the acid at a constant temperature and one reason for making sure the cubes were completely covered by the acid. (2)
hints: Which surfaces of the cube take part?
questions.solution:
Temperature affects kinetic energy / rate of diffusion [B1]
So all surfaces / the whole surface area is in contact with acid. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student used a respirometer containing soda lime to measure oxygen uptake by germinating seeds. Suggest why the apparatus was left in a water bath for 10 minutes before readings were taken, and why soda lime was used. (2)
hints: Seeds give out a gas as well as taking one in.
questions.solution:
To let the temperature (and pressure) equilibrate / stabilise [B1]
Soda lime absorbs carbon dioxide, so volume change is due to oxygen uptake only. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two features of a good scientific drawing of cells seen with an optical microscope. (2)
hints: Think about the lines you draw.
questions.solution:
Clear, continuous lines / no sketching [B1]
No shading [B1]
Label lines drawn with a ruler, not crossing, no arrowheads [B1]
Correct proportions / title / magnification or scale. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any 2.

questions.prompt: A student's drawing of onion epidermis cells has sketchy, overlapping lines, shaded nuclei, and labels with arrowheads that cross each other. Suggest two ways to improve the drawing. (2)
hints: Pick two of the faults and say how to correct them.
What should label lines look like?
questions.solution:
Use single, clear continuous lines [B1]
Do not shade (nuclei) [B1]
Use ruled label lines with no arrowheads that do not cross. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

Model answer:
Any 2.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would use potato cylinders and a range of sucrose solutions to find the water potential of the potato tissue. (3)
hints: What do you measure before and after?
How do you find the concentration where nothing changes?
questions.solution:
Cylinders of the same size; blot dry and weigh before [B1]
Place in a range of sucrose concentrations for the same time at the same temperature [B1]
Blot and reweigh; calculate percentage change in mass [B1]
Plot % change against concentration; where the line crosses 0 is the concentration with the same water potential as the tissue. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe how to make 10 cm³ of each of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution from a 1.0 mol dm⁻³ stock solution and distilled water. (3)
hints: What fraction of the final volume must be stock solution for 0.2 mol dm⁻³?
Volume of stock = final concentration ÷ stock concentration × 10.
questions.solution:
0.2: 2 cm³ stock + 8 cm³ water; 0.4: 4 + 6 [B1]
0.6: 6 + 4; 0.8: 8 + 2 [B1]
Measure with a pipette / syringe / measuring cylinder and mix. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an osmosis experiment with potato cylinders, explain why the student: (i) blotted each cylinder before weighing, (ii) calculated percentage change in mass, (iii) covered the tubes. (3)
hints: What is on the surface after removing a cylinder from solution?
Did all cylinders start with the same mass?
questions.solution:
(i) Removes surface solution, so only the mass of tissue is measured [B1]
(ii) Starting masses differ, so percentage allows comparison [B1]
(iii) Prevents evaporation, which would change the concentration / water potential of the solution. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student extracted pigment from red cabbage leaves using different solvents. Name two variables the student should keep the same. (2)
hints: Think about the solvent and timing.
questions.solution: Any two from: mass / surface area of leaf pieces; volume of solvent; time in solvent; temperature; age / part of leaf. [B2]

questions.prompt: A student investigated the effect of ethanol concentration on pigment leakage from beetroot. Name two variables the student should keep the same. (2)
hints: What could change how much pigment leaks out apart from ethanol?
Think about the pieces and conditions.
questions.solution: Any two from: temperature; size / surface area of beetroot pieces; volume of solution; time in solution; same beetroot. [B2]

questions.prompt: A student investigated the effect of temperature on pigment leakage from beetroot. Name two variables the student should keep the same. (2)
hints: Not temperature — that's the independent variable.
questions.solution: Any two from: volume of water; size / surface area of pieces; time in water; same beetroot / rinsing method. [B2]

questions.prompt: Describe how a student without a colorimeter could use a dilution series of a coloured extract to estimate the pigment concentration in their samples. (3)
hints: How do you compare colours fairly?
questions.solution:
Make a range of known concentrations by diluting the extract [B1]
Put the same volume in identical tubes [B1]
Compare the colour of each sample with the standards against a white background and record the closest match. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to use a colorimeter to measure the concentration of pigment in samples. (3)
hints: What do you set to zero first?
How do you turn absorbance into concentration?
questions.solution:
Zero / calibrate with a blank of solvent (and use the same filter / wavelength) [B1]
Measure the absorbance of known concentrations and plot a calibration curve [B1]
Measure the samples and read concentration off the curve. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a colorimeter is reset using a cuvette of solvent before measuring samples. (3)
hints: What else could absorb light apart from the pigment?
questions.solution:
Sets absorbance to zero for the solvent [B1]
So the reading is due only to the pigment [B1]
Corrects for any absorbance by the cuvette / solvent (or drift). [B1]

questions.prompt: In an enzyme investigation, every reaction was stopped after exactly 2 minutes. Explain why this was important. (2)
hints: What does the amount of product depend on?
Why must all tubes be treated the same?
questions.solution:
The amount of product depends on reaction time [B1]
Same time for every tube, so results can be compared fairly / time is a control variable. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student drew a section through an artery and a vein seen with a microscope. Give two ways to make sure the drawing is a good scientific drawing. (2)
questions.solution:
Use clear, continuous lines with no shading [B1]
Ruled label lines that don't cross / correct relative sizes of the vessels [B1]
Include a title and magnification / scale. [B1]
Any 2 of these points — max 2 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why scientific drawings should be done with a sharp pencil and should show only what is actually seen. (2)
hints: Why not draw what the textbook shows?
questions.solution:
Sharp pencil gives clear, fine lines that can be corrected [B1]
Drawing only what is seen gives an accurate record of the specimen, not an idealised one. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two features that should be included on a drawing of plant tissue seen with an optical microscope, other than the drawing itself. (2)
hints: How does a reader know what they're looking at?
How do they know the size?
questions.solution:
A title [B1]
Labels / magnification or scale bar. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two safety precautions when using a scalpel to dissect a heart. (2)
hints: What happens to the blade afterwards?
questions.solution:
Cut away from the body / on a dissecting board [B1]
Carry and store the scalpel carefully / dispose of blades in a sharps bin. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two hygiene precautions after dissecting animal tissue. (2)
hints: What should you do to your hands?
What about the bench and the tissue?
questions.solution:
Wash hands with soap and water [B1]
Disinfect the work surface / dispose of tissue in a labelled bag. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two precautions when using aseptic technique to culture bacteria on agar plates. (2)
hints: How do you sterilise the loop?
How should the plate be sealed and incubated?
questions.solution:
Flame the loop / neck of the bottle; work near a Bunsen flame [B1]
Tape the lid but do not seal completely / incubate at 25 °C, not 37 °C. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why mice in a cancer drug trial were humanely killed when their tumours reached a set size. (1)
hints: Is it ethical to let them suffer?
questions.solution: To prevent / limit suffering (ethical reason). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why scientists try to use as few animals as possible in drug trials. (1)
hints: Animals may experience pain or distress.
questions.solution: To reduce the number of animals that suffer / ethical reasons. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the mice used in drug trials are often genetically identical. (1)
hints: What else could cause differences between treated and untreated mice?
questions.solution: Reduces variation, so differences are due to the treatment (not genetic differences). [B1]

questions.prompt: Before a new cancer drug is tested on humans, suggest two further investigations scientists should carry out, and explain why. (2)
hints: Is it safe for healthy human cells?
questions.solution:
Test on human cells / tissue cultures to check toxicity to healthy cells [B1]
Test different doses / long-term effects in animals to find a safe, effective dose. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why new drugs are first tested on a small number of healthy volunteers. (2)
hints: Is the first trial testing whether it works?
What must be known before giving it to patients?
questions.solution:
To check safety / side effects [B1]
To find a safe dose before testing on patients. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why later drug trials are double-blind. (2)
hints: Who doesn't know which treatment is given?
questions.solution:
Neither patients nor doctors know who has the drug or placebo [B1]
Avoids bias in reporting / assessing results (and the placebo effect is controlled). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one advantage of using a pH probe connected to a data logger, rather than an indicator, to follow the activity of lipase. (1)
hints: How often can readings be taken?
questions.solution: Continuous / frequent readings, or more accurate / not a subjective colour judgement. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one advantage of using a colorimeter rather than judging colour by eye. (1)
hints: Is a colorimeter reading a number?
Do people see colours the same way?
questions.solution: Gives a quantitative / objective measurement (not subjective). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why measuring the volume of gas with a gas syringe is better than counting bubbles. (1)
hints: Are all bubbles the same size?
questions.solution: Bubbles vary in size, so a syringe measures the actual volume more accurately. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to spread a liquid culture of bacteria evenly over an agar plate using aseptic technique. (3)
hints: How do you sterilise a glass spreader?
How should you handle the lid?
questions.solution:
Dip spreader in ethanol and pass through a Bunsen flame (let it cool) [B1]
Lift the lid only slightly / work near a flame [B1]
Spread the culture over the whole surface; replace the lid and tape it (not fully sealed). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to sterilise an inoculating loop and use it to transfer bacteria from a broth to an agar plate. (3)
hints: How hot should the loop get?
What do you do to the neck of the bottle?
questions.solution:
Heat the loop in a Bunsen flame until red hot, then let it cool [B1]
Remove the lid, flame the neck of the bottle, take a loopful, flame the neck again and replace the lid [B1]
Lift the plate lid slightly and streak the agar; replace the lid quickly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why aseptic technique is used when culturing bacteria. (3)
hints: What could get into the culture?
questions.solution:
Prevents contamination of the culture by other microorganisms [B1]
So results are valid / only the intended bacteria grow [B1]
Prevents bacteria escaping and infecting people / the environment. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student investigated the effect of pH on the rate at which amylase breaks down starch. Describe a suitable control and explain its purpose. (3)
questions.solution:
Same volume / concentration of starch and buffer at each pH [B1]
Boiled (denatured) amylase or water instead of active amylase [B1]
Shows any change in starch is due to the enzyme (not pH alone). [B1]

questions.prompt: A student measured oxygen released when liver (containing catalase) was added to hydrogen peroxide at different temperatures. Describe a suitable control and explain its purpose. (3)
hints: What would have no active enzyme?
What else must be kept the same?
questions.solution:
Boiled liver of the same mass [B1]
Same volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide, at each temperature [B1]
Shows the oxygen is produced by the enzyme, not by spontaneous breakdown of hydrogen peroxide. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a tube without enzyme is included when using a colorimeter to measure the product of an enzyme reaction. (3)
hints: Could the substrate change colour on its own?
questions.solution:
Substrate may break down / change colour without the enzyme [B1]
Gives a baseline reading [B1]
So the difference shows the effect of the enzyme only. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to pour sterile agar into a Petri dish using aseptic technique. (3)
hints: How should you handle the bottle and lid?
questions.solution:
Use sterilised (autoclaved) agar [B1]
Flame the neck of the bottle [B1]
Lift the lid only slightly, pour, replace the lid quickly and leave to set. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to dispose of bacterial cultures and clean up safely after a microbiology practical. (3)
hints: What about the bench and your hands?
questions.solution:
Plates / cultures put in autoclave bags and autoclaved (or soaked in disinfectant) [B1]
Disinfect the work surface [B1]
Wash hands with soap. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to place antibiotic discs onto an agar plate that has been spread with bacteria, using aseptic technique. (3)
hints: How should the lid be handled?
questions.solution:
Sterilise forceps (dip in ethanol and flame) [B1]
Lift the lid slightly and place each disc gently, spaced apart [B1]
Replace the lid quickly and tape it (not fully sealed). [B1]

questions.prompt: Students tested whether garlic extract (dissolved in ethanol) kills bacteria. Describe a suitable positive control and a suitable negative control. (2)
questions.solution:
Positive: a disc / well with a known antibiotic [B1]
Negative: a disc / well with ethanol only (the solvent). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the purpose of the positive and negative controls in an investigation of an antibacterial substance. (2)
hints: What does the positive control prove?
What does the negative control rule out?
questions.solution:
Positive control shows the bacteria can be killed / the method works [B1]
Negative control shows that the solvent / disc alone has no effect, so any effect is due to the substance. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a disc soaked in ethanol, rather than a dry disc, is used as the negative control when testing a plant extract dissolved in ethanol. (2)
hints: What must the control rule out?
questions.solution:
Ethanol itself may kill / inhibit bacteria [B1]
So the control shows any effect on the test disc is due to the extract, not the solvent. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student timed how long apple tissue from two varieties took to turn brown. Variety D: 45, 52 and 48 s. Variety E: 30, 28 and 35 s. Describe a suitable results table and calculate the means to 1 decimal place. (3)
hints: Units go in the column headings, not the cells.
questions.solution:
Table with columns for variety, three repeats and mean, with units (s) in headings only [M1]
Mean for D = 48.3 s [M1]
Mean for E = 31.0 s. [A1]

questions.prompt: Volumes of oxygen collected were 12, 14 and 13 cm³ at 20 °C and 22, 25 and 21 cm³ at 30 °C. Describe a suitable results table and calculate the means to 1 decimal place. (3)
hints: Put the independent variable in the first column.
questions.solution:
Table with temperature / °C in first column, repeats and mean volume / cm³ as headings [M1]
Mean at 20 °C = 13.0 cm³ [M1]
Mean at 30 °C = 22.7 cm³. [A1]

questions.prompt: Give three rules for drawing a results table for an experiment. (3)
hints: Where does the independent variable go?
questions.solution:
Independent variable in the first column [B1]
Column headings include units (not written in cells) [B1]
Values recorded to a consistent number of decimal places / include repeats and mean. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one change that would increase the number of courtship displays recorded in a laboratory study of male fish. (1)
questions.solution: Add females / provide breeding-season conditions (e.g. temperature or day length). [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one variable that should be kept constant when comparing the calling behaviour of two frog populations. (1)
questions.solution: Temperature / time of day / number of females present / time of year. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why recordings of frog calls were made at night. (1)
questions.solution: Frogs call / breed mainly at night. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to make a calibration curve to estimate starch concentration using iodine solution and a colorimeter, and name one control variable. (3)
questions.solution:
Make a range of known starch concentrations (e.g. by dilution) [B1]
Add the same volume of iodine and measure absorbance with a colorimeter (zeroed with a blank, same filter) [B1]
Plot absorbance against concentration and draw a line / curve of best fit. Control: volume of iodine / time before reading / same cuvette. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how colour standards could be used to estimate the percentage oxygen saturation of blood samples, and name one control variable. (3)
hints: You need samples of known saturation.
questions.solution:
Prepare samples of known oxygen saturation (e.g. 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) [B1]
Put the same volume of each, and of the unknowns, in identical tubes [B1]
Compare each unknown against the standards (against a white background) and record the closest match. Control: same lighting / same volume / same tube. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a new calibration curve should be made each time a new batch of reagent is used with a colorimeter. (3)
hints: Is every batch of reagent identical?
questions.solution:
Different batches may differ in concentration / colour [B1]
So the same concentration of test substance could give a different absorbance [B1]
A new curve keeps the results accurate / comparable (and corrects for colorimeter drift). [B1]

questions.prompt: A student investigated the effect of pH on the rate of starch digestion by amylase. Name two variables the student should keep constant. (1)
hints: Not pH — that's the independent variable.
questions.solution: Two from: temperature; volume / concentration of amylase; volume / concentration of starch. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student investigated the effect of hydrogen peroxide concentration on the activity of catalase in liver. Name two variables the student should keep constant. (1)
hints: What about the source of enzyme?
questions.solution: Two from: temperature; pH; mass / size of liver; volume of hydrogen peroxide. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student investigated the effect of inhibitor concentration on an enzyme-controlled reaction. Name two variables the student should keep constant. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: temperature; pH; enzyme concentration; substrate concentration. [B1]

questions.prompt: A dye took 5 minutes to rise up a celery stalk. What other information is needed to calculate the rate of water movement? (1)
questions.solution: The distance the dye travelled (length of stalk). [B1]

questions.prompt: A potometer measured water uptake by a leafy shoot. What other information is needed to calculate the rate of water uptake per unit leaf area? (1)
hints: You need to measure the leaves.
questions.solution: The total surface area of the leaves. [B1]

questions.prompt: A seedling grew 18 mm. What other information is needed to calculate its mean growth rate? (1)
questions.solution: The time over which it grew. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a root-tip squash, explain why a stain such as toluidine blue is used, and why only the tip of the root is used. (2)
hints: What would chromosomes look like unstained?
questions.solution:
Stain binds to DNA / chromosomes, so they can be seen [B1]
Root tip contains the meristem, where cells are dividing. [B1]

questions.prompt: When making a root-tip squash, explain why you press down firmly on the coverslip but do not twist it. (2)
hints: What do you want the cells to form?
questions.solution:
Pressing spreads the cells into a single layer so light passes through [B1]
Twisting could damage / break the chromosomes or smear the cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cells should be counted in several fields of view when calculating a mitotic index. (2)
questions.solution:
Dividing cells may not be evenly distributed, so more fields are more representative [B1]
Gives a more reliable mean / reduces the effect of anomalies. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a respirometer is left to stand for a while after being placed in a water bath, before readings are taken. (1)
questions.solution: So temperature / pressure equilibrates and volume changes are due only to respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a respirometer is placed in a water bath. (1)
hints: What would change gas volume apart from respiration?
questions.solution: To keep the temperature constant (temperature affects gas volume and rate of respiration). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the purpose of a second respirometer containing glass beads instead of organisms. (1)
questions.solution: Control — shows volume changes not caused by organisms (e.g. temperature / pressure changes). [B1]

questions.prompt: In a trial of a diuretic drug, all volunteers drank the same volume of water before the trial. Suggest and explain why. (2)
hints: Why must it be the same?
questions.solution:
Water intake affects urine volume [B1]
So differences in urine volume are due to the drug only. [B1]

questions.prompt: Volunteers in a diuretic trial were asked not to exercise before or during the trial. Suggest and explain why. (2)
hints: What would sweating do to urine volume?
questions.solution:
Exercise causes water loss by sweating / changes blood flow to the kidneys [B1]
Which would reduce urine volume and affect results. [B1]

questions.prompt: Volunteers in a diuretic trial ate the same amount of salt. Suggest and explain why. (2)
hints: How does salt affect blood water potential?
questions.solution:
Salt intake affects blood water potential / ADH release [B1]
Which changes how much water is reabsorbed and so urine volume. [B1]

questions.prompt: The lids were kept on the Petri dishes during an investigation of shoot growth in IAA solutions. Explain why. (2)
hints: What would happen to the solution?
questions.solution:
Reduces evaporation, which would change IAA concentration / dry out the segments [B1]
Reduces contamination by microorganisms. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why plant tissue culture is carried out in sterile conditions. (2)
hints: What could grow on the nutrient medium?
questions.solution:
Microorganisms would grow on the nutrient-rich medium [B1]
They would compete for nutrients / damage the plant tissue. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why shoot segments were kept at a constant temperature during a growth investigation. (2)
questions.solution:
Temperature affects enzyme activity / respiration / rate of growth [B1]
So changes in growth are due only to IAA concentration. [B1]

questions.prompt: In paper chromatography, explain why the solvent level must be below the origin. (1)
hints: What would happen if the spot were under the solvent?
questions.solution: Otherwise the pigments would dissolve into the solvent pool instead of moving up the paper. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the chromatography tank is covered while the chromatogram runs. (1)
questions.solution: So the air is saturated with solvent vapour / solvent doesn't evaporate from the paper. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the spot of pigment extract is kept small and concentrated. (1)
hints: What happens to a large spot as it moves?
questions.solution: Gives sharper / better separated spots that don't overlap. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to run a paper chromatogram once the pigment spot has been applied. (2)
hints: When do you remove the paper?
questions.solution:
Place paper in solvent with the origin above the solvent level, and cover [B1]
Remove when the solvent is near the top and mark the solvent front. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how Rf values can be used to identify pigments on a chromatogram. (2)
hints: What do you compare it with?
questions.solution:
Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front [B1]
Compare with known Rf values for each pigment (in the same solvent). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to make 10 cm³ of each of 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 mmol dm⁻³ solutions from a 10 mmol dm⁻³ stock solution and distilled water. (4)
hints: Make up to 10 cm³ with water.
questions.solution:
0: 0 cm³ stock + 10 cm³ water; 2: 2 cm³ + 8 cm³ [B1]
4: 4 + 6; 6: 6 + 4 [B1]
8: 8 + 2 [B1]
Measure with pipettes / syringes and mix thoroughly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to produce and use a calibration curve to find the concentration of a substance using a colorimeter. (4)
hints: How do you read off the unknown?
questions.solution:
Prepare a range of known concentrations and add the same volume of reagent to each [B1]
Measure absorbance of each with a colorimeter [B1]
Plot absorbance against concentration and draw a line / curve of best fit [B1]
Measure the unknown and read its concentration from the curve. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to use a colorimeter to get accurate absorbance readings. (4)
questions.solution:
Use the correct filter / wavelength [B1]
Zero the colorimeter with a blank (solvent / reagent without sample) [B1]
Use the same volume in the cuvette; handle by the ridged sides, keep clean [B1]
Take readings the same time after adding the reagent. [B1]

questions.prompt: The absorbance of a urine sample was higher than that of the most concentrated standard used for the calibration curve. Suggest what should be done to find its concentration. (2)
hints: Can you read beyond the curve?
How could you bring the reading into range?
questions.solution:
Dilute the sample by a known factor and measure again [B1]
Read the concentration from the curve and multiply by the dilution factor. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to use a calibration curve to find the concentration of an unknown sample. (2)
hints: What do you measure for the sample?
Which way do you read across?
questions.solution:
Measure the absorbance of the sample under the same conditions [B1]
Find that absorbance on the y-axis, read across to the line and down to the concentration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how you would make sure that all the water has been removed from plant samples dried in an oven. (2)
hints: How do you know when no more water is lost?
questions.solution:
Weigh, return to the oven, then reweigh [B1]
Repeat until the mass stays constant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why plant samples are dried at about 80 °C rather than at a much higher temperature. (2)
hints: What could happen to organic matter at high temperature?
questions.solution:
A higher temperature could burn / decompose organic matter [B1]
So the mass would be lower than the true dry biomass. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why dried samples are cooled in a desiccator before being weighed. (2)
hints: What could dry samples absorb from the air?
What would that do to mass?
questions.solution:
Prevents the sample absorbing moisture from the air [B1]
Which would increase its mass / give an inaccurate dry mass. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain two features of an experiment design that would make a comparison of transgenic and non-transgenic fish valid. (2)
hints: What conditions must be the same?
How should the fish be related?
questions.solution:
Same conditions (temperature, food, tank size) so only the gene differs [B1]
Fish of the same age / from the same parents, reducing genetic variation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why siblings from the same parents are used as the non-transgenic control group. (2)
hints: What else could cause size differences?
questions.solution:
Siblings are genetically similar [B1]
So differences in growth are due to the inserted gene, not other genes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a large number of fish should be measured in each group. (2)
hints: What does a bigger sample give?
questions.solution:
Individuals vary in size [B1]
A large sample gives a more reliable / representative mean and allows a statistical test. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a trial of a new cancer drug, the control group received the standard drug rather than a placebo. Give two reasons why. (2)
hints: Is it ethical to give no treatment?
questions.solution:
Unethical to withhold treatment from cancer patients [B1]
Shows whether the new drug is better than the current best treatment. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why patients in a drug trial are randomly allocated to groups. (2)
hints: Could the researcher influence who gets the drug?
questions.solution:
Avoids bias in choosing who gets each treatment [B1]
Makes the groups similar (age, severity, etc.), so differences are due to the drug. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why drug trials are often double-blind. (2)
hints: Who doesn't know which treatment is given?
questions.solution:
Neither patients nor doctors know who receives which treatment [B1]
Prevents bias in reporting or assessing the results. [B1]

questions.prompt: Apart from temperature and pH, name two variables to control when growing yeast cultures to compare their growth. (2)
hints: What is in the growth medium?
How many cells at the start?
questions.solution: Two from: volume / concentration of glucose (nutrient medium); starting number / mass of yeast; oxygen supply / shaking; time. [B2]

questions.prompt: Name two variables to control when comparing the effect of different antibiotic discs on a bacterial lawn. (2)
questions.solution: Two from: disc size / concentration of antibiotic; volume of culture spread; depth of agar; incubation temperature / time. [B2]

questions.prompt: Name two variables to control when measuring the rate of respiration of yeast at different temperatures. (2)
questions.solution: Two from: glucose concentration / volume; mass / concentration of yeast; pH; time allowed to acclimatise. [B2]

questions.prompt: Give two things that must be the same to compare the respiration rate of seeds at two temperatures fairly. (2)
questions.solution:
Same mass / number / type of seeds [B1]
Same time / same capillary tube / acclimatisation time. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why drug doses in animal studies are given per kg of body mass. (1)
hints: Do larger animals have more blood and tissue?
questions.solution: Larger animals have more tissue / blood, so dosing by mass gives the same concentration / effect in each animal. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why children are usually given smaller doses of medicine than adults. (1)
questions.solution: Children have a smaller body mass, so a smaller dose gives the same concentration in the body. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why animals of similar mass are often used in a study. (1)
questions.solution: Reduces variation between animals, so differences are due to the treatment. [B1]

questions.prompt: You are given chromatography paper, a ruler, a pencil, a glass tank with a lid, a solvent and a leaf pigment extract. Describe how you would separate the pigments in the extract. (4)
hints: Where does the extract go on the paper, and why pencil?
How deep should the solvent be?
questions.solution:
Draw a pencil origin line about 1–2 cm from the bottom of the paper [B1]
Spot the extract on the line repeatedly, letting it dry between applications, to build a small concentrated spot [B1]
Stand the paper in solvent in the tank with the solvent below the origin line, lid on [B1]
Remove when the solvent front nears the top, mark the front and let the paper dry. [B1]

questions.prompt: After running a chromatogram of leaf pigments, describe how you would identify each pigment using Rf values. (4)
hints: What two distances do you measure?
What do you compare the Rf values with?
questions.solution:
Mark the solvent front as soon as the paper is removed [B1]
Measure the distance from the origin to the centre of each pigment spot [B1]
Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front [B1]
Compare Rf values with known values for the same solvent (and conditions). [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain four precautions taken when running a chromatogram of photosynthetic pigments, and why each is needed. (4)
hints: Why not use pen for the origin line?
Why keep the origin above the solvent?
questions.solution:
Origin drawn in pencil, because ink would dissolve and separate too [B1]
Origin above the solvent level, so pigments don't dissolve straight into the solvent [B1]
Small, concentrated spot (dried between applications), so the spots don't smudge into each other [B1]
Lid on the tank, so the solvent doesn't evaporate / the atmosphere stays saturated [B1]
Handle paper at the edges / wear gloves, so grease doesn't affect the run. [B1]
Any 4 of these points — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: In an experiment, tomato seeds were planted in sterilised soil and a mycorrhizal fungus culture was added to half of the pots. Suggest two reasons why the soil was sterilised. (2)
hints: What might already be living in soil?
What would that do to the control pots?
questions.solution:
To kill any mycorrhizal fungi already in the soil, so only treated pots have the fungus / control has none [B1]
To kill pathogens / other microorganisms that could affect growth (a confounding variable). [B1]

questions.prompt: In an experiment on the effect of mycorrhizal fungi, the control pots had sterilised fungal culture added to them. Suggest two reasons why. (2)
hints: What else is in the culture besides living fungus?
How does this make the comparison fair?
questions.solution:
The culture medium may contain nutrients that affect growth [B1]
So the only difference between groups is the living fungus / shows the effect is due to the fungus. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons why the pots in a plant-growth experiment were placed in random positions in the greenhouse and moved around regularly. (2)
hints: Is light and temperature the same everywhere in a greenhouse?
questions.solution:
Light intensity / temperature / humidity vary in different parts of the greenhouse [B1]
Randomising avoids bias, so differences are due to the treatment only. [B1]

questions.prompt: In the tomato experiment, the soil contained the recommended concentration of fertiliser. Suggest two reasons why this concentration was used. (2)
hints: Would results apply to farms if no fertiliser was used?
questions.solution:
It matches conditions a farmer would use, so results are relevant / realistic [B1]
So mineral ions are not limiting / plants grow normally / too much could harm plants or the fungus. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons why all plants in a growth experiment were given the same volume of water each day (except where water was the variable). (2)
hints: What happens if one plant gets more water?
What is this type of variable called?
questions.solution:
Water affects photosynthesis / growth, so it is a control variable [B1]
So any difference in growth is due to the independent variable only / results are valid. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two reasons why the same variety of tomato was used in every pot in an experiment. (2)
hints: Do different varieties grow at the same rate?
What are you trying to measure?
questions.solution:
Different varieties have different genotypes / yields / responses [B1]
So the variety isn't a confounding variable and the effect is due to the treatment. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three environmental factors that should be controlled when investigating the effect of colour of light on the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed. (2)
hints: What about CO₂ supply in water?
questions.solution:
Temperature; carbon dioxide concentration (e.g. hydrogencarbonate); light intensity. [B2]
3 correct = 2 marks; 2 correct = 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would measure the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed using a photosynthometer. (2)
questions.solution:
Collect oxygen produced in a capillary tube over a set time [B1]
Measure the length of the bubble and convert to volume (πr²l), dividing by time. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why pondweed is left for a few minutes at each light intensity before measurements are taken. (2)
questions.solution:
So the plant can acclimatise / rate becomes stable at the new condition [B1]
So results reflect the new light intensity only. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to make a 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ solution of gibberellin from a 10⁻¹ mol dm⁻³ stock solution. (1)
hints: Could be done in two steps.
questions.solution: Add 1 cm³ of stock to 99 cm³ distilled water (or two serial 1 in 10 dilutions). [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to make 10 cm³ of a 0.05 mol dm⁻³ solution from a 0.5 mol dm⁻³ stock solution. (1)
questions.solution: 1 cm³ of stock + 9 cm³ distilled water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to make 20 cm³ of a 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution from a 1.0 mol dm⁻³ stock solution. (1)
questions.solution: 4 cm³ of stock + 16 cm³ distilled water. [B1]

questions.prompt: You are given gibberellin solutions from 10⁻¹ to 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³, distilled water, six Petri dishes and 60 stem segments of varying lengths. Describe how you would investigate the effect of gibberellin concentration on stem growth. (5)
hints: Segments vary in length — how do you allow for that?
questions.solution:
Measure the starting length of each segment [B1]
Place 10 segments in each dish with the same volume of each concentration, and distilled water as a control [B1]
Keep at the same temperature / light / for the same time [B1]
Re-measure lengths after a set time (e.g. 24 h) [B1]
Calculate the mean percentage change in length for each concentration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate the effect of IAA concentration on the growth of root segments. (5)
hints: How do you make it fair?
questions.solution:
Make a range of IAA concentrations by serial dilution, plus distilled water control [B1]
Cut root segments of the same length from the same region of the root [B1]
Same number of segments and same volume of solution in each dish [B1]
Same temperature, in the dark, same time [B1]
Measure final length and calculate mean change / percentage change; repeat. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate the effect of temperature on the germination of seeds. (5)
questions.solution:
Use several temperatures, e.g. water baths / incubators at 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 °C [B1]
Same number of seeds of the same species / variety at each [B1]
Same volume of water / same substrate, same light [B1]
Count the number / percentage germinated after a set time [B1]
Repeat to calculate a mean. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how an oven and a balance could be used to find the dry mass of a sample of leaves. (2)
hints: How do you know all water has gone?
questions.solution:
Heat at about 100 °C (low enough not to burn) to evaporate water [B1]
Weigh, reheat and re-weigh until mass is constant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Freshwater shrimps were collected from a stream. Water and gravel from the same stream were put in a choice chamber with four sections at different light intensities, made using layers of black paper. 30 shrimps were placed in the centre and counted in each section after 10 minutes. Suggest and explain three features of the method that support its validity. (3)
hints: Why use water from the same stream?
questions.solution:
Same water and gravel, so other conditions like their habitat / only light varies [B1]
Black paper changes only light intensity, not temperature [B1]
Placed in the centre so no bias towards one section [B1]
10 minutes allows time to move / settle; 30 shrimps gives a reasonable sample. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Woodlice were placed in a choice chamber with a dry side and a humid side. Suggest three ways to make the investigation valid. (3)
hints: What else could differ between sides?
How many woodlice and how many repeats?
questions.solution:
Keep light / temperature the same on both sides (cover the chamber) [B1]
Release woodlice in the centre [B1]
Use many woodlice and repeat, swapping sides to avoid bias [B1]
Same time before counting. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain three ethical considerations when carrying out a choice-chamber investigation on invertebrates. (3)
questions.solution:
Handle carefully (e.g. with a soft brush) to avoid harm [B1]
Keep conditions within tolerable limits (not too dry / hot) and for a short time [B1]
Return them to their habitat afterwards. [B1]

questions.prompt: Germinating seeds were placed in a respirometer with potassium hydroxide to absorb CO₂. Before readings were taken, the apparatus was left with the tap open for 10 minutes in a water bath. Give three reasons why. (3)
hints: What needs to reach the water bath temperature?
What might the seeds need time to do?
questions.solution:
Allow the apparatus / air to reach the water bath temperature (equilibrate) [B1]
Allow pressure to equalise with the atmosphere [B1]
Allow seeds to adjust / respiration rate to become constant [B1]
Allow KOH to absorb CO₂ already present. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain the purpose of (i) the potassium hydroxide, (ii) a control tube containing glass beads, and (iii) the water bath in a respirometer experiment. (3)
hints: Why the same volume of beads?
questions.solution:
(i) Absorbs CO₂, so volume change is due to oxygen uptake only [B1]
(ii) Control with same volume of non-living material — compensates for changes in temperature / pressure [B1]
(iii) Keeps temperature constant, as temperature affects gas volume and respiration rate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a respirometer could be used to find the respiratory quotient (RQ) of germinating seeds. (3)
hints: Two runs — with and without what?
questions.solution:
Run with KOH to measure oxygen uptake (volume decrease) [B1]
Run without KOH — change is the difference between CO₂ produced and O₂ used [B1]
Calculate CO₂ produced and RQ = CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ consumed. [B1]

questions.prompt: The respirometer experiment was carried out at 20 °C. Suggest and explain why this temperature was chosen. (2)
hints: Could seeds be damaged at higher temperatures?
questions.solution:
Enzymes active / seeds respire at a measurable rate [B1]
Not so high that enzymes denature / seeds damaged / similar to natural conditions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the seeds used in a respirometer were all of the same species and the same mass. (2)
hints: Do species respire at different rates?
How does mass affect oxygen uptake?
questions.solution:
Different species may respire at different rates [B1]
Greater mass means more cells / more respiration, so mass is a control variable (or calculate rate per gram). [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why dead (boiled) seeds could be used as a control in a respirometer experiment. (2)
questions.solution:
Dead seeds don't respire [B1]
So any volume change shows the effect of other factors (temperature / pressure / microorganisms). [B1]

questions.prompt: Samples from infected lungs were spread on agar plates and colonies counted. Samples from the untreated group had to be diluted before plating, but samples from the phage-treated group did not. Explain why. (2)
hints: How many bacteria were in each sample?
Can you count colonies that merge?
questions.solution:
Untreated samples had many more bacteria — colonies would overlap / too many to count [B1]
Treated samples had fewer bacteria, so separate colonies could be counted without dilution. [B1]

questions.prompt: A sample was diluted 1 in 10 four times and 0.1 cm³ was spread on a plate, giving 42 colonies. Calculate the number of bacteria per cm³ in the original sample. (2)
Describe how to carry out a serial dilution of a bacterial culture. (2)
questions.solution:
Transfer 1 cm³ of culture to 9 cm³ sterile water / broth and mix [B1]
Repeat, transferring 1 cm³ of each dilution into the next tube, using a new sterile pipette each time. [B1]

questions.prompt: Outline how a potometer could be used to find the rate of water loss per mm² of leaf surface area. (3)
hints: How do you measure leaf area?
questions.solution:
Measure water uptake (bubble movement / volume) over a set time [B1]
Remove leaves and draw round them on graph paper (or photograph) to find total area, counting both surfaces [B1]
Divide rate by surface area. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you would set up a potometer to give reliable results. (3)
questions.solution:
Cut the shoot under water (at a slant) to stop air entering the xylem [B1]
Assemble the potometer under water / ensure no air bubbles [B1]
Seal joints with Vaseline and dry the leaves; let the plant acclimatise. [B1]

questions.prompt: When counting cells in a haemocytometer square, cells touching the top and left lines are counted but those touching the bottom and right lines are not. Suggest two reasons. (2)
hints: Would some cells be counted twice?
questions.solution:
Prevents cells being counted twice (in adjacent squares) [B1]
Gives a consistent / standard method, so counts are comparable / accurate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why several squares are counted in a haemocytometer and a mean calculated. (2)
questions.solution:
Cells are not evenly distributed / some squares are atypical [B1]
Mean is more representative / reduces the effect of anomalies. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a sample is mixed thoroughly before it is placed in a haemocytometer. (2)
questions.solution:
Cells settle / clump [B1]
Mixing ensures an even distribution so the sample is representative. [B1]

questions.prompt: Red blood cells were diluted 200 times but white blood cells only 20 times. Suggest why. (1)
questions.solution: There are far fewer white cells, so less dilution is needed to have enough to count. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a bacterial culture is diluted before counting cells. (1)
questions.solution: So there are few enough cells to count individually / they don't overlap. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a dilution of 1000 might make a cell count unreliable. (1)
questions.solution: Very few cells per square, so chance has a big effect / many squares would have zero. [B1]

questions.prompt: Ammonia concentration in soil samples was given in µg per g of soil. Suggest why these units were used. (2)
hints: Do samples have the same mass?
questions.solution:
Samples may differ in mass, so per gram allows comparison [B1]
Ammonia is present in small amounts, so µg is suitable. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the rate of photosynthesis of different leaves is often expressed per cm² of leaf. (2)
questions.solution:
Leaves have different areas [B1]
So rates per unit area can be compared fairly. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why oxygen uptake by seeds is expressed per gram per hour. (2)
questions.solution:
Different masses of seeds / different times [B1]
So results are comparable. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you could measure the growth of a bacterial population in a liquid culture. (4)
questions.solution:
Measure absorbance / turbidity with a colorimeter at intervals [B1]
Or take samples, serial dilute and plate [B1]
Count colonies after incubation and multiply by the dilution factor [B1]
Plot log of number against time. [B1]

questions.prompt: Bacterial cultures were set up in glass bottles. Suggest one method of sterilising the bottles and explain why sterilisation was needed. (2)
questions.solution:
Autoclave (or heat in oven) [B1]
Kills microorganisms already present, which could compete or affect results. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two aseptic techniques used when transferring bacteria from a culture to an agar plate. (2)
questions.solution: Two from: flame the inoculating loop until red hot and cool; flame the neck of the bottle; lift the lid of the Petri dish only slightly; work near a Bunsen flame; disinfect bench. [B2]

questions.prompt: Explain why agar plates are taped but not sealed completely and incubated at 25 °C rather than 37 °C. (2)
questions.solution:
Not sealed so oxygen gets in and anaerobic (pathogenic) bacteria don't grow [B1]
25 °C reduces the chance of growing human pathogens. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you could obtain a quantitative measure of how cloudy three river-water samples are. (3)
hints: What instrument measures light passing through?
questions.solution:
Use a colorimeter [B1]
Zero / calibrate it with distilled water (blank) [B1]
Measure absorbance / transmission of each sample with the same filter / wavelength, using a cuvette of the same size; higher absorbance = cloudier. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a calibration curve can be used to find the concentration of a substance in an unknown solution using a colorimeter. (3)
questions.solution:
Make solutions of known concentration (serial dilution) and measure their absorbance [B1]
Plot absorbance against concentration (calibration curve) [B1]
Measure the absorbance of the unknown and read off its concentration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest three variables to control when comparing cloudiness of water samples with a colorimeter. (3)
questions.solution:
Same filter / wavelength of light [B1]
Same cuvette / path length [B1]
Samples mixed / shaken the same amount before measuring / same temperature / same volume. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two safety precautions when dissecting a heart. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: cut away from body / on a board; handle scalpel carefully; wear gloves / wash hands; disinfect surfaces. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two ethical considerations when dissecting animal organs in schools. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: obtained from food industry (not killed for dissection); treated with respect; dispose properly; students may object. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how you would identify the left ventricle in a dissected heart. (1)
questions.solution: It has the thickest muscular wall. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an investigation, group I drank caffeine with sugar, group J drank caffeine without sugar, and group K drank water. Suggest one extra group that would show whether it's the combination of caffeine and sugar that causes the increase in heart rate, and explain why. (2)
hints: Which variable hasn't been tested on its own?
questions.solution:
A group given sugar without caffeine [B1]
To see the effect of sugar alone, so the combined effect can be compared. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why participants in a caffeine study were asked not to eat or drink anything else for several hours beforehand. (2)
hints: Other substances could affect heart rate.
questions.solution:
Other food / drink (e.g. caffeine in tea) could affect heart rate [B1]
So any effect is due to the drink given only. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why participants in a caffeine study should not know whether their drink contains caffeine. (2)
questions.solution:
Knowing might change their heart rate (expectation / stress / placebo effect) [B1]
Blind trial reduces bias. [B1]

questions.prompt: Starfish from tropical coral reefs were studied in tanks. Suggest two factors to keep constant so they behave normally. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: temperature (warm); salinity / sea water; pH; oxygen concentration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two variables that should be kept constant in a maggot choice-chamber experiment testing light. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: temperature; humidity; age / size of maggots; time. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why animals in a choice-chamber experiment are left to acclimatise before the experiment starts. (1)
questions.solution: So handling stress doesn't affect their movement / they behave normally. [B1]

questions.prompt: Tumour volume was measured before and after treatment, and both the change in volume and the percentage change were recorded. Explain why both were recorded. (2)
hints: Do tumours start the same size?
questions.solution:
Tumours started at different sizes, so percentage change allows comparison [B1]
Volume shows the actual size of the tumour / absolute change. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why tumour size is often measured as volume rather than diameter. (2)
questions.solution:
Tumours are three-dimensional, so volume reflects the number of cells better [B1]
Small changes in diameter mean large changes in volume. [B1]

questions.prompt: Female fish with large or small brains were each placed in a tank next to two males, one brightly coloured and one dull, and watched for 10 minutes to see which male they swam near. 45 of each type of female were used. Suggest three limitations of this investigation. (3)
hints: Does swimming near a male mean choosing to mate?
questions.solution:
Swimming near a male doesn't necessarily show mate choice / mating not observed [B1]
Only 10 minutes — behaviour may change over time [B1]
Other features of the males (size, behaviour) not controlled / same males used repeatedly [B1]
Tank conditions not natural / observer bias / position of males not swapped. [B1]
Any 3 of these points — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Suggest three ways to improve an investigation into whether female birds prefer males with longer tail feathers. (3)
questions.solution:
Use males that differ only in tail length (e.g. trim / extend feathers) [B1]
Swap the positions of the males to avoid side bias [B1]
Use many females and repeat / measure actual mating or eggs fathered. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why each female in a mate-choice experiment should only be tested once, and why the observer should not know the type of female. (3)
questions.solution:
Testing once avoids learning / previous experience affecting choice [B1]
Each female is an independent data point [B1]
Observer unaware avoids bias in recording behaviour. [B1]

questions.prompt: Beetles were released in the middle of a box, half light and half dark, and their position and mean speed recorded after 5 minutes. The light side was 37.5 °C and the dark side 35 °C. A student concluded beetles prefer the dark, move faster in light, and that light affects their behaviour. Suggest why the conclusions might not be valid. (3)
questions.solution:
Temperature also differs between sides, so it may be temperature not light (confounding variable) [B1]
Only 5 minutes / sample size / repeats unknown [B1]
No statistical test, so differences may be due to chance. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest three improvements to an investigation of the effect of light on the movement of woodlice in a choice chamber. (3)
questions.solution:
Use a heat filter / LED so temperature is the same on both sides [B1]
Use more woodlice and repeat, swapping the light side [B1]
Control humidity; release in the centre; use a statistical test. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a taxis and a kinesis, and how you could show which a woodlouse shows in response to humidity. (3)
questions.solution:
Taxis is directional; kinesis is a change in speed / rate of turning [B1]
Track woodlice paths in humid and dry areas [B1]
If they move faster / turn less in dry and slow in humid without directional movement, it is kinesis. [B1]

questions.prompt: Plant height was used instead of biomass to calculate growth rate so plants weren't destroyed. State the assumption made and why it may not be valid. (2)
questions.solution:
Assumes biomass increases in proportion to height [B1]
Plants may grow in width / leaves / roots without increasing in height. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why dry mass is the most accurate measure of plant growth, and its disadvantage. (2)
questions.solution:
Water content varies, so dry mass is a reliable measure [B1]
Plants must be killed, so growth over time can't be followed in the same plant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two non-destructive measurements of plant growth and one limitation of each. (2)
questions.solution:
Height — doesn't include width / roots [B1]
Number / area of leaves — doesn't reflect stem or root growth. [B1]

questions.prompt:
A ruler was caught after falling 64 mm. The ruler has a resolution of 1 mm. Which is the percentage uncertainty?

Choose one answer.

A  0.78%
B  1.56%
C  3.13%
D  15.6% (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
A length of 125 mm was measured with an uncertainty of ±0.5 mm. What is the percentage uncertainty?

Choose one answer.

A  0.4%
B  0.8%
C  4%
D  2.5% (1)
questions.solution: A [B1]

questions.prompt:
A distance of 40 mm was measured with an uncertainty of ±1 mm. What is the percentage uncertainty?

Choose one answer.

A  0.25%
B  1.25%
C  2.5%
D  4% (1)
questions.solution: C [B1]

questions.prompt: In a reaction-time test, one trial gave a time of 30 ms, but humans can't react in less than 45 ms. Suggest an explanation. (1)
hints: Did they react to the stimulus?
questions.solution: The person anticipated / guessed the drop rather than reacting to it. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why reaction times got shorter over the first few trials of an experiment. (1)
questions.solution: Practice / learning effect. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest what to do with an anomalous result when calculating a mean. (1)
questions.solution: Exclude it from the mean (and repeat that trial). [B1]

questions.prompt: Yeast respiration in different sugars was measured by collecting CO₂. Suggest two variables, other than temperature, to keep constant. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: concentration / volume of sugar solution; mass / concentration of yeast; pH; time allowed to acclimatise. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two ways of keeping temperature constant in a yeast respiration investigation. (1)
questions.solution: Use a thermostatically controlled water bath; let solutions reach the temperature before starting. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a layer of oil is placed on a yeast and glucose solution in an anaerobic respiration experiment. (1)
questions.solution: Stops oxygen dissolving / entering, so respiration is anaerobic. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student measured respiration by timing how long bromothymol blue took to change from blue to yellow. Explain why this is less accurate than measuring gas volume and how it could be improved. (2)
questions.solution:
The end point is subjective / colour changes gradually, so hard to judge [B1]
Use a colour standard to compare, or a colorimeter to measure absorbance. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why methylene blue is used to compare the respiration rate of yeast at different temperatures, and one limitation. (2)
questions.solution:
Methylene blue accepts electrons / H and becomes colourless — faster decolourisation means faster respiration [B1]
End point is subjective / hard to judge. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two ways to improve the reliability of a method that times a colour change. (2)
questions.solution:
Repeat and calculate a mean [B1]
Compare with a colour standard / use a white tile / same person judges each end point. [B1]

questions.prompt: A few colonies grew on plates containing an antibiotic that the bacterium is not resistant to. Suggest two reasons. (2)
questions.solution:
A mutation gave some bacteria resistance [B1]
Contamination by another species / antibiotic concentration too low / antibiotic broken down. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a control plate without antibiotic is used when testing antibiotics. (2)
questions.solution:
Shows the bacteria are viable / grow normally [B1]
So any reduction can be attributed to the antibiotic. [B1]

questions.prompt: An allergen dissolved in olive oil was applied to one ear of each mouse and olive oil alone to the other ear. Suggest and explain why. (1)
questions.solution: Control — shows any swelling is due to the allergen, not the olive oil. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why the same mice were used for both treatments (one on each ear). (1)
questions.solution: Removes variation between individual mice / each mouse is its own control. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why mice of the same age and genotype were used in an immune study. (1)
questions.solution: Age / genetics affect immune responses, so controlling them reduces variation. [B1]

questions.prompt: Woodlice were placed in a respirometer in a water bath and the movement of a coloured drop measured each minute for 5 minutes. Suggest two further variables to keep constant. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: mass / number of woodlice; volume of KOH / soda lime; time to acclimatise; volume of air in the tube. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two variables to control when comparing the respiration rates of germinating seeds of two species. (1)
questions.solution: Two from: mass of seeds; age / time since germination; temperature; volume of KOH. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the respirometer is left for 10 minutes before readings are taken. (1)
questions.solution: To let the apparatus reach the water-bath temperature / organisms acclimatise / pressure equalise. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a syringe attached to a respirometer can be used to reset the coloured drop to the start of the scale. (2)
questions.solution:
Open the tap / connect the syringe [B1]
Push the syringe plunger to move the drop back to the start, then close the tap. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a syringe on a respirometer can be used to measure the volume of oxygen used. (2)
questions.solution:
After a set time, push the syringe to return the drop to its starting position [B1]
Volume pushed in from the syringe scale equals the volume of oxygen absorbed. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the capillary tube of a respirometer must be airtight. (2)
questions.solution:
Leaks would let air in or out, so pressure / volume changes wouldn't be due to respiration [B1]
Results would be inaccurate. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest a suitable control for a respirometer experiment with woodlice and explain why it is needed. (2)
questions.solution:
Same apparatus with glass beads (same volume / mass) instead of woodlice [B1]
Shows changes due to temperature / pressure, not respiration. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a differential (two-tube) respirometer reduces the effect of temperature and pressure changes. (2)
questions.solution:
Both tubes are affected equally by changes in temperature / atmospheric pressure [B1]
So the drop only moves because of respiration in the tube with organisms. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why boiled seeds should not be used as the only control in a respirometer experiment. (2)
questions.solution:
Boiled seeds may be decomposed by microorganisms, which respire [B1]
So volume changes may still occur — glass beads are better. [B1]

questions.prompt: A mark-release-recapture study was repeated for five years. State two precautions taken each year so data could be compared. (2)
questions.solution:
Same area / plants sampled, same method and sampling effort [B1]
Same time of year / interval between samples / same weather conditions. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why long-term monitoring is needed to judge the effect of a conservation scheme on a population. (2)
questions.solution:
Populations fluctuate naturally from year to year [B1]
Long-term data show whether there's a real trend. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two ways to make sure marking an animal doesn't affect the population estimate. (2)
questions.solution:
Use a mark that doesn't make animals more visible to predators [B1]
Non-toxic / small mark that doesn't affect movement or survival and won't rub off. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two improvements to a student's drawing of a dissected gas exchange system, not including labels or a sharp pencil. (2)
questions.solution:
Use single, continuous lines (no sketching / shading) [B1]
Correct proportions / add a scale or magnification / title. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two rules for drawing biological specimens. (2)
questions.solution:
No shading; clear continuous lines [B1]
Label lines drawn with a ruler, not crossing / include magnification. [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to dissect the gas exchange system of a mammal safely. (2)
questions.solution:
Use a sharp scalpel / scissors, cutting away from the body, on a dissecting board [B1]
Wear gloves / wash hands / disinfect surfaces afterwards. [B1]

questions.prompt: In a gut model, the effect of chewing on starch digestion was tested by comparing chewed wheat with wheat chopped in a blender. Suggest a more appropriate control and explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Wheat chopped in a blender with saliva added / boiled saliva [B1]
So the only difference is the chewing action (or the enzyme), isolating its effect. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why boiled enzyme solution is used as a control in an enzyme investigation. (2)
questions.solution:
Boiling denatures the enzyme [B1]
Shows any change is due to enzyme activity, with all other components present. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how to show that saliva contains an enzyme that digests starch. (2)
questions.solution:
Mix saliva with starch and test samples with iodine over time — blue-black disappears [B1]
Control with boiled saliva / water stays blue-black. [B1]

questions.prompt: In an experiment on a fungus that helps plant growth, seed surfaces were sterilised and the soil heated to 85 °C for 2 days. Explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Kill microorganisms (including other fungi) already on seeds and in the soil [B1]
So any effect is due to the added fungus only. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the experimental pots were kept in a sterile greenhouse. (2)
questions.solution:
Prevent contamination by other microorganisms / spores [B1]
Which could affect growth and confound results. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the same species and variety of plant was used in every pot. (2)
questions.solution:
Different varieties grow at different rates / respond differently [B1]
So genotype is controlled and only the treatment varies. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the soil used contained no useful mineral ions. (1)
questions.solution: So mineral ions only come from the fertiliser added, allowing its effect to be measured. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why sand is often used instead of soil in mineral nutrition experiments. (1)
questions.solution: Sand contains almost no nutrients, so mineral supply can be controlled. [B1]

questions.prompt: Group A got heat-treated (killed) fungus with nitrate fertiliser, group B live fungus with nitrate, group C killed fungus with ammonium and group D live fungus with ammonium. Explain how groups A and C act as controls. (2)
questions.solution:
Fungus is killed but other substances from the fungus are still present [B1]
Compare A with B and C with D to show the effect of living fungus with each fertiliser. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why heat-killed fungus rather than no fungus was added to control pots. (2)
questions.solution:
Fungal material may release nutrients when broken down [B1]
So the only difference between groups is whether the fungus is alive. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why each treatment was given to several plants. (2)
questions.solution:
Plants vary, so repeats allow a mean to be calculated [B1]
SD / statistical tests can show whether differences are significant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Plants were dried in an oven at 90 °C for 3 days. Suggest what should have been done to make sure all water was removed. (2)
questions.solution:
Weigh, return to oven, and reweigh at intervals [B1]
Until the mass stays constant. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why plant material is dried at about 90 °C rather than 200 °C. (2)
questions.solution:
At high temperature, organic material would burn / decompose [B1]
So mass lost would include more than water. [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why dried samples should be cooled in a desiccator before weighing. (2)
questions.solution:
Prevents the sample absorbing water vapour from the air as it cools [B1]
So the mass recorded is the true dry mass. [B1]
